options.D: A CT scan only images the skeletal system in color

explanation: CT technology reconstructs multiple X-ray angles into detailed cross-sectional slices, whereas a standard X-ray produces a single flat projection. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why do dense structures like bone appear white on a CT monitor?

options.A: Dense tissues absorb high amounts of radiation
options.B: The computer highlights bone using artificial blue dyes
options.C: Dense tissues allow all radiation to pass straight through
options.D: Bone actively emits fluorescent light during the scan

explanation: Radiation attenuation causes dense structures to absorb more of the X-ray beam, reducing the radiation reaching the detectors and rendering them white. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h1)

question: What is the primary purpose of using contrast media during a CT scan?

options.A: To replace the need for an X-ray tube inside the gantry
options.B: To enhance the visibility of specific tissues and blood vessels
options.C: To completely block all radiation from reaching the patient
options.D: To speed up the physical movement of the scanner table

explanation: Contrast media alters radiation absorption, making target organs, blood vessels, and abnormal lesions much easier to identify. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h2)

question: When would a nurse expect oral contrast to be administered for a CT scan?

options.A: To highlight the deep blood vessels in the brain

options.C: To visualize the interior chambers of the heart muscle
options.D: To check for fractures in the long bones of the leg

explanation: Oral contrast fills the gastrointestinal tract so nurses and radiologists can easily distinguish the bowel from surrounding abdominal organs. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h2)

question: Which medical condition is most commonly evaluated emergently using a head CT scan?

options.A: Superficial scalp laceration
options.B: Bacterial meningitis infection
options.C: Acute intracranial hemorrhage
options.D: Chronic peripheral neuropathy

explanation: A head CT is the primary diagnostic tool used to quickly rule out or confirm bleeding inside the skull following trauma or stroke symptoms. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h3)

question: A patient with sudden chest pain and shortness of breath is sent for a specialized CT scan to check for which condition?

options.A: Pulmonary embolism
options.B: Essential hypertension
options.C: Chronic asthma attack
options.D: Congestive heart failure

explanation: CT pulmonary angiography is specifically utilized to visualize blood flow within the pulmonary arteries and detect blood clots. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h3)

question: Why must a nurse check serum creatinine levels before a contrast-enhanced CT scan?

options.A: To measure the body's ability to absorb oral contrast
options.B: To check for underlying systemic bacterial infections
options.C: To determine the correct amount of radiation dose required
options.D: To evaluate kidney function for clearing the contrast dye

explanation: Iodinated contrast is excreted through the kidneys, so baseline renal function must be known to prevent contrast-induced kidney injury. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h4)

question: Which medication is commonly held following an intravenous contrast procedure to prevent lactic acidosis?

options.A: Paracetamol
options.B: Metformin
options.C: Furosemide
options.D: Digoxin

explanation: Metformin is withheld if kidney function temporarily declines after contrast administration to avoid a dangerous buildup of acid in the blood. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h4)

question: What is the primary reason a patient must remain completely still during a CT scan?

options.A: To prevent motion artifact from blurring the images
options.B: To keep the intravenous contrast line from falling out
options.C: To stop the X-ray tube from overheating inside the gantry
options.D: To reduce the total amount of radiation absorbed by skin

explanation: Movement creates motion artifacts that distort the cross-sectional images, rendering them difficult for the radiologist to interpret accurately. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h5)

question: What normal physical sensation should a nurse warn a patient about when intravenous contrast is injected?

options.A: Severe muscle cramps in the lower extremities
options.B: A sharp burning pain directly in the chest
options.C: A sudden metallic taste and warm flushing feeling
options.D: Sudden numbness and tingling in both hands

explanation: A transient metallic taste and a warm flush spreading through the body are common, harmless side effects of intravenous contrast administration. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is a primary post-procedural nursing intervention after a CT scan with contrast?

options.A: Encouraging high fluid intake to flush out the contrast
options.B: Placing the patient on a clear liquid diet for a full day
options.C: Administering a high dose of intravenous diuretic medication
options.D: Keeping the patient on strict bed rest for twelve hours

explanation: Abundant fluids help the kidneys rapidly excrete the contrast medium, reducing the risk of renal complications. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h6)

question: Which symptom observed hours after a CT scan indicates a delayed allergic reaction to contrast?

options.A: Hives and skin itching
options.B: Mild fatigue and sleepiness
options.C: Temporary hair loss
options.D: A slight metallic taste

explanation: Delayed hypersensitivity reactions can occur hours or even days later, presenting commonly as pruritus, rash, or urticaria. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h6)

question: Why is the use of CT scans carefully justified by healthcare providers despite their diagnostic benefits?

options.A: Patients cannot tolerate more than one scan per calendar year
options.B: The contrast dye causes permanent kidney failure in all clients
options.C: Each scan exposes the patient to cumulative ionizing radiation
options.D: CT scanners are extremely expensive to maintain in hospitals

explanation: Ionizing radiation carries a small but real cumulative risk of cellular damage, necessitating careful clinical justification for every scan. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h7)

question: What immediate medication is required if a patient experiences severe anaphylaxis from contrast media?

options.A: Metformin
options.B: Paracetamol
options.C: Furosemide
options.D: Epinephrine

explanation: Severe allergic anaphylactic reactions compromise the airway and circulation, making epinephrine the primary life-saving emergency drug. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h7)

question: What does a PET scan primarily measure within the human body?

options.A: Electrical brain rhythms
options.B: Cellular metabolic activity
options.C: Bone density and fractures
options.D: Peripheral blood pressure

explanation: PET scans track metabolic and biochemical processes by following radiopharmaceuticals in living tissues. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h1)

question: How do PET scans differ from standard CT scans?

options.A: PET requires permanent surgical implantation of tracers
options.B: PET shows body function while CT shows body structure
options.C: PET takes less than five seconds to capture whole bodies
options.D: PET uses high-voltage sound waves instead of radiation

explanation: Standard imaging visualizes anatomy, whereas nuclear medicine highlights functional changes in cells. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which radiopharmaceutical is most commonly used in routine clinical PET scans?

options.A: Liquid barium sulfate
options.B: Radioactive iodine
options.C: Gadolinium contrast
options.D: Fluorodeoxyglucose

explanation: FDG mimics glucose and is taken up heavily by metabolically active cells. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h2)

question: A patient asks why they must rest quietly after receiving their FDG injection. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: To lower your blood pressure before entering the cold imaging room
options.B: To keep your heart rate high enough for the scanner to detect blood flow
options.C: To allow the radioactive dye to completely leave your body through sweat
options.D: To prevent muscles from taking up the sugar tracer instead of target cells

explanation: Muscle movement increases glucose consumption, which creates unwanted background noise on the scan. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h2)

question: In which clinical area is PET imaging most frequently utilized?

options.A: Orthopedics for joint casting
options.B: Obstetrics for fetal growth
options.C: Oncology for cancer staging
options.D: Dermatology for skin burns

explanation: Oncology uses PET extensively to detect malignant growths and monitor therapy success. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h3)

question: Why would a cardiologist order a PET scan for a patient with heart failure?

options.A: To view the physical size of heart valve calcifications
options.B: To check if damaged heart muscle is still alive and salvageable
options.C: To clear blood clots completely out of the coronary arteries
options.D: To measure the exact electrical conduction speed of the ventricles

explanation: Cardiac PET assesses myocardial viability to see if blood flow restoration will improve heart function. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h3)

question: How many hours of fasting are typically required before an FDG-PET scan?

options.A: No fasting is needed
options.B: Four to six hours
options.C: Thirty minutes
options.D: Twelve to twenty hours

explanation: Short-term fasting helps lower baseline blood glucose levels so the radiotracer is absorbed properly. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h4)

question: What is the primary reason high blood sugar ruins an FDG-PET scan?

options.A: Elevated blood glucose makes the patient too weak to lie flat
options.B: Sugar neutralizes the radioactive decay particles inside the veins
options.C: Excess sugar competes with the radioactive tracer for cell uptake
options.D: High glucose levels cause the scanner cameras to overheat instantly

explanation: When too much normal glucose is present, cells ignore the FDG tracer, ruining the image contrast. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h4)

question: Why must the patient empty their bladder right before the scanning phase begins?

options.A: To reduce pelvic radiation exposure and prevent image artifacts
options.B: To measure accurate fluid balance output during the procedure
options.C: To prevent the patient from feeling dizzy during the rapid spin
options.D: To test the urine sample for hidden infectious bacteria

explanation: An empty bladder limits radiation pooling near pelvic organs and stops movement caused by discomfort. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h5)

question: What is the main nursing goal during the tracer uptake waiting period?

options.A: Encouraging light exercises to speed up tracer distribution
options.B: Promoting absolute physical rest and reducing anxiety
options.C: Performing complete neurological assessments every five minutes
options.D: Administering large volumes of intravenous electrolyte fluids

explanation: Rest prevents muscles from taking up glucose, ensuring the tracer reaches targeted pathological tissues. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h5)

question: What is the most effective way for a patient to clear remaining tracers after a PET scan?

options.A: Taking strong laxatives to clean out the gastrointestinal tract
options.B: Undergoing whole-body therapeutic massage sessions daily
options.C: Drinking plenty of fluids and urinating frequently
options.D: Breathing pure oxygen through a tight facial mask

explanation: Hydration and urination help eliminate the remaining water-soluble radioactive isotopes safely. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h6)

question: A patient who just completed a PET scan wants to hold their newborn grandchild immediately. What instruction should the nurse give?

options.A: There are no restrictions because the radiation disappears instantly
options.B: Limit close contact with infants for the rest of the day as a precaution
options.C: Wait exactly two full weeks before being in the same room with children
options.D: Wash the baby thoroughly with antiseptic soap after the visit

explanation: Minimizing close exposure to vulnerable groups for several hours protects them from residual radiation. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T14#GNS123_U2_T14_h6)

question: What main type of information is gathered when taking a health history from a patient?

options.A: Laboratory data
options.B: Objective data
options.C: Subjective data
options.D: Radiological data

explanation: Subjective data is information the patient or caregiver tells you directly, which forms the core of any health history. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is taking a detailed patient history so important in nursing?

options.A: It serves primarily as a legal document for hospital billing
options.B: It guides clinical reasoning and shapes the nursing care plan
options.C: It eliminates all risks of medication administration errors
options.D: It replaces the need for physical examinations entirely

explanation: A thorough history gives you the vital clues needed to make good clinical decisions and plan the right care for your patient. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which type of question helps a patient talk freely about their symptoms in their own words?

options.A: Leading questions
options.B: Open-ended questions
options.C: Closed-ended questions
options.D: Direct interrogation

explanation: Open-ended questions encourage patients to share more details, giving you a clearer picture of what they are experiencing. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h2)

question: A newly admitted patient looks anxious and avoids eye contact. What should you do first?

options.A: Establish a calm, welcoming environment and use gentle non-verbal cues
options.B: Demand that the patient look up when speaking to clinical staff
options.C: Document that the patient is uncooperative and leave the bedside
options.D: Ask family members to answer all questions to speed up the process

explanation: Creating a safe and friendly space helps lower the patient's anxiety so they can trust you before you ask personal health questions. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which of these is an example of biographical data collected during a health history?

options.A: Surgical scar location
options.B: Current blood pressure
options.C: Heart murmur grade
options.D: Patient occupation

explanation: Biographical data covers basic background details like age, gender, and job, which help you understand their daily life and health risks. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the main reason for asking about a patient's family medical history?

options.A: To predict the exact date of discharge based on relative recovery times
options.B: To identify inherited risks for chronic conditions like hypertension or diabetes
options.C: To determine the financial status of the extended family members
options.D: To trace the legal lineage of the patient for hospital inheritance claims

explanation: Family history reveals genetic health patterns that might put the patient at risk for certain long-term illnesses. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h3)

question: In the PQRST pain assessment tool, what does the letter 'P' stand for?

options.A: Previous physical pathology
options.B: Pulse and pressure readings
options.C: Primary patient position
options.D: Provocative or palliating factors

explanation: The 'P' helps you find out what makes the pain worse or what makes it feel better. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h4)

question: A patient says a sharp chest pain started ten minutes ago while resting. Which part of the PQRST framework is this?

options.A: Quality
options.B: Timing
options.C: Severity
options.D: Region

explanation: When pain starts, how long it lasts, and how often it happens all fall under the timing category. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which part of the health history covers past hospital stays and major injuries?

options.A: Current psychosocial assessment
options.B: Past medical and surgical history
options.C: Biographical demographic data
options.D: Review of systemic organ functions

explanation: This section records all major illnesses, surgeries, injuries, and past hospital admissions a patient has experienced. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why is it important to know a patient's past surgical history before they undergo a new procedure?

options.A: To verify the exact hospital where the previous doctor trained
options.B: To update the patient's employment status in the hospital system
options.C: To identify prior reactions to anesthesia and surgical complications
options.D: To calculate the total financial cost of past healthcare visits

explanation: Knowing how a patient reacted to past surgeries or anesthesia helps the medical team keep them safe during new procedures. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h5)

question: What kind of information do you gather during a review of systems?

options.A: Surgical consent forms signed by relatives
options.B: Objective physical examination measurements and lab results
options.C: Direct observations made under a microscope
options.D: Patient-reported symptoms across various body systems

explanation: The review of systems is a checklist of symptoms the patient reports, moving step-by-step through different body parts. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the main benefit of doing a review of systems during an interview?

options.A: It serves as a legally binding contract for surgical intervention
options.B: It replaces the need to check vital signs or physical reflexes
options.C: It diagnoses the exact pathology without requiring laboratory tests
options.D: It uncovers symptoms the patient forgot to mention during the chief complaint

explanation: Going through body systems step-by-step helps catch small or forgotten details that are important for the patient's health. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h6)

question: Which of these is looked at during a lifestyle and psychosocial assessment?

options.A: Surgical instrumentation sterilization logs
options.B: Exact microscopic cell count in the blood
options.C: Use of alcohol, tobacco, or traditional remedies
options.D: Inherited genetic chromosomal abnormalities

explanation: This assessment checks daily habits and substance use that can affect the patient's health or treatment. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why should nurses ask patients if they use traditional remedies?

options.A: To replace all modern nursing interventions with local herbs
options.B: To report illegal practitioners to local law enforcement agencies
options.C: To check for potential interactions with prescribed orthodox medications
options.D: To determine the financial budget of the patient's household

explanation: Many people use local herbs alongside hospital drugs, and checking for bad drug interactions keeps the patient safe. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h7)

question: In the eyes of the law, what happens if a nursing assessment is not written down?

options.A: It is legally considered not done
options.B: It is assumed to be completed verbally
options.C: It is automatically updated by hospital management
options.D: It is classified as private personal property

explanation: If it is not documented in the patient's records, legally it is treated as though it never happened. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h8)

question: What should you avoid doing when writing down patient history findings?

options.A: Maintaining strict patient confidentiality
options.B: Using judgmental language or personal opinions
options.C: Recording subjective data in direct quotes
options.D: Writing entries promptly after the interview

explanation: Nursing documentation must stay strictly professional, factual, and free of personal bias or emotional comments. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T2#GNS123_U2_T2_h8)

question: What primary type of data does a physical examination provide for the nurse?

options.A: Financial data
options.B: Historical data
options.C: Objective data
options.D: Subjective data

explanation: Physical examinations rely on measurable and observable findings, which constitute objective clinical data. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h1)

question: Baseline health data obtained during an initial physical exam is primarily used for what purpose?

options.A: Comparing future health status changes
options.B: Fulfilling mandatory billing requirements
options.C: Replacing the patient medical history
options.D: Determining the hospital discharge date

explanation: Baseline measurements give the nurse a starting point to monitor improvement or deterioration in a patient's condition. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is proper room lighting critical during a physical examination?

options.A: To observe subtle skin color changes accurately
options.B: To prevent the nurse from dropping medical tools
options.C: To reduce the overall temperature of the room
options.D: To keep the patient awake during the procedure

explanation: Good lighting allows the clinician to detect fine details like jaundice, cyanosis, or rashes on the skin. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h2)

question: A nurse is about to examine a patient in a busy ward. What is the immediate first action to ensure a proper environment?

options.A: Ask all family members to leave the hospital
options.B: Turn off all overhead lighting in the room
options.C: Begin the physical assessment immediately
options.D: Draw bedside curtains to secure patient privacy

explanation: Securing privacy protects patient dignity and establishes a safe environment before any physical assessment begins. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the single most effective way to prevent the spread of microorganisms in clinical settings?

options.A: Using face shields
options.B: Hand hygiene
options.C: Wearing sterile gowns
options.D: Cleaning floors daily

explanation: Regular and proper hand hygiene drastically reduces the transmission of pathogens between patients and staff. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h3)

question: When must a nurse apply standard infection control precautions?

options.A: When working in surgical units only
options.B: Only when caring for patients with known infections
options.C: During every single patient encounter
options.D: After completing all documentation tasks

explanation: Standard precautions apply universally to all patients to protect against unknown or unexpected pathogen exposures. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which assessment technique involves using the sense of touch to evaluate body tissues?

options.A: Inspection
options.B: Auscultation
options.C: Palpation
options.D: Percussion

explanation: Palpation uses hands and fingers to feel for masses, tenderness, skin temperature, and moisture. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why is auscultation performed before palpation during an abdominal physical examination?

options.A: To prevent altering normal bowel sounds
options.B: To complete the assessment more quickly
options.C: To make the patient feel more relaxed
options.D: To warm up the stethoscope diaphragm

explanation: Touching or pressing the abdomen early can stimulate peristalsis, falsely changing the frequency and character of bowel sounds. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h4)

question: When does the general survey of a patient officially begin?

options.A: After finishing the systemic physical examination
options.B: During the formal review of medical history
options.C: When measuring the patient's blood pressure
options.D: The moment the nurse first meets the patient

explanation: Observation of appearance, posture, and behavior starts immediately upon initial visual contact. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the primary clinical significance of abnormal vital signs in a patient?

options.A: They confirm the exact diagnosis of a viral infection
options.B: They indicate that the patient is ready for discharge
options.C: They replace the need for a comprehensive health history
options.D: They often serve as early warnings of clinical deterioration

explanation: Shifts in vital parameters frequently flag underlying physiological instability before other symptoms become obvious. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h5)

question: What primary focus guides a respiratory system physical examination?

options.A: Pupillary reflex and cranial nerve function
options.B: Joint range of motion and muscle strength
options.C: Chest expansion and breath sounds
options.D: Bowel motility and abdominal tenderness

explanation: Respiratory exams evaluate lung ventilation and airflow through visual inspection of the chest and auscultation of breath sounds. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h6)

question: A patient reports left-sided chest pain. Which body system requires the most immediate and thorough physical examination?

options.A: Integumentary
options.B: Musculoskeletal
options.C: Reproductive
options.D: Cardiovascular

explanation: Chest pain is a classic indicator of potential cardiac distress, making the cardiovascular system the top priority for evaluation. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h6)

question: How should physical examination findings be recorded in the patient record?

options.A: At the end of the work week to save time
options.B: Using general opinions and subjective impressions
options.C: Exclusively through verbal handovers
options.D: Promptly and objectively with specific details

explanation: Documentation must rely on clear, factual, and measurable observations rather than vague or biased statements. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why is accurate and timely documentation of assessment findings essential for patient care?

options.A: It facilitates safe communication among the healthcare team
options.B: It prevents patients from asking questions about treatment
options.C: It eliminates the need for any further nursing assessments
options.D: It guarantees that the patient will recover quickly

explanation: Clear written records allow doctors, nurses, and other providers to track changes and provide safe, continuous care. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of taking baseline physical measurements on admission?

options.A: To replace the need for ongoing physical examinations
options.B: To determine the exact discharge date of the patient
options.C: To establish a foundation for evaluating future physiological changes
options.D: To diagnose specific tropical diseases without laboratory tests

explanation: Baseline measurements give nurses a starting point to compare later readings and spot patient deterioration. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why must nurses record vital signs consistently using a standard method?

options.A: To eliminate the need for doctors to visit the ward
options.B: To satisfy strict administrative paperwork requirements only
options.C: To create a reliable trend line tracking patient progress
options.D: To prevent the patient from asking questions about treatment

explanation: Consistent recording methods ensure that any changes observed over time reflect actual shifts in the patient's condition rather than measurement errors. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h1)

question: Which artery is most commonly used for routine pulse assessment in adult patients?

options.A: Radial artery
options.B: Brachial artery
options.C: Femoral artery
options.D: Carotid artery

explanation: The radial artery at the wrist is easily accessible and safe for routine pulse checks. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h2)

question: Why should a nurse count a patient's respirations without informing them beforehand?

options.A: To test the patient's hearing and attention span
options.B: To comply with emergency surgical protocols
options.C: To measure blood pressure at the exact same time
options.D: To prevent the patient from consciously altering their breathing rate

explanation: Patients tend to change how fast or slow they breathe if they know they are being watched. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h2)

question: What equipment is standard for measuring adult height accurately in a clinic?

options.A: Centimeter tape measure
options.B: Sphygmomanometer
options.C: Tympanic thermometer
options.D: Stadiometer

explanation: A stadiometer provides a fixed vertical scale designed specifically for accurate height measurement. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h3)

question: A bedridden patient cannot stand on the ward scale. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Force the patient to stand up briefly despite weakness
options.B: Use alternative anthropometric indicators like mid-upper arm circumference
options.C: Refuse to record any nutritional data until discharge
options.D: Guess the weight based on visual inspection to save time

explanation: Alternative measurements provide vital nutritional data when standard standing scales cannot be used. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h3)

question: Where is the normal apex beat located in a healthy adult?

options.A: Third right intercostal space at the sternal border
options.B: Sixth right intercostal space at the midclavicular line
options.C: Fourth left intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
options.D: Fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line

question: What does a displaced apex beat typically indicate during a physical examination?

options.A: Cardiac enlargement or structural heart disease
options.B: Temporary anxiety caused by hospital admission
options.C: Dehydration from inadequate fluid intake
options.D: Normal physical development in young adults

explanation: When the heart enlarges, the point of maximal impulse shifts away from its normal anatomical position. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is the normal baseline range for a fetal heart rate per minute?

options.A: 60 to 100 beats
options.B: 110 to 160 beats
options.C: 80 to 120 beats
options.D: 140 to 180 beats

explanation: A healthy resting fetal heart rate falls within the 110 to 160 beats per minute range. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why are Leopold's maneuvers performed before trying to auscultate the fetal heart?

options.A: To check the mother's blood pressure response
options.B: To determine fetal position and locate the best site for listening
options.C: To stimulate uterine contractions during early labor stages
options.D: To measure the exact weight of the unborn baby

explanation: Palpating the abdomen helps the nurse find the fetus's back, where the heartbeat is heard most clearly. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h5)

question: What should the nurse do immediately after measuring a patient's vital signs?

options.A: Disregard normal values and only document abnormal findings
options.B: Record the exact numerical values immediately in the patient chart
options.C: Wait for the doctor to arrive before writing anything down
options.D: Memorize the numbers until the end of the shift

explanation: Immediate documentation prevents memory errors and ensures all healthcare team members have current data. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why is knowing standard normal physiological ranges critical for clinical practice?

options.A: It simplifies the hospital discharge summary process
options.B: It guarantees the patient will recover without medication
options.C: It removes the need to report findings to senior nursing staff
options.D: It allows the nurse to spot abnormal trends and escalate care

explanation: Familiarity with normal ranges helps nurses quickly identify when a patient's condition is worsening. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T4#GNS123_U2_T4_h6)

question: What level of prevention does routine health screening primarily fall under?

options.A: Tertiary prevention
options.B: Primary prevention
options.C: Quaternary prevention
options.D: Secondary prevention

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early detection and prompt intervention of asymptomatic diseases during their preclinical phase. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why is health screening classified differently from primary prevention methods like vaccination?

options.A: Screening targets individuals who already show severe clinical symptoms
options.B: Vaccination is performed only inside tertiary care hospitals
options.C: Screening aims to detect hidden disease in apparently healthy people
options.D: Vaccination reverses existing chronic illness without medications

explanation: Screening is designed to catch unrecognized conditions early, whereas primary prevention stops the initial onset of disease altogether. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h1)

question: The main goal of implementing routine health screening in a community is to achieve what outcome?

options.A: Cure terminal illnesses permanently
options.B: Decrease hospital bed capacity permanently
options.C: Eliminate the need for diagnostic laboratory tests
options.D: Reduce morbidity and mortality through early detection

explanation: Catching diseases early allows for prompt treatment, which directly lowers complication rates and death. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h2)

question: A clinic nurse reviews a patient file and notes a strong family history of diabetes. What is the immediate objective of screening this client?

options.A: Identify asymptomatic blood glucose abnormalities early
options.B: Prescribe long-term insulin therapy immediately
options.C: Reverse genetic predispositions to insulin resistance
options.D: Diagnose the patient with clinical type 1 diabetes

explanation: High-risk clients are screened to catch hidden metabolic changes before overt symptoms develop. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h2)

question: Why is fasting strictly required before collecting blood for a lipid profile?

options.A: To ensure the patient remains completely conscious during the test
options.B: To prevent falsely elevated postprandial triglyceride levels
options.C: To reduce the total volume of blood drawn from the arm
options.D: To prevent sudden allergic reactions to the collection needle

explanation: Food intake directly alters blood lipid concentrations, making fasting necessary for an accurate baseline reading. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary reason for providing written instructions alongside verbal explanations for a screening test?

options.A: To speed up the physical assessment in a busy ward
options.B: To ensure the client remembers complex steps at home
options.C: To protect the hospital legally if a test fails
options.D: To replace the need for direct nurse-patient communication

explanation: Clients often forget verbal instructions once they leave the clinic environment, making written guides vital for compliance. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h3)

question: How can severe patient anxiety directly impact the accuracy of routine screening measurements?

options.A: It destroys cellular samples collected during diagnostic swabs
options.B: It prevents the kidneys from producing urine samples
options.C: It permanently alters baseline genetic test markers
options.D: It causes temporary spikes in blood pressure and heart rate

explanation: Stress activates the sympathetic nervous system, leading to elevated vital signs that do not reflect the true resting baseline. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h4)

question: A patient scheduled for a breast cancer screening exam expresses intense fear of a positive result. What is the best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Acknowledge their fear and explain the procedure steps calmly
options.B: Tell them there is zero chance the result will be positive
options.C: Cancel the screening session to protect their mental health
options.D: Refer them immediately to a psychiatric inpatient ward

explanation: Validating emotions and providing clear information helps reduce anxiety and builds trust for the screening process. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h4)

question: What does a false-positive result in a health screening indicate?

options.A: The test shows disease presence when the person is actually healthy
options.B: The patient failed to follow pre-screening fasting rules
options.C: The laboratory lost the client sample before analysis
options.D: The test completely misses an existing and advanced disease

explanation: A false positive incorrectly suggests an abnormality exists, causing unnecessary worry until confirmatory tests are done. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why is obtaining voluntary informed consent critical even for routine community health screenings?

options.A: It eliminates all financial costs associated with the laboratory
options.B: It respects patient autonomy and right to self-determination
options.C: It legally forces the patient to follow up if results are abnormal
options.D: It guarantees the screening test will yield a normal result

explanation: Every individual retains the legal and ethical right to decide what medical procedures happen to their own body. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary reason for calibrating diagnostic screening equipment before use?

options.A: To guarantee accurate and reliable measurement readings
options.B: To make the equipment look newer to incoming patients
options.C: To extend the manufacturer warranty on the device
options.D: To reduce the electrical power consumed by the machine

explanation: Calibration ensures that instruments like sphygmomanometers or glucometers provide correct data, preventing misdiagnosis. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which factor is most important when setting up a screening station in a community outreach setting?

options.A: Using decorative lighting to create a relaxing spa mood
options.B: Storing all medical supplies in an unlocked hallway box
options.C: Placing the registration desk outside the main building
options.D: Ensuring visual and auditory privacy for clients

explanation: Privacy encourages clients to share sensitive health histories honestly without fear of being overheard by others. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h6)

question: What action must a nurse take immediately after discovering an abnormal screening result?

options.A: Prescribe curative medications without consulting a physician
options.B: Discard the result record to protect patient confidentiality
options.C: Wait until the client schedules their next annual checkup
options.D: Provide a structured referral pathway for confirmatory testing

explanation: Screenings are not final diagnoses; abnormal findings require prompt follow-up and confirmation by specialized diagnostic tests. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h7)

question: A nurse is explaining a screening report to a patient who has limited health literacy. What communication strategy should the nurse use?

options.A: Speak in complex medical terminology to sound professional
options.B: Direct the client to search for answers on social media
options.C: Use simple terms and ask the client to repeat the plan
options.D: Hand over the technical laboratory printout without comment

explanation: Clear communication ensures understanding, and the teach-back method confirms that the client comprehends their next steps. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T5#GNS123_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is the basic functional unit of the kidney responsible for urine production?

options.A: Glomerulus
options.B: Ureter
options.C: Loop of Henle
options.D: Nephron

explanation: The nephron is the microscopic structural and functional unit of the kidney that filters blood and forms urine. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h1)

question: During which phase of urine formation does the body reclaim essential nutrients back into the bloodstream?

options.A: Glomerular filtration
options.B: Bowman capsule collection
options.C: Tubular reabsorption
options.D: Tubular secretion

explanation: Tubular reabsorption moves water and vital solutes out of the filtrate and back into the peritubular capillaries. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which type of urine sample is best for detecting pregnancy and concentrated substances?

options.A: Timed twenty-four hour specimen
options.B: Random spot specimen
options.C: First morning specimen
options.D: Catheterized specimen

explanation: The first morning sample is the most concentrated because urine accumulates in the bladder overnight. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h2)

question: Why do we use a clean-catch midstream technique for urine cultures?

options.A: It measures the exact volume produced over a set time
options.B: It stops red blood cells from entering the collection cup
options.C: It prevents skin germs from contaminating the bacterial culture
options.D: It ensures the bladder is completely empty before testing

explanation: Washing the urethral area and letting the initial stream flush away external organisms prevents false-positive culture results. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h2)

question: Finding nitrites on a routine urine dipstick test usually points to which condition?

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.B: Glomerular nephritis
options.C: Urinary tract infection
options.D: Renal tubular acidosis

explanation: Certain bacteria reduce urinary nitrates to nitrites, signaling a likely bacterial infection in the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h3)

question: What is the main reason urine dipsticks must be stored away from moisture and heat?

options.A: To keep the container sterile for patient testing
options.B: To stop the plastic strips from bending out of shape
options.C: To ensure the color chart remains bright and readable
options.D: To prevent chemical damage to the reactive pads

explanation: Exposure to environmental moisture and heat alters the chemical reagents on the pads, leading to false results. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h3)

question: What are the small tube-shaped structures formed in the kidney tubules that can show up in urine sediment?

options.A: Casts
options.B: Calculi
options.C: Crystals
options.D: Clots

explanation: Casts are formed when protein precipitates within the renal tubules and takes on the shape of the lumen. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h4)

question: What does finding many white blood cells and white blood cell casts in urine sediment usually mean?

options.A: Severe dehydration causing salt buildup
options.B: Contamination of the sample with normal vaginal secretions
options.C: Normal breakdown of blood cells after heavy exercise
options.D: Active inflammation or infection in the urinary tract

explanation: White blood cells and their casts signify an active inflammatory process, often due to a kidney infection or severe bladder infection. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h4)

question: What bacterial count in a urine sample usually confirms a significant urinary tract infection?

options.A: 10^5 CFU/mL
options.B: 10^2 CFU/mL
options.C: 10^1 CFU/mL
options.D: 10^8 CFU/mL

explanation: A bacterial count of 10^5 CFU/mL or higher in a clean-catch sample is the standard benchmark for significant bacteriuria. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h5)

question: A patient's urine culture report shows bacterial growth with an antibiotic labeled as 'resistant'. What does this mean for treatment?

options.A: The patient is allergic to that particular pharmaceutical agent
options.B: That specific drug will not successfully kill the infecting bacteria
options.C: The laboratory made an error during testing
options.D: The drug should be given at double the standard dose to work

explanation: A resistant label indicates the pathogen is not inhibited by that antibiotic, meaning the drug should be avoided. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h5)

question: How should you start the collection process for an accurate 24-hour urine test?

options.A: Collect all urine starting immediately with the first morning void
options.B: Save the very first morning urine sample in a separate small container
options.C: Have the patient empty the bladder completely and discard that urine
options.D: Force fluids for two hours before starting the official collection timer

explanation: Discarding the first morning void marks zero time; starting with an empty bladder ensures old urine is not counted in the test. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h6)

question: Why are 24-hour urine collections necessary for certain laboratory tests?

options.A: Substance levels change throughout the day, so a total daily measurement is needed
options.B: Bacteria take a full day to grow large enough to view under a microscope
options.C: Single spot samples cannot be processed by automated hospital lab machines
options.D: Kidneys only filter specific proteins during sleep

explanation: Many substances vary in concentration across hours, so a 24-hour pool provides an accurate average daily output. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h6)

question: Why does a urine sample left at room temperature for over two hours give unreliable results?

options.A: Bacteria multiply and cells break down, changing the findings

options.C: Reagents on the test strips stop reacting with fluid
options.D: The plastic collection container begins to dissolve

explanation: Prolonged room temperature delay causes bacterial overgrowth and cellular breakdown, leading to false test values. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h7)

question: How should a nurse instruct a female patient to clean her genital area before a clean-catch urine collection?

options.A: Scrub the area vigorously in a circular motion
options.B: Wash using standard bath soap and rinse with tap water
options.C: Wipe from front to back using antiseptic wipes
options.D: Clean from back to front to reach the lower area

explanation: Wiping from front to back prevents the introduction of germs from the anal area into the urinary opening. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T6#GNS123_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is the main reason doctors and nurses check blood test results for patients in the hospital?

options.A: To lower the cost of the hospital stay
options.B: To replace physical checks entirely
options.C: To check if treatment is working and guide care
options.D: To figure out the exact discharge date

explanation: Laboratory results give clear numbers that help track how a patient is doing and show whether current treatments are helping. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why do nurses look at how lab results change over time instead of just looking at one single result?

options.A: Hospital rules do not allow looking at single results
options.B: Trends show if the patient is getting better or worse
options.C: Single values change too slowly to be useful
options.D: Single lab values are always written down incorrectly

explanation: Comparing results over time helps you see the direction an illness is taking and tells you if the treatment is working. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h1)

question: What is the normal range for white blood cells in a healthy adult?

options.B: 4.2 to 5.4 million/mcL
options.D: 12 to 18 g/dL

explanation: A white blood cell count between 4,000 and 11,000/mcL is considered normal for healthy adults. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h2)

question: Which part of the blood mainly carries oxygen around the body?

options.A: White blood cells
options.B: Platelets
options.C: Plasma proteins
options.D: Red blood cells

explanation: Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, which picks up oxygen in the lungs and delivers it to the rest of the body. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h2)

question: A high number of neutrophils on a blood test usually points to which problem?

options.A: Severe iron deficiency
options.B: An active allergic reaction
options.C: A sudden bacterial infection
options.D: A long-term viral infection

explanation: Neutrophils are the first immune cells to multiply and rush to the scene to fight off bacterial infections. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h3)

question: What does a significant drop in hemoglobin and hematocrit mean?

options.A: Dehydration
options.B: Anemia
options.C: Polycythemia
options.D: High white blood cell count

explanation: Low hemoglobin and hematocrit levels show that the blood has a reduced ability to carry enough oxygen to the tissues. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h3)

question: Which blood test is used specifically to monitor patients taking warfarin?

options.A: Hemoglobin
options.B: Platelet count
options.C: INR
options.D: PTT

explanation: The International Normalized Ratio helps standardize PT results across labs so patients on blood thinners like warfarin stay at a safe dose. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h4)

question: Which test is used mainly to monitor patients receiving intravenous heparin?

options.A: Serum electrolyte panel
options.B: Prothrombin Time
options.C: Complete blood count
options.D: Partial Thromboplastin Time

explanation: Partial Thromboplastin Time measures how long it takes blood to clot, which increases during heparin treatment. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h4)

question: A patient with a dangerously abnormal potassium level is at the highest risk for which complication?

options.A: Sudden vision loss
options.B: Numbness in the hands and feet
options.C: Irregular heart rhythms
options.D: Fluid in the lungs

explanation: Potassium plays a direct role in regulating the electrical signals that keep the heart beating steadily. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which pair of lab tests is mainly used to check how well the kidneys are working?

options.A: PT and INR
options.B: Hemoglobin and platelets
options.C: Sodium and potassium
options.D: Creatinine and blood urea nitrogen

explanation: Both creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels go up when the kidneys struggle to filter waste products from the blood. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h5)

question: What does an arterial blood gas test primarily measure?

options.A: Blood clotting speed and platelets
options.B: Bone marrow cell production
options.C: Kidney filtration and waste clearance
options.D: Acid-base balance and oxygen levels

explanation: Arterial blood gases give direct readings of blood pH, dissolved oxygen, and carbon dioxide in the arteries. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why would a nurse need an arterial blood gas test for a patient in severe respiratory distress?

options.A: To check how fast platelets are clumping
options.B: To check current blood sugar levels
options.C: To see how well the lungs are exchanging gases
options.D: To measure total iron stored in the body

explanation: Arterial blood gases show how well oxygen is getting into the bloodstream and how effectively the lungs are clearing out carbon dioxide. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h6)

question: What is the very first thing a nurse must do before collecting a blood sample from a patient?

options.A: Pick out the correct colored lab tubes
options.B: Leave a tight rubber band on the arm for five minutes
options.C: Write patient names on the tubes before entering the room
options.D: Check the patient's identity using two unique details

explanation: Confirming the patient's identity prevents mislabeling samples and keeps diagnostic testing safe. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h7)

question: Why should a nurse avoid drawing blood from an arm that has an active IV fluid drip running into it?

options.A: it breaks basic hand hygiene rules
options.B: It makes the needle poke hurt much more
options.C: It dilutes the blood sample and messes up the lab results
options.D: It causes permanent paralysis of the arm

explanation: IV fluids mix with the blood sample, making electrolyte and hemoglobin levels look falsely high or low. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h7)

question: What should a nurse do immediately after receiving a critically abnormal lab result?

options.A: Give the patient a double dose of their prescribed drugs
options.B: Quickly report the result to the doctor and write it down
options.C: Wait until the end of the shift to mention it during handover
options.D: Throw away the report and ask for a repeat test tomorrow

explanation: Critical lab values require urgent reporting and quick medical action to keep the patient safe from sudden worsening. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h8)

question: Why is writing down exact notes about critical lab results so important for nursing practice?

options.A: It stops patients from reading their own medical charts
options.B: It fulfills hospital billing department requests
options.C: It replaces the need to talk during shift handovers
options.D: It protects you legally and keeps patient care safe and continuous

explanation: Clear nursing notes prove that urgent steps were taken promptly to protect the patient from harm. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T7#GNS123_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the primary function of blood group antigens located on red blood cells?

options.A: They act as surface markers recognized by the immune system.
options.B: They transport oxygen molecules throughout the systemic circulation.
options.C: They regulate the osmotic pressure inside the vascular space.
options.D: They prevent the clotting of blood inside normal blood vessels.

explanation: Antigens are unique molecules on red blood cells that determine blood type and trigger immune reactions if foreign. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why does a transfusion reaction occur when incompatible blood is given to a patient?

options.A: The total blood volume drops rapidly due to sudden fluid evaporation.
options.B: Recipient white blood cells permanently lose their ability to fight infection.
options.C: Donor plasma proteins immediately dissolve the recipient blood vessel walls.
options.D: Host antibodies attack and destroy the foreign donor red blood cells.

explanation: Incompatible transfusions cause the recipient's antibodies to bind with donor antigens, resulting in cell destruction. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which antibodies are naturally present in the plasma of a person with blood group A?

options.A: Anti-A antibodies
options.B: Both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
options.C: No antibodies are present
options.D: Anti-B antibodies

explanation: Blood group A individuals have A antigens on their cells and circulating anti-B antibodies in their plasma. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h2)

question: Blood group O is often called the universal red cell donor because...

options.A: it can safely receive blood from any other ABO group without testing.
options.B: its plasma contains high levels of both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
options.C: it contains special clotting factors that prevent immediate transfusion reactions.
options.D: its red blood cells lack both A and B surface antigens.

explanation: Lacking A and B antigens means recipient antibodies have nothing to attack on the donor red blood cells. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h2)

question: How do anti-Rhesus antibodies typically develop in an individual who is Rh-negative?

options.A: Through exposure to environmental bacteria during early childhood development
options.B: Through dietary intake of iron-rich foods during the third trimester
options.C: Through prior exposure to Rh-positive blood via transfusion or pregnancy
options.D: They are present at birth alongside natural ABO system antibodies

explanation: Anti-Rh antibodies are not naturally occurring and require sensitization through previous exposure to the D antigen. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h3)

question: A pregnant woman is Rh-negative and her husband is Rh-positive. What is the main clinical concern for future pregnancies?

options.A: Hemolytic disease of the newborn due to maternal anti-D antibody crossing the placenta
options.B: Severe iron-deficiency anemia in the mother caused by active red cell destruction
options.C: Complete absence of ABO blood group antigens in the developing fetus
options.D: Immediate maternal rejection of the placenta during the first trimester of gestation

explanation: Sensitized Rh-negative mothers produce antibodies that attack subsequent Rh-positive fetal red blood cells. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h3)

question: What reaction indicates a positive result during standard bedside or laboratory blood typing?

options.A: Rapid separation of plasma from the cellular layers
options.B: Complete dissolution of the entire blood sample
options.C: A sudden change of the blood color to bright green
options.D: Agglutination or clumping of the red blood cells

explanation: Clumping occurs when antibodies in the test serum bind to matching antigens on the red blood cells. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why are commercial antisera used when performing a routine blood type test?

options.A: To sterilize the blood sample and prevent bacterial contamination during testing
options.B: To preserve the fragile red blood cells for microscopic evaluation later
options.C: To dissolve abnormal clots that form naturally inside the specimen tube
options.D: To identify specific antigens on the red blood cells through visible clumping

explanation: Known antibodies in antisera react with unknown patient antigens to reveal the blood group. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a blood cross-match before a transfusion?

options.A: To measure the total fluid volume contained in the donor unit
options.B: To sterilize the blood bag against viral and bacterial pathogens
options.C: To determine the exact hemoglobin level of the donor unit
options.D: To detect any unexpected antibodies between donor and recipient

explanation: Cross-matching ensures compatibility by testing recipient serum against donor red cells for adverse reactions. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h5)

question: Which samples are combined in the laboratory to perform a standard cross-match test?

options.A: Donor plasma and recipient white blood cells
options.B: Donor serum and commercial anti-A antibodies
options.C: Recipient whole blood and sterile saline solution
options.D: Recipient serum and donor red blood cells

explanation: The test checks if antibodies in the patient's serum will attack the red blood cells of the donor. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h5)

question: What does a major cross-match specifically test in the laboratory?

options.A: Donor whole blood against commercial saline
options.B: Recipient plasma against recipient platelets
options.C: Recipient serum against donor red blood cells
options.D: Donor serum against recipient red blood cells

explanation: A major cross-match mixes the patient's serum with donor cells to prevent severe transfusion reactions. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h6)

question: Why is the minor cross-match performed less frequently with modern packed red cell transfusions?

options.A: Minor cross-matching only applies to platelet concentrates and cryoprecipitate.
options.B: Most donor plasma containing active antibodies has been removed from the product.
options.C: Routine ABO and Rhesus typing completely eliminates the need for any laboratory testing.
options.D: Donor red blood cells destroy all foreign plasma proteins upon contact.

explanation: Packed red cells contain minimal plasma, reducing the risk from donor antibodies directed at the recipient. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h6)

question: Why must a nurse remain closely with the patient during the first fifteen minutes of a blood transfusion?

options.A: The blood pump requires constant manual adjustment to prevent air embolism.
options.B: Standard hospital policy prohibits nurses from leaving the bedside entirely.
options.C: Most acute hemolytic reactions occur during the initial phase of administration.
options.D: Patients frequently fall asleep and pull out their peripheral IV lines.

explanation: Severe immune reactions typically present quickly after the first few milliliters of incompatible blood enter circulation. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h7)

question: Two nurses are at the bedside preparing to hang a unit of packed red blood cells. What must they verify together?

options.A: Patient identity, blood group, unit serial number, and expiration date
options.B: Exact weight of the blood bag and manufacturing laboratory address
options.C: Patient room number, primary physician name, and total hospital bill
options.D: Donor occupation, geographic origin, and previous donation history

explanation: Independent bedside double-checking prevents catastrophic clerical errors resulting in incompatible transfusions. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is the FIRST action a nurse must take if a patient shows signs of an acute transfusion reaction?

options.A: Stop the blood transfusion immediately and keep the vein open with saline.
options.B: Administer prescribed antipyretic medications and continue monitoring vital signs.
options.C: Collect a fresh midstream urine sample for routine laboratory microscopy.
options.D: Slow down the infusion rate by half and notify the blood bank technician.

explanation: Stopping the infusion prevents further entry of incompatible blood while maintaining IV access for emergency drugs. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T8#GNS123_U2_T8_h8)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Loin or lower back pain accompanied by fever and chills
options.B: Sudden loss of hearing in both ears during the infusion
options.C: Severe itching confined strictly to the palms of the hands
options.D: Painless swelling of the parotid glands near the jawline

question: What is the main purpose of a U&E (Urea and Electrolytes) blood test?

options.A: Kidney function and fluid balance
options.B: Red blood cell oxygen capacity
options.C: Blood clotting factor levels
options.D: Liver enzyme production rates

explanation: A U&E panel checks how well the kidneys are filtering waste and shows the balance of fluids and salts in the body. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h1)

question: When do doctors and nurses usually order a U&E test?

options.A: Exclusively prior to outpatient eye surgery
options.B: Only when diagnosing inherited bone disorders
options.C: To confirm the presence of a skin infection
options.D: During emergency room evaluations and routine admissions

explanation: U&E tests are ordered broadly in emergency and ward settings to quickly check for fluid and kidney problems. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h1)

question: What is the normal blood level for potassium in adults?

options.A: 96 to 106 mmol/L
options.B: 2.5 to 6.7 mmol/L
options.C: 135 to 145 mmol/L
options.D: 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L

explanation: Normal serum potassium is kept between 3.5 and 5.0 mmol/L to keep the heart and muscles working properly. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h2)

question: Which body systems work together to keep fluids and electrolytes balanced?

options.A: Heart valves and gastrointestinal tract only
options.B: Kidneys, lungs, and endocrine system
options.C: Liver, spleen, and peripheral nerves
options.D: Skin, skeletal muscles, and lymphatic vessels

explanation: Fluid balance relies on the kidneys, lungs, and hormones working together to regulate water and salts. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h2)

question: Where is urea primarily synthesized in the human body?

options.A: Liver
options.B: Pancreas
options.C: Skeletal muscle
options.D: Kidneys

explanation: Urea is a nitrogenous waste product created in the liver as a result of protein metabolism before being excreted by the kidneys. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h3)

question: Why is creatinine often a better marker of kidney function than urea?

options.A: It changes instantly when a patient eats a heavy meal
options.B: It is less affected by diet and hydration status than urea
options.C: It does not require glomerular filtration to be cleared
options.D: It is produced by the kidneys rather than skeletal muscles

explanation: Creatinine stays steady because it depends on muscle mass, whereas urea can change quickly if a patient is dehydrated. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h3)

question: Which electrolyte is most important for keeping the heart rhythm stable?

options.A: Chloride
options.B: Potassium
options.C: Calcium
options.D: Sodium

explanation: Potassium plays a key role in the electrical activity of heart muscle cells. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the main job of bicarbonate in the blood?

options.A: Providing energy for active cellular transport
options.B: Acting as a chemical buffer to regulate pH
options.C: Directly regulating resting blood pressure levels
options.D: Transporting oxygen molecules to peripheral tissues

explanation: Bicarbonate neutralizes acid in the blood to keep the body's pH at a safe level. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h4)

question: Which type of medication often requires regular U&E blood tests?

options.A: Antibiotics
options.B: Bronchodilators
options.C: Diuretics
options.D: Antihistamines

explanation: Diuretics make the body lose water and can upset salt levels, making regular U&E checks necessary. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h5)

question: A patient arrives at the ward with severe vomiting and diarrhea. What is the best initial blood test to run?

options.A: Liver function test profile
options.B: Sputum microscopy analysis
options.C: Urea and electrolytes panel
options.D: Fasting blood glucose test

explanation: Severe vomiting and diarrhea cause rapid fluid loss, making a U&E essential to check for dehydration and electrolyte imbalances. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h5)

question: What is the primary clinical danger associated with severe hyperkalemia?

options.A: Uncontrolled hypertension
options.B: Fatal cardiac arrhythmias
options.C: Rapid muscle wasting
options.D: Severe peripheral edema

explanation: High serum potassium disrupts electrical conduction in the heart, leading to dangerous and potentially lethal rhythm disturbances. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h6)

question: What does a high urea-to-creatinine ratio usually suggest in an adult patient?

options.A: Pre-renal failure due to dehydration
options.B: Primary glomerular destruction
options.C: Excessive dietary carbohydrate intake
options.D: Chronic liver cirrhosis

explanation: When the body is low on fluids, the kidneys hold onto more urea, making the ratio go up. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h6)

question: What can happen if a tourniquet is left on too long during a blood draw?

options.A: Artificial lowering of serum creatinine levels
options.B: Complete destruction of all plasma proteins
options.C: Immediate clotting of the collection tube
options.D: False elevation of potassium through hemolysis

explanation: Leaving a tourniquet on too long breaks open red blood cells, releasing potassium and giving a falsely high lab result. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h7)

question: Why should blood for a U&E test not be drawn from an arm with an active IV drip?

options.A: It dilutes the sample with intravenous fluids, leading to inaccurate results
options.B: It increases the risk of spreading a systemic infection
options.C: It causes immediate collapse of the peripheral veins
options.D: It creates severe pain and bruising at the puncture site

question: Which medication is given first to protect the heart during severe high potassium levels?

options.A: Furosemide injection
options.B: Sodium bicarbonate
options.C: Calcium gluconate
options.D: Regular normal saline

explanation: Calcium gluconate stabilizes the heart muscle membrane against high potassium while other treatments work to lower it. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h8)

question: Why are insulin and glucose given together to treat high potassium?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing hypoglycemia
options.B: To shift potassium from the blood into the cells
options.C: To stimulate rapid renal excretion of urea
options.D: To filter excess potassium out through the glomeruli

explanation: Insulin pushes potassium out of the bloodstream and into the cells, while glucose is added so the patient's blood sugar doesn't drop too low. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T9#GNS123_U2_T9_h8)

question: What is the primary biological purpose of inflammation in the human body?

options.A: To stop all metabolic activity in affected areas
options.B: To permanently increase local blood pressure
options.C: To destroy healthy host tissue and cells
options.D: To remove tissue injury causes and begin repair

explanation: Inflammation serves as a defense mechanism to clear harmful agents and heal damaged tissue. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why can the inflammatory response sometimes cause damage to the host?

options.A: It permanently deactivates the immune system
options.B: It can be excessive or directed inappropriately
options.C: It completely stops blood flow to organs
options.D: It is always caused by malignant cell growth

explanation: Overactive or misdirected immune responses lead to collateral damage in healthy tissues. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which white blood cell type dominates during acute inflammation?

options.A: Neutrophils
options.B: Eosinophils
options.C: Lymphocytes
options.D: Macrophages

explanation: Neutrophils are the primary and rapid responders in acute inflammatory reactions. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h2)

question: What pathological feature distinguishes chronic inflammation from acute inflammation?

options.A: Immediate local pain and heat
options.B: Vascular proliferation and fibrosis
options.C: Rapid resolution of tissue swelling
options.D: Presence of active neutrophils

explanation: Chronic inflammation involves long-term tissue remodeling, including fibrosis and new blood vessel formation. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h2)

question: What physiological change directly causes rubor during acute inflammation?

options.A: Deposition of collagen fibers
options.B: Lymphatic vessel blockage
options.C: Vasodilation of local blood vessels
options.D: Decreased cellular metabolism

explanation: Vasodilation increases blood volume in the microvasculature, leading to visible redness. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h3)

question: Chemical mediators such as prostaglandins contribute directly to which cardinal sign?

options.A: Heat
options.B: Pain
options.C: Loss of function
options.D: Redness

explanation: Prostaglandins and bradykinins sensitize nerve endings, generating the sensation of pain at the injury site. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the movement of leukocytes toward the site of injury called?

options.A: Vasodilation
options.B: Diapedesis
options.C: Margination
options.D: Chemotaxis

explanation: Chemotaxis is the chemical-guided movement of white blood cells toward the source of injury. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why does increased vascular permeability occur early in acute inflammation?

options.A: To prevent white blood cells from leaving blood vessels
options.B: To allow protein-rich fluid to enter the interstitial tissue
options.C: To speed up systemic blood circulation through the heart
options.D: To permanently close damaged local capillary networks

question: Which organ produces acute-phase proteins like C-reactive protein during systemic inflammation?

options.A: Spleen
options.B: Kidneys
options.C: Liver
options.D: Pancreas

explanation: The liver synthesizes and releases large amounts of acute-phase proteins when stimulated by inflammatory cytokines. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h5)

question: What lab finding is most commonly associated with an ongoing acute inflammatory response?

options.A: Elevated C-reactive protein levels
options.B: Reduced erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.C: High serum albumin concentrations
options.D: Decreased white blood cell count

explanation: CRP rises sharply in the bloodstream during inflammatory states, making it a key diagnostic marker. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h5)

question: A patient with a localized leg wound develops a fever and elevated heart rate. What do these findings indicate?

options.A: The patient is experiencing normal resting physiology
options.B: The inflammatory process has completely resolved
options.C: The inflammation has remained strictly local
options.D: The local injury has triggered a systemic response

explanation: Fever and tachycardia reflect systemic involvement rather than isolated local changes. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which nursing action is most important when monitoring a limb with acute soft tissue inflammation?

options.A: Limiting all patient movement to prevent joint stiffness
options.B: Measuring extremity circumference to track changes in edema
options.C: Restricting fluid intake to stop inflammatory exudate production
options.D: Applying continuous direct heat to speed up cellular repair

explanation: Regular measurement provides objective data on whether swelling is worsening or improving. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary pharmacological action of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs?

options.A: Inhibiting cyclooxygenase enzymes to reduce prostaglandins
options.B: Increasing local blood flow to clear cellular debris
options.C: Stimulating the bone marrow to produce more neutrophils
options.D: Blocking all nerve transmission in the central nervous system

explanation: NSAIDs block the COX pathway, preventing the formation of pain-producing prostaglandins. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why is cold therapy recommended during the first 24 to 48 hours after an acute soft tissue injury?

options.A: It triggers immediate vasodilation to bring more white blood cells
options.B: It permanently removes all damaged collagen fibers from the area
options.C: It increases local cellular metabolism to speed up tissue healing
options.D: It causes vasoconstriction to minimize local swelling and pain

explanation: Cold constricts local blood vessels, decreasing fluid leakage into tissues and numbing nerve endings. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T1#GNS123_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is a primary long-term consequence of uncontrolled chronic inflammation in organs?

explanation: Nurses must track the patient's breathing response and watch out for common medication side effects like tachycardia. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T13#GNS123_U3_T13_h7)

question: What severe complication can result from prolonged, untreated severe dyspnoea?

options.A: Permanent skin tanning
options.B: Enhanced muscle growth
options.C: Increased bone density
options.D: Respiratory failure

explanation: Inability to maintain adequate gas exchange over time leads directly to respiratory failure and dangerous tissue hypoxia. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T13#GNS123_U3_T13_h8)

question: Why is patient education on avoiding environmental triggers critical for chronic breathlessness?

options.A: It eliminates all bacteria present in the lung alveoli
options.B: It cures the underlying genetic defect causing the disease
options.C: It prevents sudden acute exacerbations of airway narrowing
options.D: It replaces the need for any regular medical check-ups

explanation: Limiting exposure to smoke, dust, and allergens stops the inflammatory cascade that triggers acute breathing attacks. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T13#GNS123_U3_T13_h8)

question: Where does excess fluid collect when a patient has peripheral oedema?

options.A: Directly in the lymphatic ducts
options.B: Within the interstitial spaces
options.C: Inside the cellular cytoplasm
options.D: Inside the vascular lumen

explanation: Oedema is the collection of fluid outside the blood vessels, specifically in the spaces between tissue cells. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T14#GNS123_U3_T14_h1)

question: What does the presence of oedema tell the nurse about the body?

options.A: Total destruction of the renal cortex
options.B: An absolute absence of plasma proteins
options.C: An alteration in normal fluid balance
options.D: Complete failure of the hepatic system

explanation: Swelling shows that fluid filtration from blood vessels has overtaken the normal reabsorption mechanisms. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T14#GNS123_U3_T14_h1)

question: Which pressure force pulls fluid back into the capillary blood vessels?

options.A: Interstitial hydrostatic pressure
options.B: Atmospheric pressure
options.C: Capillary hydrostatic pressure
options.D: Plasma oncotic pressure

explanation: Circulating proteins, mainly albumin, create an osmotic pull that draws fluid back into the circulation. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T14#GNS123_U3_T14_h2)

question: A patient with severe liver disease has low blood protein levels. What causes their oedema?

options.A: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
options.B: Elevated interstitial oncotic pressure
options.C: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure
options.D: Reduced interstitial hydrostatic pressure

explanation: Low albumin production reduces the pulling pressure that normally keeps fluid inside the blood vessels. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T14#GNS123_U3_T14_h2)

question: What term describes a severe, generalised accumulation of fluid across the entire body?

options.A: Myxoedema
options.B: Anasarca
options.C: Lymphoedema
options.D: Ascites

explanation: Anasarca is the medical term for massive, widespread swelling affecting the whole body. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T14#GNS123_U3_T14_h3)

question: An isolated swollen ankle from a sprained ligament is an example of what type of oedema?

options.A: Generalised oedema
options.B: Systemic oedema
options.C: Localised oedema
options.D: Dependent oedema

explanation: When swelling is restricted to a single site of injury, it is classified as localised oedema. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T14#GNS123_U3_T14_h3)

question: How does liver cirrhosis lead to fluid retention?

options.A: Impaired synthesis of blood proteins
options.B: Obstruction of major lymphatic trunks
options.C: Excessive dietary salt intake
options.D: Primary destruction of nephron units

explanation: A damaged liver cannot make enough albumin, which lowers blood oncotic pressure and causes fluid to leak into tissues. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T14#GNS123_U3_T14_h4)

question: Which condition is most likely to cause generalised fluid overload and fluid in the lungs?

options.A: Congestive heart failure
options.B: An acute insect sting
options.C: A localised muscle tear
