options.B: To make sure the patient's blood pressure remains stable during the blood draw
options.C: To allow the white blood cell count time to normalize naturally
options.D: To ensure the laboratory technician is available to process the blood immediately

explanation: If we give antibiotics first, they might kill the germs in our lab sample, leaving us guessing about what infection we are fighting! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T6#GNS213_U1_T6_h4)

question: A patient is admitted with suspected infective endocarditis. Which test is best for directly viewing the valve growths?

options.A: Standard 12-lead ECG
options.B: Chest X-ray
options.C: Echocardiogram
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: An echocardiogram uses sound waves (like an ultrasound for the heart) to let doctors actually see those moving valve growths clearly. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T6#GNS213_U1_T6_h4)

question: How long do patients usually need antibiotic treatment for infective endocarditis?

options.A: Four to six weeks
options.B: Six months to a year
options.C: One to two weeks
options.D: Three to five days

explanation: Germs hiding inside heart valve growths are very hard for drugs to reach. That's why patients need a long course of IV antibiotics, usually 4 to 6 weeks. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T6#GNS213_U1_T6_h5)

question: Why is colchicine sometimes given along with NSAIDs to treat pericarditis?

options.A: To dissolve existing blood clots inside the heart chambers
options.B: To destroy resistant bacterial strains in the bloodstream
options.C: To permanently lower the patient's resting heart rate
options.D: To help prevent future episodes of the condition from returning

explanation: Colchicine is a helpful anti-inflammatory medicine added to treatment to stop pericarditis from coming back to trouble the patient again. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T6#GNS213_U1_T6_h5)

question: Which of these is a common reason a patient with infective endocarditis might need surgical valve replacement?

options.A: Temporary joint pain in the lower extremities
options.B: Heart failure caused by severe valve damage
options.C: A slight elevation in white blood cell count
options.D: Mild fatigue during routine daily activities

explanation: When an infection destroys the heart valves so badly that the heart starts failing or fluid overloads the body, surgery becomes necessary to fix or replace the valve. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T6#GNS213_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is a major nursing priority right after a patient has heart valve surgery for endocarditis?

options.A: Stopping all antibiotic medications once the patient leaves the operating room
options.B: Encouraging immediate heavy physical exercise to strengthen the heart muscle
options.C: Restricting fluid intake completely to prevent any swelling
options.D: Monitoring closely for signs of infection and evaluating neurological status for emboli

explanation: Great nursing care here means staying alert! We watch for any lingering infection and check the patient's brain function (neurological status) to catch any loose clots early. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T6#GNS213_U1_T6_h6)

question: What common complication happens when pieces of a heart valve growth break off and travel in the bloodstream?

options.A: Bone fracture
options.B: Kidney stones
options.C: Stroke
options.D: Asthma attack

explanation: When those infected clumps break free, they travel through blood vessels and can block blood flow to the brain, leading to a stroke. Spotting this early saves lives! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T6#GNS213_U1_T6_h7)

question: Why must high-risk heart patients take antibiotics before certain dental procedures?

options.A: Dental manipulation can introduce bacteria into the bloodstream, which may latch onto damaged heart valves.
options.B: Dental medications frequently interact negatively with cardiac drugs like digoxin.
options.C: Tooth decay directly causes inflammation of the outer pericardial sac.
options.D: Local anesthetics used by dentists weaken the heart muscle permanently.

explanation: Gum bleeding during dental work lets mouth bacteria sneak into the bloodstream. For a vulnerable heart, prophylactic antibiotics act like a shield! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T6#GNS213_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is the name of the thick muscular middle layer of the heart wall that pumps blood?

options.A: Myocardium
options.B: Epicardium
options.C: Pericardium
options.D: Endocardium

explanation: The myocardium is the muscular middle layer of the heart that does the hard work of contracting and pumping blood to the body! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why is inflammation affecting any layer of the heart considered a serious medical concern?

options.A: It exclusively affects the lungs and has no impact on circulation
options.B: It only causes temporary skin rashes on the chest wall
options.C: It can severely compromise the heart's ability to pump blood effectively
options.D: It instantly stops all electrical activity without warning

explanation: Swelling and damage to heart tissues disrupt the normal pumping action, which can lead to heart failure and poor circulation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which position usually helps make chest pain feel better when a patient has pericarditis?

options.A: Reclining deeply with legs elevated
options.B: Lying completely flat on the back
options.C: Sitting upright and leaning forward
options.D: Turning sharply onto the left side

explanation: Leaning forward pulls the heart away from surrounding tissues, reducing painful friction and giving the patient sweet relief. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h2)

question: What creates that scratchy 'pericardial friction rub' sound heard through a stethoscope?

options.A: Blood leaking backward through a faulty valve
options.B: Blood rushing too fast through narrowed coronary arteries
options.C: Rough, inflamed heart sac layers rubbing against each other
options.D: Air trapped inside the chest cavity

explanation: Think of it like sandpaper: when the pericardial layers get rough from inflammation, they scratch against each other with every heartbeat, creating that distinct sound. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is the most common cause of myocarditis?

options.A: Viruses
options.B: Fungi
options.C: Parasites
options.D: Prions

explanation: Viruses are the top culprits behind myocarditis worldwide, often attacking the heart muscle after a normal viral infection. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h3)

question: How does myocarditis usually affect the function of the heart muscle?

options.A: It thickens the coronary arteries completely
options.B: It turns the heart muscle hard like bone
options.C: It weakens the muscle walls and lowers pumping efficiency
options.D: It permanently opens up all the valves

explanation: Because inflammation damages the muscle tissue, the heart struggles to squeeze hard, leading to reduced pumping power. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h3)

question: What do we call the infected clumps of platelets and germs that grow on heart valves in endocarditis?

options.A: Atheromas
options.B: Vegetations
options.C: Aneurysms
options.D: Thromboemboli

explanation: In infective endocarditis, clusters of bacteria, platelets, and fibrin build up on the valves like little growths called vegetations. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h4)

question: A patient with endocarditis has small, painful reddish bumps on their finger pads. What are these called?

options.A: Petechiae
options.B: Roth spots
options.C: Osler's nodes
options.D: Janeway lesions

explanation: Osler's nodes are tender, painful bumps that pop up on fingers and toes due to immune complexes settling there. Remember: O for 'Ouch' in Osler's! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h4)

question: Which medication is often given alongside NSAIDs to stop pericarditis from coming back?

options.A: Warfarin
options.B: Digoxin
options.C: Atropine
options.D: Colchicine

explanation: Colchicine works brilliantly alongside NSAIDs to calm down stubborn inflammation and prevent flare-ups. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why do patients with endocarditis need to take antibiotics for many weeks instead of just a few days?

options.A: Pills take a very long time to reach the stomach
options.B: Heart valves have no blood supply and drugs can't reach them easily
options.C: Bacteria hiding inside valve vegetations are hard for drugs to reach
options.D: Short courses always cause skin allergies

explanation: The clumps of bacteria and platelets (vegetations) don't have their own blood vessels, so it takes a long, steady course of antibiotics to fully wipe them out. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why is strict bed rest ordered during the early, active phase of myocarditis?

options.A: To lower the workload on the inflamed heart muscle
options.B: To stop blood clots from forming in the legs
options.C: To stop the kidneys from making too much urine
options.D: To keep the patient's blood pressure high

explanation: Resting lowers the heart rate and reduces the amount of work the heart has to do, giving the sore muscle time to heal. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h6)

question: Which nursing action is most important for tracking fluid buildup in a patient with heart inflammation?

options.A: Doing reflex checks on both arms
options.B: Checking the patient's vision every four hours
options.C: Testing grip strength twice a day
options.D: Checking daily weights and tracking intake and output

explanation: Tracking daily weights and fluid charts is your best early warning system for fluid retention and failing heart function. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h6)

question: What emergency procedure is used to drain extra fluid from around the heart during cardiac tamponade?

options.A: Thoracentesis
options.B: Cardioversion
options.C: Pericardiocentesis
options.D: Paracentesis

explanation: Pericardiocentesis involves gently passing a needle into the pericardial sac to draw out fluid and relieve dangerous pressure on the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h7)

question: What classic set of signs points to cardiac tamponade?

options.A: Slow pulse, flushed skin, and high temperature
options.B: High BP, strong pulses, and clear breath sounds
options.C: Fast breathing, pinpoint pupils, and quiet tummy
options.D: Low BP, muffled heart sounds, and swollen neck veins

explanation: Known as Beck's triad, these three signs (low blood pressure, muffled heart tones from fluid, and distended neck veins) are huge red flags for tamponade! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h7)

question: Why must nurses stress finishing the full course of antibiotics for heart infections?

options.A: Patients will need pills for the rest of their lives
options.B: Incomplete doses make you immune to everything
options.C: Antibiotics expire very quickly in hot weather
options.D: Stopping early can cause the infection to roar back

explanation: Stopping antibiotics early leaves the toughest germs alive, allowing the infection to bounce right back stronger than before. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h8)

question: What routine self-care practice is strongly emphasized to patients at risk for infective endocarditis to prevent bacteria from entering the bloodstream?

options.A: Refusing all routine vaccinations at local health clinics
options.B: Drinking large quantities of palm wine daily
options.C: Maintaining good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups
options.D: Avoiding all physical exercise for the rest of their lives

explanation: Oral bacteria can easily enter the bloodstream during dental procedures or daily hygiene, making dental care a primary prevention target for endocarditis. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h8)

question: What is the main difference between primary and secondary heart tumours?

options.A: Secondary tumours never affect heart valves
options.B: Primary tumours are always malignant growths
options.C: Primary tumours start directly inside the heart tissues
options.D: Secondary tumours only occur in children

explanation: Primary cardiac tumours originate within the heart itself, whereas secondary tumours spread to the heart from other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h1)

question: How do heart tumours usually cause problems with normal heart function?

options.A: By blocking blood flow and damaging valves
options.B: By instantly causing complete electrical heart block
options.C: By destroying red blood cells in the ventricles
options.D: By permanently lowering blood pressure

explanation: Tumours inside the heart chambers or walls physically block blood movement and interfere with valve closure. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h1)

question: What is the most common type of primary heart tumour in adults?

options.A: Fibroelastoma
options.B: Myxoma
options.C: Angiosarcoma
options.D: Rhabdomyoma

explanation: Myxomas represent the majority of primary heart tumours, most often found in the left atrium. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h2)

question: A patient has an angiosarcoma of the heart. Which chamber is most commonly involved?

options.A: Left atrium
options.B: Left ventricle
options.C: Right atrium
options.D: Interventricular septum

explanation: Malignant primary cardiac angiosarcomas show a strong preference for the right-sided heart chambers, particularly the right atrium. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h2)

question: Which type of cancer most commonly spreads (metastasizes) to the heart?

options.A: Brain cancer
options.B: Lung cancer
options.C: Prostate cancer
options.D: Colon cancer

explanation: Lung malignancies are the leading cause of secondary, metastatic cardiac involvement in clinical practice. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h3)

question: Secondary heart tumours most frequently involve which layer of the heart?

options.A: Endocardium
options.B: Papillary muscle
options.C: Aortic valve
options.D: Pericardium

explanation: Secondary cancer cells typically travel to the pericardial space, frequently resulting in fluid accumulation around the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h3)

question: Why can symptoms of a heart tumour look like other conditions such as mitral stenosis?

options.A: Because all cardiac growths alter the electrical conduction system
options.B: Because tumours always cause high blood pressure
options.C: Because tumours can physically block blood flow through heart valves
options.D: Because secondary tumours immediately destroy heart muscle cells

explanation: An atrial myxoma can sit over the mitral valve, mimicking valvular stenosis by blocking blood flow into the ventricle. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which symptom category includes unexplained fever, tiredness, and weight loss in a patient with a heart tumour?

options.A: Embolic manifestations
options.B: Obstructive symptoms
options.C: Valvular regurgitation
options.D: Constitutional signs

explanation: Tumours can release inflammatory proteins into the bloodstream, producing systemic signs that resemble chronic infection or malignancy. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h4)

question: What is the first and most common imaging tool used to check for heart masses?

options.A: Echocardiography
options.B: Chest X-ray
options.C: Coronary angiography
options.D: Electrocardiography (ECG)

explanation: An echocardiogram is non-invasive, widely available, and highly effective for visualizing heart chambers and masses. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why might a doctor order a cardiac MRI along with an ultrasound when investigating a heart tumour?

options.A: To check for blockages inside the coronary arteries only
options.B: To better show tissue details and the exact borders of the mass
options.C: To measure the electrical activity of the heart muscle
options.D: To instantly dissolve blood clots around the tumour

explanation: Cardiac MRI provides detailed tissue characterization to help differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is the standard treatment to completely remove a primary benign heart myxoma?

options.A: Radiation therapy alone
options.B: Systemic chemotherapy
options.C: Surgical removal
options.D: Long-term blood thinners

explanation: Surgically removing a benign primary tumour prevents dangerous complications like stroke or sudden cardiac death. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h6)

question: How are secondary, spreading heart tumours usually managed in patients?

options.A: With routine antibiotics to prevent infection
options.B: With electrical shock to restore normal heart rhythm
options.C: With supportive therapy and treatment targeting the primary cancer
options.D: With immediate heart transplantation as the first choice

explanation: Because secondary tumours represent widespread disease, management focuses on comfort, symptom relief, and treating the primary cancer source. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why is continuous heart monitoring (telemetry) essential after a patient has surgery to remove a heart tumour?

options.A: To watch for irregular heartbeats caused by touching the heart muscle during surgery
options.B: To prevent the myxoma tissue from growing back in the atrium
options.C: To evaluate how well the lungs are taking in oxygen
options.D: To measure the exact pumping power of the left ventricle

explanation: Surgical work on heart tissue frequently irritates the conduction system, increasing the risk of post-operative heart rhythm disturbances. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h7)

question: What critical assessment should a nurse perform regularly to check for blood clots breaking loose after heart surgery?

options.A: Inspecting the surgical wound for skin redness
options.B: Listening to bowel sounds in all four quadrants
options.C: Checking peripheral pulses and neurological status
options.D: Measuring the patient's waistline every four hours

explanation: Monitoring neurological signs and limb perfusion helps identify any debris or micro-emboli dislodged during the operation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h7)

question: What is the typical long-term outlook for a patient who has a benign heart myxoma successfully removed?

options.A: Guarded, requiring lifetime chemotherapy
options.B: Uncertain, because they always spread later
options.C: Poor, leading quickly to organ failure
options.D: Excellent, with high long-term survival rates

explanation: Complete surgical removal of a benign myxoma typically cures the condition and restores normal life expectancy. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical complication of malignant heart tumours?

options.A: Bits of the tumour breaking off and blocking blood vessels
options.B: Complete natural disappearance of the tumour without treatment
options.C: Severe heart failure due to heart muscle damage
options.D: Dangerous irregular heartbeats leading to cardiac arrest

explanation: Malignant cardiac tumours do not spontaneously disappear; instead, they progress and cause heart failure, arrhythmias, and emboli. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the primary cause of blunt cardiac injury in civilian settings?

options.A: Iatrogenic catheterization
options.B: Stab wounds from knives
options.C: Gunshot wounds
options.D: Motor vehicle collisions

explanation: Blunt cardiac injury most frequently results from rapid deceleration forces during vehicular accidents. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why can a normal initial ECG still miss a heart contusion?

options.A: Heart muscle damage changes can show up gradually over several hours
options.B: Bruises heal on their own in the first few minutes
options.C: Pain meds hide the heart's true electrical pattern
options.D: ECGs only check the upper chambers of the heart

explanation: Cellular damage to the heart muscle evolves over time, which means early ECG results can look completely normal even when an injury is present. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h1)

question: What are the three classic signs of Beck's triad in cardiac tamponade?

options.A: Slow heart rate, strong pulses, wide pulse pressure
options.B: Fast heart rate, windpipe shift, quiet breath sounds
options.C: Low blood pressure, swollen neck veins, muffled heart sounds
options.D: High blood pressure, flat neck veins, loud heart sounds

explanation: Beck's triad consists of hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds, which together point to acute cardiac tamponade. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h2)

question: Why do patients with cardiac tamponade develop swollen neck veins?

options.A: Too much IV fluid is given too quickly
options.B: Fluid in the sac around the heart blocks blood from returning
options.C: Trauma directly stimulates the fight-or-flight nervous system
options.D: The aortic valve suddenly stops closing properly

explanation: Fluid building up in the pericardial space squeezes the heart chambers, making it hard for blood to flow back easily from the jugular veins. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h2)

question: What is the main bedside ultrasound tool used to check for fluid around the heart after trauma?

options.A: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage
options.B: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma
options.C: Barium swallow study
options.D: Chest magnetic resonance imaging

explanation: The FAST scan is quick, non-invasive, and very effective for spotting blood around the heart in emergency situations. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h3)

question: Why might a regular chest X-ray look completely normal in someone with a sharp stab wound to the heart?

options.A: Stab wounds instantly seal themselves with small clots
options.B: Patients always hold their breath during chest X-rays
options.C: A small amount of blood in the heart sac does not change the heart's outline on X-ray
options.D: X-rays cannot pass through the front chest wall muscles

explanation: Even a small amount of blood trapped in the pericardium can cause a life-threatening emergency without making the heart shadow look enlarged on a standard X-ray. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h3)

question: What size of intravenous access is best when resuscitating a trauma patient?

options.A: Small pediatric butterfly needles
options.B: Central lines placed in the foot
options.C: Subcutaneous infusion ports
options.D: Large-bore peripheral lines

explanation: Large-bore IV lines allow fluids and blood products to be pushed in rapidly when a patient is in shock. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h4)

question: What is a major risk of giving IV fluids too aggressively during penetrating heart injuries?

options.A: It instantly turns an irregular heart rhythm back to normal
options.B: It can knock loose fragile blood clots and worsen bleeding
options.C: It immediately fixes muffled heart sounds and low blood pressure
options.D: It fully repairs damaged heart valve flaps

explanation: Pushing blood pressure up too fast can blow out the delicate clots holding a heart wound together, leading to more internal bleeding. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h4)

question: What surgical material is often used to keep stitches from tearing through delicate heart muscle?

options.A: Wooden splints
options.B: Elastic bands
options.C: Pledgets
options.D: Metal staples

explanation: Small felt pledgets help spread out the tension so stitches do not tear through fragile heart tissue during repairs. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h5)

question: A patient recovering from heart surgery develops a fever, sharp chest pain when breathing, and a rubbing sound on the chest. What is the most likely issue?

options.A: Tension pneumothorax
options.B: Post-pericardiotomy syndrome
options.C: Aortic aneurysm
options.D: Infectious subacute endocarditis

explanation: Inflammation of the outer lining of the heart following surgery or trauma often shows up as post-pericardiotomy syndrome. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T9#GNS213_U1_T9_h5)

question: What is the primary function of the upper respiratory tract?

options.A: Filter, warm, and humidify incoming air
options.B: Produce red blood cells for gas transport
options.C: Generate electrical impulses for breathing rhythm
options.D: Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide at cellular level

explanation: The upper structures prepare the inspired air by cleaning and conditioning it before deep lung entry. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which structure prevents food from entering the trachea during swallowing?

options.A: Pharynx
options.B: Larynx
options.C: Epiglottis
options.D: Soft palate

explanation: The epiglottis acts as a lid that closes over the larynx during swallowing to protect the airway. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why does the trachea have C-shaped rings of cartilage?

options.A: To keep the airway open during breathing
options.B: To absorb oxygen directly into the blood
options.C: To produce sound vibrations for the voice
options.D: To contract and push food down the throat

explanation: The rigid hyaline cartilage rings prevent the tracheal walls from collapsing during pressure changes in respiration. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h2)

question: What structural change happens as bronchi divide into smaller bronchioles?

options.A: The tubes become rigid and fixed in diameter
options.B: Cartilage rings disappear and smooth muscle increases
options.C: Skeletal muscle attaches to control voluntary breathing
options.D: Bone replaces cartilage to support heavy lung tissue

explanation: Smaller bronchioles lose their cartilage support and rely heavily on smooth muscle tone to adjust airway diameter. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the main function of pulmonary surfactant?

options.A: Trap dust particles and bacteria in the airway
options.B: Lower surface tension to prevent alveolar collapse
options.C: Maintain fluid balance inside the pleural cavity
options.D: Transport oxygen molecules through the blood plasma

explanation: Surfactant reduces the cohesive forces of water molecules inside the alveoli, stopping them from sticking together and collapsing. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h3)

question: Which cells form the primary thin barrier for gas exchange in the lungs?

options.A: Alveolar macrophages
options.B: Ciliated columnar cells
options.C: Type I alveolar cells
options.D: Type II alveolar cells

explanation: Type I cells create a flat, simple squamous sheet that keeps the diffusion distance between air and blood extremely short. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h3)

question: What happens to the diaphragm during inspiration?

options.A: It contracts and flattens downward
options.B: It relaxes and domes upward
options.C: It vibrates to create vocal sounds
options.D: It remains stationary while ribs move

explanation: Contraction of the dome-shaped diaphragm pulls it downward, increasing the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h4)

question: A patient has a condition that prevents normal relaxation of chest muscles. Which phase of ventilation is directly impaired?

options.A: Gas diffusion
options.B: Inspiration
options.C: Expiration
options.D: Surfactant production

explanation: Quiet expiration relies on the passive relaxation of inspiratory muscles to decrease thoracic volume and push air out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h4)

question: How is the majority of oxygen transported in the blood?

options.A: Dissolved directly in the blood plasma
options.B: Bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells
options.C: Converted into stable bicarbonate molecules
options.D: Attached to white blood cells for defense

explanation: The vast majority of oxygen molecules attach to the iron-containing heme groups of hemoglobin for systemic delivery. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h5)

question: What physical principle drives oxygen across the alveolar-capillary membrane?

options.A: Active cellular transport
options.B: Partial pressure gradient
options.C: Electrical charge attraction
options.D: Hydrostatic blood pressure

explanation: Gases move passively from an area of higher partial pressure to an area of lower partial pressure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h5)

question: Where are the primary neural centers that control the basic rhythm of breathing located?

options.A: Medulla oblongata and pons
options.B: Cerebellum and basal ganglia
options.C: Cerebrum and cerebral cortex
options.D: Hypothalamus and pituitary gland

explanation: The brainstem houses the neural pacemaker networks that automatically generate the breathing cycle. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the most powerful chemical stimulus that triggers an increase in the rate of breathing?

options.A: Critically low levels of dissolved oxygen
options.B: Decreased body temperature during rest
options.C: Elevated carbon dioxide levels in the blood
options.D: High concentration of plasma proteins

explanation: Rising carbon dioxide leads to increased hydrogen ions and acidity, strongly stimulating central chemoreceptors to speed up ventilation. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T1#GNS213_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary function of the respiratory system that gets disrupted during disorders?

options.A: Nutrient absorption
options.B: Blood filtration
options.C: Fluid balance control
options.D: Gas exchange

explanation: The main job of the respiratory system is moving oxygen into the blood and removing carbon dioxide. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why do patients experience shortness of breath when they have a respiratory problem?

options.A: The kidneys are retaining too much water
options.B: The heart is pumping too much blood to the muscles
options.C: The stomach is pushing upward against the diaphragm
options.D: The body is trying to fix low oxygen or high carbon dioxide levels

explanation: Think of shortness of breath as an alarm bell! It's your body's clever way of telling you it needs more oxygen or needs to blow off extra carbon dioxide. Great effort! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h1)

question: What term is used to describe shortness of breath that occurs specifically when a patient lies flat?

options.A: Tachypnea
options.B: Apnea
options.C: Bradypnea
options.D: Orthopnea

explanation: Orthopnea is breathing difficulty that worsens when lying down and improves when sitting upright. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h2)

question: A patient wakes up gasping for air two hours after falling asleep and has to sit by the window to breathe. What is this called?

options.A: Acute bronchial asthma
options.B: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
options.C: Simple sleep apnea
options.D: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

explanation: You're doing great! Waking up suddenly in the middle of the night feeling starved for air is known as paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND). It's a classic sign often seen in heart issues. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h2)

question: What does a rust-colored sputum sample often point toward?

options.A: Simple dehydration
options.B: Severe throat irritation
options.C: Pneumococcal pneumonia
options.D: Common viral cold

explanation: Rust-colored sputum contains blood mixed with inflammatory exudate, which is typical of pneumococcal pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h3)

question: Why is pink and frothy sputum an urgent sign that nurses must report immediately?

options.A: It is a normal byproduct of taking cough syrup
options.B: It means the patient is swallowing too much saliva
options.C: It indicates fluid backing up into the air sacs from the heart
options.D: It shows the patient has been smoking too many cigarettes

explanation: Well done! Pink and frothy sputum tells us fluid is leaking into the tiny air sacs in the lungs (pulmonary edema)—definitely something you want to catch and report fast! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h3)

question: What is the medical term for coughing up blood from the lungs?

options.A: Epistaxis
options.B: Hemothorax
options.C: Hematemesis
options.D: Hemoptysis

explanation: Hemoptysis refers specifically to blood that comes up from the respiratory system through coughing. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h4)

question: Why do many lung diseases cause sharp chest pain only when the patient takes a deep breath?

options.A: Air is getting trapped inside the stomach muscles
options.B: The main airway is swelling shut during inhalation
options.C: The heart muscle is stretching too hard against the ribcage
options.D: The inflamed lining of the lungs rubs against the chest wall during movement

explanation: Think of it like a skin scrape rubbing against clothing: when the pleural lining of the lungs gets inflamed, every deep breath causes those sore layers to rub together and hurt! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h4)

question: What physical sign involves a bluish color of the skin due to low oxygen in the blood?

options.A: Jaundice
options.B: Pallor
options.C: Cyanosis
options.D: Erythema

explanation: Cyanosis is the bluish tint seen on the skin and lips when deoxygenated hemoglobin levels rise. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h5)

question: Why might a severely anemic patient NOT show a blue skin color (cyanosis) even when their oxygen is dangerously low?

options.A: Their skin is naturally thicker and hides color changes better
options.B: Anemia causes the blood vessels to dilate and turn the skin red instead
options.C: They do not have enough red blood cells or hemoglobin to display the blue color
options.D: Their lungs absorb extra oxygen from the surrounding air

explanation: You're getting the hang of it! Cyanosis needs enough hemoglobin (the stuff in red blood cells that carries oxygen) to show that blue tint. If a patient is severely anemic, they simply don't have enough to show the color! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h5)

question: Which breath sound is described as a continuous musical whistle heard when airways are narrowed?

options.A: Crackles
options.B: Wheezes
options.C: Rhonchi
options.D: Stridor

explanation: Wheezes are high-pitched musical sounds created when air flows through constricted bronchial tubes. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h6)

question: A nurse listens with a stethoscope and hears moist, popping sounds at the lung bases of a patient with heart failure. What are these sounds called?

options.A: Friction rubs
options.B: Crackles
options.C: Wheezes
options.D: Rhonchi

explanation: Great job! Crackles sound just like Velcro pulling apart or bubbles popping, caused by fluid opening up those tiny air sacs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is finger clubbing typically associated with in chronic conditions?

options.A: Rapid dehydration from fever
options.B: Sudden bacterial throat infections
options.C: Long-term low oxygen levels in the blood
options.D: A temporary lack of dietary vitamins

explanation: Finger clubbing develops gradually as a result of chronic hypoxia and tissue changes in the extremities. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h7)

question: Why do many patients with severe, long-term lung disease experience noticeable weight loss and muscle wasting?

options.A: The physical effort of breathing uses up enormous amounts of energy
options.B: Their digestive tracts stop absorbing nutrients completely
options.C: They deliberately avoid eating to prevent shortness of breath
options.D: Liver damage prevents them from storing body fat

explanation: Think about how hard it is to run a race—now imagine working that hard just to breathe all day! That heavy effort burns massive amounts of energy and leads to weight loss. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h7)

question: What is the very FIRST thing a nurse should do when a patient suddenly gets severe shortness of breath?

options.A: Help the patient sit up and check their oxygen delivery
options.B: Leave the room immediately to find the attending doctor
options.C: Document the exact time the symptoms started
options.D: Have the patient lie flat on their back for rest

explanation: Patient comfort and breathing come first! Always help them sit upright and check their oxygen before you start writing notes or running off. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT helpful to include when charting about a patient's cough?

options.A: Factors that make the coughing worse
options.B: The color and amount of any sputum produced
options.C: The brand of soap used in the hospital room
options.D: Whether the cough is dry or productive

explanation: You got it! The soap brand won't change lung assessment findings, but details about sputum, triggers, and cough type are clinical gold! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T10#GNS213_U2_T10_h8)

question: What is the normal resting respiratory rate for a healthy adult?

options.A: 8 to 11 breaths per minute
options.B: 22 to 30 breaths per minute
options.C: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
options.D: 35 to 40 breaths per minute

explanation: A normal, healthy adult at rest breathes between 12 and 20 times every minute. Rates outside this range can indicate underlying respiratory or metabolic problems. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why is cyanosis considered a poor early indicator of hypoxia?

options.A: It only appears after severe oxygen shortage has already developed
options.B: It is easily confused with normal pigmentation changes in the skin
options.C: It disappears completely when the patient stands up
options.D: It only occurs when the patient is holding their breath

explanation: Cyanosis is a late sign of low oxygen in the blood. Restlessness and confusion show up much earlier, so nurses must not wait for blue skin to give oxygen. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of the huff coughing technique?

options.A: To measure the total lung capacity of the patient
options.B: To force air deeply into closed alveoli sacs
options.C: To prevent the tongue from blocking the throat
options.D: To move mucus upward without collapsing the airways

explanation: Huff coughing keeps the vocal cords open while the patient exhales sharply, helping push mucus up from the lower airways safely. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h2)

question: A patient with thick lung secretions refuses to drink water because of nausea. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Force the patient to drink a full cup of water immediately
options.B: Report the fluid refusal and suggest IV hydration or anti-nausea medication
options.C: Document that the patient refuses care and leave the room
options.D: Stop all respiratory treatments until the nausea goes away on its own

explanation: Good hydration thins out thick mucus so it can be cleared easily. Addressing nausea and providing fluids through alternative routes helps maintain airway clearance. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h2)

question: Which oxygen delivery device provides the most precise and controlled oxygen concentration?

options.A: Non-rebreather mask
options.B: Standard nasal cannula
options.C: Simple face mask
options.D: Venturi mask

explanation: The Venturi mask uses interchangeable adapters to mix exact amounts of room air with oxygen, delivering a very specific percentage of gas. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h3)

question: Why must nurses enforce strict fire safety rules around patients receiving oxygen therapy?

options.A: Oxygen strongly supports combustion and makes fires spread much faster
options.B: Electrical equipment creates sparks that turn oxygen into a liquid
options.C: Patients on oxygen are more likely to fall asleep while smoking
options.D: Oxygen tanks will automatically explode if they touch plastic

explanation: While oxygen itself does not burn, it feeds fires vigorously, turning small sparks into dangerous blazes instantly. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h3)

question: When a patient needs both a bronchodilator and an inhaled corticosteroid, why should the bronchodilator be used first?

options.A: It stops the side effects of the steroid from harming the heart
options.B: It neutralizes stomach acid that might interfere with breathing
options.C: It opens the airways so the steroid can reach deeper into the lungs
options.D: It cleans the mouth so the patient does not develop a fungal infection

explanation: Using the bronchodilator first widens the bronchial tubes, allowing the corticosteroid to penetrate further down into the respiratory tree. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h4)

question: A patient is prescribed a metered-dose inhaler without a spacer and complains that the medicine just hits their throat. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Instruct the patient to hold their breath for five minutes after inhaling
options.B: Call the doctor to change the prescription to a skin patch
options.C: Advise the patient to obtain and use a spacer device to improve drug delivery
options.D: Tell the patient to swallow the medicine instead of breathing it in

explanation: Spacers act as a holding chamber that slows down the spray, preventing medication from depositing in the mouth and throat instead of the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h4)

question: What is the best initial position for a patient experiencing acute respiratory distress?

options.A: High Fowler's position
options.B: Flat on the back
options.C: Trendelenburg position
options.D: Left lateral recovery position

explanation: Sitting upright in high Fowler's position allows gravity to lower the diaphragm, giving the lungs maximum room to expand and making breathing easier. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h5)

question: How does pursed-lip breathing help a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?

options.A: It forces extra oxygen directly into the bloodstream through the mouth
options.B: It relaxes the stomach muscles to improve digestion
options.C: It stops the patient from coughing up thick mucus plugs
options.D: It slows down exhalation and keeps airways open longer

explanation: Pursed-lip breathing creates back-pressure in the airways, preventing them from collapsing too early and helping trap less air in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T11#GNS213_U2_T11_h5)

question: What is the main job of our respiratory system?

options.A: Producing red blood cells
options.B: Bringing in oxygen and removing carbon dioxide
options.C: Regulating body temperature
options.D: Filtering bacteria out of the bloodstream

explanation: Spot on! The lungs trade gases with every breath we take—bringing in fresh oxygen our body loves and blowing out waste carbon dioxide. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why do lung problems often affect the rest of the body?

options.A: Lung infections spread directly to the brain within hours
options.B: Every organ relies heavily on a steady supply of oxygen from the lungs
options.C: Poor breathing causes the stomach to stop digesting food completely
options.D: The heart stops pumping blood when the lungs become inflamed

explanation: You got it! If the lungs aren't working well, oxygen delivery drops, and every single tissue in the body starts to suffer. Oxygen is food for our cells! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h1)

question: What do we call a dangerously low level of oxygen in the blood?

options.A: Hemothorax
options.B: Atelectasis
options.C: Hypoxemia
options.D: Hypercapnia

explanation: Well done! 'Hypo-' means low, and 'oxemia' refers to oxygen in the blood. Put them together and you have hypoxemia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which type of breathing problem involves a dangerous buildup of carbon dioxide?

options.A: A buildup of carbon dioxide due to poor ventilation
options.B: A sudden drop in oxygen caused by fluid in the alveoli
options.C: High blood pressure inside the arteries of the lungs
options.D: A complete collapse of the lung tissue from air in the chest

explanation: Correct! When a patient isn't moving air in and out well enough (poor ventilation), carbon dioxide gets trapped inside. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h2)

question: What actually is 'cor pulmonale'?

options.A: Bleeding into the chest cavity following trauma
options.B: An infection of the lining surrounding the lungs
options.C: Right-sided heart failure caused by long-term lung disease
options.D: A sudden collapse of a lung lobe due to a blocked airway

explanation: You nailed it. Long-term lung trouble makes the heart work extra hard on the right side, eventually leading to right-sided heart failure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h3)

question: A patient develops cor pulmonale from chronic lung disease. What sign might you spot as a nurse?

options.A: A sudden spike in blood glucose levels
options.B: Sudden sharp chest pain and absent breath sounds
options.C: Bright red blood coming up when coughing
options.D: Swollen lower legs and distended neck veins

explanation: Spot on! Since the right side of the heart is struggling to pump forward, fluid backs up into the body, causing swollen legs and puffy neck veins. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h3)

question: In simple terms, what is atelectasis?

options.A: An abnormal collection of air in the pleural cavity
options.B: A severe bacterial infection inside the lung tissue
options.C: The collapse or closure of a lung resulting in reduced gas exchange
options.D: High pressure inside the blood vessels of the lungs

explanation: Correct! Atelectasis happens when tiny air sacs (alveoli) deflate or collapse, making it harder to trade gases. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h4)

question: How does fluid in the chest cavity (pleural effusion) make it hard to breathe?

options.A: Fluid enters the alveoli and destroys the natural surfactant
options.B: It blocks the main windpipe and chugs off air supply
options.C: Fluid physically presses against the lung, stopping it from expanding fully
options.D: It forces the heart to beat too fast, causing sudden shock

explanation: You got it! The fluid takes up space in the chest and squeezes the lung from the outside, so it can't puff up nicely when breathing in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h4)

question: What fills the chest space when a patient has a hemothorax?

options.A: Air
options.B: Serous fluid
options.C: Blood
options.D: Pus

explanation: Easy and clear! 'Hemo' means blood, and 'thorax' means chest. It's blood inside the chest cavity. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h5)

question: Why is a tension pneumothorax such a major emergency?

options.A: Trapped air builds up pressure and shifts the heart and major blood vessels
options.B: It stops the kidneys from producing urine within minutes
options.C: It floods both lungs with thick, yellow mucus
options.D: It causes an immediate massive infection in the bronchial tubes

explanation: Correct! Trapped air keeps stacking up like a balloon, pushing everything in the chest sideways and stopping blood from returning to the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h5)

question: If a patient holds onto too much carbon dioxide because they aren't breathing deeply enough, what acid-base imbalance happens?

options.A: Respiratory alkalosis
options.B: Respiratory acidosis
options.C: Metabolic acidosis
options.D: Metabolic alkalosis

explanation: Well done! Carbon dioxide acts like an acid in the body. If it builds up in the lungs, the blood becomes too acidic—hence respiratory acidosis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h6)

question: A patient is having a panic attack and breathing way too fast. What are they at risk for?

options.A: Metabolic acidosis
options.B: Metabolic alkalosis
options.C: Respiratory alkalosis
options.D: Respiratory acidosis

explanation: Spot on! Breathing too fast blows off too much carbon dioxide. Losing too much acid makes the blood basic (alkaline), causing respiratory alkalosis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h6)

question: What is usually the very first clue that a patient's oxygen level is dropping?

options.A: A drop in body temperature
options.B: Swelling in the feet
options.C: Restlessness and confusion
options.D: Severe chest pain

explanation: You got it! The brain is super sensitive to oxygen. When it starts running low, the patient often gets fidgety, anxious, or confused before anything else happens. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h7)

question: Which sign tells you a patient is struggling and working extra hard to breathe?

options.A: Use of accessory muscles in the neck during inhalation
options.B: Warm and dry skin across the chest and arms
options.C: A slow and steady heart rate below 60 beats per minute
options.D: Quiet and effortless breathing sounds throughout both lung fields

explanation: Correct! When normal breathing isn't enough, the body recruits extra muscles in the neck and shoulders to help pull air in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h7)

question: Why do we teach pursed-lip breathing to patients with chronic lung issues?

options.A: It lowers the patient's blood pressure immediately
options.B: It stops all coughing episodes within a few minutes
options.C: It replaces the need for using oxygen therapy
options.D: It keeps airways open longer and helps expel trapped air

explanation: Well done! Breathing out through pursed lips creates a gentle back-pressure, stopping tiny airways from collapsing too soon. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h8)

question: What is the best way to help prevent atelectasis in a patient after surgery?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload in the chest
options.B: Administering a strong sleeping pill to ensure total rest
options.C: Encouraging regular deep breathing and incentive spirometry
options.D: Keeping the patient completely flat in bed to rest the lungs

explanation: Spot on! Getting the patient to take deep breaths and use their incentive spirometer pops those little air sacs wide open and keeps the lungs clear. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T12#GNS213_U2_T12_h8)

question: What is the main job of the mucociliary escalator in our airways?

options.A: Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide in the tiny air sacs
options.B: Making surfactant to keep the lungs from collapsing
options.C: Filtering big dust bits right inside the nose
options.D: Sweeping trapped dirt and mucus upward toward the throat

explanation: Think of the mucociliary escalator like a tiny conveyor belt in your respiratory tract. It uses beating hair-like cilia and mucus to push dust and germs up to your throat so you can swallow or cough them out cleanly! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h1)

question: Which nursing action is a great example of secondary prevention for respiratory health?

options.A: Running a community talk on the dangers of smoking
options.B: Teaching an asthma patient how to use their inhaler properly
options.C: Giving the yearly flu shot to a healthy adult
options.D: Screening high-risk factory workers with routine breathing tests

explanation: Secondary prevention is all about early detection! Screening tests help catch signs of trouble early, before a patient even notices symptoms. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h1)

question: What is the single biggest preventable cause of chronic lung disease (COPD) worldwide?

options.A: Childhood asthma attacks
options.B: Inhaling coal dust at work
options.C: Smoke from indoor cooking fires
options.D: Tobacco smoke exposure

explanation: Tobacco smoke is tough on the airways and air sacs over time. Because people can choose to avoid or quit it, it stands out as the number one preventable cause of COPD globally. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h2)

question: A patient living in a rural home with poor kitchen ventilation uses wood for daily cooking and now has a lasting cough. What is the best primary prevention advice?

options.A: Give them a course of strong oral antibiotics right away
options.B: Recommend using a quick-relief rescue inhaler every day
options.C: Order a chest X-ray to check for tuberculosis
options.D: Advise the family to switch to cleaner cooking fuel and improve kitchen airflow

explanation: Primary prevention stops the problem before it starts or worsens. Fixing indoor smoke exposure removes the root environmental trigger keeping that cough going! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h2)

question: Why do people need to take the influenza vaccine every single year?

options.A: The government needs yearly numbers for health records
options.B: The vaccine turns toxic if stored for more than a year
options.C: The flu virus mutates and changes its shape from year to year
options.D: Immunity from last year's shot completely disappears in six months

explanation: Flu viruses are clever changelings! They undergo constant changes (antigenic drift), so scientists update the vaccine annually to match whatever strain is currently spreading. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h3)

question: Which group of people benefits the most from herd immunity against respiratory infections?

options.A: Young adults working in busy office buildings
options.B: Older adults who get their flu shots on time
options.C: People who are too young or have weak immune systems to get vaccines
options.D: Healthy athletes training outdoors

explanation: Herd immunity acts like a protective shield. When most of the community is vaccinated, it stops the germ from spreading to vulnerable people who cannot take vaccines themselves. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h3)

question: In occupational health, what is the FIRST and best line of defense against workplace air hazards?

options.A: Putting up exhaust fans in the work area
options.B: Giving workers certified face masks or respirators
options.C: Rotating shifts so workers spend less time near the hazard
options.D: Completely removing or replacing the dangerous material

explanation: Elimination and substitution are top priorities in safety. If you get rid of the hazard entirely, nobody has to rely on masks or fans to stay safe! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h4)

question: Which of these is a classic lung disease caused by breathing in mineral dust at work?

options.A: Cystic fibrosis
options.B: Silicosis
options.C: Acute bronchitis
options.D: Lobar pneumonia

explanation: Silicosis happens when workers breathe in tiny crystalline silica dust, often found in mining, construction, or masonry jobs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h4)

question: What is the main reason for doing screening spirometry on healthy workers who are at high risk?

options.A: To measure how much oxygen is floating in the blood
options.B: To cure existing chronic lung disease
options.C: To catch early breathing trouble before any symptoms show up
options.D: To find out which exact bacteria is causing an infection

explanation: Spirometry is a breathing test that can spot small changes in lung function long before a worker starts feeling short of breath. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a goal of secondary prevention in respiratory health?

options.A: Finding small pulmonary nodules on routine diagnostic imaging
options.B: Reversing the genetic mutations that cause inherited lung disorders
options.C: Identifying early airway obstruction using breathing tests
options.D: Catching latent infections before they become active and contagious

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early detection and treatment of existing disease, not genetic modification or primary prevention of DNA mutations. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the main goal of tertiary prevention for someone living with COPD?

options.A: Slowing down the disease and preventing troublesome complications
options.B: Preventing airway inflammation back when they were a child
options.C: Screening healthy family members for hidden lung issues
options.D: Completely curing the permanent damage in the air sacs

explanation: Tertiary prevention steps in after a chronic illness is already present. The aim is to help the patient manage symptoms, stay active, and avoid severe flare-ups. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h6)

question: What activities are normally included in a pulmonary rehabilitation program?

options.A: Supervised exercise training and breathing exercises
options.B: Continuous high-dose antibiotic therapy
options.C: Long-term isolation so the patient avoids all outside air
options.D: Surgical replacement of damaged lung tissue

explanation: Pulmonary rehab is wonderful for chronic lung patients! It combines guided physical activity and breathing techniques to help them breathe easier and build stamina. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h6)

question: How does a nurse best show public health advocacy regarding breathing disorders?

options.A: Doing deep lung biopsies in local health clinics
options.B: Isolating every single person with a seasonal flu
options.C: Supporting policies that cut down air pollution and tobacco use
options.D: Prescribing strong bronchodilators to people in the neighborhood

explanation: Advocacy goes beyond the hospital bedside. Nurses advocate by supporting healthier environments, clean air policies, and community tobacco control. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h7)

question: A nurse is teaching an asthma patient how to use an inhaler. What is the best way to make sure the teaching worked?

options.A: Explaining the complex chemistry of the aerosol drug
options.B: Giving the patient a textbook chapter to read at home
options.C: Telling a family member to always give the medicine for them
options.D: Demonstrating the technique and asking the patient to show it back

explanation: Return demonstration is the gold standard of patient education! It lets you watch the patient do it themselves so you know they truly understand the steps. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T13#GNS213_U2_T13_h7)

question: What is the primary anatomical purpose of a tracheostomy tube?

options.A: Prevent aspiration of gastric contents
options.B: Measure arterial blood gas pressures
options.C: Deliver medications directly to the lungs
options.D: Bypass an upper airway obstruction

explanation: A tracheostomy creates an artificial airway directly into the trachea, bypassing any blockage located in the upper respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h1)

question: A patient with severe Guillain-Barré syndrome needs a tracheostomy mainly for which reason?

options.A: Correcting severe metabolic acidosis from kidney failure
options.B: Treating an acute bacterial pneumonia infection
options.C: Managing thick tracheal secretions and respiratory weakness
options.D: Preventing sudden cardiac arrest during sleep

explanation: Neuromuscular disorders cause weak coughs and poor breathing, requiring an artificial airway for secretion clearance and ventilation support. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which tracheostomy component is removed immediately after the tube is inserted?

options.A: Outer cannula
options.B: Pilot balloon
options.C: Inner cannula
options.D: Obturator

explanation: The obturator guides the outer cannula during insertion and must be removed right away so the patient can breathe through the tube. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h2)

question: What is the main function of the inner cannula in a tracheostomy set?

options.A: It guides the doctor during the initial surgical cut
options.B: It inflates to stop liquid from entering the lungs
options.C: It connects the breathing machine to the patient
options.D: It can be removed and cleaned to prevent mucus plugs

explanation: The inner cannula collects dried secretions and can be taken out for cleaning or replacement without disturbing the outer tube. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h2)

question: What critical equipment must always remain at the bedside of a patient with a new tracheostomy?

options.A: A sterile surgical scalpel for emergency re-incision
options.B: An extra mechanical ventilator machine
options.C: A spare tracheostomy tube of the same size
options.D: A container of sterile normal saline for drinking

explanation: An identical spare tube must be readily available at the bedside for immediate reinsertion if the current tube accidentally falls out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h3)

question: When should suctioning be applied during tracheostomy care?

options.A: While pushing the catheter down the tube
options.B: Before the patient is given any extra oxygen
options.C: Only while withdrawing the catheter
options.D: Continuously during both insertion and withdrawal

explanation: Suctioning during withdrawal protects the delicate lining of the trachea from trauma and tissue damage. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h4)

question: Why is it dangerous to suction a tracheostomy tube for longer than fifteen seconds?

options.A: It forces mucus deeper down into the tiny air sacs
options.B: It removes too much oxygen and causes low blood oxygen levels
options.C: It permanently damages the automatic cough reflex nerves
options.D: It causes the inner cannula to melt from the vacuum pressure

explanation: Prolonged suctioning removes air along with secretions, which rapidly depletes oxygen reserves and leads to dangerous hypoxia and heart arrhythmias. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h4)

question: What is the primary emergency action when a newly placed tracheostomy tube accidentally falls out?

options.A: Cover the open neck hole with a dry gauze pad
options.B: Administer rescue breaths using an oxygen mask on the face
options.C: Wait calmly for the surgical team to arrive at the bedside
options.D: Attempt immediate reinsertion using a spare tube

explanation: A fresh tracheostomy tract closes rapidly, making immediate tube reinsertion vital to maintain a patent airway. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h5)

question: What physical sign indicates that air has leaked into the tissues surrounding the tracheostomy stoma?

options.A: Loud whistling sounds coming from inside the mouth
options.B: A crackling feeling under the skin when touched
options.C: Bright red blood dripping continuously from the outer edge
options.D: A sudden drop in the patient's blood pressure reading

explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema creates crepitus, a characteristic crackling sensation felt when palpating the skin around the neck due to trapped air. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h5)

question: What must a patient demonstrate before a tracheostomy tube can be safely removed?

options.A: Normal breathing rates while sleeping for two full nights
options.B: Effective cough and ability to protect their own airway
options.C: Ability to speak clearly without any finger covering
options.D: Complete healing of the neck skin incision scar

explanation: Decannulation requires proof that the patient can clear their own secretions and breathe independently without aspirating. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h6)

question: How is the open tracheostomy wound typically managed after the tube is removed?

options.A: Left completely open to the air without any dressing
options.B: Covered with an airtight dressing to heal on its own
options.C: Sutured tightly closed right away by the surgeon
options.D: Packed with antiseptic gauze until new skin grows

explanation: An occlusive dressing seals the stoma to prevent air leakage, allowing the tissue to close naturally over time. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T14#GNS213_U2_T14_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of an under-water seal drainage system?

options.A: To flush the pleural cavity with sterile saline solution
options.B: To measure daily urine output in critically ill patients
options.C: To deliver humidified oxygen directly into the lungs
options.D: To restore negative pressure in the pleural space

explanation: The drainage system removes air and fluid while preventing outside air from entering, which restores the normal negative pressure needed for lung expansion. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h1)

question: Why does the distal end of the chest tube sit beneath water in the seal chamber?

options.A: To humidify the air entering the patient's chest
options.B: To warm the drainage fluid before it hits the collection chamber
options.C: To dilute blood coming from the pleural cavity
options.D: To act as a one-way valve preventing air return

explanation: Submerging the tube in water allows trapped air and fluid to bubble out of the chest while blocking outside air from flowing backward. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h1)

question: An accumulation of blood in the pleural cavity is called what?

options.A: Hemothorax
options.B: Empyema
options.C: Chylothorax
options.D: Pneumothorax

explanation: Hemothorax specifically describes blood gathering inside the pleural space, typically following injury or surgical procedures. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h2)

question: A patient with a stab wound to the chest develops respiratory distress and absent breath sounds on one side. What condition is most likely present?

options.A: Pneumothorax
options.B: Bronchial asthma
options.C: Myocardial infarction
options.D: Pulmonary edema

explanation: Chest trauma often introduces air into the pleural space, collapsing the lung and causing sudden respiratory distress with absent breath sounds. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h2)

question: What is a major advantage of modern plastic disposable chest drainage units over older glass bottles?

options.A: They do not require connection to a patient chest tube
options.B: They completely eliminate the need for any nursing monitoring
options.C: They are less prone to breakage and easier to handle
options.D: They prevent the formation of any drainage fluid entirely

explanation: Disposable plastic units replace fragile glass bottles, reducing accident risks and simplifying setup in busy hospital wards. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h3)

question: How do dry suction chest drainage systems regulate suction compared to wet systems?

options.A: They use chemical tablets dissolved in water to generate vacuum pressure
options.B: They require continuous manual pumping by the nursing staff
options.C: They rely purely on gravity without any external suction source
options.D: They use a built-in mechanical regulator instead of a water column

explanation: Dry systems use a dial or regulator to control suction levels, removing the need to monitor water evaporation in a suction chamber. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h3)

question: What position should a nurse place a patient in for chest tube insertion?

options.A: Trendelenburg position
options.B: Prone flat on the bed
options.C: Left lateral decubitus
options.D: Semi-Fowler's or upright

explanation: Sitting upright or in semi-Fowler's position allows gravity to shift fluid or air and gives the clinician safer access to the pleural space. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h4)

question: Why must a nurse tape all tubing connections in a chest drainage system immediately after insertion?

options.A: To prevent accidental disconnection and entry of room air
options.B: To increase the speed of fluid drainage into the collection chamber
options.C: To stop the water in the seal chamber from evaporating
options.D: To comply with hospital branding and aesthetic guidelines

explanation: Secure taping stops air from leaking into the system or pleural space, which would cause a tension pneumothorax. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h4)

question: What does 'tidaling' in the water seal chamber indicate during patient breathing?

options.A: A dangerous air leak inside the patient's chest wall
options.B: Total obstruction of the drainage tubing by blood clots
options.C: Patency of the chest tube and pleural communication
options.D: Evaporation of the sterile water inside the water seal

explanation: The rhythmic rising and falling of water with respiration shows that the tube is open and transmitting pressure changes from the pleural cavity. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h5)

question: A nurse notices that tidaling in the water seal chamber has suddenly stopped. What is a likely initial nursing action?

options.A: Turn off the wall suction source permanently
options.B: Immediately pull out the chest tube from the patient
options.C: Inject sterile water directly into the pleural cavity
options.D: Check the tubing for kinks or dependent loops

explanation: A sudden stop in tidaling often points to mechanical blockage like a kink or a dependent loop trapping fluid, which needs checking before panicking. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h5)

question: Where must the chest drainage system always be positioned relative to the patient?

options.A: Below the level of the chest
options.B: Resting comfortably on the patient's abdomen
options.C: At the exact height of the bed mattress
options.D: Suspended directly above the patient's head

explanation: Gravity ensures fluid drains away from the chest cavity; placing the unit higher would cause drainage to flow back into the pleural space. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h6)

question: A patient with a chest tube is being transferred to the radiology department for an X-ray. What should the nurse NOT do?

options.A: Clamp the chest tube during transport
options.B: Monitor vital signs before and after transport
options.C: Ensure the tubing is free of dependent loops
options.D: Keep the drainage unit below chest level

explanation: Routine clamping during transport is dangerous because air or fluid cannot escape, rapidly leading to a tension pneumothorax. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h6)

question: What is the immediate nursing action if a chest tube becomes disconnected from the drainage unit?

options.A: Submerge the end of the tube in sterile water
options.B: Wrap the open end tightly with adhesive tape
options.C: Milk the tubing to clear out any blood clots
options.D: Run to find the attending surgeon immediately

explanation: Placing the tube tip in sterile water re-establishes an immediate water seal, stopping room air from rushing into the pleural space. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h7)

question: The chest tube accidentally pulls completely out of the patient's chest wall. Which dressing should the nurse apply first?

options.A: Sterile petrolatum gauze taped on three sides
options.B: Dry cotton gauze held in place with tight elastic
options.C: An iodine-soaked sponge packed deep into the wound
options.D: An airtight plastic wrap sealed on all four sides

explanation: Petrolatum gauze taped on three sides acts as a valve, allowing trapped air to escape while preventing outside air from entering the wound. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h7)

question: What breathing instruction is given to a patient just as the chest tube is being pulled out?

options.A: Exhale all air completely and hold your breath out
options.B: Take rapid, shallow breaths through your mouth
options.C: Breathe normally while coughing continuously
options.D: Take a deep breath, hold it, and bear down

explanation: Performing the Valsalva maneuver increases intrathoracic pressure, preventing air from rushing into the pleural space when the tube comes out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h8)

question: What clinical criteria typically indicate that a patient is ready for chest tube removal?

options.A: Ability to walk around the ward without assistance
options.B: Complete absence of any food or water intake
options.C: Normal body temperature for at least 12 hours
options.D: Lung re-expansion and minimal fluid drainage

explanation: Doctors remove chest tubes once imaging confirms the lung is fully expanded and drainage volume has dropped to safe baseline levels. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T15#GNS213_U2_T15_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of placing an endotracheal tube?

options.A: To prevent the patient from speaking during surgery
options.B: To measure the exact blood pressure of the lungs
options.C: To deliver oral medications directly to the stomach
options.D: To secure a patent airway and provide ventilation

explanation: An endotracheal tube keeps the airway open so oxygen can reach the lungs and carbon dioxide can escape. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h1)

question: A patient with a severe head injury and Glasgow Coma Scale of 6 requires intubation mainly for what reason?

options.A: Correction of severe metabolic acidosis
options.B: Prevention of normal swallowing reflexes
options.C: Protection against aspiration and airway collapse
options.D: Immediate removal of excess cerebrospinal fluid

explanation: Low GCS scores mean loss of protective airway reflexes, placing the patient at high risk of aspiration. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h1)

question: Why is pre-oxygenation performed before inserting an endotracheal tube?

options.A: To build up an oxygen reserve during the procedure
options.B: To force fluid out of the lower lung fields
options.C: To calm the patient down before sedation is given
options.D: To expand the chest wall for easier tube insertion

explanation: Pre-oxygenation replaces lung nitrogen with oxygen, delaying the onset of dangerous desaturation while the airway is manipulated. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h2)

question: The primary check for a laryngoscope blade before intubation involves verifying what component?

options.A: The flexibility of the metal tip
options.B: The brightness and security of the light bulb
options.C: The presence of a rubber cuff on the blade
options.D: The exact weight of the handle

explanation: A working light source is essential for visualizing the glottis and vocal cords inside a dark pharynx. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of giving a neuromuscular blocker during intubation?

options.A: To relax skeletal muscles and ease tube insertion
options.B: To stop all electrical activity in the heart
options.C: To increase natural saliva production in the mouth
options.D: To lower the patient's heart rate and blood pressure

explanation: Neuromuscular blocking agents paralyze the jaw and vocal cords so the tube can pass without trauma. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h3)

question: A patient given propofol for intubation suddenly drops their blood pressure significantly. What best explains this response?

options.A: The drug increases sympathetic nervous system activity
options.B: Fluid overload occurred prior to the drug administration
options.C: The patient was already in severe septic shock
options.D: Propofol causes systemic vasodilation and myocardial depression

explanation: Induction agents frequently lower blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels and reducing the pumping strength of the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h3)

question: What head and neck position helps align the airway axes for intubation?

options.A: The Trendelenburg position
options.B: The high Fowler position
options.C: The left lateral decubitus position
options.D: The sniffing position

explanation: The sniffing position aligns the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes to provide a direct line of sight to the vocal cords. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h4)

question: In which hand should the clinician hold the laryngoscope during the intubation procedure?

options.A: Both hands simultaneously
options.B: Either hand interchangeably
options.C: The right hand
options.D: The left hand

explanation: Laryngoscopes are designed for the left hand to allow the right hand to manipulate the tube and suction. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h4)

question: What is the gold standard bedside method to confirm correct endotracheal tube placement?

options.A: Observing equal rise of the abdomen
options.B: Checking for fogging inside the plastic tube
options.C: Measuring the length of the tube at the lip
options.D: End-tidal carbon dioxide detection

explanation: Detecting exhaled carbon dioxide proves the tube is inside the respiratory tree rather than the esophagus. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h5)

question: A nurse auscultates breath sounds after intubation and hears gurgling over the epigastrium with absent breath sounds on the left. What action is required?

options.A: Secure the tube firmly in place and request a chest X-ray
options.B: Increase the flow rate on the mechanical ventilator
options.C: Push the tube an additional five centimeters deeper
options.D: Immediately deflate the cuff, remove the tube, and re-oxygenate

explanation: Gurgling over the stomach indicates esophageal intubation, requiring immediate removal and bag-valve-mask ventilation. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h5)

question: What is the recommended range for endotracheal tube cuff pressure?

options.A: 40 to 50 cmH2O
options.B: 60 to 70 cmH2O
options.C: 20 to 30 cmH2O
options.D: 5 to 10 cmH2O

explanation: Maintaining cuff pressure in this range seals the airway without cutting off blood supply to the tracheal mucosa. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h6)

question: Why is keeping the head of the bed elevated important for an intubated patient?

options.A: To increase blood flow to the brain and face
options.B: To prevent the endotracheal tube from slipping out
options.C: To reduce the risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia
options.D: To make it easier for the patient to swallow saliva

explanation: Elevation prevents gastric contents and oral secretions from pooling above the cuff and trickling down into the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h6)

question: Which mnemonic helps nurses troubleshoot sudden distress in an intubated patient?

options.A: A.B.C.D.
options.B: R.A.C.E.
options.C: D.O.P.E.
options.D: S.O.A.P.

explanation: The DOPE mnemonic stands for Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, and Equipment failure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h7)

question: A patient with an endotracheal tube suddenly develops absent breath sounds on the left side and tracheal deviation. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Esophageal intubation
options.B: Mucus plug in the tube
options.C: Accidental extubation
options.D: Tension pneumothorax

explanation: Sudden lung collapse causes absent breath sounds on the affected side and shifts the trachea away from the pressure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h7)

question: What is the primary sign of laryngeal edema after tube removal?

options.A: Bradycardia
options.B: Wheezing
options.C: Hypertension
options.D: Stridor

explanation: Stridor is a high-pitched breathing sound caused by narrowing of the upper airway from swelling after extubation. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h8)

question: What action should a nurse take immediately after extubating a patient?

options.A: Apply supplemental oxygen and monitor breathing closely
options.B: Encourage the patient to eat a large meal right away
options.C: Perform immediate suctioning down into the trachea
