options.D: Place the patient flat on their back without a pillow

explanation: Patients require oxygen support and close observation for respiratory distress or airway swelling immediately following extubation. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h8)

question: What is the main reason a doctor performs a diagnostic thoracentesis?

options.A: To permanently seal the pleural space shut
options.B: To collect pleural fluid for laboratory analysis
options.C: To measure continuous pulmonary artery pressure
options.D: To deliver aerosolized antibiotics into the lungs

explanation: Diagnostic thoracentesis involves drawing a small fluid sample to identify the underlying cause of an effusion, such as infection or cancer. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h1)

question: A patient is struggling to breathe because of a massive buildup of fluid in the chest. Which type of procedure is needed?

options.A: Therapeutic thoracentesis
options.B: Routine diagnostic tap
options.C: Continuous lavage procedure
options.D: Prophylactic thoracentesis

explanation: Removing a large volume of fluid relieves lung compression and restores normal breathing capacity, which defines therapeutic intervention. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h1)

question: Where should the needle be placed when performing a thoracentesis?

options.A: Immediately below the upper rib
options.B: Through the center of the sternum
options.C: Directly across the middle rib
options.D: Immediately above the lower rib

explanation: Neurovascular bundles run along the lower edge of ribs, so insertion must occur over the upper border of the lower rib to prevent bleeding. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h2)

question: Why do healthcare providers usually drain pleural fluid from the back part of the chest?

options.A: The diaphragm sits higher on the anterior side
options.B: The chest wall is thinnest near the clavicle
options.C: Fluid naturally accumulates in the dependent posterior bases
options.D: Intercostal blood vessels are completely absent posteriorly

explanation: Gravity causes free-flowing pleural fluid to pool in the lower back regions of a patient who is sitting up. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h2)

question: What is the best position for a patient getting a thoracentesis?

options.A: Sitting upright and leaning forward
options.B: Lying flat on the unaffected side
options.C: Flat on the back with arms extended
options.D: Prone with a pillow under the chest

explanation: Leaning forward spreads the ribs apart and moves abdominal organs away from the needle path. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h3)

question: Which lab test is most important for a nurse to check before a thoracentesis?

options.A: Coagulation studies like platelets and INR
options.B: Total serum protein and albumin values
options.C: Thyroid stimulating hormone concentration
options.D: Fast blood glucose and HbA1c levels

explanation: Normal clotting times and adequate platelets prevent excessive bleeding into the chest cavity during the needle puncture. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h3)

question: What should the nurse tell the patient to do while the needle is inside the chest?

options.A: Avoid coughing or sudden movements
options.B: Take rapid deep breaths continuously
options.C: Talk loudly to report chest pain
options.D: Cough forcefully every ten seconds

explanation: Sudden body movements or coughing can cause the lung tissue to hit the needle tip, increasing the risk of accidental lung puncture. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h4)

question: A patient suddenly turns pale, starts sweating, and feels dizzy during a thoracentesis. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Quickly withdraw more fluid to lower pressure
options.B: Increase the rate of intravenous fluids
options.C: Ask the patient to lie flat on the floor
options.D: Stop the procedure and notify the clinician

explanation: Sudden distress or a vasovagal reaction means the procedure must be paused or stopped immediately for safety. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h4)

question: What test is routinely ordered right after a thoracentesis is finished?

options.A: Chest X-ray
options.B: Brain CT scan
options.C: Abdominal ultrasound
options.D: Electrocardiogram

explanation: A chest X-ray checks that the lung has expanded properly and rules out a collapsed lung. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h5)

question: How should a patient be positioned right after the thoracentesis is complete?

options.A: Upright in a chair with arms raised overhead
options.B: Flat on the abdomen with head turned aside
options.C: On the unaffected side for a short duration
options.D: In a strict Trendelenburg position for two hours

explanation: Lying on the good side helps seal the puncture site on the treated side and encourages full lung expansion. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h5)

question: Which sign points to re-expansion pulmonary edema after fluid is removed from the chest?

options.A: Sudden sharp pain in the lower abdomen
options.B: Inability to move the lower extremities
options.C: Frothy pink sputum and severe cough
options.D: High fever with generalized skin rash

explanation: When a collapsed lung expands too quickly, fluid can leak into the tiny air sacs, causing a heavy cough and frothy pink sputum. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h6)

question: Which finding after a thoracentesis suggests a collapsed lung that needs urgent attention?

options.A: Stable blood pressure and normal heart rate
options.B: Absent breath sounds on the affected side
options.C: Mild soreness around the sterile bandage
options.D: Low-grade fever twelve hours post-procedure

explanation: Air leaking into the pleural space pushes the lung away from the chest wall, leading to muffled or totally absent breath sounds on that side. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h6)

question: What is the main goal of using a mechanical ventilator in the hospital?

options.A: Cure the underlying pulmonary infection
options.B: Permanently replace natural lung function
options.C: Eliminate the need for arterial blood gases
options.D: Support breathing while the body heals

explanation: Mechanical ventilation is a temporary support measure that helps maintain oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange until the patient's lungs recover. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h1)

question: In hypercapnic respiratory failure, what problem is the body experiencing?

options.A: Eliminate carbon dioxide effectively from the blood
options.B: Generate sufficient negative intrapleural pressure
options.C: Prevent fluid accumulation in the alveolar spaces
options.D: Maintain adequate arterial oxygen saturation levels

explanation: Hypercapnic failure happens when a patient cannot breathe out enough air, causing carbon dioxide to build up in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h1)

question: Which ventilator setting lets the patient breathe on their own between the machine's regular breaths?

options.A: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure
options.B: Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation
options.C: Control Mode Ventilation
options.D: Assist-Control Ventilation

explanation: This mode delivers set breaths while still allowing the patient to take their own breaths in between. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h2)

question: A recovering patient starts every breath on their own and just needs a gentle pressure push from the machine. Which mode works best?

options.A: Pressure Support Ventilation
options.B: Inverse Ratio Ventilation
options.C: High-Frequency Oscillation
options.D: Controlled Mechanical Ventilation

explanation: Pressure support helps patients do the work of breathing themselves by giving an extra push when they take a breath. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h2)

question: What is the main reason for adding PEEP (Positive End-Expiratory Pressure) to a ventilator?

options.A: Reduce the total minute volume requirement of the lungs
options.B: Prevent alveolar collapse at the end of expiration
options.C: Lower the fraction of inspired oxygen to room air
options.D: Increase the peak inspiratory pressure limit safely

explanation: PEEP leaves a small amount of pressure in the lungs at the end of each breath to keep the tiny air sacs from closing up. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h3)

question: Why do modern ventilators often use smaller tidal volumes for patients?

options.A: They prevent overdistention and injury to delicate lung tissue
options.B: They eliminate the requirement for humidified oxygen delivery
options.C: They decrease the need for continuous arterial blood gas monitoring
options.D: They allow patients to tolerate higher levels of carbon dioxide

explanation: Using smaller breath volumes based on the patient's body size protects the lungs from being stretched too far and getting damaged. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h3)

question: What piece of emergency equipment must always be kept right at the bedside of a patient on a ventilator?

options.A: Manual resuscitation bag and mask
options.B: Continuous end-tidal carbon dioxide capnometer
options.C: Tracheostomy insertion surgical tray
options.D: A backup mechanical ventilator machine

explanation: A manual bag-valve-mask must always be ready at hand to manually breathe for the patient if the power fails or the machine acts up. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h4)

question: A patient on a ventilator suddenly becomes restless and the high-pressure alarm starts ringing. What should you check first?

options.A: Silence the alarm permanently to reduce environmental noise
options.B: Auscultate breath sounds and check for tube obstruction
options.C: Administer a large dose of a neuromuscular blocking agent
options.D: Increase the fraction of inspired oxygen concentration immediately

explanation: High-pressure alarms usually mean something is blocking the airway or the tube has moved, so listening to breath sounds helps find the issue fast. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h4)

question: When is the best time to suction the airway of a patient on a ventilator?

options.A: Strictly every two hours regardless of patient clinical status
options.B: Immediately before every scheduled medication administration time
options.C: Only when the high-pressure ventilator alarm sounds continuously
options.D: Based on clinical indicators like secretions or coarse breath sounds

explanation: Suctioning should only be done when you actually see or hear secretions, because doing it too often can hurt the airway lining. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h5)

question: Why is regular mouth care with chlorhexidine so important for ventilated patients?

options.A: It eliminates the need for humidified circuit air
options.B: It reduces bacterial colonization that leads to pneumonia
options.C: It prevents the rubber tube from sticking to oral mucosa
options.D: It stimulates salivary gland function during heavy sedation

explanation: Germs love to gather in the mouth of a ventilated patient; keeping the mouth clean cuts down on bacteria sliding into the lungs to cause pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h5)

question: At what angle should the head of the bed be kept to help prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia?

options.A: 90 degrees upright
options.B: Flat on the mattress
options.C: 30 to 45 degrees
options.D: 10 to 15 degrees

explanation: Keeping the head of the bed elevated stops saliva and stomach contents from trickling down into the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h6)

question: What complication can happen when a patient breathes very high levels of oxygen for a long time?

options.A: Acute upper airway muscle atrophy
options.B: Sudden tension pneumothorax formation
options.C: Oxygen toxicity and alveolar damage
options.D: Severe endotracheal tube obstruction

explanation: Too much pure oxygen creates harmful molecules that can break down the delicate walls of the air sacs in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h6)

question: What is the main goal of a Spontaneous Breathing Trial before taking a patient off the ventilator?

options.A: Verify correct placement of the endotracheal tube
options.B: Determine the maximum peak inspiratory pressure limit
options.C: Assess the patient's ability to breathe without support
options.D: Cleanse the large airways of thick pooled secretions

explanation: This test checks if the patient's body is strong enough to handle breathing on their own before the breathing tube is pulled out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h7)

question: A patient struggles and gets very tired during a breathing trial. What should the nurse do next?

options.A: Proceed with extubation and administer high-flow oxygen
options.B: Increase the fraction of inspired oxygen and wait another hour
options.C: Remove the artificial airway and insert a nasal cannula
options.D: Return the patient to previous ventilator support settings

explanation: If a patient fails the trial, it means their breathing muscles need more rest, so you put them back on the ventilator support settings. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T18#GNS213_U2_T18_h7)

question: What calculation determines a client's smoking pack-year history?

options.A: Packs per day multiplied by years smoked
options.B: Total packs smoked divided by months active
options.C: Cigarettes per day divided by age in years
options.D: Years smoked added to total daily cigarettes

explanation: Pack-years are calculated by multiplying the average number of packs smoked daily by the total number of years the person has smoked. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is it important to ask about occupational history during a respiratory assessment?

options.A: Inhaled toxins and dust can cause chronic lung diseases
options.B: Physical labor directly increases baseline lung volume
options.C: Work stress is the primary trigger for acute asthma
options.D: Employers require health records for factory insurance

explanation: Long-term exposure to airborne irritants like coal dust, asbestos, or agricultural fumes damages lung tissue over time. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h1)

question: What is the correct sequence for a respiratory physical examination?

options.A: Auscultation, percussion, inspection, palpation
options.B: Percussion, auscultation, palpation, inspection
options.C: Palpation, inspection, auscultation, percussion
options.D: Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation

explanation: Respiratory assessment always starts with inspection before touching or listening to prevent altering breath sounds. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h2)

question: What does a dull percussion note over lung tissue usually indicate?

options.A: Normal air trapping within the alveoli
options.B: Acute inflammation of the upper trachea
options.C: Fluid or solid mass in the lung tissue
options.D: Hyperinflation typical of severe asthma

explanation: Dull sounds replace normal resonance when fluid, blood, or solid tumors replace air in the pleural space or alveoli. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which breath sound is best described as continuous, high-pitched, and musical?

options.A: Wheezes
options.B: Stridor
options.C: Crackles
options.D: Rhonchi

explanation: Wheezes are musical, whistling sounds produced when air flows through narrowed or constricted lower airways. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h3)

question: A client with left-sided heart failure has fine, popping sounds at the lung bases. What are these called?

options.A: Rhonchi
options.B: Wheezes
options.C: Friction rubs
options.D: Crackles

explanation: Crackles are generated when fluid pops open collapsed small airways and alveoli during inspiration. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of collecting a sputum sample for culture?

options.A: To measure the exact daily volume of fluid loss
options.B: To identify the specific bacteria causing an infection
options.C: To check the client's current blood oxygen level
options.D: To calculate total lung capacity and air trapping

explanation: Sputum cultures isolate pathogens so doctors can prescribe the correct antibiotic therapy. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which blood test provides the most accurate measurement of the client's acid-base balance?

options.A: Complete blood count
options.B: Electrolyte panel
options.C: Arterial blood gases
options.D: Random blood glucose

explanation: ABG analysis measures pH, carbon dioxide, and bicarbonate directly from arterial blood to evaluate gas exchange and acid-base status. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why does severe respiratory distress frequently trigger intense psychological anxiety?

options.A: Air hunger and suffocation directly threaten basic survival
options.B: Hospital rooms are typically cold and poorly ventilated
options.C: Sedative medications cause acute panic as a side effect
options.D: Lack of oxygen damages the frontal lobe permanently

explanation: Difficulty breathing triggers an instinctive panic response because oxygen deprivation is interpreted by the brain as an immediate threat to life. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which entry represents the most accurate clinical documentation of a respiratory assessment?

options.A: Respiratory status is fine, oxygen saturation is stable on room air
options.B: No distress noted, client breathing normally while resting in bed
options.C: Client feels a bit short of breath today, lungs sound mostly clear
options.D: Respirations 24/min, shallow, bilateral wheezes heard in lower lobes, client leaning forward

explanation: Specific quantitative data and clear objective observations provide an accurate baseline for evaluating future changes. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary function of the nasal cavity during respiration?

options.A: Producing surfactant for alveoli
options.B: Regulating systemic blood pressure
options.C: Warming and filtering inspired air
options.D: Exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide

explanation: The nasal cavity prepares air for the lungs by adjusting its temperature and trapping dust with mucous membranes. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which respiratory structure marks the boundary between the upper and lower respiratory tracts?

options.A: Trachea
options.B: Bronchi
options.C: Larynx
options.D: Pharynx

explanation: The larynx is traditionally considered the dividing point where the upper airway transitions into the lower respiratory structures. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which pathogen type causes the majority of upper respiratory tract infections?

options.A: Bacteria
options.B: Fungi
options.C: Parasites
options.D: Viruses

explanation: Rhinoviruses and other viral agents are responsible for the vast majority of common upper airway infections like the common cold. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h2)

question: What physiological change causes nasal congestion during an upper airway infection?

options.A: Constriction of respiratory muscles
options.B: Collapse of the cartilaginous rings
options.C: Decreased production of mucus
options.D: Vasodilation and mucosal edema

explanation: Inflammation causes local blood vessels to dilate and tissues to swell, narrowing the nasal passages and causing congestion. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h2)

question: A patient with acute laryngitis is most likely to exhibit which symptom?

options.A: Severe chest pain
options.B: Abdominal tenderness
options.C: Inspiratory wheezing
options.D: Hoarseness of voice

explanation: Laryngitis involves inflammation of the vocal cords, which directly alters phonation and causes hoarseness. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h3)

question: A nurse assesses a client with a severe throat infection and notes difficulty swallowing. What term describes this finding?

options.A: Dyspnea
options.B: Dyspepsia
options.C: Dysphasia
options.D: Dysphagia

explanation: Dysphagia refers to difficulty or pain when swallowing, commonly associated with acute pharyngitis or tonsillitis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary diagnostic tool used for most routine upper airway infections?

options.A: Sputum cytology
options.B: Computed tomography scan
options.C: Clinical history and physical exam
options.D: Magnetic resonance imaging

explanation: Most upper respiratory infections are diagnosed based on presenting signs and symptoms without needing complex laboratory testing. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why is a throat culture performed when a rapid antigen test is negative?

options.A: To determine the patient's blood type
options.B: To measure the exact oxygen saturation level
options.C: To catch bacterial infections missed by rapid testing
options.D: To assess lung capacity and airflow

explanation: Rapid tests have high specificity but lower sensitivity, so cultures are used to confirm negative streptococcal results if suspicion remains high. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why are antibiotics NOT recommended for the treatment of the common cold?

options.A: Antibiotics are too expensive for routine use
options.B: Colds always resolve within twenty-four hours
options.C: Colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria
options.D: Viral infections make antibiotics completely inactive

explanation: Antibacterial medications target bacterial cell walls and processes, rendering them completely ineffective against viral pathogens. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which class of medication is prescribed to treat confirmed streptococcal pharyngitis?

options.A: Antibiotics
options.B: Antifungals
options.C: Bronchodilators
options.D: Antivirals

explanation: Streptococcus pyogenes is a bacterium, requiring appropriate antibiotic therapy to clear the infection and prevent secondary complications. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h5)

question: A patient with an upper airway infection is encouraged to increase oral fluid intake primarily for which reason?

options.A: To thin respiratory secretions for easier clearance
options.B: To prevent the development of kidney stones
options.C: To increase systemic blood pressure levels
options.D: To flush out excess circulating white blood cells

explanation: Adequate hydration helps liquefy thick mucus secretions, making them much easier for the patient to mobilize and expel. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which clinical sign indicates immediate danger of upper airway obstruction in an infected patient?

options.A: Stridorous breathing sounds
options.B: Mild throat discomfort
options.C: Low-grade evening fever
options.D: Clear nasal drainage

explanation: Stridor is a high-pitched, turbulent sound indicating significant narrowing or obstruction of the upper airway requiring urgent intervention. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the main risk if a patient stops taking prescribed antibiotics early when feeling better?

options.A: Return of the infection and bacterial resistance
options.B: Permanent damage to the lower respiratory tract
options.C: Immediate development of a severe viral illness
options.D: Complete immunity against future respiratory bugs

explanation: Stopping antibiotics prematurely allows surviving bacteria to multiply and develop resistance to future pharmacological treatments. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h7)

question: Which practice is most effective in preventing the transmission of upper respiratory infections?

options.A: Using over-the-counter nasal sprays daily
options.B: Frequent and thorough hand hygiene
options.C: Taking daily multi-vitamin supplements
options.D: Avoiding all outdoor physical exercise

explanation: Respiratory pathogens are frequently spread via contaminated hands touching the face, making handwashing the best preventative measure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T3#GNS213_U2_T3_h7)

question: Which structure helps protect your airway from food and liquid during swallowing?

options.A: Larynx
options.B: Bronchus
options.C: Alveoli
options.D: Trachea

explanation: The larynx includes the epiglottis, which shuts over the windpipe when you swallow to keep food out of your lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why can even a little swelling in the upper airway make it hard to breathe?

options.A: The upper airway is naturally narrow, so swelling blocks it fast
options.B: Mucus production completely stops during inflammation
options.C: The lungs fail to expand when the pharynx swells
options.D: Cartilage rings in the larynx instantly collapse

explanation: Because passages like the pharynx are already tight spaces, even mild swelling leaves less room for air to pass through. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h1)

question: What happens inside a person's airway when something blocks it?

options.A: Blood pressure drops rapidly
options.B: Oxygen diffusion speeds up
options.C: Lung compliance improves
options.D: Airway resistance increases

explanation: Any physical blockage makes it much harder for air to flow through, which raises airway resistance. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h2)

question: What is the ultimate danger if an airway blockage is not cleared?

options.A: Metabolic alkalosis from hyperventilation
options.B: Hypoxic brain injury and death
options.C: Excessive carbon dioxide elimination
options.D: Chronic pulmonary hypertension

explanation: When air cannot get in, the body is cut off from oxygen, leading quickly to brain damage and life-threatening failure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h2)

question: In an unconscious patient lying flat on their back, what is the most common cause of airway blockage?

options.A: Enlarged thyroid tissue
options.B: Accumulated pleural fluid
options.C: Severe bronchial spasm
options.D: The tongue falling back

explanation: When a person loses consciousness, their throat muscles relax, allowing the tongue to slip backward and block the airway. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which condition involves sudden, severe soft tissue swelling in the upper airway due to an allergic reaction?

options.A: Pleural effusion
options.B: Pulmonary embolism
options.C: Chronic bronchitis
options.D: Angioedema

explanation: Angioedema causes rapid swelling beneath the skin and mucous membranes, which can quickly close off the airway. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the name of the high-pitched whistling sound heard when someone breathes in with a partially blocked upper airway?

options.A: Crackles
options.B: Stridor
options.C: Wheezing
options.D: Rhonchi

explanation: Stridor is a harsh, high-pitched sound created when air forces its way through a narrowed upper airway. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why is a bluish skin color (cyanosis) usually a late sign that a patient is lacking oxygen?

options.A: Peripheral vessels constrict to hide the blue coloration initially
options.B: The brain masks skin color changes until total cardiac arrest occurs
options.C: Pulse oximeters detect hypoxia long before visual color changes begin
options.D: A large amount of unoxygenated hemoglobin must build up before skin changes color

explanation: The blood must carry a high percentage of oxygen-deprived cells before the blue tint actually shows on the skin. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why should you hold off on sending an unstable, choking patient for an X-ray?

options.A: Radiation exposure worsens the underlying inflammatory response
options.B: Moving the patient to the radiology department improves oxygenation
options.C: Immediate airway stabilization is far more critical than finding the exact cause
options.D: X-ray machines cannot capture images of soft tissue swelling in the neck

explanation: Keeping the patient breathing takes priority over taking pictures; an unstable airway must be secured first. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the very first step when checking a patient who might have an airway blockage?

options.A: Looking, listening, and feeling at the mouth and nose
options.B: Ordering an immediate computed tomography scan
options.C: Drawing arterial blood gases for baseline pH
options.D: Inserting a rigid bronchoscope into the trachea

explanation: Quick clinical checks start with observing chest movement, listening for breath sounds, and feeling for airflow. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the first physical maneuver to try for a conscious adult who is choking badly on an object?

options.A: Inhaler administration
options.B: Endotracheal intubation
options.C: Abdominal thrusts
options.D: Cricothyroidotomy

explanation: Abdominal thrusts push up on the diaphragm to force trapped air out and dislodge the object. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h6)

question: If a choking patient suddenly passes out, what should the nurse do next?

options.A: Administer an intravenous corticosteroid immediately
options.B: Lower the patient to the floor and start chest compressions
options.C: Perform blind finger sweeps to clear the oral cavity
options.D: Place the patient in a high Fowler position and apply oxygen

explanation: When an obstructed patient loses consciousness, chest compressions help create enough pressure to clear the blockage. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which medication is often given through a nebulizer to quickly shrink swelling in the upper airway?

options.A: Morphine
options.B: Salbutamol
options.C: Furosemide
options.D: Epinephrine

explanation: Epinephrine causes blood vessels in the airway lining to constrict, rapidly reducing dangerous swelling. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h7)

question: When would a doctor perform a surgical cricothyroidotomy instead of normal tube placement through the mouth?

options.A: When foreign body removal is successful after back blows
options.B: When arterial blood gases show mild metabolic acidosis
options.C: When severe facial trauma or swelling blocks the upper airway completely
options.D: When the patient has a mild chronic cough and normal oxygen levels

explanation: A surgical airway is an emergency backup used when swelling or trauma makes normal breathing tubes impossible to insert. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is a key nursing duty right after an artificial airway is put in place?

options.A: Keeping the suction catheter inserted continuously
options.B: Monitoring respiratory status and securing the tube properly
options.C: Allowing the patient to consume oral fluids immediately
options.D: Removing the stabilization tape every hour for skin checks

explanation: Watching the patient closely and keeping the tube secure ensures they get enough air and prevents accidental slips. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h8)

question: What advice should a nurse give to someone at high risk for choking?

options.A: Chew food thoroughly and eat in an upright position
options.B: Take large bites to stimulate swallowing reflexes
options.C: Lie flat immediately after finishing every large meal
options.D: Avoid drinking water during meals to prevent dilution

explanation: Sitting upright and chewing food well makes swallowing much safer and lowers the chance of choking. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T4#GNS213_U2_T4_h8)

question: Which structure keeps the airway open by providing rigid support?

options.A: Stratified squamous layers
options.B: Smooth muscle bands
options.C: Cartilaginous rings
options.D: Elastic ligament fibers

explanation: Structures like the thyroid and cricoid cartilages give the upper airway the mechanical strength needed to resist collapse. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which structure acts as the main valve to prevent food from entering the airway during swallowing?

options.A: Cricoid cartilage
options.B: Epiglottis
options.C: Soft palate
options.D: Thyroid notch

explanation: The epiglottis folds downward over the laryngeal inlet during a swallow to divert food safely into the esophagus. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h1)

question: In Nigerian road transport accidents, what causes blunt upper airway trauma most commonly?

options.A: Side window
options.B: Rearview mirror
options.C: Passenger seat
options.D: Steering wheel

explanation: Direct anterior impact against a steering wheel or handlebar frequently crushes the laryngeal cartilages against the cervical spine. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h2)

question: Why does rapid tissue swelling in the neck become a life-threatening emergency?

options.A: It causes immediate failure of the left ventricle
options.B: It paralyzes the diaphragm through nerve damage
options.C: It quickly narrows the rigid upper airway lumen
options.D: It stops the production of pulmonary surfactant

explanation: The neck contains tight fascial compartments where even minor edema severely restricts airflow through the upper airway. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h2)

question: What is the term for a high-pitched sound that points to a partial upper airway blockage?

options.A: Rhonchi
options.B: Wheezing
options.C: Stridor
options.D: Crackles

explanation: Stridor is classic turbulent airflow noise generated when the upper airway passages are narrowed by edema or injury. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h3)

question: What does a crackling sensation under the neck skin (crepitus) indicate in a trauma patient?

options.A: Swelling of the thyroid gland from blunt force
options.B: Severe infection tracking up from the mediastinum
options.C: Air leaking from a disrupted airway into soft tissues
options.D: Accumulation of fluid in the pleural space

explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema occurs when air escapes through a tear in the trachea or larynx into the surrounding neck tissues. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h3)

question: Why is blind orotracheal intubation dangerous when a patient has severe laryngeal trauma?

options.A: It can convert a partial airway tear into a complete transection
options.B: It stimulates the vagus nerve to cause tachycardia
options.C: It introduces too much oxygen into the pleural cavity
options.D: It prevents the administration of intravenous fluids

explanation: Pushing a rigid tube through a fractured, swollen larynx can worsen tissue displacement and cause total airway loss. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h4)

question: What emergency procedure is typically done when intubation fails due to severe neck trauma?

options.A: Tracheostomy tube removal
options.B: Thoracentesis
options.C: Pericardiocentesis
options.D: Cricothyroidotomy

explanation: A surgical or needle cricothyroidotomy provides immediate access through the cricothyroid membrane below the level of laryngeal damage. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the main reason for doing a tracheostomy after laryngeal fracture surgery?

options.A: To facilitate easier delivery of oral nutrition
options.B: To prevent the development of a pneumothorax
options.C: To allow the patient to resume normal speech immediately
options.D: To divert airflow past the surgical site and promote healing

explanation: Bypassing the larynx with a tracheostomy tube protects the surgical repairs from the mechanical stress of breathing and coughing. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which class of medication is sometimes given early to reduce mucosal swelling in airway trauma?

options.A: Diuretics
options.B: Beta-blockers
options.C: Corticosteroids
options.D: Antihistamines

explanation: Steroids help decrease acute inflammatory edema in the upper respiratory tissues, reducing the risk of sudden obstruction. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h5)

question: What is a common long-term complication after severe upper airway trauma heals?

options.A: Permanent lower lobe collapse
options.B: Chronic airway stenosis
options.C: Permanent diaphragmatic hernia
options.D: Chronic pulmonary hypertension

explanation: Scar tissue formation during the healing of laryngeal or tracheal injuries often results in abnormal narrowing of the airway lumen. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h6)

question: Permanent changes in a patient's voice after neck trauma are usually caused by damage to which structure?

options.A: Carotid sinus baroreceptor
options.B: Superior cervical ganglion
options.C: Recurrent laryngeal nerve
options.D: Phrenic nerve bundle

explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the vocal cords, and injury to it leads to hoarseness or permanent voice alteration. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h6)

question: A patient with a new tracheostomy tube shows thick mucus and mild breathing distress. What is the immediate nursing action?

options.A: Administer a dose of oral antitussive medication
options.B: Place the patient flat on their back to rest
options.C: Remove the tracheostomy ties to inspect the stoma
options.D: Perform sterile suctioning of the tracheostomy tube

explanation: Clearing accumulated mucus via suctioning directly relieves the obstruction and restores effective ventilation in artificial airways. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h7)

question: Why is a formal swallowing check necessary before letting a patient eat after laryngeal surgery?

options.A: To prevent food and liquids from entering the repaired airway
options.B: To ensure the patient has regained their normal voice tone
options.C: To test for allergic reactions to hospital food
options.D: To check if the stomach can absorb oral medications

explanation: Swallowing coordination is often temporarily impaired after neck trauma, risking aspiration into the respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T5#GNS213_U2_T5_h7)

question: Which parts of the body are involved in a lower respiratory tract infection?

options.A: Sinuses, tonsils, and Eustachian tubes
options.B: Nose, pharynx, and larynx
options.C: Oral cavity and epiglottis
options.D: Trachea, bronchi, and alveoli

explanation: Think of the larynx as the dividing line! Anything below it—like the windpipe (trachea), breathing tubes (bronchi), and air sacs (alveoli)—makes up the lower respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why are lower respiratory infections generally more serious than upper respiratory ones?

options.A: They cause severe localized pain in the nose.
options.B: They only happen to people with heart disease.
options.C: They directly interfere with oxygen exchange in the air sacs.
options.D: They are always completely resistant to drugs.

explanation: You've got this! When an infection hits the tiny air sacs (alveoli) deep in the lungs, it blocks oxygen from getting into the blood, making it much harder to breathe. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h1)

question: What is the most common bacteria that causes pneumonia outside of the hospital?

options.A: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.B: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.C: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.D: Influenza virus type A

explanation: Also known simply as pneumococcus, this bug is the leading culprit behind everyday community-acquired pneumonia. Great to keep in mind for clinicals! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h2)

question: A patient develops a fever, cough, and shortness of breath five days after being admitted to the surgical ward for a knee replacement. How is this infection classified?

options.A: Hospital-acquired pneumonia
options.B: Aspiration pneumonia
options.C: Community-acquired pneumonia
options.D: Primary acute bronchitis

explanation: Any pneumonia symptoms appearing 48 hours or longer after a patient is admitted to a healthcare facility are classified as hospital-acquired or nosocomial pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h2)

question: What main change happens inside the tiny air sacs (alveoli) during pneumonia?

options.A: The walls permanently stretch and lose stretchiness.
options.B: Blood flow to the lungs completely stops overnight.
options.C: Fluid, pus, and cellular debris fill up the spaces.
options.D: The breathing tubes stretch out and trap air.

explanation: As the body fights the infection, fluid and white blood cells flood the alveoli. That's why air has such a hard time getting in! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h3)

question: Why does a ventilation-perfusion mismatch happen when someone has a severe lung infection?

options.A: Blocked air sacs still get blood flow, but can't get fresh air.
options.B: The throat swells up and stops breathing completely.
options.C: The heart pumps blood way too slowly for the lungs.
options.D: Mucus plugs in the windpipe block blood from reaching the heart.

explanation: Think of it as a mismatch: blood is flowing past the air sacs ready to pick up oxygen, but because they are full of fluid, there's no fresh air waiting for them. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h3)

question: When listening to the chest of a patient with lung consolidation, what sound do you usually hear?

options.A: Crackles
options.B: A friction rub in the neck
options.C: Stridor
options.D: Borborygmi

explanation: You'll hear crackles (or rales)! They sound like tiny popping noises when fluid-filled air sacs suddenly snap open as the patient breathes in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h4)

question: A patient with pneumonia says their chest hurts sharply every time they take a deep breath. What's the most likely reason?

options.A: Sudden spasms of the chest muscles
options.B: Extra pressure inside the right side of the heart
options.C: Inflamed lung linings rubbing against the chest wall
options.D: Irritation of the main breathing tubes in the throat

explanation: That sharp pain is called pleuritic chest pain. It happens when the inflamed outer lining of the lungs (pleura) rubs against the chest wall with every breath. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h4)

question: Which test is mostly used to confirm if a patient has fluid or consolidation in their lungs?

options.A: Chest X-ray
options.B: Abdominal ultrasound
options.C: Electrocardiogram
options.D: Magnetic resonance imaging

explanation: A simple chest X-ray is fast, easy, and gives a clear picture of cloudy areas or fluid buildup in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why do nurses collect a sputum sample *before* starting the patient on antibiotics?

options.A: To check if the patient is allergic to drugs
options.B: To clear out the airways so they can breathe right away
options.C: To measure the red blood cell count in the airway
options.D: To find the exact germ so the right antibiotic can be given

explanation: Getting the sample first ensures the lab can grow and identify the exact bacteria without antibiotics masking the results. Smart nursing practice! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h5)

question: What is the main medicine used to treat a confirmed bacterial lower respiratory infection?

options.A: Antibiotics
options.B: Antihistamines
options.C: Antifungals
options.D: Antivirals

explanation: Since it's a bacterial infection, antibiotics are needed to target and stop those specific germs from multiplying. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h6)

question: Why are bronchodilators sometimes given along with antibiotics for a lung infection?

options.A: To dry up all fluid inside the chest cavity
options.B: To bring down the patient's fever
options.C: To directly kill the bacteria in the air sacs
options.D: To relax tight airways and make breathing easier

explanation: Bronchodilators relax the muscles around the breathing tubes, opening them up so air flows more smoothly. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which nursing action helps a hospitalized patient cough up thick mucus more easily?

options.A: Encouraging fluids and deep breathing exercises
options.B: Keeping the patient lying flat in bed all day
options.C: Restricting water to prevent fluid buildup in the lungs
options.D: Giving strong sleeping pills to stop the cough

explanation: Water is a natural thinner for mucus! Combined with deep breathing and controlled coughing, it helps clear the airways safely. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is your top assessment priority when caring for a patient with a severe lung infection?

options.A: Measuring the belly size every four hours
options.B: Checking reflexes in the legs
options.C: Checking for swollen feet
options.D: Monitoring breathing rate, depth, and oxygen levels

explanation: Respiratory status comes first! Keeping a close eye on breathing and oxygen saturation helps you catch any sudden downturn early. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is an empyema?

options.A: A collapsed section of lung from mucus
options.B: A blood clot traveling from the leg to the lungs
options.C: A pocket of pus collected in the pleural space
options.D: A permanent stretching of the main breathing tubes

explanation: An empyema happens when a lung infection spreads into the space around the lungs, forming a pocket of pus that usually needs to be drained. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h8)

question: What complication happens if a localized lung infection spreads directly into the patient's bloodstream?

options.A: Sepsis
options.B: Pulmonary embolism
options.C: Pneumothorax
options.D: Pulmonary fibrosis

explanation: When germs escape the lungs and enter the general circulation, they can trigger a body-wide, dangerous inflammatory response known as sepsis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h8)

question: Which preventive measure is especially recommended to protect older adults from bacterial pneumonia?

options.A: Taking daily antibiotics just in case
options.B: Staying indoors all the time
options.C: Pneumococcal vaccination
options.D: Using a home air humidifier

explanation: Vaccines are a powerful shield! The pneumococcal vaccine helps older adults and high-risk patients fight off dangerous strains of pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h9)

question: Why does cigarette smoking greatly increase a person's risk of getting a lower respiratory infection?

options.A: It puts extra oxygen in the blood, which attracts germs.
options.B: It seals the air sacs shut so no air enters.
options.C: It paralyzes and destroys the tiny hairs (cilia) that sweep dirt out of the airways.
options.D: It stops the stomach from making acid.

explanation: Smoke damages the cilia—the microscopic brooms of the respiratory tract. Without them working, mucus and germs get trapped in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h9)

question: Which layer of the pleura hugs the outer surface of the lungs tightly?

options.A: Mediastinal pleura
options.B: Parietal pleura
options.C: Diaphragmatic pleura
options.D: Visceral pleura

explanation: You've got this! Think of the visceral pleura as the inner skin that sticks right onto the lung tissue. Great job keeping up with your anatomy! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h1)

question: What happens in the chest when your diaphragm contracts during a breath in?

options.A: The pleural space fills entirely with air
options.B: Positive pressure forces air out of the lungs
options.C: Negative pressure is created to pull air in
options.D: Pressure inside the chest equals atmospheric pressure

explanation: When the diaphragm moves down, it opens up space and lowers the pressure inside, drawing air naturally into your lungs. Beautiful concept to master! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h1)

question: In a condition called hemothorax, what main substance builds up in the pleural space?

options.A: Serous fluid
options.B: Blood
options.C: Atmospheric air
options.D: Purulent pus

explanation: The name gives it a great clue—'hemo' always points to blood! You are doing fantastic learning these clinical terms. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h2)

question: If a patient has a large left-sided tension pneumothorax, which way is the trachea likely to shift?

options.A: Tracheal deviation toward the left side
options.B: Downward displacement of the liver
options.C: Tracheal deviation toward the right side
options.D: No movement of the mediastinal structures

explanation: Think of it like a crowded room: pressure builds up on the left and pushes everything over toward the healthy right side. You're building solid emergency nursing instincts! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h2)

question: What kind of sound do you usually hear when tapping (percussing) over an area filled with fluid like a pleural effusion?

options.A: Vesicular resonance
options.B: Hyperresonance
options.C: Dullness
options.D: Tympany

explanation: Fluid dampens the vibration, giving a flat, dull sound instead of a hollow ring. Keep practicing your physical assessment skills—they get easier every day! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why might a patient with a collapsed lung (pneumothorax) have absent breath sounds on that side?

options.A: Heart sounds are louder than normal lung sounds
options.B: Air in the pleural space separates the lung from the chest wall, muffling sounds
options.C: Inflammation of the trachea prevents air movement
options.D: Bronchial secretions completely block the mainstem bronchi

explanation: Because air is trapped outside the lung, it acts like a thick cushion blocking the sound from reaching your stethoscope. Makes complete sense when you picture it! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h3)

question: What is the main reason a nurse or doctor performs a thoracentesis for a pleural effusion?

options.A: To deliver continuous oxygen directly into the lung tissue
options.B: To permanently seal the pleural space against future leaks
options.C: To measure direct arterial blood pressure inside the thorax
options.D: To remove fluid for diagnostic analysis and relieve pressure

explanation: It's a win-win procedure: we take out some fluid so the lab can test it, and the patient instantly finds it easier to breathe. You're thinking like a real clinician! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h4)

question: Which quick test is most commonly used at the bedside to check for a collapsed lung?

options.A: Chest X-ray
options.B: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.C: Pulmonary function testing
options.D: Bronchoscopy

explanation: A quick chest X-ray gives us an immediate picture of what's going on inside the chest cavity. Keep up the great diagnostic thinking! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h4)

question: What is the main job of the water-seal chamber in a chest drainage setup?

options.A: To deliver humidified oxygen directly into the pleural space
options.B: To allow air to escape from the chest while preventing outside air from entering
options.C: To apply high-pressure suction to reinflate collapsed tissue
options.D: To measure the total volume of blood lost over twenty-four hours

explanation: It acts like a smart one-way valve—letting trapped air bubble out, but never letting room air sneak back in. Brilliant piece of bedside engineering! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h5)

question: You notice continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber of a chest tube system. What does this usually mean?

options.A: An expected amount of residual blood loss
options.B: An air leak somewhere in the tubing or insertion site
options.C: Blockage of the chest tube drainage lumen
options.D: Normal lung re-expansion and healing

explanation: While tiny occasional bubbles can be normal, continuous bubbling is like a leaky bicycle tire telling us air is getting in where it shouldn't. Excellent clinical observation! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h5)

question: A patient's chest tube accidentally slips out of the drainage machine. What is your very first nursing move?

options.A: Call the physician immediately before taking action
options.B: Immerse the end of the chest tube in sterile water
options.C: Remove the dressing and inspect the insertion site
options.D: Clamp the chest tube securely with metal hemostats

explanation: Plunging the tube into sterile water instantly recreates a water seal and stops room air from rushing into the chest. Quick thinking saves lives here! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why must a chest drainage system always stay lower than the patient's chest level?

options.A: To ensure the suction motor runs quietly without disturbing the patient
options.B: To use gravity effectively and prevent fluid from flowing backward into the pleural space
options.C: To make it easier for the patient to ambulate around the room
options.D: To prevent the water-seal chamber from evaporating too quickly

explanation: Gravity is our best friend here; keeping the collection box down ensures fluid drains away from the patient, not back into them. You've got a bright future in ward nursing! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary cause of occupational lung diseases?

options.A: Smoking cigarettes without using a proper filter
options.B: Breathing in harmful workplace dusts and chemicals
options.C: Severe bacterial infections caught in the community
options.D: Inherited genetic defects of the respiratory tract

explanation: These conditions are directly caused by inhaling hazardous substances present in the work environment over a long period. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why is early recognition of occupational lung diseases so critical for patients?

options.A: Treatment only works during the first week of coughing
options.B: The lung tissue scarring is usually permanent once it forms
options.C: Employers will immediately pay compensation before it spreads
options.D: Infections will spread to the brain within a few hours

explanation: Because the damage caused by dust accumulation leads to irreversible fibrosis, catching the condition early helps prevent further exposure and worsening illness. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which size of inhaled dust particles is most dangerous because it reaches the alveoli?

options.A: Particles measuring between 50 and 100 micrometers
options.B: Large clumps visible to the naked human eye
options.C: Moisture droplets trapped in the nasal hair
options.D: Particles measuring less than 2.5 micrometers

explanation: Very small respirable dust particles bypass upper airway defenses and travel deep into the gas-exchanging regions of the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h2)

question: What happens when alveolar macrophages try to swallow heavy loads of mineral dust?

options.A: They burst and release chemicals that cause scar tissue formation
options.B: They travel out of the lungs through the sweat glands
options.C: They turn into red blood cells to improve oxygen transport
options.D: They successfully dissolve the mineral dust into harmless sugar

explanation: When macrophages cannot digest toxic dust like silica, they break down and release inflammatory signals that trigger permanent lung fibrosis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h2)

question: Which group of occupational lung diseases is caused by inhaling mineral dusts like silica and asbestos?

options.A: Pneumoconiosis
options.B: Simple Bronchitis
options.C: Occupational Asthma
options.D: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis

explanation: Pneumoconiosis is the medical term for fibrotic lung diseases caused by the accumulation of mineral dusts in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h3)

question: A baker who develops sudden wheezing and chest tightness after inhaling flour dust at work is most likely suffering from which condition?

options.A: Asbestos-related pleural plaque
options.B: Occupational asthma
options.C: Bacterial lobar pneumonia
options.D: Coal worker's pneumoconiosis

explanation: Exposure to organic sensitizers like flour triggers an allergic airway response characterized by bronchospasm, which defines occupational asthma. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h3)

question: What is a major source of crystalline silica dust exposure for workers in many Nigerian local communities?

options.A: Operating commercial transport buses in traffic
options.B: Fishing in coastal rivers and marine lagoons
options.C: Artisanal gold mining and stone quarrying
options.D: Weaving traditional cotton fabrics by hand

explanation: Unregulated mining and quarrying activities frequently expose local Nigerian workers to high levels of dangerous silica dust. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why are informal sector workers in developing regions often at a higher risk for occupational lung disease?

options.A: Government laws completely ban safety masks in local factories
options.B: The tropical climate causes dust particles to become radioactive
options.C: They frequently lack proper personal protective equipment and health monitoring
options.D: Their lungs are naturally weaker than those of corporate office workers

explanation: The absence of safety gear, safety regulations, and routine medical checkups in informal industries greatly increases the risk of chronic lung injury. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is typically the earliest symptom experienced by someone developing an occupational lung disease?

options.A: A persistent cough and shortness of breath with exertion
options.B: Sudden paralysis of both lower extremities
options.C: Complete loss of the sense of taste and smell
options.D: Bright yellow coloration of the skin and eyes

explanation: Early lung damage usually manifests as a mild, dry cough and breathlessness that only appears when the person engages in physical work or exercise. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h5)

question: Why is taking a thorough work history so crucial when diagnosing respiratory problems?

options.A: Many lung diseases take years to develop and link directly to past job exposures
options.B: Work history determines the exact blood type of the individual
options.C: Doctors are legally required to record the patient's salary level
options.D: It helps prove whether the patient has a contagious viral infection

explanation: Because symptoms often appear long after the actual dust exposure occurred, a detailed job history is the key to identifying the root cause. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is the most important first step in managing any patient diagnosed with an occupational lung disease?

options.A: Transferring the patient to a warm tropical climate
options.B: Removing the worker from further exposure to the harmful dust
options.C: Advising the patient to start smoking tobacco to coat the lungs
options.D: Starting immediate high-dose chemotherapy sessions

explanation: Stopping ongoing exposure to the hazardous agent is essential to prevent further lung destruction and worsening fibrosis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h6)

question: A nurse is teaching breathing techniques to a patient with severe lung fibrosis. Which method should the nurse demonstrate to help ease shortness of breath?

options.A: Holding the breath for two minutes after each deep sigh
options.B: Breathing exclusively through the mouth while running fast
options.C: Rapid shallow panting to increase carbon dioxide retention
options.D: Pursed-lip breathing to help keep airways open longer

explanation: Pursed-lip breathing creates gentle backpressure in the airways, preventing them from collapsing prematurely and easing shortness of breath. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h6)

question: What is the term for right-sided heart failure caused by long-term lung disease?

options.A: Cor pulmonale
options.B: Myocardial infarction
options.C: Rheumatic carditis
options.D: Infective endocarditis

explanation: Cor pulmonale refers to enlargement and failure of the right ventricle resulting from high blood pressure in the pulmonary blood vessels due to lung disease. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h7)

question: Why do patients with advanced occupational lung diseases have an increased risk of heart failure?

options.A: Respiratory failure lowers the body temperature until the heart stops beating
options.B: The inhaled mineral dust travels directly into the heart muscle and clogs valves
options.C: Scarred lung tissue restricts blood flow, forcing the right heart to pump much harder
options.D: Lung damage causes the patient to drink excessive amounts of salty water

explanation: Destruction of the pulmonary capillary bed increases vascular resistance, putting immense strain on the right side of the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is considered the single most effective approach to managing occupational lung diseases?

options.A: Prescribing expensive daily antibiotic tablets
options.B: Performing routine lung transplant surgery on all workers
options.C: Administering oxygen therapy during night shifts only
options.D: Primary prevention and stopping exposure to dust

explanation: Because lung scarring cannot be reversed, stopping the inhalation of harmful dusts before disease starts is the only foolproof solution. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of routine spirometry testing in an industrial occupational health clinic?

options.A: To test the employee's hearing capacity against machine noise
options.B: To check if the worker has contracted a stomach ulcer
options.C: To measure the exact body weight and fat percentage of workers
options.D: To detect early drops in lung function before symptoms appear

explanation: Regular spirometry allows nurses and occupational health officers to spot early breathing impairments so corrective safety steps can be taken immediately. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T8#GNS213_U2_T8_h8)

question: What is the main job of pulmonary surfactant inside the tiny air sacs (alveoli)?

options.A: To stimulate the diaphragm to contract during inspiration
options.B: To warm incoming air before it reaches the bronchioles
options.C: To transport oxygen directly into the bloodstream
options.D: To lower surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse

explanation: You've got this! Surfactant acts like a special coating that reduces surface tension inside the tiny air sacs, keeping them open and stable so breathing is easy. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h1)

question: What happens inside your chest when your diaphragm contracts to take in a normal breath?

options.A: Surface tension increases to make the lung tissue stiffer
options.B: Intrapleural pressure decreases to draw air into the lungs
options.C: Intrapleural pressure increases to force air out of the lungs
options.D: The chest wall pushes inward to compress the lung tissue

explanation: Great thinking! When your diaphragm moves down and your chest expands, the pressure inside drops below the outside air pressure, naturally sucking air in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h1)

question: What is the main physical problem for a patient with an obstructive lung disorder?

options.A: Inability of the chest wall to expand at all
options.B: Total absence of blood flow through the capillaries
options.C: Complete destruction of the pulmonary surfactant
options.D: Difficulty getting air out of the lungs quickly

explanation: Spot on! Obstructive diseases narrow or trap air inside the airways, making it really hard for patients to breathe air out fast. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h2)

question: How do restrictive lung disorders mainly affect how the lungs work?

options.A: They trap large volumes of stale air inside the alveoli
options.B: They increase airway resistance specifically during expiration
options.C: They decrease the total capacity and expansion of the lungs
options.D: They lower the heart rate to slow down blood circulation

explanation: You're doing great! Restrictive disorders make the lung tissue or chest wall stiff, so the lungs just cannot expand to hold a normal volume of air. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h2)

question: What causes a high ventilation-perfusion mismatch, like when someone has a pulmonary embolism?

options.A: Air reaches the alveoli, but blood flow is blocked
options.B: Deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs entirely through a shunt
options.C: Blood flows normally, but the airways are completely filled with pus
options.D: Surface tension drops so low that the alveoli permanently swell

explanation: Well done! A pulmonary embolism blocks blood flow past the air sacs, meaning air gets in fine, but there's no blood there to pick it up. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h3)

question: Why does a pulmonary shunt cause very low blood oxygen that doesn't easily fix with standard oxygen therapy?

options.A: Excess carbon dioxide blocks the hemoglobin binding sites permanently
options.B: Surfactant production stops completely, causing widespread lung collapse
options.C: Blood bypasses unventilated alveoli, so it never gets oxygen to pick up
options.D: The heart pumps too slowly to push blood through the narrowed pulmonary veins

explanation: Exactly. If blood flows past collapsed or fluid-filled sacs without getting oxygen, adding extra oxygen to room air can't reach that blocked blood! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h3)

question: Which major structural change happens in the lungs of someone with emphysema?

options.A: Thickening of the pleural space with fibrous scar tissue
options.B: Destruction of alveolar walls and loss of lung elasticity
options.C: Permanent blockage of the main pulmonary artery by clots
options.D: Excessive production of watery fluid inside the pleural cavity

explanation: You got it! Emphysema breaks down the walls of the air sacs and destroys the elastic fibers, making it hard for the lungs to bounce back when breathing out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why do advanced emphysema patients often end up with a flattened diaphragm and hard-working breathing muscles?

options.A: Scar tissue in the pleural lining pulls the diaphragm upward into the neck
options.B: Loss of pulmonary blood flow weakens the intercostal muscle fibers
options.C: Thick mucus plugs block the trachea and force the chest wall to expand
options.D: Air trapping hyperinflates the lungs and pushes the diaphragm downward

explanation: Makes total sense! Trapped air keeps the chest inflated like a balloon, flattening the diaphragm and making it tired and less efficient. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the primary change in lung tissue for a patient with pulmonary fibrosis?

options.A: Accumulation of watery transudate in the pleural cavity
options.B: Dilation and destruction of the small alveolar air sacs
options.C: Hypersecretion of thick mucus in the large main bronchi
options.D: Replacement of normal lung tissue with stiff scar tissue

explanation: Brilliant! Pulmonary fibrosis is all about chronic inflammation turning healthy lung tissue into stiff, non-stretchy scar tissue. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h5)

question: Which of these is considered an extrinsic cause of a restrictive lung disease?

options.A: Chronic bronchitis from smoking
options.B: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
options.C: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
options.D: Severe scoliosis of the spine

explanation: You're doing awesome. 'Extrinsic' means the problem is outside the lung tissue itself—like a curved spine (scoliosis) squeezing the chest wall. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h5)

question: What is cor pulmonale?

options.A: Infection of the heart valves resulting from severe pneumonia
options.B: Narrowing of the coronary arteries due to chronic low blood oxygen
options.C: Weakening of the left ventricle caused by systemic high blood pressure
options.D: Right heart failure caused by primary lung or pulmonary vascular disease

explanation: Spot on! Cor pulmonale happens when lung problems create high pressure in the pulmonary vessels, forcing the right side of the heart to struggle and eventually fail. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h6)

question: How does long-term high blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension) directly change the heart?

options.A: It shrinks the left atrium because less blood returns from the lungs
options.B: It causes the heart valves to stretch and leak due to low blood pressure
options.C: It weakens the left ventricle by reducing blood flow through the aorta
options.D: It causes the right ventricle to thicken and enlarge from working too hard

explanation: You've got it! Just like lifting heavy weights makes a bicep grow, the right ventricle bulks up (hypertrophies) when it has to push against high lung pressures. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h6)

question: What main trigger causes the kidneys to release erythropoietin in patients with chronic lung disease?

options.A: High levels of red blood cells in circulation
options.B: Increased blood pressure in the right atrium
options.C: Persistent low blood oxygen levels
options.D: Reduced production of pulmonary surfactant

explanation: Brilliant! When the kidneys sense low oxygen (hypoxemia) over a long time, they release erythropoietin to tell the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h7)

question: Why does long-term low blood oxygen sometimes lead to secondary polycythemia?

options.A: The liver releases clotting factors to repair damaged alveolar walls
options.B: The bone marrow responds to inflammation by producing excess white blood cells
options.C: The body tries to carry more oxygen by making extra red blood cells
options.D: Dehydrated blood vessels concentrate the existing red blood cells rapidly

explanation: You're nailing this! Making extra red blood cells is the body's clever way of packing more oxygen-carriers into the blood when air supply is low. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h7)

question: What is the innermost layer of the gastrointestinal tract wall called?

options.A: Muscularis externa
options.B: Mucosa
options.C: Serosa
options.D: Submucosa

explanation: The mucosa is the innermost layer lining the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract, specialized for absorption and secretion. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h1)

question: Venous blood from the gastrointestinal tract flows directly to which organ first?

options.A: Heart
options.B: Kidneys
options.C: Liver
options.D: Spleen

explanation: Blood from the GI tract travels via the hepatic portal system to the liver for nutrient processing before entering general circulation. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which enzyme found in saliva begins the chemical digestion of carbohydrates?

options.A: Salivary amylase
options.B: Pancreatic lipase
options.C: Trypsin
options.D: Pepsinogen

explanation: Salivary amylase is secreted by salivary glands into the mouth to start breaking down starches into simpler sugars. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h2)

question: What prevents food from entering the trachea during the act of swallowing?

options.A: Thyroid cartilage
options.B: Soft palate
options.C: Epiglottis
options.D: Uvula

explanation: The epiglottis folds down over the larynx during swallowing to divert food safely into the esophagus. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which gastric cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?

options.A: Parietal cells
options.B: Chief cells
options.C: Mucous neck cells
options.D: G cells

explanation: Parietal cells in the gastric glands produce both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h3)

question: Why is intrinsic factor produced by the stomach clinically critical?

options.A: It stimulates the release of pancreatic juices
options.B: It breaks down complex proteins into peptides
options.C: It is required for vitamin B12 absorption
options.D: It protects the stomach lining from ulcers

explanation: Intrinsic factor binds to vitamin B12, allowing it to be absorbed later in the terminal ileum. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h3)

question: What are the tiny lymphatic capillaries located inside intestinal villi called?

options.A: Sinusoids
options.B: Microvilli
options.C: Plicae
options.D: Lacteals

explanation: Lacteals absorb dietary fats and fat-soluble vitamins that are too large to enter blood capillaries directly. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h4)

question: How do structural modifications like villi and microvilli affect small intestinal function?

options.A: They produce hormones that control the release of bile from the gallbladder
options.B: They greatly increase the surface area available for nutrient absorption
options.C: They slow down peristalsis to allow for complete gastric emptying
options.D: They secrete large amounts of hydrochloric acid to sterilize chyme

explanation: Plicae, villi, and microvilli expand the internal surface area of the small intestine exponentially to maximize nutrient uptake. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary function of bile salts in digestion?

options.A: Neutralizing stomach acid
options.B: Digesting complex proteins
options.C: Absorbing vitamin B12
options.D: Emulsifying dietary fats

explanation: Bile salts break large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase to work on. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why is the secretion of bicarbonate by the pancreas essential?

options.A: It provides the color pigment found in normal stool
options.B: It neutralizes acidic chyme entering from the stomach
options.C: It stimulates insulin production in response to blood glucose
options.D: It prevents gallstones from forming in the biliary ducts

explanation: Bicarbonate neutralizes the harsh stomach acid, protecting the intestinal lining and optimizing enzyme pH levels. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h5)

question: What are the pocket-like sacs along the length of the colon called?

options.A: Villi
options.B: Haustra
options.C: Rupae
options.D: Crypts

explanation: Haustra are small pouches formed by the contraction of the teniae coli muscle bands along the large intestine. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which muscle makes up the voluntary external sphincter of the anal canal?

options.A: Elastic cartilage
options.B: Smooth muscle
options.C: Cardiac muscle
options.D: Skeletal muscle

explanation: The external anal sphincter is composed of skeletal muscle, allowing conscious, voluntary control over defecation. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which neural network primarily controls gastrointestinal motility and muscle tone?

options.A: Submucosal plexus
options.B: Myenteric plexus
options.C: Somatic nerve plexus
options.D: Cervical nerve plexus

explanation: The myenteric plexus, or Auerbach's plexus, is located between the muscle layers and governs gut motility. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary function of segmentation movements in the small intestine?

options.A: Preventing the backward flow of gastric contents
options.B: Absorbing water from undigested food waste
options.C: Propelling food rapidly toward the large intestine
options.D: Mixing chyme thoroughly with digestive enzymes

explanation: Segmentation uses alternating contractions to back-and-forth mix chyme with digestive juices for optimal absorption. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h7)

question: In what order should a nurse perform a physical assessment of the abdomen?

options.A: Inspect, auscultate, percussion, palpate
options.B: Percuss, palpate, inspect, auscultate
options.C: Auscultate, inspect, palpate, percussion
options.D: Palpate, auscultate, percussion, inspect

explanation: Auscultation is performed before palpation so that manual pressure does not artificially alter natural bowel sounds. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h8)

question: Why must a nurse listen to bowel sounds before pressing on a patient's abdomen?

options.A: It confirms the correct placement of the stethoscope diaphragm
options.B: Auscultation warms up the abdominal wall muscles
options.C: Palpation can stimulate or alter bowel motility and sounds
options.D: Pressing too hard may cause immediate vomiting

explanation: Physical manipulation from palpation can alter gut activity, leading to inaccurate auscultation findings if done first. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T1#GNS213_U3_T1_h8)

question: Which substance do stomach cells release to neutralize acid and protect the lining?

options.A: Bicarbonate
options.B: Bile salts
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Amylase

explanation: Bicarbonate is secreted with mucus to form a chemical shield that protects the stomach lining from acid. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T10#GNS213_U3_T10_h1)

question: Why can taking NSAID painkillers lead to stomach ulcers?

options.A: They block protective prostaglandin synthesis
options.B: They stop the production of hydrochloric acid
options.C: They increase the concentration of pepsinogen
options.D: They directly bind to and dissolve tight junctions

explanation: Prostaglandins normally help maintain the stomach's protective lining. Blocking them reduces mucus and bicarbonate, leaving the tissue vulnerable to damage. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T10#GNS213_U3_T10_h1)

question: GERD (acid reflux) happens mainly due to a problem with which ring of muscle?

options.A: Pyloric sphincter
options.B: Lower esophageal sphincter
options.C: Upper esophageal sphincter
options.D: Ileocecal valve

explanation: The lower esophageal sphincter relaxes when it shouldn't, allowing stomach acid to flow backward into the esophagus. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T10#GNS213_U3_T10_h2)

question: How does Helicobacter pylori survive in the acidic environment of the stomach?

options.A: Releasing bile to digest the mucosal lining
options.B: Producing urease to neutralize surrounding acid
options.C: Consuming excess dietary iron from gastric juices
options.D: Forming a hard calcium shell around itself

explanation: H. pylori releases an enzyme called urease, which breaks down urea into ammonia and neutralizes the acid right around the bacteria. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T10#GNS213_U3_T10_h2)

question: What is a main feature that separates Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis?

options.A: Absence of fistulas and deep tissue fissures
options.B: Superficial crypt abscesses restricted to the colon
options.C: Continuous mucosal inflammation starting in the rectum
options.D: Transmural wall involvement with skip lesions

explanation: Crohn's disease affects the entire thickness of the bowel wall in patchy sections, unlike ulcerative colitis which causes continuous superficial inflammation. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T10#GNS213_U3_T10_h3)

question: Why might a patient with inflammatory bowel disease develop a bowel obstruction?

options.A: Crohn's disease causing deep transmural scarring and strictures
options.B: Ulcerative colitis causing diffuse superficial mucosal bleeding
options.C: H. pylori infection forming a mechanical blockage in the duodenum
options.D: Acute gastritis causing massive submucosal fluid accumulation
