options.B: Excreting large amounts of bicarbonate into the urine
options.C: Reabsorbing excess potassium ions into the bloodstream
options.D: Stopping all glomerular filtration to save blood buffers

explanation: By eliminating acidic hydrogen ions and retaining alkaline bicarbonate, the kidneys restore normal blood pH levels. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T1#GNS213_U4_T1_h5)

question: Which male accessory gland surrounds the upper portion of the urethra just below the bladder?

options.A: Pituitary gland
options.B: Adrenal gland
options.C: Prostate gland
options.D: Bulbourethral gland

explanation: The prostate gland wraps around the male urethra, meaning its enlargement can directly obstruct urine flow. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T1#GNS213_U4_T1_h6)

question: A male patient experiences urinary hesitancy due to a swollen prostate. What anatomical structure is being compressed?

options.A: Ureter
options.B: Ejaculatory duct
options.C: Urethra
options.D: Vas deferens

explanation: The prostate gland directly encircles the urethra, so swelling narrows the channel and impairs urination. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T1#GNS213_U4_T1_h6)

question: What female reproductive organ lies directly posterior to the urinary bladder?

options.A: Fallopian tube
options.B: Ovary
options.C: Uterus
options.D: Cervix

explanation: The uterus rests directly behind and slightly superior to the urinary bladder in the female pelvis. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T1#GNS213_U4_T1_h7)

question: Weakening of the pelvic floor muscles after childbirth can directly affect which urinary function in women?

options.A: Continence control
options.B: Renal acid secretion
options.C: Ureteral peristalsis
options.D: Glomerular filtration rate

explanation: Pelvic floor support is vital for maintaining urethral closure pressure, and weakness often leads to stress incontinence. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T1#GNS213_U4_T1_h7)

question: Which part of the nervous system stimulates the detrusor muscle to contract during urination?

options.A: Somatic motor system
options.B: Sympathetic nervous system
options.C: Enteric nervous system
options.D: Parasympathetic nervous system

explanation: Parasympathetic pathways drive bladder contraction and internal sphincter opening during the micturition reflex. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T1#GNS213_U4_T1_h8)

question: What role does the external urethral sphincter play in controlling urination?

options.A: It provides voluntary skeletal muscle control over the release of urine
options.B: It produces stretch receptor signals to notify the brain of fullness
options.C: It automatically contracts whenever the bladder is completely empty
options.D: It pumps residual urine back into the kidneys via reflex action

explanation: The external sphincter is made of skeletal muscle, allowing conscious control over when to start or stop urinating. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T1#GNS213_U4_T1_h8)

question: Which organ in the urinary system is injured most often during trauma?

options.A: Ureter
options.B: Bladder
options.C: Kidney
options.D: Urethra

explanation: The kidney is the most frequently injured upper urinary tract organ because of its position and major blood supply. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h1)

question: Why do pelvic fractures often lead to lower urinary tract trauma?

options.A: The pelvis stores the main blood supply for the kidneys
options.B: The bony pelvis closely encases the bladder and urethra
options.C: Pelvic bones produce sharp bone fragments that dissolve tissue
options.D: Fractures cut off all nerve supply to the lower abdomen

explanation: Because the pelvic bones sit right next to the bladder and urethra, bone displacement during a fracture can easily damage these structures. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h1)

question: A gunshot wound to the abdomen is an example of what type of trauma?

options.A: Penetrating trauma
options.B: Deceleration trauma
options.C: Iatrogenic trauma
options.D: Blunt trauma

explanation: Penetrating trauma happens when an object like a bullet or knife breaks through the skin and internal tissues. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h2)

question: A patient in a high-speed car crash is at high risk for which type of internal injury?

options.A: Localized inflammation from chronic urinary tract infection
options.B: Clean surgical cuts along the lining of the bladder
options.C: Superficial scratches on the external perineal skin
options.D: Rapid deceleration shearing forces on the renal pedicle

explanation: Sudden stopping in high-speed crashes creates pulling forces that can tear the main blood vessels attached to the kidneys. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h2)

question: A completely shattered kidney with torn main blood vessels is classified as which injury grade?

options.A: Grade V
options.B: Grade III
options.C: Grade I
options.D: Grade II

explanation: Grade V is the most severe level of kidney injury, involving a shattered organ or completely torn blood vessels. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h3)

question: What separates a Grade IV kidney injury from lesser grades?

options.A: Superficial cortical tearing less than one centimeter in depth
options.B: Presence of a simple contusion confined to the outer capsule
options.C: Complete separation of the kidney from the adrenal gland
options.D: Involvement of the renal collecting system or major blood vessels

explanation: Grade IV injuries reach deeper into the kidney's urine-collecting system or involve bleeding from major renal blood vessels. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h3)

question: What is a classic sign of a posterior urethral injury in male patients?

options.A: A low-lying, soft prostate gland
options.B: Blood at the urinary meatus
options.C: Immediate and painless urination
options.D: Excessive enlargement of both testes

explanation: Seeing blood at the urethral opening is a strong warning sign of damage somewhere along the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h4)

question: A patient with a pelvic fracture has blood at the meatus and cannot urinate. What is the correct nursing action?

options.A: Insert a rigid latex urinary catheter immediately to drain the bladder
options.B: Encourage oral fluid intake until spontaneous voiding occurs
options.C: Withhold catheterization and report findings for a retrograde urethrogram
options.D: Perform digital rectal examination to force the prostate downward

explanation: Passing a catheter blindly can worsen a urethral tear, so imaging studies must be done first to check the area. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h4)

question: What physical sign is typical of a penile fracture?

options.A: Inability to feel lower extremity pulses
options.B: Complete absence of scrotal skin
options.C: Persistent, painless erection lasting hours
options.D: Eggplant deformity from rapid bruising

explanation: Tearing of the internal tissues causes severe bleeding under the skin, giving the penis a swollen, dark appearance. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h5)

question: Why is immediate surgery necessary for a suspected testicular rupture?

options.A: To prevent the development of permanent lower limb paralysis
options.B: To preserve testicular viability and long-term endocrine function
options.C: To eliminate the need for any postoperative pain medication
options.D: To stop immediate bleeding into the peritoneal cavity

explanation: Early surgical repair prevents tissue death and protects the testicle's ability to produce hormones and sperm. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h5)

question: What imaging test is best for evaluating a stable patient with a kidney injury?

options.A: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage
options.B: Plain abdominal radiograph
options.C: Computed tomography scan
options.D: Magnetic resonance imaging

explanation: A CT scan with contrast gives clear, detailed pictures of kidney damage, bleeding, and urine leaks. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h6)

question: What does blood in the urine (hematuria) usually indicate during a trauma assessment?

options.A: Complete cessation of glomerular filtration
options.B: Definite destruction of the urinary bladder dome
options.C: Severe infection present prior to the trauma event
options.D: Possible injury anywhere along the urinary tract

explanation: Hematuria simply signals that trauma has affected some part of the urinary system, from the kidneys down to the urethra. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h6)

question: What is the main goal of conservative management for minor kidney injuries?

options.A: Allowing natural healing while monitoring closely for complications
options.B: Forcing rapid diuresis to flush out blood clots from the bladder
options.C: Preventing the patient from moving out of the hospital bed for weeks
options.D: Ensuring immediate surgical removal of the damaged kidney

explanation: Most minor kidney bruises and cuts heal on their own with supportive care and close observation. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h7)

question: A patient resting with a mild kidney injury develops a fast heart rate and falling blood pressure. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Encourage the patient to get out of bed to stimulate circulation
options.B: Notify the surgical team immediately for signs of ongoing bleeding
options.C: Administer oral sleeping pills to help the patient rest quietly
options.D: Decrease intravenous fluid infusion rates to prevent fluid overload

explanation: Dropping blood pressure and a fast pulse can mean internal bleeding is getting worse, requiring urgent medical review. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of a suprapubic catheter placed during bladder surgery?

options.A: To divert urine away from the bladder repair site
options.B: To deliver concentrated antibiotics directly to the kidneys
options.C: To allow the patient to walk immediately without a bag
options.D: To measure accurate intra-abdominal pressure hourly

explanation: A suprapubic catheter drains urine directly through the lower abdomen, keeping the healing bladder empty and free from tension. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h8)

question: Why is keeping a urinary catheter clear and open so important after urinary surgery?

options.A: Continuous high pressure prevents the formation of normal scar tissue
options.B: Blocked catheters automatically cause permanent kidney failure within minutes
options.C: Urine must back up into the renal pelvis to lubricate internal tissue
options.D: Clots and kinks cause bladder spasms and strain surgical suture lines

explanation: Clear drainage prevents urine buildup and painful spasms that could pull apart fresh surgical stitches. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h8)

question: What long-term complication can develop from kidney scarring after trauma?

options.A: Chronic hypotension
options.B: Hypertension
options.C: Pulmonary embolism
options.D: Diabetes mellitus

explanation: Kidney scarring can reduce blood flow inside the organ, activating hormone pathways that lead to high blood pressure later on. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h9)

question: A patient treated for a urethral injury returns months later reporting a weak urine stream. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Urethral stricture formation
options.B: Permanent loss of both testes
options.C: Spontaneous bladder rupture
options.D: Acute kidney stone disease

explanation: As the urethra heals, scar tissue can form and narrow the passage, leading to a weak urine stream and straining. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T10#GNS213_U4_T10_h9)

question: What is the primary reason for establishing trust during a genitourinary assessment?

options.A: To eliminate the requirement for formal medical documentation
options.B: To prevent the need for diagnostic laboratory tests
options.C: To speed up the physical examination process
options.D: To encourage the patient to share sensitive health details

explanation: Genitourinary symptoms involve private bodily functions, making trust essential for an honest and accurate patient history. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why must a nurse evaluate both the urinary and reproductive systems together?

options.A: Patients cannot distinguish between urinary and reproductive pain
options.B: Issues in one system often directly affect the other
options.C: The anatomical structures share the exact same nerve supply
options.D: Hospital policies mandate performing both exams simultaneously

explanation: Because the urinary and reproductive systems share close anatomical proximity and pathways, pathology in one frequently impacts the other. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h1)

question: What medical term is used to describe pain or a burning sensation when passing urine?

options.A: Nocturia
options.B: Dysuria
options.C: Proteinuria
options.D: Hematuria

explanation: Dysuria is the clinical term for painful or difficult urination, commonly reported during infections. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h2)

question: A patient reports waking up three times every night to pass urine. What term should the nurse document?

options.A: Enuresis
options.B: Nocturia
options.C: Polyuria
options.D: Oliguria

explanation: Nocturia specifically refers to interrupted sleep caused by the need to void during the night. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which physical assessment technique is used to check for kidney tenderness at the back?

options.A: Inspection
options.B: Percussion
options.C: Retraction
options.D: Auscultation

explanation: Great job! Gently tapping (percussing) the costovertebral angle at the back helps us check if the kidneys are inflamed or tender. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h3)

question: When gently pressing on the lower abdomen of a healthy adult, what should you normally expect?

options.A: The urethra should feel tender and slightly thickened
options.B: The urinary bladder is not palpable unless distended
options.C: The ureters should be clearly felt along the flank
options.D: Both kidneys should feel firm and easily movable

explanation: Spot on! When the bladder is empty, it hides safely deep in the pelvis. You only feel it when it is full and distended with urine. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which blood tests are most commonly used to evaluate kidney filtration function?

options.A: Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen
options.B: White blood cell count and hemoglobin
options.C: Serum electrolytes and platelet count
options.D: Prothrombin time and international normalized ratio

explanation: Creatinine and blood urea nitrogen are waste products filtered by the kidneys, making them reliable indicators of renal function. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why is proper cleaning of the urethral meatus required before collecting a clean-catch urine sample?

options.A: To decrease burning sensations caused by dysuria during the collection
options.B: To stimulate the bladder muscles and encourage full voiding
options.C: To prevent bacteria from the skin from contaminating the urine culture
options.D: To ensure the specific gravity remains within normal limits

explanation: Skin flora can easily enter the urine stream during collection, leading to false-positive culture results. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary advantage of using an ultrasound for genitourinary assessment?

options.A: It requires general anesthesia for every patient
options.B: It provides a biopsy of the kidney tissue automatically
options.C: It does not expose the patient to radiation
options.D: It measures blood pressure inside the renal arteries

explanation: Ultrasound relies on sound waves rather than ionizing radiation, making it a safe diagnostic imaging option. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which finding is considered a normal, expected temporary side effect following a cystoscopy procedure?

options.A: Mild burning during urination and slight pink-tinged urine
options.B: Inability to feel the need to urinate for several weeks
options.C: Severe lower abdominal pain radiating to the shoulders
options.D: Complete absence of urine output for twenty-four hours

explanation: Passing the scope through the urethra causes minor irritation and mucosal trauma, leading to temporary burning and light bleeding. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h5)

question: What type of data includes measurable physical signs and laboratory test results?

options.A: Objective data
options.B: Anecdotal data
options.C: Historical data
options.D: Subjective data

explanation: Objective data consists of observable and measurable facts gathered through physical examination and diagnostic testing. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h6)

question: Why is accurate documentation of genitourinary assessment findings essential for patient care?

options.A: It establishes a reliable baseline to monitor treatment progress
options.B: It replaces the need for verbal communication between shift nurses
options.C: It guarantees that no further diagnostic tests will be needed
options.D: It eliminates the legal liability of the healthcare facility

explanation: Clear documentation provides a factual record that allows the healthcare team to track changes in a patient's condition over time. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T2#GNS213_U4_T2_h6)

question: What primary body system does an intravenous pyelogram evaluate?

options.A: Gastrointestinal system
options.B: Cardiovascular system
options.C: Urinary system
options.D: Respiratory system

explanation: An IVP is specifically designed to image the kidneys, ureters, and bladder using a radiopaque contrast dye. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is a contrast medium injected intravenously during an IVP?

options.A: To highlight urinary structures on X-rays
options.B: To prevent infection during the procedure
options.C: To flush out small kidney stones completely
options.D: To numb the urinary tract structures

explanation: The radiopaque dye is filtered by the kidneys and makes the internal urinary tract visible on X-ray imaging. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h1)

question: A common clinical indication for performing an IVP is...

options.A: Essential hypertension
options.B: Suspected urolithiasis
options.C: Acute appendicitis
options.D: Peptic ulcer disease

explanation: IVP is frequently used to locate kidney stones and assess urinary tract obstructions. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h2)

question: How does an IVP help a patient with recurrent urinary tract infections?

options.A: It measures the exact daily fluid intake
options.B: It kills bacteria hiding in the bladder
options.C: It strengthens the detrusor muscle tone
options.D: It identifies underlying structural blockages

explanation: Structural anomalies cause urine stasis, which leads to frequent infections that an IVP can help visualize. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which condition is an absolute contraindication for an IVP procedure?

options.A: History of childhood asthma
options.B: Controlled essential hypertension
options.C: Known allergy to iodinated contrast
options.D: Mild urinary tract infection

explanation: Patients with a known iodine allergy are at high risk for severe anaphylaxis when exposed to contrast dye. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why must metformin be withheld from patients receiving iodinated contrast media?

options.A: It stops the contrast dye from working
options.B: It increases the risk of lactic acidosis
options.C: It causes immediate severe hypoglycemia
options.D: It lowers the blood pressure too quickly

explanation: If renal function drops after contrast administration, metformin accumulates and can lead to dangerous lactic acidosis. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary reason for administering a laxative before an IVP?

options.A: To stimulate rapid urine production by the kidneys
options.B: To relax the abdominal wall muscles fully
options.C: To prevent severe post-procedure constipation
options.D: To clear fecal matter that obscures imaging

explanation: Stool and gas in the bowel block clear views of the kidneys and ureters on the X-ray plates. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h4)

question: A patient scheduled for an IVP asks why they must empty their bladder right before the test starts. The best nursing response is...

options.A: To make it easier to insert the intravenous line
options.B: To provide a fresh urine sample for laboratory testing
options.C: To prevent accidental leakage during the procedure
options.D: To obtain an accurate baseline image before dye is given

explanation: An empty bladder allows the initial scout film to clearly show baseline anatomical structures without urine interference. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the purpose of the initial scout film taken during an IVP?

options.A: To check bowel prep and find existing stones
options.B: To numb the skin before needle insertion
options.C: To test the patient for iodine allergies
options.D: To measure the exact volume of the bladder

explanation: The scout film confirms the bowel is clean and identifies any stones visible before dye administration. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why are abdominal compression bands sometimes used during an IVP procedure?

options.A: To keep the patient safely positioned on the table
options.B: To prevent the contrast dye from reaching the bladder
options.C: To stimulate peristalsis and clear remaining bowel gas
options.D: To slow down urine flow and enhance system filling

explanation: Compression over the lower ureters temporarily holds urine in the kidneys to make the collecting system clearer. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h5)

question: A normal sensation a patient may report during the intravenous contrast injection is...

options.A: A warm flushing feeling and metallic taste
options.B: Intense shivering and high fever
options.C: Severe sharp pain in the lower back
options.D: Sudden numbness in both lower limbs

explanation: Patients commonly experience a temporary warm flush and a strange taste immediately after contrast enters the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h6)

question: Why is encouraging high fluid intake important immediately after an IVP?

options.A: To prevent dehydration from fasting
options.B: To help flush out the contrast dye
options.C: To stimulate normal bowel movements
options.D: To keep the bladder muscle stretched

explanation: Abundant fluids promote rapid diuresis, clearing the nephrotoxic contrast medium from the kidneys. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h6)

question: Which symptom indicates a severe, life-threatening reaction to contrast media?

options.A: Localized warmth in the face
options.B: Bronchospasm and laryngeal edema
options.C: Mild metallic taste in the mouth
options.D: Transient nausea and mild vomiting

explanation: Airway swelling and breathing difficulty are signs of severe anaphylaxis requiring immediate emergency care. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h7)

question: A patient develops hives and shortness of breath during contrast injection. What is the immediate nursing action?

options.A: Send the patient back to the ward
options.B: Ask the patient to take slow, deep breaths
options.C: Stop the contrast infusion immediately
options.D: Wait to see if the symptoms clear up

explanation: Stopping the trigger is the first step in managing any acute adverse drug reaction. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h7)

question: What does a filling defect observed on an IVP film typically suggest?

options.A: Extreme renal hyperfunction
options.B: Complete absence of blood supply
options.C: Normal rapid urinary flow
options.D: Calculi, blood clots, or tumors

explanation: A filling defect represents a mass or stone taking up space and blocking the normal flow of contrast dye. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h8)

question: How does hydronephrosis present on an IVP image?

options.A: Multiple tiny stones spread evenly
options.B: Shrunken and scarred renal contours
options.C: Dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces
options.D: Complete absence of the urinary bladder

explanation: Obstruction causes urine to back up, leading to noticeable swelling and enlargement of the renal collecting system. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T3#GNS213_U4_T3_h8)

question: What primary renal structures are inflamed in acute glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Ureteral lining
options.B: Collecting ducts
options.C: Loop of Henle
options.D: Renal glomeruli

explanation: Acute glomerulonephritis specifically targets the glomeruli, which are the main filtering units responsible for blood purification. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h1)

question: Reduced glomerular filtration rate in acute glomerulonephritis directly leads to which clinical finding?

options.A: Complete absence of blood in urine
options.B: Excessive urine output
options.C: Marked drop in blood pressure
options.D: Fluid retention and edema

explanation: When the kidneys fail to filter waste and fluid properly, water and sodium accumulate, causing characteristic swelling. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h1)

question: What type of immune reaction primarily drives the tissue damage in acute glomerulonephritis?

options.A: IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity
options.B: Delayed cell-mediated lysis
options.C: Immune complex deposition
options.D: Direct bacterial invasion of tissue

explanation: Circulating antigen-antibody complexes get trapped in the glomerular membrane, initiating the destructive inflammatory response. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h2)

question: The complement cascade is activated in acute glomerulonephritis primarily to do what?

options.A: Flush out trapped red blood cells safely
options.B: Recruit inflammatory cells to the glomeruli
options.C: Prevent sodium reabsorption in the tubules
options.D: Repair damaged basement membrane cells directly

explanation: Complement activation releases chemical signals that attract white blood cells, which inadvertently worsen tissue injury while fighting complexes. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h2)

question: What bacterial organism is the classic antecedent cause of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.B: Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus
options.C: Escherichia coli
options.D: Staphylococcus aureus

explanation: Throat or skin infections caused by this specific streptococcal strain frequently precede the immune response targeting the kidneys. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h3)

question: A Nigerian child presenting with acute glomerulonephritis following a skin infection should be evaluated for which common local pathogen?

options.A: Staphylococcus aureus
options.B: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.C: Salmonella typhi
options.D: Neisseria meningitidis

explanation: Tropical skin infections and pyoderma caused by staphylococcal bacteria are frequent triggers for immune complex kidney injury in the region. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h3)

question: What gives the urine its characteristic cola-colored appearance in acute glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Bile pigment accumulation
options.B: Excreted red blood cells
options.C: High concentration of urea
options.D: Bacterial waste byproducts

explanation: Damaged glomerular capillaries allow red blood cells to leak into the urine, which turns dark brown or cola-colored as they degrade. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h4)

question: A patient with acute glomerulonephritis exhibits morning facial puffiness and dark urine. Which assessment finding requires immediate nursing attention?

options.A: Crackles heard at the lung bases
options.B: Generalized yellowish skin pallor
options.C: A slight elevation in body temperature
options.D: Mild fatigue during morning care

explanation: Basal lung crackles indicate pulmonary congestion resulting from severe fluid overload, which can quickly lead to heart failure or pulmonary edema. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which specific laboratory finding is most indicative of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Elevated Antistreptolysin O titer
options.B: Decreased serum creatinine levels
options.C: Absence of protein in urine
options.D: Elevated serum sodium levels

explanation: An elevated ASO titer confirms recent exposure to streptococcal bacteria, helping link the antecedent infection to the current kidney injury. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h5)

question: What happens to serum C3 complement levels during the active phase of acute glomerulonephritis?

options.A: They fluctuate wildly every hour
options.B: They rise sharply to fight the infection
options.C: They drop due to active consumption
options.D: They remain entirely unchanged

explanation: The ongoing immune complex reaction consumes complement proteins in the blood, leading to characteristically low C3 serum levels. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary pharmacological goal of administering loop diuretics in acute glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Increase systemic protein synthesis
options.B: Replenish depleted complement C3 proteins
options.C: Relieve fluid overload and hypertension
options.D: Destroy residual streptococcal bacteria

explanation: Loop diuretics force the kidneys to excrete excess water and sodium, lowering blood pressure and easing circulatory strain. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why is penicillin prescribed for a patient diagnosed with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

options.A: To eradicate any remaining streptococcal organisms
options.B: To lower systemic vascular resistance directly
options.C: To prevent secondary bacterial pneumonia
options.D: To repair the damaged glomerular basement membrane

explanation: Antibiotics clear out persistent bacteria from the body, stopping further antigen production even though they do not reverse existing kidney inflammation. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h6)

question: Which nursing intervention provides the most reliable daily indicator of fluid balance in a child with glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Checking skin turgor over the sternum
options.B: Weighing the child at the same time daily
options.C: Measuring abdominal girth every evening
options.D: Counting the number of wet diapers

explanation: Daily weights offer an objective measurement of fluid retention or loss, bypassing the inaccuracies often found in measuring fluid intake and output. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h7)

question: What is NOT a primary monitoring responsibility of the nurse caring for a client with acute glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Monitoring blood pressure every four hours
options.B: Administering daily blood transfusions
options.C: Checking urine for blood and protein
options.D: Tracking strict fluid intake and output

explanation: Routine blood transfusions are not standard care for acute glomerulonephritis unless severe anemia develops, which is uncommon compared to fluid management needs. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h7)

question: What triggers hypertensive encephalopathy in a patient with acute glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Direct bacterial colonization of the cerebral cortex tissue
options.B: Massive protein loss leading to brain tissue edema
options.C: Severe systemic dehydration causing cerebral ischemia
options.D: Acute cerebral vessel vasospasm from severe blood pressure elevation

explanation: Extremely high blood pressure forces cerebral blood vessels to spasm, causing neurological symptoms like headaches, confusion, and seizures. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h8)

question: A patient with acute glomerulonephritis suddenly develops severe headache, vomiting, and confusion. What is the immediate nursing priority?

options.A: Encourage oral fluids to flush the kidneys
options.B: Administer a prescribed daily multivitamin
options.C: Collect a fresh midstream urine specimen
options.D: Check and record blood pressure immediately

explanation: These neurological signs point toward hypertensive encephalopathy, making immediate blood pressure assessment and intervention critical. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h8)

question: What is the typical long-term outlook for a child recovering from acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Inevitable progression to end-stage renal disease
options.B: Complete recovery with normal kidney function
options.C: Development of chronic kidney stones
options.D: Permanent requirement for daily dialysis

explanation: Unlike adults, the vast majority of pediatric patients heal completely from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis without permanent damage. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h9)

question: Which urinary abnormality can persist for months even after a patient's kidney function has fully normalized?

options.A: Severe glycosuria
options.B: Microscopic hematuria
options.C: Complete absence of urine
options.D: Frank macroscopic blood clots

explanation: It is normal for tiny amounts of blood to remain detectable under a microscope for months after all other clinical symptoms have cleared. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T4#GNS213_U4_T4_h9)

question: What happens to the glomeruli in chronic glomerulonephritis over time?

options.A: Healthy membrane tissue regenerates quickly
options.B: The renal artery suddenly widens
options.C: Nephrons grow larger and filter faster
options.D: Fibrous scar tissue replaces working kidney tissue

explanation: Chronic inflammation causes permanent damage, leading to fibrosis and the replacement of normal glomerular structures with scar tissue. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why do people with chronic glomerulonephritis often feel fine in the early stages?

options.A: Urine output stops completely on day one
options.B: Healthy nephrons work harder to make up for damaged ones over years
options.C: Blood pressure stays very low until total failure happens
options.D: Symptoms only show up after eating heavy protein

explanation: The slow progression allows compensatory mechanisms in remaining nephrons to maintain balance until severe damage accumulates. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which cells in the kidney produce the extra proteins that cause scarring in the glomerulus?

options.A: Osteoclasts
options.B: Erythrocytes
options.C: Squamous cells
options.D: Mesangial cells

explanation: Inflammatory stimulation causes mesangial cells to multiply and overproduce matrix proteins, leading to scarring of the glomerulus. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h2)

question: How does immune damage lead to a lower kidney filtration rate?

options.A: Antibodies push extra water out into the tubules
options.B: White blood cells block the ureter completely
options.C: Inflammation and scarring narrow the tiny blood vessels and slow blood flow
options.D: The renal pelvis reabsorbs all filtered fluid

explanation: Immune injury triggers cellular proliferation and fibrosis, which physically narrows the filtering capillaries and drops the filtration rate. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which of these long-term body conditions can lead to chronic kidney damage?

options.A: Iron deficiency anemia
options.B: Chronic peptic ulcer
options.C: Essential thrombocythemia
options.D: Systemic hypertension

explanation: Sustained high blood pressure damages the delicate blood vessels within the kidneys, accelerating the loss of functional glomeruli. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which condition is NOT a common cause of chronic glomerulonephritis?

options.A: Unresolved acute glomerulonephritis
options.B: Acute bacterial pneumonia
options.C: Systemic lupus erythematosus
options.D: IgA nephropathy

explanation: Pneumonia affects the respiratory system primarily and is not a direct primary cause of chronic glomerular injury. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h3)

question: What is a common sign you might see on a patient's face in the morning when they lose protein through their urine?

options.A: Yellowing of the eyes
options.B: Protruding eyeballs
options.C: A rash on the trunk
options.D: Swelling around the eyes

explanation: Hypoalbuminemia reduces plasma oncotic pressure, frequently manifesting as swelling around the eyes upon waking. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why do patients with advanced chronic kidney disease often develop anemia?

options.A: Frequent hospital blood tests drain all iron
options.B: Uremic toxins destroy platelets in the blood
options.C: Strict diets stop vitamin C absorption
options.D: Damaged kidneys stop making enough erythropoietin hormone

explanation: The failing kidneys lose their endocrine function, failing to signal the bone marrow to produce sufficient red blood cells. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h4)

question: What would an ultrasound scan show that points to chronic kidney disease rather than an acute injury?

options.A: An enlarged renal pelvis
options.B: Fluid collected around the kidney
options.C: Small, shrunken kidneys on both sides
options.D: Only one kidney visible

explanation: Chronic disease causes extensive fibrosis and tissue loss, resulting in visibly smaller kidneys on imaging. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why might a doctor skip doing a kidney biopsy in very late-stage chronic kidney disease?

options.A: Ultrasound is always better at showing cell details
options.B: The procedure causes permanent vision loss
options.C: Blood urea must be zero for local anesthesia to work
options.D: Too much scarring makes it impossible to tell what caused the original damage

explanation: When nephrons are completely replaced by scar tissue, the specific original cause is often obscured beyond recognition. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which medication group is often given to lower pressure inside the glomerulus and reduce protein in the urine?

options.A: ACE inhibitors
options.B: Calcium channel blockers
options.C: Loop diuretics
options.D: Beta blockers

explanation: ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arterioles more than afferent arterioles, lowering pressure within the glomerulus and reducing protein leak. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the main reason for cutting down on dietary protein in chronic kidney disease?

options.A: To keep blood albumin high and prevent clots
options.B: To help the basement membrane grow back fast
options.C: To lower the buildup of nitrogen waste products in the blood
options.D: To prevent iron deficiency anemia

explanation: Lowering protein intake reduces the burden of metabolizing nitrogen, easing symptoms of uremia and protecting remaining nephrons. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the most accurate way to check daily fluid balance in a patient with chronic kidney disease?

options.A: Counting how many times they urinate
options.B: Checking their daily body weight
options.C: Checking skin elasticity
options.D: Measuring arm size with a tape

explanation: Weighing the patient daily under standard conditions provides the most reliable data on acute fluid retention or loss. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h7)

question: Why must patients with kidney failure avoid eating too much potassium?

options.A: Potassium causes severe swelling around the eyes
options.B: Damaged kidneys cannot clear potassium well, which can cause dangerous heart rhythms
options.C: Potassium stops blood pressure medications from working
options.D: High potassium destroys red blood cells instantly

explanation: Impaired glomerular filtration leads to potassium retention, which can cause fatal heart rhythm disturbances if dietary intake is not controlled. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the final stage of chronic kidney disease that requires dialysis or a transplant called?

options.A: End-stage renal disease
options.B: Chronic pyelonephritis
options.C: Acute tubular necrosis
options.D: Nephrotic syndrome flare

explanation: When nephron destruction is nearly complete, the condition is termed end-stage renal disease, requiring dialysis or transplantation. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h8)

question: Why do patients in late-stage kidney failure often develop metabolic acidosis?

options.A: The liver makes too much lactic acid from a poor diet
options.B: The kidneys fail to clear hydrogen ions and keep enough bicarbonate
options.C: Drinking less water makes glucose ferment in the bladder
options.D: High blood pressure pushes acid out into body tissues

explanation: Damaged nephrons lose their ability to regulate acid-base balance, leading to an accumulation of hydrogen ions and depletion of buffers. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary characteristic of acute renal failure?

options.A: Slow decrease in glomerular filtration rate
options.B: Gradual scarring of nephrons over years
options.C: Sudden loss of kidney function
options.D: Permanent destruction of renal cortex

explanation: Acute renal failure happens rapidly over hours or days, unlike chronic kidney disease which develops slowly. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h1)

question: Azotemia in acute renal failure refers to the buildup of what substances?

options.A: Red blood cells
options.B: Urea and creatinine
options.C: Sodium and water
options.D: Plasma proteins

explanation: When the kidneys fail suddenly, they cannot filter nitrogenous wastes like urea and creatinine, causing them to accumulate in the blood. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h1)

question: Severe dehydration leading to reduced renal blood flow is classified as what type of cause?

options.A: Glomerular
options.B: Intrarenal
options.C: Postrenal
options.D: Prerenal

explanation: Prerenal causes involve a sudden drop in blood flow to the kidneys before any structural damage to the organ occurs. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h2)

question: An enlarged prostate blocking urine flow out of the bladder is an example of which category?

options.A: Intrinsic failure
options.B: Postrenal failure
options.C: Intrarenal failure
options.D: Prerenal failure

explanation: Postrenal causes involve any mechanical obstruction of the urinary tract downstream from the kidneys. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h2)

question: During which phase of acute renal failure does urine output drop below 400 mL daily?

options.A: Oliguric phase
options.B: Diuretic phase
options.C: Recovery phase
options.D: Onset phase

explanation: The oliguric phase is marked by a sharp decrease in urine output alongside a buildup of metabolic wastes. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h3)

question: Why does high-volume urine output occur during the diuretic phase of recovery?

options.A: The kidneys are suddenly working twice as hard
options.B: Damaged tubules cannot yet concentrate urine properly
options.C: Fluid overload medications force water out
options.D: Glomerular filtration rate becomes excessively high

explanation: As the kidneys begin to heal during the diuretic phase, nephrons excrete large amounts of water and waste before tubular reabsorption function fully returns. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h3)

question: Which electrolyte imbalance in acute renal failure poses the most immediate danger to the heart?

options.A: Hyponatremia
options.B: Hypocalcemia
options.C: Hyperkalemia
options.D: Hypermagnesemia

explanation: Elevated potassium levels severely disrupt cardiac electrical activity, potentially causing fatal arrhythmias. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h4)

question: A patient with acute renal failure exhibits deep, rapid breathing. What is the primary reason for this?

options.A: Direct neurological damage to the brainstem
options.B: Pulmonary edema filling the alveoli with fluid
options.C: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis
options.D: Severe anxiety caused by uremic toxins

explanation: Kussmaul breathing is a deep, rapid respiratory pattern used to blow off carbon dioxide and compensate for acid buildup in the blood. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a renal ultrasound in suspected acute renal failure?

options.A: To calculate daily electrolyte balance
options.B: To test for specific urinary tract infections
options.C: To rule out urinary tract obstruction
options.D: To measure exact glomerular filtration rate

explanation: An ultrasound quickly visualizes the kidneys and ureters to check for swelling or blockages causing postrenal failure. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h5)

question: Which laboratory values are expected to rise significantly in a patient with acute renal failure?

options.A: Hemoglobin and hematocrit percentages
options.B: Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen
options.C: Serum albumin and total protein levels
options.D: White blood cell and platelet counts

explanation: Failing kidneys fail to clear nitrogenous waste products, causing both serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen to accumulate. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h5)

question: Which medication is administered intravenously to protect the heart during severe hyperkalemia?

options.A: Furosemide
options.B: Calcium gluconate
options.C: Regular insulin
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate

explanation: Calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac cell membrane against the toxic effects of high serum potassium. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h6)

question: Why is regular insulin often given alongside glucose to treat acute hyperkalemia?

options.A: To stimulate the kidneys to excrete extra potassium
options.B: To prevent dangerous hypoglycemia from developing
options.C: To drive potassium ions back inside the cells
options.D: To increase overall glomerular filtration rate

explanation: Insulin promotes the movement of potassium from the extracellular fluid into the intracellular space, temporarily lowering blood levels. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h6)

question: What is the most accurate daily indicator of a patient's fluid balance status?

options.A: Daily body weight measurement
options.B: Total fluid intake calculation
options.C: Hourly blood pressure readings
options.D: Routine skin turgor assessment

explanation: A kilogram gained or lost directly corresponds to a liter of fluid retained or lost, making daily weights the most reliable fluid monitor. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h7)

question: During the oliguric phase, why is careful fluid management critical for the patient?

options.A: To prevent the development of permanent chronic renal failure
options.B: To encourage the kidneys to produce normal urine volume
options.C: To prevent life-threatening fluid overload and pulmonary edema
options.D: To reduce the frequency of painful hemodialysis sessions

explanation: Because the kidneys cannot excrete water adequately, unmanaged fluid intake quickly leads to congestion in the lungs and circulation. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h7)

question: What happens to the remaining healthy nephrons early in chronic renal failure?

options.A: They undergo hyperfiltration and hypertrophy.
options.B: They stop producing urine completely.
options.C: They immediately scar and shut down.
options.D: They multiply to replace damaged tissue.

explanation: Healthy nephrons work harder and grow larger to compensate for lost tissue before eventually failing themselves. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h1)

question: The primary underlying process of chronic renal failure is best described as...

options.A: the gradual and irreversible destruction of nephron units.
options.B: a sudden and completely reversible loss of blood flow.
options.C: an acute obstruction of the lower urinary tract.
options.D: a temporary infection of the renal pelvis and tubules.

explanation: CKD is characterized by slow, permanent damage to the kidney structure over a long period. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h1)

question: The two leading global and local causes of chronic renal failure are...

options.A: malaria and typhoid fever.
options.B: hypertension and diabetes mellitus.
options.C: viral hepatitis and tuberculosis.
options.D: peptic ulcers and asthma.

explanation: High blood pressure and high blood sugar place continuous strain on the renal vasculature, driving most cases of CKD. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h2)

question: A patient with long-standing hypertension presents with rising creatinine. What process caused this kidney damage?

options.A: Acute autoimmune destruction of the ureters
options.B: Direct bacterial invasion of the renal parenchyma
options.C: Chronic pressure injury to small renal blood vessels
options.D: Obstruction of the bladder outlet by scar tissue

explanation: Persistent high blood pressure thickens and narrows the blood vessels supplying the kidneys, starving them of blood supply. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h2)

question: A glomerular filtration rate below which value defines Stage 5 kidney failure?

options.A: 60 mL/min/1.73m²
options.B: 15 mL/min/1.73m²
options.C: 90 mL/min/1.73m²
options.D: 30 mL/min/1.73m²

explanation: Stage 5 represents end-stage renal disease where GFR drops below 15 mL/min/1.73m², requiring dialysis or transplant. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h3)

question: Why is staging chronic kidney disease based on GFR clinically useful?

options.A: It guides treatment decisions and predicts progression risk.
options.B: It measures the immediate daily urine output accurately.
options.C: It determines the exact infectious agent in the blood.
options.D: It cures the underlying cause of the renal injury.

explanation: Knowing the stage helps clinicians plan dietary changes, medication adjustments, and prepare the patient for replacement therapy. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h3)

question: Normocytic anemia in chronic renal failure is primarily caused by...

options.A: destruction of red blood cells in the spleen.
options.B: decreased production of erythropoietin by the kidneys.
options.C: an inadequate dietary intake of Vitamin C.
options.D: daily blood loss through the gastrointestinal tract.

explanation: Failing kidneys fail to produce enough erythropoietin, the hormone that stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h4)

question: Which electrolyte imbalance is the most life-threatening complication in a patient with advanced renal failure?

options.A: Hyperkalemia
options.B: Hypermagnesemia
options.C: Hyponatremia
options.D: Hypocalcemia

explanation: High blood potassium levels directly disrupt the electrical conduction system of the heart, causing fatal arrhythmias. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h4)

question: What ultrasound finding strongly supports a diagnosis of chronic rather than acute renal failure?

options.A: Small, shrunken kidneys
options.B: Complete absence of both kidneys
options.C: Enlarged, swollen kidneys
options.D: Dilation of the renal pelvis only

explanation: Chronic disease causes scarring and atrophy over time, making the kidneys appear small on imaging, whereas acute injury often keeps them normal or large. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h5)

question: Why is serum creatinine preferred over blood urea nitrogen when estimating kidney function?

options.A: Urea levels are easily influenced by dietary protein and hydration.
options.B: Urea does not pass through the glomerular membrane at all.
options.C: Creatinine is produced at a slower and completely unstable rate.
options.D: Creatinine levels rise only during acute systemic infections.

explanation: Blood urea nitrogen fluctuates with protein intake, bleeding, and fluid status, making creatinine a steadier marker for baseline filtration. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h5)

question: The primary role of phosphate binders in patients with chronic renal failure is to...

options.A: stimulate the bone marrow to produce red blood cells.
options.B: prevent the absorption of dietary phosphorus in the gut.
options.C: increase the renal excretion of excess potassium ions.
options.D: lower systemic blood pressure by dilating blood vessels.

explanation: Phosphate binders attach to phosphorus from food in the digestive tract, preventing it from entering the bloodstream where it causes bone and vascular damage. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h6)

question: Why are ACE inhibitors frequently prescribed in early chronic renal failure?

options.A: They stimulate the renal tubules to reabsorb more sodium.
options.B: They reduce pressure inside the glomeruli to slow down damage.
options.C: They replace the hormone erythropoietin lost by the kidneys.
options.D: They directly destroy uremic toxins circulating in the blood.

explanation: By dilating the efferent arterioles, ACE inhibitors lower the high pressure inside the filtering units, preserving remaining nephron function. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h6)

question: What type of vascular access is preferred and most durable for long-term hemodialysis?

options.A: Arteriovenous fistula
options.B: Percutaneous subclavian line
options.C: Central venous catheter
options.D: Temporary jugular cannula

explanation: An AV fistula created by joining an artery and vein provides the most reliable blood flow and lowest infection risk for regular dialysis. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h7)

question: How does peritoneal dialysis primarily filter waste products from the blood?

options.A: By stimulating the ureters to flush toxins out through natural urination
options.B: By filtering blood directly through the muscular walls of the bladder
options.C: By using the patient's peritoneal membrane inside the abdomen
options.D: By pumping blood through an artificial machine outside the body

explanation: Peritoneal dialysis uses the rich network of blood vessels in the abdominal lining to filter wastes across the membrane into instilled fluid. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h7)

question: A patient with chronic renal failure gains 2 kilograms in two days. What is the most likely nursing interpretation?

options.A: Rapid muscle mass growth from high protein intake
options.B: Sudden improvement in daily glomerular filtration rate
options.C: Successful rehydration from drinking enough water
options.D: Acute fluid retention due to failing renal excretion

explanation: Rapid weight gain in a renal patient almost always indicates that the kidneys are retaining fluid rather than building true body tissue. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h8)

question: Which dietary restriction is most critical to prevent cardiac arrhythmias in severe renal failure?

options.A: Vitamin C
options.B: Iron
options.C: Potassium
options.D: Calcium

explanation: Limiting high-potassium foods like bananas and oranges prevents dangerous accumulations that can stop the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T7#GNS213_U4_T7_h8)

question: What is the main finding in the urine of someone with nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Complete lack of urine
options.B: High amounts of protein
options.C: Sugar in the urine
options.D: Frank blood

explanation: Damage to the filtering membrane of the kidney allows large amounts of blood proteins to leak into the urine. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h1)

question: Why does widespread swelling happen in patients with nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Blocked lymph vessels stop normal skin drainage
options.B: High salt intake overworks the kidney tubes
options.C: High heart output pushes blood into the legs
options.D: Low blood protein levels pull fluid out of vessels into tissues

explanation: Losing blood proteins lowers the pressure that keeps fluid inside blood vessels, causing it to leak into surrounding tissues. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h1)

question: What is the most frequent cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children?

options.A: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
options.B: Minimal change disease
options.C: Diabetic glomerulosclerosis
options.D: Membranous nephropathy

explanation: Minimal change disease is responsible for the vast majority of primary nephrotic syndrome cases in children. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h2)

question: When a diabetic patient develops nephrotic syndrome, how is this type classified?

options.A: A birth defect present since early pregnancy
options.B: Kidney failure caused entirely by heavy metal poisoning
options.C: An infection limited strictly to the renal pelvis
options.D: Kidney damage triggered by a whole-body disease

explanation: Secondary nephrotic syndrome happens when a systemic illness, like diabetes, damages the tiny blood vessels in the kidneys. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h2)

question: Which blood test result usually drops low in a patient with nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Serum triglycerides
options.B: Serum cholesterol
options.C: Serum albumin
options.D: 24-hour urine protein

explanation: Constantly losing protein through the urine causes a significant drop in circulating blood albumin levels. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h3)

question: A patient presents with puffy eyes and foamy urine. Which test confirms the main problem?

options.A: Random blood glucose test for diabetes
options.B: Electrocardiogram to check heart rhythm
options.C: Twenty-four-hour urine protein test
options.D: Complete blood count to check for infection

explanation: Measuring protein released over 24 hours directly shows the amount of leakage coming from the kidneys. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h3)

question: What is the standard first-line medication used to treat minimal change disease?

options.A: Beta-blockers
options.B: Blood thinners
options.C: Corticosteroids
options.D: Loop diuretics

explanation: Corticosteroids like prednisone are the main treatment to calm the immune response causing the kidney leak. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h4)

question: Why are ACE inhibitors prescribed for patients with nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: To reduce pressure inside the kidney filters and lower protein loss
options.B: To lower blood cholesterol and fat levels
options.C: To prevent deep vein blood clots
options.D: To stimulate bone marrow to make red blood cells

explanation: ACE inhibitors relax the kidney blood vessels, reducing pressure inside the filters to slow down protein loss. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h4)

question: Which diet change is most important for managing swelling in nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Increasing fluid intake
options.B: Restricting dietary sodium
options.C: Eating more carbohydrates
options.D: Restricting potassium

explanation: Limiting salt intake prevents the body from holding onto extra water and making the swelling worse. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h5)

question: Why is a very high protein diet discouraged for chronic protein loss in the kidneys?

options.A: It causes dangerous jumps in blood potassium
options.B: It triggers severe allergic reactions
options.C: It forces remaining kidney filters to work harder and worsens scarring
options.D: It stops the liver from making cholesterol

explanation: Eating too much protein makes the working nephrons strain harder, increasing filtration pressure and speeding up kidney damage. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h5)

question: Losing which protective substance puts nephrotic patients at high risk for infection?

options.A: Antibodies or immunoglobulins
options.B: Erythropoietin
options.C: Calcium
options.D: Platelets

explanation: Losing immunoglobulins in the urine strips the body of the antibodies it needs to fight off common bacterial germs. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h6)

question: What is an important nursing action for a hospitalized patient with generalized swelling?

options.A: Applying warm compresses to puffy eyelids
options.B: Checking daily weights at the same time every day
options.C: Massaging swollen legs to move trapped fluid
options.D: Encouraging high fluid intake to flush the kidneys

explanation: Weighing the patient daily gives the most accurate, objective measure of fluid gain or loss during treatment. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h6)

question: What early sign of a returning condition should patients watch for at home?

options.A: Loss of appetite for sweets
options.B: Sudden increase in eyesight
options.C: Sudden weight gain and facial puffiness
options.D: Changes in hair texture

explanation: Water building back up from protein loss quickly shows up as facial swelling and sudden weight gain. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h7)

question: What instruction is critical for a patient taking long-term steroids?

options.A: Double the dose if your joints feel stiff
options.B: Take the medication only on an empty stomach
options.C: Stop the drug right away if you gain a little weight
options.D: Never stop taking the medication suddenly without a doctor's advice

explanation: Stopping steroids abruptly can cause serious adrenal gland problems and bring back the kidney disease. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h7)

question: What main change inside a cell starts the growth of a tumor?

options.A: Genetic mutations causing uncontrolled cell division
options.B: Rapid dehydration of surrounding tissue layers
options.C: Permanent reduction in local blood supply
options.D: Complete cessation of cellular metabolism

explanation: Tumors start when changes in the cell's genes stop normal cell cycle controls, leading to rapid and unstopped cell multiplication. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h1)

question: Why do different organs in the urinary and reproductive systems develop different types of cancer?

options.A: Bacterial flora vary extensively throughout the upper and lower urinary tracts
options.B: Urinary pH levels fluctuate differently in every anatomical chamber
options.C: Each organ possesses unique cellular structures and specific functional stimuli
options.D: All genitourinary tissues share identical embryonic origin pathways

explanation: Prostate, kidney, and bladder tissues have different baseline cell types and hormone exposures, which change how cancerous growths develop in each area. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h1)

question: What is a key feature of a benign tumor in the urinary system?

options.A: It actively invades adjacent blood vessels and lymphatic channels
options.B: It grows aggressively and destroys surrounding organ architecture
options.C: It consistently recurs after complete local surgical excision
options.D: It remains encapsulated and lacks the ability to metastasize

explanation: Benign growths stay enclosed within a protective capsule and do not spread to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h2)

question: Working closely with which chemical substance heavily increases a person's risk of getting bladder cancer?

options.A: Aniline dyes
options.B: Agricultural limestone
options.C: Processed food additives
options.D: Household laundry bleach

explanation: Industrial chemicals like aniline dyes are well-known risk factors linked to transitional cell cancer of the bladder. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h2)

question: What is the most common early sign of bladder cancer?

options.A: Severe bilateral flank pain
options.B: Painless gross hematuria
options.C: Sudden erectile dysfunction
options.D: High-grade intermittent fever

explanation: Seeing blood in the urine without feeling any pain is the classic first warning sign of bladder tumors. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h3)

question: A patient with a painless lump or swelling in the scrotum should be checked for which condition?

options.A: Testicular cancer
options.B: Renal cell carcinoma
options.C: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
options.D: Chronic pyelonephritis

explanation: An unexplained, painless firmness or swelling in the scrotum is a major warning sign for testicular germ cell tumors. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h3)

question: Which procedure allows a doctor to look directly inside the bladder and take tissue samples?

options.A: Renal arteriography
options.B: Intravenous pyelogram
options.C: Abdominal ultrasound
options.D: Cystoscopy

explanation: Inserting a thin scope through the urethra into the bladder lets the healthcare team directly see and sample internal growths. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h4)

question: A patient has painless blood in the urine and unexplained weight loss. Which test is best to look directly at the bladder lining?

options.A: Prostate palpation
options.B: Cystoscopy
options.C: Scrotal thermography
options.D: Uroflowmetry study

explanation: Direct viewing using a cystoscope is the standard method for finding the exact source of bleeding inside the bladder. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h4)

question: What is the main goal of hormone therapy that blocks androgens in prostate cancer care?

options.A: To eradicate bacterial infections within the prostatic ducts
options.B: To stimulate normal renal tubular regeneration
options.C: To dissolve obstructive urinary stones in the bladder
options.D: To suppress testosterone production and slow tumor growth

explanation: Prostate cancer cells need testosterone and other androgens to multiply, so blocking these hormones helps slow down the cancer. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h5)

question: Why is the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine put directly into the bladder for some bladder cancer patients?

options.A: To trigger a local immune response that destroys remaining cancer cells
options.B: To lubricate the urethral canal prior to repeated catheterizations
options.C: To alter urine chemistry and dissolve small crystal formations
options.D: To permanently paralyze the detrusor muscle and prevent spasms

explanation: Placing this medicine directly into the bladder wakes up local immune cells to attack and destroy any leftover cancer cells. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h5)

question: A patient who just had prostate surgery feels a strong, sudden urge to urinate around their catheter. What should the nurse check first?

options.A: Inflate the catheter retention balloon with extra sterile water
options.B: Clamp the drainage tubing for two hours to rest the bladder
options.C: Check the patency of the urinary catheter and drainage tubing
options.D: Immediately administer a potent oral narcotic analgesic

explanation: Bladder spasms around a catheter usually happen because the tubing is pinched, blocked, or irritated, stopping normal drainage. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h6)

question: What is the most important nursing duty when caring for a patient with a new urinary stoma (uroostomy)?

options.A: Encouraging heavy lifting to strengthen abdominal wall muscles
options.B: Assessing stoma color and ensuring secure appliance seal integrity
options.C: Applying antibiotic ointment to the mucosal surface every hour
options.D: Irrigating the conduit daily with normal saline to prevent stones

explanation: Checking that the stoma has good blood supply, shown by a pink or red color, and keeping urine from leaking onto the skin are key nursing tasks. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h6)

question: Pelvic floor muscle training is commonly given to help patients manage which post-surgery problem?

options.A: Urinary incontinence
options.B: Peristomal hernia
options.C: Testicular atrophy
options.D: Renal tubular acidosis

explanation: Kegel exercises help strengthen the muscles around the urinary sphincter, improving bladder control after pelvic or prostate surgery. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h7)

question: Which symptom in a patient treated for bladder cancer must be reported to the doctor right away?

options.A: Gradual hair thinning from aging
options.B: Recurring gross hematuria
options.C: Mild transient fatigue after walking
options.D: Occasional mild muscle stiffness

explanation: Blood returning in the urine after treatment is a warning sign that the cancer might be coming back in the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T9#GNS213_U4_T9_h7)

question: What is the main job of vitamin D made in the skin?

options.A: Enhancing red blood cell production
options.B: Regulating blood glucose levels
options.C: Preventing bacterial skin infections
options.D: Promoting calcium absorption in the gut

explanation: Vitamin D made in the skin changes into an active form that helps the intestines absorb calcium from the food you eat. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h1)

question: How does the skin help lower a high body temperature?

options.A: Constricting blood vessels to trap heat internally
options.B: Dilating dermal blood vessels and producing sweat
options.C: Increasing subcutaneous fat deposition for insulation
options.D: Shedding outer epidermal cells to release body heat

explanation: Blood vessels widen to bring warm blood close to the skin surface to release heat, while sweat evaporation cools the body down. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h1)

question: Which skin cell type is mainly responsible for producing protective skin color?

options.A: Langerhans cells
options.B: Keratinocytes
options.C: Merkel cells
options.D: Melanocytes

explanation: Melanocytes make melanin, the pigment that absorbs ultraviolet light to protect deep skin cells from damage. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h2)

question: How does the outer layer of the skin (epidermis) get its nutrients?

options.A: Absorption of moisture from the external air
options.B: Diffusion from blood vessels in the dermis
options.C: Direct capillary loops reaching the outer surface
options.D: Active transport via lymphatic vessel networks

explanation: The epidermis does not have its own blood supply, so nutrients soak upward from the blood vessels in the layer beneath it. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h2)

question: Where on the body is the clear skin layer called the stratum lucidum found?

options.A: Face and neck
options.B: Abdomen and chest
options.C: Eyelids and lips
options.D: Palms and soles

explanation: The stratum lucidum is a clear, protective layer found only in areas of thick skin that deal with a lot of friction, like the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h3)

question: What is the main feature of cells in the deepest layer of the epidermis (stratum basale)?

options.A: Complete keratinization
options.B: Incipient cellular apoptosis
options.C: Rapid mitotic division
options.D: Accumulation of lipid droplets

explanation: The stratum basale contains cells that constantly divide to create new cells that push upward toward the skin surface. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h3)

question: What type of tissue makes up the reticular layer of the dermis?

options.A: Loose areolar connective tissue
options.B: Simple columnar epithelium
options.C: Dense irregular connective tissue
options.D: Stratified squamous epithelium

explanation: The reticular layer is packed with thick collagen fibers running in different directions to give the skin strength and toughness. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h4)

question: Dermal papillae help form which unique feature on the hands and feet?

options.A: Fingerprints
options.B: Hair follicles
options.C: Nail matrices
options.D: Sweat pores

explanation: Bumps from the upper dermal layer push up against the epidermis, creating the unique ridges we know as fingerprints and footprints. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h4)

question: What is the main type of tissue found in the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer)?

options.A: Epithelial tissue
options.B: Hyaline cartilage
options.C: Adipose tissue
options.D: Skeletal muscle

explanation: The hypodermis is mostly made of fat tissue (adipose tissue), which helps insulate the body, provide padding, and store energy. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h5)

question: What is the job of oil (sebaceous) glands in the skin?

options.A: Anchoring epidermal layers to underlying muscle
options.B: Lubricating and waterproofing skin and hair
options.C: Providing immune defense against bacterial invasion
options.D: Regulating core body temperature via evaporation

explanation: Sebaceous glands produce oil (sebum) that keeps the skin soft and stops it from losing too much water. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h5)

question: A patient gets a pressure sore over the tailbone from lying in bed too long. What happens first to cause this tissue breakdown?

options.A: Hypersecretion of sebum blocking epidermal pores
options.B: Atrophy of melanocytes leading to radiation damage
options.C: Compression of blood vessels in the dermis and hypodermis
options.D: Accelerated mitotic division in the stratum basale

explanation: Constant pressure squeezes blood vessels shut, cutting off oxygen and nutrients to the skin layers and causing cells to die. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h6)

question: Why do nurses check skin turgor over the collarbone (clavicle) or chest instead of the back of the hand in older adults?

options.A: The clavicle has higher concentration of sweat glands for fluid testing
options.B: Loss of subcutaneous fat in the hands creates false dehydration readings
options.C: Skin on the hand lacks the collagen fibers necessary for elasticity
options.D: Blood flow to the extremities prevents accurate moisture measurement

explanation: Older adults lose fat and skin elasticity in their hands, so checking the chest or collarbone gives a much truer picture of hydration. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h6)

question: What is a flat, discolored skin lesion that is less than 1 cm wide called?

options.A: Papule
options.B: Nodule
options.C: Plaque
options.D: Macule

explanation: A macule is a flat, distinct, discolored area on the skin surface with a diameter of less than 1 cm, such as a regular freckle. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h1)

question: Why is skin turgor checked over the clavicle or forearm during a physical assessment?

options.A: To evaluate the patient's overall hydration status
options.B: To measure the exact blood pressure in the upper body
options.C: To check for localized muscle weakness under the skin
options.D: To determine if the patient has a superficial fungal infection

explanation: Skin turgor reflects how quickly the skin returns to its normal flat position, which helps nurses estimate body fluid volume and hydration. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h1)

question: What diagnostic procedure involves placing small amounts of suspected allergens on the back under tape for 48 hours?

options.A: Wood's light exam
options.B: Patch testing
options.C: Skin scraping
options.D: Punch biopsy

explanation: Patch testing is specifically designed to diagnose contact dermatitis by exposing the skin to small, controlled amounts of potential allergens. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a skin biopsy in dermatology?

options.A: To obtain tissue samples for definitive microscopic diagnosis
options.B: To instantly kill bacteria inside a deep skin abscess
options.C: To remove unwanted benign moles for cosmetic reasons
options.D: To rehydrate severely dry and cracking skin layers

explanation: A biopsy removes a small piece of skin tissue so a pathologist can examine it under a microscope to confirm diseases like skin cancer or severe inflammation. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h2)

question: Why are ointment-based topical medications usually preferred over creams for thick, scaly skin lesions?

options.A: Ointments can be applied in very thick layers without any side effects
options.B: Ointments trap moisture effectively and penetrate thick skin better
options.C: Ointments dry out quickly and prevent any staining of clothing
options.D: Ointments wash off easily with plain water during normal bathing

explanation: The heavy, oil-based nature of ointments creates a barrier that locks in moisture, making them ideal for dry, thickened, or hyperkeratotic skin conditions. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h3)

question: What local complication can happen if topical corticosteroids are used in thick layers for too long?

options.A: Complete numbness of the area
options.B: Skin thinning and atrophy
options.C: Excessive permanent tanning
options.D: Rapid growth of thick hair

explanation: Prolonged and improper application of potent topical steroids breaks down collagen in the skin, resulting in thinning, fragility, and striae. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h3)

question: Which dressing type is made from seaweed and is best suited for wounds with heavy drainage?

options.A: Dry gauze sponge
options.B: Transparent film
options.C: Alginate
options.D: Hydrocolloid

explanation: Alginate dressings absorb large amounts of wound exudate by forming a soft gel, making them ideal for bleeding or heavily draining wounds. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h4)

question: What is the primary clinical goal of performing debridement on a chronic wound?

options.A: To eliminate the need for proper patient nutrition and hydration
options.B: To completely seal the wound shut without needing any sutures
options.C: To stop all blood circulation directly underneath the skin surface
options.D: To remove dead tissue and encourage healthy new cell growth

explanation: Necrotic or dead tissue acts as a barrier to healing and a breeding ground for bacteria; removing it lets healthy granulation tissue form. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h4)

question: What term describes the thickening of the skin caused by chronic scratching and rubbing?

options.A: Maceration
options.B: Excoriation
options.C: Lichenification
options.D: Desquamation

explanation: Lichenification refers to thickened, leathery skin markings that develop after a patient repeatedly scratches or rubs an itchy area over a long period. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h5)

question: A patient with a fungal skin infection in the groin area asks how to prevent spreading it and getting it again. What should the nurse advise?

options.A: Apply thick occlusive petroleum jelly over the area all day
options.B: Wash the skin vigorously with harsh antiseptic soap every hour
options.C: Keep the skin folds clean and dry, and do not share towels
options.D: Wear heavy synthetic clothing to trap warm air near the skin

explanation: Fungi thrive in warm, moist places, so keeping the skin dry and avoiding shared personal items like towels stops transmission and growth. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h5)

question: What is the immediate priority when caring for a patient who has just suffered a severe burn injury?

options.A: Applying antibiotic ointment to all blistered areas
options.B: Calculating the total body surface area burned
options.C: Inserting a large-bore intravenous line for pain meds
options.D: Securing the airway and assessing breathing

explanation: Airway stability always comes first in trauma and burn management because smoke inhalation or laryngeal edema can quickly cause suffocation. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h6)
