question: Why do patients with extensive major burns require large volumes of intravenous fluid resuscitation in the first 24 hours?

options.A: Patients cannot swallow any oral liquids because of severe mouth pain
options.B: Fluid shifts out of the blood vessels into surrounding tissues cause shock
options.C: Burned skin immediately absorbs excess water directly from the intravenous tubing
options.D: Intravenous fluids are needed to cool the internal body temperature down

explanation: Increased capillary permeability in severe burns causes plasma to leak rapidly into interstitial spaces, risking severe hypovolemic shock if not replaced. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h6)

question: Which validated tool is commonly used in clinical practice to assess a patient's risk for developing pressure injuries?

options.A: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.B: Braden Scale
options.C: Morse Fall Scale
options.D: APGAR Score

explanation: The Braden Scale evaluates sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction/shear to score a patient's pressure injury risk. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h7)

question: What is the primary physiological mechanism that causes pressure injuries to form over bony prominences?

options.A: Excessive surface sweat softens the outer skin layer until it tears
options.B: Prolonged pressure cuts off capillary blood flow, causing tissue ischemia
options.C: Bacterial growth multiplies rapidly inside healthy sweat glands
options.D: The body's immune system attacks normal skin cells by mistake

explanation: When external pressure exceeds normal capillary pressure, blood flow stops, starving the tissues of oxygen and nutrients and causing cell death. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h7)

question: Why is addressing psychosocial well-being particularly important for patients with visible, chronic skin conditions?

options.A: Visible skin problems can cause embarrassment, anxiety, and social withdrawal
options.B: Emotional stress directly stops all topical medications from working
options.C: Mental health counseling replaces the need for any physical wound care
options.D: Patients with skin disorders never experience physical pain, only worry

explanation: Chronic and visible dermatological conditions frequently affect body image and self-esteem, making psychological support an important part of holistic care. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h8)

question: What is the best way for a nurse to ensure a patient can safely manage complex wound care and dressing changes at home?

options.A: Tell the patient to wait until the wound heals entirely on its own
options.B: Assume the family knows what to do because dressing changes are simple
options.C: Ask the patient to read a medical textbook chapter before leaving the hospital
options.D: Provide written instructions and have the patient demonstrate the technique back

explanation: Return demonstration combined with written instructions ensures the patient or caregiver actually understands and can perform the steps correctly at home. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T10#GNS213_U5_T10_h8)

question: What is the main job of healthy skin when it comes to protection?

options.A: Regulating the body's hormones
options.B: Making complex carbohydrates
options.C: Producing red blood cells
options.D: Acting as a barrier against germs

explanation: You got this! Healthy skin acts like a natural shield, stopping harmful germs from entering the body. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h1)

question: Why do patients with skin problems easily get secondary bacterial infections?

options.A: They produce an excess amount of oils
options.B: Their immune systems are permanently shut down
options.C: Topical medications attract environmental toxins
options.D: Broken skin allows bacteria to enter deeper tissues

explanation: Spot on! When the skin has cracks or sores, the body loses its first line of defense, making it easy for bacteria to sneak in. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h1)

question: Which substance does the body overproduce during healing, leading to keloids?

options.A: Melanin
options.B: Fibrin
options.C: Collagen
options.D: Keratin

explanation: Great job! Keloids form when the skin makes too much collagen while trying to repair itself. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h2)

question: A patient has a thick scar right across their elbow joint. What problem can this cause over time?

options.A: Reduced range of motion in the arm
options.B: Complete loss of skin sensation
options.C: Permanent hair loss on the forearm
options.D: Spontaneous bleeding from the scar

explanation: Well done! Thick scars over joints act like tight rubber bands, making it hard to move that body part fully. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h2)

question: How can a simple skin infection turn into a body-wide emergency?

options.A: Surface bacteria travel straight to the bone marrow
options.B: The skin produces too much sweat
options.C: Pathogens and toxins enter the general bloodstream
options.D: Local inflammation causes instant kidney failure

explanation: Exactly! Once germs break past local tissues and get into the blood circulation, they can cause trouble all over the body. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h3)

question: A patient with a bad skin infection suddenly has a high fever, fast heart rate, and low blood pressure. What is happening?

options.A: Chronic contact dermatitis
options.B: Systemic sepsis
options.C: Superficial fungal infection
options.D: Localized scar formation

explanation: Spot on! These are classic warning signs that an infection has spread into the bloodstream, leading to dangerous sepsis. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h3)

question: What common symptom of skin conditions often keeps patients awake at night?

options.A: Complete paralysis
options.B: Intense itching
options.C: Severe joint locking
options.D: Sudden blindness

explanation: You nailed it! Itching (pruritus) tends to act up at night, making it really hard for skin patients to get restful sleep. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h4)

question: Why should nurses care about the mental health of patients with visible skin problems?

options.A: Depression automatically cures the skin condition
options.B: Mental distress stops creams from absorbing
options.C: Psychological issues prevent any infections
options.D: Emotional stress can worsen physical skin flare-ups

explanation: Great thinking! The mind and skin are closely linked, so stress and anxiety can actually make skin rashes worse. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h4)

question: Which part of the hand is best to use when checking a patient's skin temperature?

options.A: The knuckles
options.B: The palm
options.C: The back of the hand
options.D: The fingertips

explanation: Correct! The skin on the back of our hands is thinner and much more sensitive to feeling temperature changes. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h5)

question: Which lab test does a nurse watch closely when checking for a worsening skin infection?

options.A: Total red blood cell count
options.B: Serum potassium level
options.C: White blood cell count
options.D: Fasting blood glucose level

explanation: You got it! White blood cells are our immune system soldiers, so high numbers tell us the body is fighting an infection. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h5)

question: What is the main goal of putting emollients on dry, damaged skin?

options.A: To keep the skin hydrated and protect its barrier
options.B: To numb deep nerve endings and stop pain
options.C: To permanently kill all surface bacteria
options.D: To bleach dark scars back to normal tone

explanation: Spot on! Emollients soften and lock moisture into dry skin, helping the natural barrier heal and stop cracking. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h6)

question: Why must a patient finish all their antibiotics even if their skin looks completely better?

options.A: To kill all bacteria and prevent drug resistance
options.B: To stop topical creams from staining clothes
options.C: To guarantee that scar tissue never forms
options.D: To keep the skin from changing color

explanation: Brilliant! Stopping early leaves the toughest germs alive, which can cause the infection to return stronger than before. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T11#GNS213_U5_T11_h6)

question: What is the primary mode of transmission for Mycobacterium tuberculosis?

options.A: Airborne droplets from infected individuals
options.B: Vector-borne transmission through mosquito bites
options.C: Direct contact with contaminated skin wounds
options.D: Ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products

explanation: TB bacteria spread through the air when a person with active disease coughs or sneezes, allowing others to inhale the droplets into their lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h1)

question: What does a positive Mantoux test result primarily indicate?

options.A: Immunity acquired from a recent bacterial cold
options.B: Complete resistance against future infections
options.C: The presence of active, contagious lung disease
options.D: Exposure to the tuberculosis bacterium in the past

explanation: The TST only shows that the body's immune system has encountered the TB bacteria, creating a hypersensitivity reaction, but it cannot tell if the infection is active or dormant. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h1)

question: What type of immune reaction causes the raised bump during a Mantoux test?

options.A: Immediate antibody production
options.B: Complement system activation
options.C: Cell-mediated hypersensitivity
options.D: Innate inflammatory defense

explanation: Think of this as your immune cells (T-cells) rushing to the spot and throwing a little party that takes a day or two to show up as a firm lump! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h2)

question: Why must a patient return 48 to 72 hours after getting a Mantoux injection?

options.A: To ensure the PPD liquid does not leak out of the skin layers
options.B: To receive a second booster dose in the exact same location
options.C: To allow enough time for the delayed immune reaction to peak
options.D: To prevent the injection site from becoming infected with bacteria

explanation: The cellular immune response takes two to three days to build enough local induration to be accurately measured by a healthcare provider. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h2)

question: What is the standard dose of PPD administered during a Mantoux test?

options.A: 1.0 mL containing 50 tuberculin units
options.B: 0.1 mL containing 5 tuberculin units
options.C: 0.5 mL containing 10 tuberculin units
options.D: 2.0 mL containing 100 tuberculin units

explanation: The standard diagnostic dose for standard PPD screening is exactly 0.1 mL, which equals 5 tuberculin units. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h3)

question: Which syringe and needle setup is best for giving a Mantoux skin test?

options.A: A 1-mL tuberculin syringe with a short 27-gauge fine needle
options.B: A 5-mL syringe with a blunt-tip drawing needle
options.C: An insulin syringe marked in units with a permanent attached needle
options.D: A 3-mL syringe with a large 21-gauge intramuscular needle

explanation: You need a tiny syringe to measure tiny drops accurately, and a short, fine needle helps you slide the fluid right into the top layers of the skin! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h3)

question: What visual sign immediately confirms a successful intradermal PPD injection?

options.A: A flat red rash spreading on the arm
options.B: A small droplet of bright red blood
options.C: Immediate bruising around the needle
options.D: A pale raised skin bleb or wheal

explanation: A proper intradermal injection creates a distinct bump or wheal on the skin surface, showing the fluid is trapped in the correct layer. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h4)

question: What should you do right after pulling the needle out of a PPD injection site?

options.A: Pat the area gently with cotton without rubbing it
options.B: Massage the skin vigorously to help absorb the fluid
options.C: Apply a tight pressure bandage to stop any bleeding
options.D: Clean the skin again with a fresh alcohol swab

explanation: Hands off that bubble! Rubbing or massaging can push the fluid away or mess up the skin test results. Just a gentle dab if needed. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h4)

question: When reading a Mantoux test, what part of the skin reaction do you actually measure?

options.A: The hard, raised area of tissue known as induration
options.B: The dark bruising caused by the needle puncture
options.C: The total diameter of visible surface redness
options.D: The size of the initial wheal left after the injection

explanation: Don't measure the redness! Feel for the edges of that firm, hard bump underneath (the induration)—that's what tells the real story. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h5)

question: What should you do if your patient shows up for their Mantoux reading at 96 hours (4 days) instead of 72 hours?

options.A: Measure the induration carefully and record it as normal
options.B: Document the reading as positive due to delayed reaction
options.C: Consult a physician to prescribe prophylactic antibiotics
options.D: Consider the test invalid and schedule a repeat screening

explanation: Time is key! After 72 hours, the immune reaction starts fading away, making the results unreliable. It's best to repeat the test. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h5)

question: Which induration measurement is considered positive for a patient with no known risk factors for tuberculosis?

options.A: 15 millimeters or more
options.B: 5 millimeters or more
options.C: 10 millimeters or more
options.D: 20 millimeters or more

explanation: For healthy individuals with no known exposure risks, the cut-off threshold for a positive test is 15 millimeters or greater. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h6)

question: Why is a smaller bump size (5 mm) counted as positive for patients living with HIV?

options.A: They are more likely to have allergic reactions to the PPD liquid
options.B: They process the antigen much faster than healthy people
options.C: Their weakened immune systems cannot produce large inflammatory lumps
options.D: Their skin is thinner and harder to measure accurately

explanation: Because their immune systems are fighting harder battles, they can't throw a massive inflammatory response. So, even a smaller firm bump is a big red flag we take seriously! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h6)

question: What is a frequent cause of a false-positive Mantoux test in individuals from other countries?

options.A: Prior vaccination with the BCG vaccine
options.B: Having a severe viral cold during testing
options.C: Receiving the injection too deep in the skin
options.D: Taking daily multi-vitamin supplements

explanation: The BCG vaccine, given in many countries to prevent childhood TB, can cause the immune system to react to PPD, creating a false-positive skin test. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h7)

question: Which factor can cause a false-negative Mantoux result in someone who actually has TB?

options.A: Receiving a fresh dose of the PPD antigen
options.B: Reading the test exactly at 48 hours
options.C: Severe immunosuppression from advanced HIV
options.D: Having a history of latent tuberculosis infection

explanation: If the immune system is deeply suppressed, it might not put up any fight at all, leaving you with a blank (false-negative) skin test even if TB is present. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h7)

question: What instructions should a nurse give a patient regarding care of the Mantoux injection site?

options.A: Massage ointment into the skin to reduce swelling
options.B: Keep the area clean, dry, and uncovered without scratching
options.C: Apply a medicated adhesive bandage over the bleb immediately
options.D: Wash the site vigorously with hot soapy water twice a day

explanation: Patients should leave the site alone, avoiding scratching or covering it, to ensure the local skin reaction remains undisturbed until it is read. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h8)

question: What is the best next step for a patient who comes back with a strongly positive Mantoux test?

options.A: Discharge the patient with instructions to return next year
options.B: Refer the patient for a chest X-ray and clinical evaluation
options.C: Immediately start a full course of multi-drug TB treatment
options.D: Administer a second booster Mantoux test on the other arm

explanation: A positive skin test is a warning sign, not a final diagnosis. We always send them for a chest X-ray to check if their lungs are clear or if the infection is active. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T12#GNS213_U5_T12_h8)

question: What is the main reason doctors order a skin snip test?

options.A: Detecting dermal microfilariae of Onchocerca volvulus
options.B: Culturing bacterial pathogens in cellulitis
options.C: Measuring deep dermal thickness for burn assessment
options.D: Identifying fungal elements in superficial tinea

explanation: You got this! A skin snip is specifically used to catch tiny parasite larvae (microfilariae) hiding in the skin layers. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h1)

question: Which patient symptom from an endemic region makes you suspect they might need a skin snip test?

options.A: Chronic intense itching and skin changes
options.B: Severe joint pain and high spiking fevers
options.C: Painful fluid-filled blisters on the lips
options.D: Sudden respiratory distress with wheezing

explanation: Spot on! Onchocerciasis (river blindness) is famous for causing stubborn, severe itching, bumps, and changes in skin texture where the parasite lives. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h1)

question: Which piece of patient history is most critical for a nurse to check before a skin snip?

options.A: A history of bleeding disorders or anticoagulant use
options.B: Previous surgery for appendicitis years ago
options.C: Mild seasonal allergies to pollen and dust
options.D: A childhood diagnosis of uncomplicated asthma

explanation: Safety first! Because a skin snip involves a tiny cut, we always check if the patient bleeds easily or takes blood thinners. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h2)

question: A patient scheduled for a skin snip is very anxious about pain. What is your best first response?

options.A: Cancel the procedure immediately without consulting the doctor
options.B: Administer general anesthesia to keep the patient completely asleep
options.C: Explain the procedure steps and reassure them about local anesthetic use
options.D: Tell the patient that the procedure is entirely painless and quick

explanation: Great nursing judgement! Walking patients through the steps and letting them know local numbing will be used calms their nerves. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h2)

question: Why is local anesthetic WITHOUT epinephrine typically chosen for a skin snip?

options.A: Epinephrine causes severe systemic hypertension
options.B: Epinephrine instantly destroys the surgical scalpel blade
options.C: Local anesthetics cannot be mixed with epinephrine under any rule
options.D: Vasoconstriction can interfere with parasite emergence from the tissue

explanation: Exactly. We want blood vessels to stay open so the tiny live parasites can easily crawl out of the skin sample into our liquid solution. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h3)

question: What is the main goal of placing the harvested skin sample into normal saline or water?

options.A: To sterilize the sample from any surface bacterial contamination
options.B: To encourage the microfilariae to emerge out into the fluid
options.C: To dissolve the tissue completely so only DNA remains
options.D: To preserve the tissue for permanent paraffin embedding

explanation: Spot on! The liquid tricks the live microfilariae into crawling right out of the skin snippet so we can spot them under the microscope. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h3)

question: How deep should the blade go when performing a standard skin snip?

options.A: Superficially into the dermis without deep cutting
options.B: Strictly through the dead outer stratum corneum layer
options.C: Deep into the subcutaneous fat layer for fat cells
options.D: Through the entire muscle layer down to the bone

explanation: You got it! Since the little parasites hang out in the upper skin layers (dermis), we only need a very shallow snip. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h4)

question: What does the clinician usually do right before cutting the skin with the scalpel?

options.A: Elevating a small cone of skin using a sterile needle
options.B: Applying deep pressure to stop all local circulation
options.C: Stretching the skin tightly in four opposite directions
options.D: Massaging the area vigorously to numb it faster

explanation: Correct! Lifting a tiny tent of skin helps the clinician snip just the right top layer safely without cutting too deep. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h4)

question: What causes the microfilariae to leave the skin sample and enter the liquid?

options.A: Active migration of the living parasites into the fluid
options.B: Electrical current passed directly through the glass vial
options.C: Chemical digestion of skin cells by strong laboratory acids
options.D: Mechanical centrifugation at high speeds in the machine

explanation: Well done! The living parasites actively wiggle and crawl out of the skin tissue into the surrounding water or saline. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h5)

question: Why is proper labeling crucial when taking skin snips from different body parts of the same patient?

options.A: To speed up the microscope staining process safely
options.B: To calculate the exact financial cost of laboratory processing
options.C: To determine how much local anesthetic was injected
options.D: To track which anatomical site yielded the parasites

explanation: Spot on! Parasite concentration can differ across body sites, so knowing the exact spot helps doctors measure how heavy the infection is. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h5)

question: What is your immediate nursing action right after the skin snip is taken?

options.A: Scrubbing the bleeding wound vigorously with soap
options.B: Applying direct pressure to the site until bleeding stops
options.C: Suturing the tiny wound closed with heavy nylon thread
options.D: Placing an ice pack directly on the open raw tissue

explanation: Correct! Simple direct pressure stops any minor bleeding at the tiny biopsy site before putting a bandage on. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h6)

question: A patient calls two days post-procedure reporting mild redness and tenderness. What should you advise?

options.A: Scrape the bandage off and wash the wound with harsh bleach
options.B: Come in immediately for emergency surgical debridement
options.C: Stop all prescribed medications and start strong intravenous antibiotics
options.D: Reassure the patient that mild tenderness is normal, but watch for worsening signs

explanation: You nailed it! A little bit of soreness during healing is totally normal, but we always teach patients what red flags (like pus or spreading redness) to watch out for. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T13#GNS213_U5_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary function of the integumentary system?

options.A: Producing red blood cells for systemic circulation
options.B: Acting as a barrier against environmental pathogens
options.C: Regulating blood pressure through vascular constriction
options.D: Synthesizing essential complex carbohydrates for energy

explanation: The skin forms the body's first line of physical defense against external harms and microorganisms. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why must a nurse look at skin changes when thinking about overall health?

options.A: Skin checks mean you never need blood tests
options.B: Skin changes often point to internal diseases
options.C: Skin is completely separate from internal organs
options.D: Systemic illnesses rarely change how skin looks

explanation: Many internal conditions like anemia or systemic infections present outward physical signs on the skin or mucous membranes. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h1)

question: What information should you ask about first when seeing a new skin lesion?

options.A: Past surgeries that have nothing to do with the skin
options.B: Family history of distant relatives with scars
options.C: The brand of soap used at home
options.D: When it started and how it has changed

explanation: Knowing when a skin problem started and how it changed helps determine its acuity and potential cause. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h2)

question: A patient has a sudden rash after using a new cream. What history is most important?

options.A: A timeline of recent product use
options.B: Childhood immunization records
options.C: Dietary intake of carbs and proteins
options.D: Surgical history from ten years ago

explanation: Contact dermatitis or adverse reactions require a clear timeline linking the exposure to the symptom onset. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which tool is best for measuring the exact size of a skin lesion?

options.A: A standard stethoscope
options.B: A sterile cotton swab
options.C: An ophthalmoscope lens
options.D: A ruler or tape measure

explanation: Precise documentation of lesion dimensions requires a metric measuring device. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h3)

question: Why is natural lighting preferred when checking skin color?

options.A: It removes the need to wear gloves
options.B: Artificial bulbs use too much electricity
options.C: It prevents distortion of true skin tones and cyanosis
options.D: Patients feel more relaxed under sunlight

explanation: Artificial lighting can cast yellowish or bluish hues that mask subtle changes like jaundice or pallor. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h3)

question: What does poor skin turgor usually mean in a patient?

options.A: High blood pressure
options.B: Extra fatty tissue under the skin
options.C: A local bacterial infection
options.D: Fluid volume deficit or dehydration

explanation: Skin that remains tented after pinching reflects a loss of elastic recoil due to dehydration. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h4)

question: Where is the best place to check skin turgor in an older adult?

options.A: At the tip of the nose or earlobe
options.B: Across the lower leg calf muscle
options.C: Over the clavicle or sternum
options.D: On the back of the fingers

explanation: The clavicle or sternum provides an accurate assessment site because skin on the hands is often chronically sun-damaged and loose. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h4)

question: What is the main feature of a primary skin macule?

options.A: It is a deep crater going into the dermis
options.B: It contains clear fluid inside a blister
options.C: It is a flat, non-elevated change in skin color
options.D: It is a raised solid mass larger than two centimeters

explanation: A macule is strictly a flat discoloration, such as a freckle, with no elevation or depression. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h5)

question: How do secondary skin lesions differ from primary lesions?

options.A: Secondary lesions develop from changes to existing primary lesions
options.B: Primary lesions only appear during childhood infections
options.C: Primary lesions only develop on moist surfaces
options.D: Secondary lesions are always cancerous growths

explanation: Secondary lesions form as a consequence of trauma, scratching, or natural evolution of an initial primary skin eruption. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h5)

question: What solution is added to skin scrapings to check for fungus?

options.A: A dilute vinegar mixture
options.B: Normal saline solution
options.C: Potassium hydroxide (KOH)
options.D: Hydrogen peroxide antiseptic

explanation: KOH dissolves keratin debris in skin scrapings, making fungal hyphae visible under microscopy. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h6)

question: Why would a doctor order a skin biopsy?

options.A: To treat a mild skin infection instantly
options.B: To replace the need for physical inspections
options.C: To check blood pressure and hydration levels
options.D: To get tissue for a clear microscopic examination

explanation: A biopsy allows pathologists to examine cellular architecture to confirm diagnoses like malignancy or chronic inflammatory disorders. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h6)

question: Which detail is essential when writing notes about a skin lesion?

options.A: A guess of the financial cost of care
options.B: The brand name of soap used in the ward
options.C: The exact body location and measured size
options.D: The nurse's opinion on the patient's hygiene

explanation: Objective measurements and specific locations provide a baseline to evaluate whether treatment is working over time. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h7)

question: Why are vague chart notes about skin conditions a problem?

options.A: They automatically break hospital billing rules
options.B: They stop you from accurately tracking changes over time
options.C: They prevent patients from talking to visitors
options.D: They cause physical pain for the patient

explanation: Precise, objective descriptions ensure that subsequent healthcare providers can accurately monitor healing or worsening of skin findings. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T2#GNS213_U5_T2_h7)

question: What is the main reason a doctor performs a skin biopsy?

options.A: To completely remove a large area of infected tissue
options.B: To obtain a tissue sample for microscopic examination
options.C: To drain purulent fluid from a deep subcutaneous abscess
options.D: To deliver topical medications directly to the dermis

explanation: You've got this! A skin biopsy simply means taking a tiny piece of skin so the lab can look at it closely under a microscope to figure out what's going on. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h1)

question: A patient has a stubborn rash that won't go away with standard treatment, so a skin biopsy is ordered. What is the goal?

options.A: Confirm a definitive diagnosis and guide treatment
options.B: Decontaminate the skin surface from bacterial flora
options.C: Remove all inflamed nerve endings causing itching
options.D: Prevent the rash from spreading to other body parts

explanation: When standard creams don't work, a biopsy helps pin down the exact problem so the healthcare team can choose the right medicine that actually works. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h1)

question: Which biopsy tool uses a tiny round, cookie-cutter blade to take a full-depth core of skin?

options.A: Punch biopsy
options.B: Excisional biopsy
options.C: Incisional biopsy
options.D: Shave biopsy

explanation: Think of a punch biopsy like a tiny apple corer! It uses a small, hollow circular blade to get a clean sample going through all the skin layers. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h2)

question: A patient has a deep, suspicious mole that needs to be completely removed with a clear border of healthy skin. Which method is best?

options.A: Shave biopsy
options.B: Punch biopsy core
options.C: Excisional biopsy
options.D: Superficial scraping

explanation: An excisional biopsy takes out the entire lesion plus a small safety margin of healthy skin around it—great when we need total removal, like checking for melanoma. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h2)

question: Which medication history is crucial to check before doing a skin biopsy?

options.A: Anticoagulant or blood-thinning medications
options.B: Daily multivitamin and mineral supplements
options.C: Prescription oral birth control pills
options.D: Over-the-counter daily calcium tablets

explanation: Always check for blood thinners! They can make bleeding hard to stop during and after the procedure, so the team needs a heads-up. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h3)

question: A patient scheduled for a small skin biopsy is panicking because they are sure it means they have cancer. How should the nurse reply?

options.A: Confirm that the doctor strongly suspects a malignant tumor
options.B: Suggest that the patient cancel the procedure until they feel calmer
options.C: Tell the patient not to worry because skin problems are never serious
options.D: Explain that biopsies are done to check many different conditions, not just cancer

explanation: It's totally normal for patients to worry about the 'C-word.' Gently reminding them that biopsies check for simple rashes, fungus, and routine infections too can be a huge relief. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h3)

question: Why do doctors often add epinephrine to the local numbing medicine for a skin biopsy?

options.A: To constrict blood vessels and reduce bleeding
options.B: To neutralize acidic pH levels in the local tissue
options.C: To completely eliminate the initial stinging sensation
options.D: To speed up the healing time of the skin wound

explanation: Epinephrine makes blood vessels temporarily narrow (vasoconstriction), which keeps the workspace nice and clear of blood and helps the numbing medicine last longer. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h4)

question: Why should local numbing medicine with epinephrine be avoided when doing a biopsy right on the tip of the nose?

options.A: It makes the skin too soft for the punch blade to cut
options.B: It completely stops the local anesthetic from numbing the skin
options.C: It can cause severe restricted blood flow and tissue death
options.D: It reacts poorly with standard skin antiseptic solutions

explanation: Places like the nose tip have end-arteries with no backup blood supply. Adding epinephrine there can cut off circulation completely and cause the tissue to die (necrosis). [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h4)

question: After cleaning the skin with an antiseptic and before giving the numbing injection, what is the next important step?

options.A: Suturing the edges of the anticipated wound
options.B: Placing sterile surgical drapes over the patient
options.C: Applying direct pressure to collapse blood vessels
options.D: Allowing the antiseptic solution to dry completely

explanation: Patience is key! Antiseptics need a little air-drying time to actually kill the germs before the skin barrier is opened up. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h5)

question: After a punch biopsy on the arm, a little blood keeps oozing out. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Flush the open wound with sterile hydrogen peroxide
options.B: Remove the newly placed sutures to inspect the base
options.C: Apply direct firm pressure with sterile gauze
options.D: Immediately apply a full-thickness skin graft

explanation: Simple, direct pressure with sterile gauze is your best friend for stopping minor bleeding before doing anything else. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h5)

question: How long should a patient keep their fresh biopsy bandage clean, dry, and in place?

options.A: 5 to 7 full days
options.B: Until stitches fall out
options.C: 24 to 48 hours
options.D: At least two weeks

explanation: Leaving the first bandage on for 24 to 48 hours gives the skin a chance to start forming its natural protective seal against germs. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h6)

question: Why do we recommend putting petroleum jelly on a healing biopsy site instead of letting a hard crust form?

options.A: Ointment prevents the local anesthetic from wearing off too early
options.B: Petroleum jelly contains strong antibiotics to kill all skin bacteria
options.C: It prevents the sutures from dissolving before the skin closes
options.D: A moist environment helps new skin cells migrate and heal faster

explanation: Skin cells love moisture! Keeping the wound soft with ointment lets new skin cells slide across and close the gap much faster than when a dry, crunchy scab is in the way. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h6)

question: Which sign points strongly to a wound infection after a skin biopsy?

options.A: A thin line of pink tissue along the suture line
options.B: Temporary numbness fading after the local anesthetic wears off
options.C: Spreading redness, warmth, and purulent drainage
options.D: Mild itching around the edges of the adhesive bandage

explanation: Redness that keeps spreading, feeling hot to the touch, pus (purulent drainage), and worsening pain are classic red flags that bacteria have moved in. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h7)

question: Two days after a punch biopsy, a patient calls to say there is a firm, painful, purple lump right under their stitches. What likely happened?

options.A: Normal epithelialization
options.B: Superficial epidermal cyst
options.C: Hematoma formation
options.D: Suture hypersensitivity

explanation: When blood gets trapped and pools under the closed skin, it forms a tender, purple bump called a hematoma. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h7)

question: What liquid solution is standard for preserving a skin biopsy sample on its way to the lab?

options.A: 10% neutral buffered formalin
options.B: Normal sterile saline solution
options.C: Hydrogen peroxide antiseptic
options.D: Isopropyl alcohol 70 percent

explanation: Neutral buffered formalin is the go-to liquid fixative. It stops the tissue from breaking down so the pathologist can examine the cells clearly. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h8)

question: Why is writing a detailed clinical history on the lab form so important when sending off a skin biopsy?

options.A: It determines how much money the laboratory will bill the patient's insurance
options.B: It dictates the type of suture material that should be used in the clinic
options.C: It proves to the hospital administration that the procedure was strictly necessary
options.D: It guides the pathologist on what specific features to look for under the microscope

explanation: Pathologists aren't mind readers! Giving them details like the patient's age and what the rash looked like helps them zoom in on the right clues under the microscope. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T3#GNS213_U5_T3_h8)

question: What skin layer is damaged in a superficial first-degree burn?

options.A: The subcutaneous fat layer
options.B: Both epidermis and deep dermis
options.C: Only the epidermis
options.D: Underlying muscle and bone

explanation: Superficial burns affect strictly the outer epidermal layer, causing localized redness and mild pain without blistering. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h1)

question: Why are full-thickness burns frequently described as painless at the injury site?

options.A: Edema quickly compresses local sensory nerve fibers
options.B: The body releases massive amounts of natural endorphins
options.C: Cold water first-aid numbs the deep nerve pathways
options.D: Nerve endings in the dermis are completely destroyed

explanation: Complete destruction of dermal tissue ruins the sensory nerve endings responsible for transmitting pain signals. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h1)

question: What percentage of TBSA is assigned to the entire anterior trunk in an adult?

options.A: 36 percent
options.B: 9 percent
options.C: 18 percent
options.D: 27 percent

explanation: The anterior trunk covering the chest and abdomen accounts for 18% of the total body surface area in adults. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h2)

question: A patient has burns to the entire right arm and the front of the chest. What is the calculated TBSA?

options.A: 27 percent
options.B: 18 percent
options.C: 9 percent
options.D: 36 percent

explanation: The right arm equals 9% and the anterior trunk equals 18%, totaling 27% TBSA. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h2)

question: The primary physiological shift causing burn shock is...

options.A: massive fluid movement from blood vessels into tissues
options.B: excessive production of red blood cells in bone marrow
options.C: sudden blockage of major coronary arteries by blood clots
options.D: rapid electrolyte retention causing severe fluid overload

explanation: Increased capillary permeability causes fluid to leak out of the vascular space, leading to profound hypovolemia. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h3)

question: Why does acute kidney injury frequently threaten patients during the early phase of severe burns?

options.A: Intravenous fluids dilute all essential body electrolytes
options.B: Urinary catheters block normal urine flow completely
options.C: Reduced cardiac output drops renal blood flow sharply
options.D: Direct heat exposure burns the kidneys through the back

explanation: Hypovolemia and lowered cardiac output drastically decrease perfusion to the kidneys, leading to ischemic renal failure. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h3)

question: Which sign strongly suggests a potential inhalation injury in a burn patient?

options.A: Singed nasal hairs and facial burns
options.B: Cold extremities with weak peripheral pulses
options.C: High fever and productive yellow cough
options.D: Dry skin and absent bowel sounds

explanation: Facial burns and soot around the nose or mouth warn of impending airway thermal and chemical damage. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h4)

question: Why is ice water strictly avoided when cooling a fresh burn injury?

options.A: Freezing temperatures permanently numb all local skin reflexes
options.B: Extreme cold causes local vasoconstriction and deepens tissue injury
options.C: Ice melts too quickly and complicates accurate TBSA calculation
options.D: Cold water reacts chemically with exposed subcutaneous fat

explanation: Severe cold causes intense blood vessel constriction, worsening tissue ischemia and converting partial-thickness burns into full-thickness wounds. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h4)

question: How is the total fluid volume calculated using the Parkland formula for an adult burn patient?

options.A: 6 mL multiplied by body weight in kg and TBSA percentage
options.B: 4 mL multiplied by body weight in kg and TBSA percentage
options.C: 2 mL multiplied by body weight in kg and TBSA percentage
options.D: 9 mL multiplied by body weight in kg and TBSA percentage

explanation: The standard Parkland formula uses 4 mL of crystalloid per kilogram of body weight per percentage of TBSA burned. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary clinical parameter nurses use to evaluate the success of burn fluid resuscitation?

options.A: Body core temperature readings
options.B: Hourly urine output volume
options.C: Resting heart rate frequency
options.D: Daily fasting blood glucose

explanation: Urine output is the most reliable, sensitive indicator of adequate kidney and systemic organ perfusion during fluid resuscitation. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h5)

question: What type of skin graft uses tissue taken from the patient's own body?

options.A: Allograft
options.B: Xenograft
options.C: Autograft
options.D: Heterograft

explanation: An autograft involves harvesting healthy skin from an unburned area of the same patient, ensuring permanent acceptance. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h6)

question: Why is early surgical debridement and eschar removal clinically necessary in deep burns?

options.A: It restores normal skin sensation and sweating capabilities immediately
options.B: It eliminates the need for any subsequent intravenous fluid therapy
options.C: It eliminates dead tissue that promotes bacterial growth and infection
options.D: It completely stops all local inflammation and systemic edema formation

explanation: Necrotic eschar is rich in protein and lacks blood supply, making it an ideal medium for rapid bacterial proliferation and sepsis. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h6)

question: The primary metabolic response following a major burn injury is...

options.A: total cessation of protein synthesis throughout the body
options.B: a hypermetabolic state with rapid breakdown of body tissue
options.C: rapid stabilization of basal energy expenditure within days
options.D: profound metabolic slowing with significant weight gain

explanation: Severe burns trigger massive catabolism, rapidly breaking down lean muscle mass and energy reserves to fuel the stress response. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h7)

question: Why is early enteral feeding preferred over parenteral nutrition in major burn patients?

options.A: It preserves gut integrity and prevents bacterial translocation
options.B: It stops the release of cortisol and other stress hormones
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for intravenous access lines
options.D: It is absorbed much faster without requiring active digestion

explanation: Feeding nutrients directly into the gastrointestinal tract maintains mucosal structure and stops gut bacteria from leaking into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h7)

question: What is the most common cause of death in patients who survive the initial phase of a major burn?

options.A: Spontaneous bone fractures
options.B: Severe hypertension
options.C: Infection and sepsis
options.D: Chronic kidney stones

explanation: Compromised immune defenses and open wound beds make systemic infection and sepsis the primary lethal complication after initial survival. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing an escharotomy on a circumferential chest burn?

options.A: To remove all deep dermal nerve endings and eliminate local pain
options.B: To harvest viable skin grafts directly from the thoracic wall
options.C: To relieve constrictive pressure and restore adequate chest expansion
options.D: To stop the ongoing systemic release of inflammatory cytokines

explanation: Tight, inelastic burn eschar restricts breathing as edema swells underneath; cutting through it relieves the tourniquet effect. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T4#GNS213_U5_T4_h8)

question: Which germ causes leprosy?

options.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.B: Streptococcus pyogenes
options.C: Mycobacterium leprae
options.D: Treponema pallidum

explanation: Spot on! Leprosy is caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It loves to hang out in cooler parts of the body like the skin and outer nerves. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h1)

question: Why do patients with leprosy often get burns or cuts on their hands and feet without realizing it?

options.A: Circulatory failure prevents blood flow to the fingers and toes.
options.B: Chronic skin dryness makes the epidermis fragile and prone to tearing.
options.C: The pathogen directly causes bones in the digits to dissolve.
options.D: Bacteria destroy sensory nerve fibers, causing local anesthesia.

explanation: You've got it! Because the bacteria damage the nerves, the skin loses its ability to feel pain or touch, making injuries easy to miss. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h1)

question: To call leprosy 'paucibacillary', what is the highest number of skin lesions a patient can have?

options.A: Ten lesions
options.B: Twenty lesions
options.C: Five lesions
options.D: Two lesions

explanation: Great job! 'Pauci' means few. Having 5 or fewer skin lesions puts it in the paucibacillary category. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h2)

question: What is a major sign of nerve damage in advanced leprosy during a physical check?

options.A: Painful joint swelling and generalized muscle rigidity
options.B: Sudden widespread bruising and petechiae on the skin
options.C: Spastic paralysis with hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.D: Enlarged, tender nerve trunks and sensory loss

explanation: Spot on! The bacteria attack the nerves directly, making them swollen, painful to touch, and causing the skin over them to lose feeling. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h2)

question: Which of these is a classic, go-to sign of leprosy?

options.A: Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck
options.B: Severe joint pain and morning stiffness
options.C: High fever and generalized body rash
options.D: Definite loss of sensation in a skin patch

explanation: Correct! A pale or reddish skin patch that has completely lost its feeling is a major clue for leprosy. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h3)

question: Why do nurses check (palpate) peripheral nerves during a leprosy assessment?

options.A: The bacterium multiplies exclusively inside superficial lymph nodes.
options.B: Infected nerves often become enlarged, tender, and thickened.
options.C: Nerve palpation measures the exact systemic white blood cell count.
options.D: It stimulates local blood flow to clear dormant pathogens faster.

explanation: You nailed it! Feeling for swollen or tender nerves helps us spot where the infection is causing trouble. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h3)

question: Why do we treat leprosy with a combination of drugs (MDT) instead of just one antibiotic?

options.A: To eliminate the need for any follow-up clinical evaluations
options.B: To prevent the bacterium from developing drug resistance
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing the medications
options.D: To speed up the immediate regeneration of damaged nerve fibers

explanation: Brilliant! Using multiple drugs stops the clever leprosy bacteria from learning how to fight off the treatment. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h4)

question: How long does standard multidrug therapy (MDT) last for multibacillary leprosy?

options.A: Twelve to twenty-four months
options.B: Five years or lifelong
options.C: Exactly six months
options.D: Two to four weeks

explanation: Correct! Multibacillary cases need a longer treatment stretch, usually 12 to 24 months, to clear the heavy germ load. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h4)

question: What is the most important daily protection for a leprosy patient whose feet have lost feeling?

options.A: Soaking the feet in hot water daily to stimulate blood flow
options.B: Applying strong chemical antiseptics to unbroken skin daily
options.C: Wearing well-fitted, protective footwear at all times
options.D: Binding the toes tightly together to prevent accidental stubbing

explanation: Spot on! Since they can't feel pain, good shoes protect their soles from everyday cuts, stones, and ulcers. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h5)

question: A patient on clofazimine panics because their skin is turning a dark brownish-red. What should you tell them?

options.A: Scrub the discolored skin vigorously with medicated soap during daily hygiene routines.
options.B: Explain that this is a common, harmless side effect that will gradually fade after treatment stops.
options.C: Report an emergency adverse drug reaction to the primary prescriber for medication substitution.
options.D: Advise the patient to stop taking all multidrug therapy medications immediately.

explanation: You got it! Clofazimine is known for changing skin color, but it's completely safe and temporary. Reassuring the patient goes a long way! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h5)

question: Which drug class is mainly used to calm down severe leprosy reactions and save nerves from permanent damage?

options.A: Antifungal agents
options.B: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.C: Corticosteroids
options.D: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

explanation: Correct! Corticosteroids like prednisolone are superstars at calming down dangerous inflammation during leprosy flare-ups. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h6)

question: What sign makes a Type 2 leprosy reaction (ENL) different from a Type 1 reaction?

options.A: Crops of painful, tender subcutaneous red nodules across the body
options.B: Slow fading of existing hypopigmented patches over several months
options.C: Complete absence of systemic symptoms like fever and joint aches
options.D: Sudden loss of motor function without any associated skin changes

explanation: Spot on! Type 2 reactions bring along painful red bumps under the skin (ENL) plus fever and body aches. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h6)

question: What is the best message to share with the community to help stop leprosy stigma?

options.A: Permanent physical deformities are an unavoidable outcome regardless of when treatment begins.
options.B: Isolation within a separate facility is legally required until all skin lesions vanish entirely.
options.C: The disease is fully curable with multidrug therapy and loses infectiousness quickly once treatment starts.
options.D: Casual handshakes and sharing meals are the primary ways the infection spreads between neighbors.

explanation: Brilliant! Teaching people that leprosy is curable and stops spreading quickly with treatment helps chase away fear and stigma. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h7)

question: What is the main goal of physical rehabilitation for someone recovering from advanced leprosy?

options.A: Restoring functional independence and improving quality of life
options.B: Accelerating the natural destruction of persistent dormant bacilli
options.C: Replacing all damaged nerve tissue with synthetic nerve grafts
options.D: Eliminating the need for daily skin and eye self-examinations

explanation: You've got it! Rehabilitation is all about helping patients regain their independence, manage disabilities, and live fulfilling lives. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T5#GNS213_U5_T5_h7)

question: What is the primary cellular defect responsible for depigmentation in vitiligo?

options.A: Destruction of melanocytes
options.B: Proliferation of keratinocytes
options.C: Atrophy of hair follicles
options.D: Overproduction of sebum

explanation: Vitiligo occurs when the pigment-producing cells known as melanocytes are destroyed or stop functioning, leading to white patches on the skin. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h1)

question: A patient with psoriasis is most likely to present with which physical finding?

options.A: Transient itchy wheals
options.B: Deep painful subcutaneous nodules
options.C: Diffuse depigmented patches
options.D: Silvery scales on red plaques

explanation: Psoriasis speeds up the life cycle of skin cells, causing cells to build up rapidly on the surface and form thick, silvery scales on red, inflamed plaques. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h1)

question: What primary mechanism underlies most chronic inflammatory skin disorders like psoriasis?

options.A: Bacterial colonization of pores
options.B: Immune-mediated tissue attack
options.C: Fungal infection of the dermis
options.D: Primary nutritional deficiency

explanation: Conditions like psoriasis and various types of dermatitis are driven by abnormal immune responses where immune cells target normal skin components. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h2)

question: Why do environmental factors like intense sunlight often worsen certain inflammatory skin conditions?

options.A: Radiation acts as a trigger for immune flare-ups
options.B: Sunlight removes all protective surface bacteria
options.C: Heat directly destroys subcutaneous fat cells
options.D: Humidity causes immediate bacterial resistance

explanation: Ultraviolet radiation and intense heat can irritate sensitive skin and provoke localized or systemic immune responses that worsen inflammation. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h2)

question: Which diagnostic procedure uses a special ultraviolet light to check for skin fluorescence?

options.A: Skin punch biopsy
options.B: Potassium hydroxide prep
options.C: Wood's lamp examination
options.D: Allergic patch testing

explanation: A Wood's lamp emits black light that causes certain pigments or infectious organisms on the skin to fluoresce, aiding in the diagnosis of conditions like vitiligo. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a skin biopsy for a chronic rash?

options.A: To destroy actively growing fungal colonies
options.B: To measure systemic blood antibody levels
options.C: To cure localized autoimmune skin destruction
options.D: To examine tissue architecture under a microscope

explanation: A tissue sample is taken during a biopsy so pathologists can analyze cellular structure and confirm the exact cause of chronic skin lesions. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h3)

question: What is the main therapeutic goal of prescribing topical corticosteroids for inflammatory skin conditions?

options.A: To stimulate rapid growth of new skin cells
options.B: To reduce localized inflammation and itching
options.C: To eradicate superficial bacterial infections
options.D: To increase local sweat gland production

explanation: Topical corticosteroids work by suppressing the local immune response, which successfully decreases redness, swelling, and severe itching. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h4)

question: When are systemic immunosuppressants typically considered in the management of skin disorders?

options.A: As the first line of defense for mild localized hives
options.B: To prevent normal scarring after a minor skin scrape
options.C: When topical treatments fail to control widespread disease
options.D: To immediately cure acute superficial fungal infections

explanation: Systemic medications carry higher risks of side effects and are reserved for severe or generalized skin disorders unresponsive to topical therapy. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h4)

question: A patient with severe eczema has broken skin from intense scratching. Which nursing action is most critical?

options.A: Encourage vigorous towel drying after every bath
options.B: Apply harsh antiseptic scrubs to remove all bacteria
options.C: Monitor the lesions for signs of secondary infection
options.D: Restrict all fluid intake to reduce skin moisture

explanation: Broken skin creates an entry point for pathogens, making regular assessment for bacterial infection a top priority for nursing care. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h5)

question: Why is breaking the itch-scratch cycle an essential focus in dermatological nursing care?

options.A: Friction stops topical medications from being absorbed
options.B: Nail pressure permanently stops local sweat production
options.C: Scratching worsens tissue damage and invites infection
options.D: Scratching increases systemic blood pressure rapidly

explanation: Mechanical trauma from scratching further damages the epidermal barrier, deepens lesions, and introduces harmful bacteria into the skin. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h5)

question: Which advice is most appropriate for a patient managing an inflammatory skin condition in a hot climate?

options.A: Wear tight synthetic fabrics to trap cool air
options.B: Wear loose clothing made from breathable cotton
options.C: Avoid all forms of skin moisturizers and oils
options.D: Use heavily scented soaps to remove excess sweat

explanation: Cotton garments allow better air circulation and reduce sweat accumulation, minimizing skin irritation compared to synthetic materials. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h6)

question: What is a major social challenge that nurses must help patients navigate regarding chronic skin disorders in Nigeria?

options.A: Stigma due to misconceptions about contagion
options.B: Total prohibition from eating local food items
options.C: Immediate loss of all employment opportunities
options.D: Mandatory quarantine in public health centers

explanation: Many chronic skin disorders are non-contagious, but public misunderstandings often lead to social stigma and isolation, requiring targeted patient and community education. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T6#GNS213_U5_T6_h6)

question: Which cells make up the large majority of the outer layer of your skin (the epidermis)?

options.A: Melanocytes
options.B: Fibroblasts
options.C: Adipocytes
options.D: Keratinocytes

explanation: Keratinocytes are the most common cells in the epidermis! As they mature and move upward, they form a tough, protective shield for your body. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h1)

question: What is the main job of the skin's natural lipids (fats) found between skin cells?

options.A: They fight off local germs like your body's immune system
options.B: They make skin pigment to block the sun's rays
options.C: They give the deeper skin layer its stretch and bounce
options.D: They act like mortar to lock in moisture and keep germs out

explanation: Think of skin cells like bricks and these lipids like the mortar between them. This oily seal keeps your hydration locked in and prevents harmful invaders from entering. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h1)

question: Which skin-dwelling cell releases histamine when an early inflammation or allergy starts?

options.A: Melanocytes
options.B: Adipocytes
options.C: Mast cells
options.D: Keratinocytes

explanation: Mast cells hold onto histamine and release it when triggered, which kickstarts blood flow and swelling during an inflammatory response. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h2)

question: Why does a patch of skin get red and swollen when it becomes inflamed?

options.A: Oil glands overproduce and trap water under the skin
options.B: Lymph channels completely shut down to trap toxins
options.C: Skin cells multiply rapidly to form a shield
options.D: Blood vessels widen and leak fluid into the nearby tissue

explanation: When inflammation hits, blood vessels open wider (causing redness) and let fluid seep into the tissue (causing that puffy swelling). [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h2)

question: How would you best describe a skin macule?

options.A: A solid, elevated lump deep in the skin
options.B: A fluid-filled blister larger than one centimeter
options.C: A flat, unraised change in skin color
options.D: A raised, hard plateau made of merged bumps

explanation: A macule is completely flat. You can't feel it by running your finger over it—it's simply a change in color, like a freckle. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h3)

question: A patient has a tiny, clear, fluid-filled blister on their lip from a cold sore. What is the proper medical term for this lesion?

options.A: Pustule
options.B: Nodule
options.C: Vesicle
options.D: Macule

explanation: A vesicle is a small, fluid-filled blister right on or near the top layer of skin, commonly seen in viral flare-ups like herpes labialis. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h3)

question: Which specific nerve fibers in the skin are responsible for sending itch signals to the brain?

options.A: Pacinian touch receptors
options.B: Unmyelinated C-fibers
options.C: Meissner corpuscle endings
options.D: Large myelinated A-alpha fibers

explanation: Unmyelinated C-fibers are specialized nerve endings in our skin that pick up itch (pruritic) signals and carry them to the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h4)

question: Why does scratching an itchy spot usually make the itch worse in the long run?

options.A: It numbs the skin permanently and causes local damage
options.B: It damages the skin cells, releasing more inflammatory chemicals
options.C: It stops the spinal cord from blocking pain signals
options.D: It speeds up nerve signals so they reach the brain faster

explanation: Scratching feels good for a second, but it actually injures the skin cells. This damage releases histamines and cytokines, fueling the dreaded itch-scratch cycle! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h4)

question: What special enzyme do ringworm and other fungus types use to break into the outer skin layers?

options.A: Keratinase
options.B: Bradykinin
options.C: Collagenase
options.D: Histamine

explanation: Dermatophytic fungi release keratinase, an enzyme that literally digests the tough keratin protein found in your outer skin, hair, and nails. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h5)

question: What causes the intense, driving itch of a scabies mite infestation?

options.A: The mites block blood flow and cause minor tissue death
options.B: An allergic reaction to the mites' waste and proteins in the skin
options.C: The mites chew directly through deep nerve endings
options.D: The mites secrete histamine directly from their mouths

explanation: That severe scabies itch isn't just from crawling—it's your immune system throwing an allergic reaction to the proteins and feces the mites leave behind in their tunnels. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h5)

question: A weak spot in which specific structural protein is strongly linked to the skin barrier breakdown in eczema (atopic dermatitis)?

options.A: Collagen
options.B: Keratin
options.C: Elastin
options.D: Filaggrin

explanation: Filaggrin is a vital protein that helps pack skin cells tightly together. When filaggrin is deficient, the skin barrier weakens, letting moisture out and irritants in. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h6)

question: What drives the extremely fast skin cell growth seen in plaque psoriasis?

options.A: Cold weather triggers massive mast cell breakdown
options.B: The body attacks and destroys pigment cells in the base layer
options.C: Bacteria directly eat away at the outer skin layer
options.D: T-cells release chemical signals that speed up skin cell division

explanation: In psoriasis, hyperactive T-cells release inflammatory chemicals that tell skin cells to multiply way too fast, piling up into those thick, silvery scales. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h6)

question: During wound healing, which cell type rushes in to build new collagen and repair the tissue matrix?

options.A: Keratinocytes
options.B: Mast cells
options.C: Melanocytes
options.D: Fibroblasts

explanation: Fibroblasts are the master builders of healing skin! They migrate into wounds during the repair phase to pump out fresh collagen and rebuild the tissue. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h7)

question: What is the main difference between a keloid scar and a normal hypertrophic scar?

options.A: Hypertrophic scars only happen after burns, while keloids happen after minor cuts
options.B: Keloids have weak collagen while hypertrophic scars have none
options.C: Keloids grow past the original edges of the wound, whereas hypertrophic scars do not
options.D: Hypertrophic scars shrink on their own, but keloids stay forever

explanation: The giveaway for a keloid is its stubborn tendency to keep growing outward, marching past the boundaries of the original injury, unlike a hypertrophic scar which stays within bounds. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T7#GNS213_U5_T7_h7)

question: What do we call skin changes that show up directly as the very first sign of a disease process?

options.A: Vascular lesions
options.B: Primary lesions
options.C: Purpuric lesions
options.D: Secondary lesions

explanation: Spotting primary lesions helps you catch skin conditions right at the beginning before they change. You've got this! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h1)

question: Why is good lighting so important when checking a patient's skin?

options.A: To accurately observe subtle changes in color and moisture
options.B: To prevent the patient from feeling nervous during the exam
options.C: To warm up the skin surface before touching it
options.D: To make the physical examination finish much faster

explanation: Great lighting is your best friend! It helps you spot tiny color shifts and moisture levels so you never miss a detail. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h1)

question: What is a flat, colored spot on the skin that is less than 1 cm wide called?

options.A: Papule
options.B: Plaque
options.C: Vesicle
options.D: Macule

explanation: Think of a simple freckle or flat mole—that's a macule! It's just a flat, colored spot on the skin. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h2)

question: How can you easily tell the difference between a vesicle and a bulla?

options.A: A vesicle contains pus while a bulla contains clear serum only
options.B: A vesicle appears on mucous membranes while a bulla appears on nails
options.C: A vesicle is smaller than 1 cm while a bulla is larger than 1 cm
options.D: A vesicle is solid and raised while a bulla is completely flat

explanation: Both are fluid-filled blisters! The only real difference is their size—bullae are just the bigger ones over 1 cm. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h2)

question: Which secondary skin lesion looks like a narrow crack going down into the skin layer?

options.A: Fissure
options.B: Ulcer
options.C: Lichenification
options.D: Excoriation

explanation: Picture chapped lips or dry, cracked heels—that's a fissure. It's a sharp, linear crack in the skin. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h3)

question: What causes skin to become thick, rough, and leathery, a condition we call lichenification?

options.A: A sudden bacterial infection inside a hair follicle
options.B: Rapid accumulation of watery fluid underneath a bulla
options.C: Chronic scratching and rubbing over a long period
options.D: Exposure to intense ultraviolet sunlight without protection

explanation: When a patient keeps scratching the same spot over and over, the skin fights back by getting thick and leathery. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h3)

question: What do we call those tiny, pinpoint red or purple spots caused by tiny bleeding vessels under the skin?

options.A: Petechiae
options.B: Pustules
options.C: Macules
options.D: Vesicles

explanation: Petechiae are those little pinpoint spots that show up when tiny blood vessels (capillaries) leak a bit of blood. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h4)

question: Why don't petechiae and purpura turn white when you press your finger on them?

options.A: Blood has leaked entirely outside the blood vessels into the tissue
options.B: The underlying capillaries are permanently dilated from heat
options.C: The skin has become too thick from chronic scratching
options.D: There is an overproduction of clear serum inside the blister

explanation: Since the red blood cells have escaped right out into the skin tissue, pressing on top won't make the color go away. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h4)

question: What is the clinical term for an uncomfortable skin feeling that makes you really want to scratch?

options.A: Excoriation
options.B: Lichenification
options.C: Diascopy
options.D: Pruritus

explanation: Pruritus is just the medical word for itching! You'll see it all the time in clinical notes. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h5)

question: Why should nurses worry when a patient has severe, ongoing itching?

options.A: It proves that the topical medication is working effectively
options.B: It always indicates that a patient has systemic kidney failure
options.C: Scratching breaks the skin barrier and increases infection risk
options.D: It prevents the formation of primary lesions like macules

explanation: The itch-scratch cycle damages the skin's natural defense shield, making it super easy for germs and bacteria to get in. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h5)

question: Which skin sign strongly points to a liver problem or high bilirubin levels?

options.A: Pallor
options.B: Petechiae
options.C: Cyanosis
options.D: Jaundice

explanation: Jaundice gives the skin and eyes a yellowish tint because bilirubin is building up in the body. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h6)

question: A patient comes in with a sudden, all-over body rash and a high fever. What should you as a nurse suspect first?

options.A: A potential systemic infection or drug reaction
options.B: A localized injury from scratching a simple insect bite
options.C: A normal physiological change due to aging skin
options.D: A benign primary lesion that requires no follow-up

explanation: When a rash is all over the body AND comes with a fever, it's usually a sign that something is going on inside the whole body, not just the skin. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h6)

question: What is the best way to write down a skin problem in a patient's nursing chart?

options.A: Write the single word 'rash' to save precious time
options.B: Provide precise dimensions, color, and anatomical location
options.C: Guess the exact disease name without checking physical signs
options.D: Record only what the family members report about the spots

explanation: Be specific! Writing down exact measurements, colors, and where it is on the body helps the whole healthcare team track changes accurately. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h7)

question: Why is it so helpful to note the exact pattern and layout of skin lesions?

options.A: It helps identify specific disease patterns and tracks treatment response
options.B: It proves that secondary lesions always turn into primary lesions
options.C: It eliminates the need to record vital signs during the shift
options.D: It guarantees that the patient will stop scratching immediately

explanation: Many skin conditions have a signature look or layout. Spotting this pattern makes it much easier to figure out what's wrong and if the treatment is working! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h7)

question: What is the main job of the skin as a body organ?

options.A: Filtering waste products directly from the bloodstream
options.B: Regulating the production of major digestive enzymes
options.C: Serving as a primary defense against pathogens and fluid loss
options.D: Producing red blood cells for systemic circulation

explanation: Great job! Think of your skin as your body's natural raincoat and security guard rolled into one—it keeps germs out and your precious body fluids in. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h1)

question: Why is keeping the skin intact a major focus in nursing care?

options.A: Intact skin completely prevents all forms of physical aging
options.B: A break in the skin creates a direct pathway for infection
options.C: It eliminates the need for any routine patient hygiene
options.D: Healthy skin regulates the body's internal blood pressure

explanation: Spot on! Once that protective skin barrier gets broken, it opens a wide door for germs to slip right in and cause trouble. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h1)

question: When is the best time to put lotion or moisturizer on the skin?

options.A: Right before taking a hot shower or bath
options.B: Exclusively before going to sleep at night
options.C: Immediately after bathing while the skin is still damp
options.D: Only when the skin begins to crack and bleed

explanation: You got it! Putting cream on slightly damp skin traps that moisture right where you want it, keeping dryness far away. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h2)

question: Why can using harsh, strong soaps every day damage the skin?

options.A: They permanently block all normal sweat gland secretions
options.B: They strip away the natural protective lipid barrier
options.C: They increase the thickness of the subcutaneous fat layer
options.D: They cause an immediate and permanent loss of skin pigment

explanation: Exactly! Harsh soaps wash away your skin's friendly natural oils, leaving it dry, angry, and irritated. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h2)

question: What do vitamins A, C, and E mainly do for your skin?

options.A: Increasing the overall thickness of the subcutaneous fat layer
options.B: Acting as primary cleansers for the epidermal surface
options.C: Directly producing melanin to determine skin color
options.D: Acting as antioxidants to protect cells from oxidative stress

explanation: Spot on! These vitamins act like little bodyguards, fighting off nasty molecules that try to damage your skin cells. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h3)

question: How does severe dehydration affect the skin?

options.A: It permanently changes the natural pigmentation of the skin
options.B: It speeds up the healing rate of minor skin abrasions
options.C: It causes an overproduction of natural skin oils
options.D: It reduces blood flow and impairs cellular metabolism

explanation: Well done! When your body lacks water, blood flow to the skin slows down, starving the cells and making the skin weak and fragile. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h3)

question: What is a major risk of spending too much time under strong ultraviolet (UV) sunlight?

options.A: Faster regeneration of damaged subcutaneous tissue
options.B: Enhanced production of protective surface lipids
options.C: Increased risk of skin cancers and premature aging
options.D: Permanent increase in the skin's moisture content

explanation: Correct! UV rays mess with skin cell DNA, which over time can cause early wrinkles and serious skin growths. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h4)

question: A hospital cleaner gets red, itchy hands from wearing waterproof gloves for hours. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: A sudden increase in the natural skin oil production
options.B: An excessive dietary intake of vitamin C and protein
options.C: Sweat trapped inside the gloves causing irritant contact dermatitis
options.D: Exposure to ultraviolet light while working indoors

explanation: You nailed it! Trapped sweat softens the skin barrier, making it super easy for irritation and redness to flare up. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h4)

question: What is the main reason pressure injuries (bedsores) develop?

options.A: Sustained mechanical pressure cutting off capillary blood flow
options.B: A sudden and severe deficiency in dietary vitamin A
options.C: An allergic reaction to harsh chemical cleaning soaps
options.D: Excessive exposure to natural ultraviolet sunlight

explanation: Spot on! When someone stays in one position too long, body weight pinches tiny blood vessels shut, starving the tissue of oxygen until it breaks down. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h5)

question: Why is dragging a patient straight across bedsheets a bad idea for their skin?

options.A: It completely blocks the production of natural skin oils
options.B: It forces moisture deep into the subcutaneous fat layer
options.C: It creates friction and shear forces that damage skin and blood vessels
options.D: It causes an immediate drop in the patient's systemic blood pressure

explanation: Correct! Pulling someone across rough sheets creates friction and tears tiny blood vessels underneath. Always lift, never drag! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h5)

question: In the ABCDE guide for checking moles, what does the letter 'D' stand for?

options.A: Density
options.B: Depth
options.C: Diameter
options.D: Dryness

explanation: You got it! 'D' is for Diameter—moles that are growing larger than 6 millimeters need a doctor's attention. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h6)

question: What is the main goal of doing regular skin self-examinations?

options.A: Detecting skin abnormalities at an early, treatable stage
options.B: Restoring lost moisture to severely dry epidermal layers
options.C: Completely preventing any future skin injuries from occurring
options.D: Eliminating the need for daily hygiene and moisturizing

explanation: Spot on! Catching skin changes early means any issues can be treated quickly before they turn into something serious. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T9#GNS213_U5_T9_h6)

question: Why are elderly patients much more prone to skin tears?

options.A: Their skin cells regenerate at an unusually rapid pace
options.B: Their blood circulation is much faster than in younger adults
options.C: Their epidermis thins and subcutaneous fat decreases
options.D: Their sweat glands produce excessive amounts of natural oils
