explanation: Think of the HbA1c test as a memory log! Because sugar sticks to red blood cells for their 120-day lifespan, this test shows us the big picture of how blood sugar has been managed over the last few months. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T14#GNS222_U2_T14_h7)

question: Which set of lab tests is primarily ordered to check how well the thyroid gland is working?

options.A: Serum sodium and potassium levels
options.B: Morning cortisol and ACTH levels
options.C: Fasting glucose and HbA1c levels
options.D: TSH, T3, and T4 levels

explanation: Spot on! Checking TSH (the boss hormone from the pituitary) along with T3 and T4 (the actual thyroid hormones) gives a complete picture of thyroid health. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T14#GNS222_U2_T14_h7)

question: What is the main job of endocrine glands in our body?

options.A: Filtering waste products out of liquid blood
options.B: Secreting hormones directly into the bloodstream
options.C: Producing digestive enzymes for the stomach
options.D: Pumping oxygenated blood to body tissues

explanation: Spot on! Endocrine glands don't use ducts. They release their chemical messengers (hormones) straight into nearby blood vessels to reach organs all over the body. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h1)

question: Why can a tiny hormone imbalance affect the whole body?

options.A: Metabolic disorders always destroy the nervous system first.
options.B: Hormones travel through the blood to control multiple distant organs.
options.C: Hormones directly replace the need for cellular oxygen.
options.D: Endocrine glands are physically connected to every organ system.

explanation: You got it! Because hormones ride the bloodstream everywhere, an excess or shortage acts like a ripple effect, changing how many different organs function. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h1)

question: Which test is most commonly used to check hormone levels when doctors suspect an endocrine problem?

options.A: Serum blood tests
options.B: Lumbar punctures
options.C: Bone marrow biopsies
options.D: Sputum cultures

explanation: Correct! Drawing a sample of blood lets the lab measure the exact circulating amounts of specific hormones to see what's going on. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h2)

question: A patient needs a morning blood test for specific hormone levels. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Ensure the blood is drawn precisely at the ordered morning hour because hormones fluctuate daily.
options.B: Draw the blood immediately after the patient takes their evening sleeping pills.
options.C: Delay the blood draw for three days until the patient eats a high-fat diet.
options.D: Collect the sample at any convenient time during the afternoon visiting hours.

explanation: Well done! Many hormones follow a strict daily (diurnal) rhythm, so timing is everything to get an accurate baseline result. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h2)

question: Which of these is a common nursing diagnosis for a patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Impaired Urinary Elimination from infection
options.B: Risk for Peripheral Neurovascular Dysfunction
options.C: Ineffective Airway Clearance
options.D: Risk for Unstable Blood Glucose Level

explanation: Exactly! When diabetes is uncontrolled, keeping blood sugar within a safe range is tough, making glucose instability the primary nursing focus. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h3)

question: Why is 'Disturbed Body Image' a common nursing diagnosis for conditions like Cushing's syndrome?

options.A: Visible physical changes like weight gain and facial swelling alter a person's appearance.
options.B: Hormonal imbalances cause permanent memory loss and confusion.
options.C: Severe muscle weakness prevents the patient from looking in a mirror.
options.D: Patients lose their sense of hearing and balance due to inner ear fluid shifts.

explanation: Spot on. Cushing's brings noticeable body changes, like round 'moon facies' and weight shifts, which can be really tough on a patient's self-esteem. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h3)

question: What is the main goal of setting short-term targets for a patient with a metabolic disorder?

options.A: To eliminate the need for any future nursing assessments
options.B: To permanently cure the underlying chronic endocrine disease
options.C: To achieve immediate stabilization of dangerous lab values
options.D: To replace the physician's medical treatment orders

explanation: Correct! Short-term goals are all about stepping back from the edge—like pulling a patient away from dangerously high or low blood sugar right now. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h4)

question: What makes a well-written nursing goal?

options.A: Focused entirely on hospital routines
options.B: Written only by the attending physician
options.C: Measurable and patient-centered
options.D: Vague and open-ended for flexibility

explanation: You got it! Goals must be clear and measurable so you can easily check if your patient is actually getting better. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h4)

question: As a nurse, what is your key responsibility when giving medications for hormone disorders?

options.A: Monitoring for expected therapeutic effects and potential adverse reactions
options.B: Prohibiting the patient from eating any food for 48 hours
options.C: Prescribing the initial starting dosage based on daily weight
options.D: Manufacturing synthetic hormone replacements in the hospital pharmacy

explanation: Exactly! You are the patient's safety net—watching closely to see if the drug is helping and checking for any scary side effects. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h5)

question: Your patient with diabetes just took rapid-acting insulin. When is it most critical to make sure they have food?

options.A: Whenever the laboratory technician draws a blood sample
options.B: Only when the patient reports feeling extremely thirsty
options.C: At the time of peak insulin action to prevent hypoglycemia
options.D: Exactly six hours before the insulin injection is given

explanation: Well done! Rapid-acting insulin drops blood sugar fast. Food needs to hit their system right when the insulin peaks to stop blood sugar from crashing too low. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h5)

question: Which of these is a life-threatening emergency caused by severely out-of-control diabetes?

options.A: Diabetes Insipidus
options.B: Metabolic Syndrome
options.C: Gestational Diabetes
options.D: Diabetic Ketoacidosis

explanation: Spot on! DKA involves dangerously high blood sugar, severe dehydration, and acid buildup, needing urgent emergency care. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h6)

question: What is the first thing you should do when caring for a patient having an Addisonian crisis?

options.A: Administering intravenous hydrocortisone and fluid replacement
options.B: Restricting all oral and intravenous sodium intake immediately
options.C: Encouraging heavy physical exercise to stimulate adrenal output
options.D: Preparing the patient for emergency surgical removal of the pancreas

explanation: Correct! An Addisonian crisis means the body lacks vital cortisol, causing shock and crashing blood pressure. They need IV steroids and fluids right away. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h6)

question: What vital instruction must you give a patient who is taking prescribed corticosteroid therapy?

options.A: Double the dose whenever you feel stressed
options.B: Never stop taking the medication abruptly
options.C: Take the pills only once a month
options.D: Stop the drug immediately if you gain weight

explanation: You got it! Stopping steroids suddenly can shock the body because the adrenal glands go to sleep while on the medication. They must be tapered off slowly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h7)

question: Why is teaching self-monitoring skills so important for clients with chronic metabolic conditions?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for any future doctor appointments.
options.B: It allows the patient to diagnose other people in their community.
options.C: It proves that nurses no longer need to assess hospital clients.
options.D: It empowers patients to catch small imbalances before they become emergencies.

explanation: Spot on! When patients know how to check themselves, they stay in control and can spot warning signs before things turn into an emergency. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of the evaluation step in the nursing process?

options.A: To write the initial medical diagnosis for the patient chart
options.B: To perform the physical head-to-toe baseline assessment
options.C: To administer emergency medications during a crisis
options.D: To determine if the patient met the established care goals

explanation: Exactly! Evaluation is where you check the patient's progress to see if your care plan actually worked or needs a tweak. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h8)

question: Your patient's blood glucose is still dangerously high despite your nursing interventions. What should you do next?

options.A: Remove all diabetes education materials from the chart
options.B: Collaborate with the healthcare team to revise the care plan
options.C: Discharge the patient immediately because goals were achieved
options.D: Document that the patient refused to cooperate with therapy

explanation: Well done! If the goal isn't met, nursing isn't over. You team up with the doctors and colleagues to try a new, better approach. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T15#GNS222_U2_T15_h8)

question: What is the most common spark that sets off a sudden metabolic or endocrine emergency?

options.A: A sudden physical stressor or infection
options.B: A sudden drop in room temperature
options.C: Drinking too much water too fast
options.D: Eating too much high-fat food

explanation: You've got this! When infections or physical stress hit the body, they demand extra energy, easily pushing a delicate hormone balance right over the edge into an emergency. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h1)

question: Why do endocrine problems usually cause a full-body crisis instead of just a local issue?

options.A: Hormones only work when the patient is under severe stress
options.B: Endocrine organs are all connected directly to the brain
options.C: Hormones travel through the bloodstream to affect many organs
options.D: Endocrine glands store large amounts of toxic waste products

explanation: Think of hormones like mail carriers circulating through the blood vessels. Because they travel everywhere, trouble in just one gland can quickly shake up multiple body systems at once! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h1)

question: Which lab finding helps you spot Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) because it is usually missing in HHS?

options.A: Severe lack of fluid in the body
options.B: Presence of ketones and acidosis
options.C: Extremely high blood glucose levels
options.D: Altered level of consciousness

explanation: Great clinical thinking! DKA involves heavy fat breakdown that produces acidic ketones, whereas HHS spikes the sugar sky-high without major ketoacidosis. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h2)

question: A patient arrives with a blood glucose of 900 mg/dL, severe dehydration, confusion, but zero ketones in the urine. What's the likely condition?

options.A: Thyrotoxic Storm
options.B: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
options.C: Acute Adrenal Insufficiency
options.D: Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State

explanation: Spot on! Massive blood sugar and severe dehydration without ketones is the classic picture of HHS rather than DKA. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h2)

question: What term describes the brain-specific trouble that happens when blood glucose drops too low?

options.A: Osmotic diuresis
options.B: Neuroglycopenia
options.C: Ketoacidosis
options.D: Thyrotoxicosis

explanation: Break it down: 'neuro' for brain, 'glyco' for sugar, 'penia' for low. It simply means the brain is starving for sugar! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h3)

question: Why does a sudden dip in blood sugar so quickly lead to confusion and fainting?

options.A: Low sugar causes the brain cells to instantly swell with extra fluid
options.B: The liver stops sending oxygen to the head during sugar crashes
options.C: Nerves stop producing insulin when blood sugar drops below normal
options.D: The brain relies entirely on a continuous supply of circulating glucose

explanation: Unlike other tissues, your brain cells don't store fuel. When blood glucose takes a dive, the brain feels it instantly! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h3)

question: What are the classic red flags of a thyrotoxic storm?

options.A: Dangerous high fever and rapid heart rate
options.B: Sudden numbness in the lower legs
options.C: Low body temperature and slow breathing
options.D: Severe dehydration with zero ketones

explanation: Think of a thyrotoxic storm as the body's engine revving completely out of control—leading to high fever, severe tremors, and a racing heart (tachycardia). [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h4)

question: A patient with untreated hypothyroidism is admitted with a body temp of 33°C, a very slow pulse, and low consciousness. What is happening?

options.A: Thyrotoxic storm
options.B: Addisonian crisis
options.C: Myxedema coma
options.D: Diabetic ketoacidosis

explanation: You're doing great! Severe, slow-moving hypothyroidism that drops body temperature and causes unresponsiveness is called a myxedema coma. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h4)

question: Which main hormone is dangerously low during an adrenal crisis?

options.A: Insulin
options.B: Vasopressin
options.C: Thyroxine
options.D: Cortisol

explanation: Cortisol is our primary stress hormone. When the adrenal glands fail to pump it out, the body struggles to handle even basic stress. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h5)

question: Why can suddenly stopping long-term steroid medications trigger an adrenal crisis?

options.A: Stopping steroids causes the liver to destroy all circulating glucose
options.B: Steroid pills turn into toxic acid inside the stomach lining
options.C: The adrenal glands become lazy and stop making natural cortisol
options.D: The thyroid gland reacts by shutting down body temperature controls

explanation: When you take external steroids for a long time, your adrenals take a break from making their own. If you stop abruptly, they can't bounce back fast enough! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h5)

question: Which physical check is commonly done at the bedside to test for low calcium levels (hypoparathyroidism)?

options.A: Fruity breath odor
options.B: Chvostek's sign
options.C: Pupillary reflex
options.D: Kussmaul breathing

explanation: Tapping lightly on the facial nerve near the cheek to watch for a twitch is known as Chvostek's sign—a classic clue for low calcium! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h6)

question: How does hyperparathyroidism usually impact a patient's bones?

options.A: It forces extra calcium to deposit, making bones overly thick
options.B: It triggers rapid bone growth that crushes nearby nerve roots
options.C: It stops blood flow to the joints, causing cartilage to melt
options.D: It pulls calcium out of bones, making them weak and painful

explanation: Too much parathyroid hormone acts like a withdrawal slip, pulling calcium right out of the skeleton and leaving bones fragile and aching. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h6)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a microvascular complication of diabetes?

options.A: Peripheral stroke
options.B: Carotid atherosclerosis
options.C: Diabetic retinopathy
options.D: Coronary artery disease

explanation: Retinopathy targets the tiny capillaries inside the eyes, making it a classic microvascular ('small vessel') complication. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h7)

question: What is the main difference between microvascular and macrovascular diabetic complications?

options.A: If the condition affects the upper or lower body
options.B: Whether the patient feels pain or numbness
options.C: The size of the damaged blood vessels
options.D: How fast the symptoms appear after a meal

explanation: It's all in the name! Micro means tiny vessels (like in the eyes and kidneys), while macro means larger arteries (like heart and brain vessels). [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h7)

question: What is the very first nursing priority when a patient arrives with a suspected endocrine emergency?

options.A: Assess airway, breathing, and circulation
options.B: Wait for family to bring medical history records
options.C: Send the patient for an immediate MRI scan
options.D: Offer the patient a high-protein meal

explanation: No matter the diagnosis, ABCs always come first! Keeping the airway, breathing, and circulation stable is the number one life-saving step. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h8)

question: Why is keeping a patient on a continuous heart monitor so crucial during a severe electrolyte or hormone shift?

options.A: Rapid shifts in minerals can trigger dangerous heart rhythms
options.B: Blood pressure cuffs cannot measure pulses during a crisis
options.C: Patients with hormone imbalances always have blocked arteries
options.D: Endocrine organs share direct nerve pathways with heart muscle

explanation: Your heart muscle loves stable electrolytes. When minerals like potassium and calcium fluctuate wildly, the heart's electrical rhythm can become dangerously unstable. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T16#GNS222_U2_T16_h8)

question: What is the main goal of secondary prevention in endocrine and metabolic disorders?

options.A: Providing end-of-life palliative comfort
options.B: Preventing the initial onset of the disease
options.C: Catching early signs through regular screening
options.D: Reversing long-standing organ damage

explanation: Spot-on! Secondary prevention is all about catching hidden problems early through screening tests before they become severe. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h1)

question: Why are metabolic and endocrine disorders considered such a big deal for public health?

options.A: They only affect elderly populations in rural areas
options.B: They are easily cured with a single antibiotic
options.C: They cause widespread and systemic complications
options.D: They never require long-term medical management

explanation: Because our hormones control so many different body systems, when something goes wrong here, it affects the whole body. Great thinking! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h1)

question: How many minutes of moderate exercise per week are generally recommended for primary prevention?

options.A: Exactly 30 minutes
options.B: Up to 500 minutes
options.C: At least 150 minutes
options.D: No more than 60 minutes

explanation: That's right! Health guidelines suggest a minimum of 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly to keep our metabolism humming nicely. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h2)

question: A patient asks how to lower their risk of type 2 diabetes. What is the best starting advice a nurse can give?

options.A: Sleep for at least 12 hours every night without exercising
options.B: Eliminate all carbohydrates completely from every meal
options.C: Take a daily low-dose insulin injection to rest the pancreas
options.D: Adopt a diet high in fiber and increase daily physical activity

explanation: Spot on! Eating healthy fiber and staying active directly fights insulin resistance, which is the root cause of type 2 diabetes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h2)

question: Which test is commonly used to check a patient's long-term blood sugar control over the past three months?

options.A: Hemoglobin A1c assay
options.B: Serum potassium level
options.C: Urinalysis for protein
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: Correct! The HbA1c test gives us a wonderful 3-month picture of how well blood glucose has been managed. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h3)

question: Why is secondary prevention so crucial for conditions like type 2 diabetes?

options.A: The disease often develops silently without early symptoms
options.B: Symptoms are always too painful to ignore
options.C: Early detection makes the condition completely disappear
options.D: Screening tests are expensive and rarely performed

explanation: Exactly! Type 2 diabetes can creep up quietly for years without symptoms, making routine screening an absolute lifesaver. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of tertiary prevention in nursing care?

options.A: Preventing complications in established chronic diseases
options.B: Curing genetic disorders before birth
options.C: Stopping healthy people from ever getting sick
options.D: Screening asymptomatic populations for hidden risk

explanation: Well done! Tertiary prevention steps in after a diagnosis to help patients manage their condition and avoid further complications. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h4)

question: You are caring for a patient with long-standing diabetes. Which assessment is key for tertiary prevention of microvascular issues?

options.A: Measuring handgrip strength using a dynamometer
options.B: Palpating superficial lymph nodes in the neck
options.C: Asking about daily recreational screen time habits
options.D: Checking urine for microalbumin and performing foot exams

explanation: Spot on! Checking urine for tiny amounts of protein (microalbumin) and inspecting the feet regularly helps catch early kidney and nerve damage. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h4)

question: Why is the "return-demonstration" method so effective when teaching a patient to test their blood glucose?

options.A: It proves the patient has memorized all medical terminology
options.B: It saves time compared to traditional verbal explanations
options.C: It confirms the patient can perform the skill correctly and safely
options.D: It eliminates the need for any written instructions

explanation: That's right! Having the patient show you how they do it ensures they truly grasp the steps before managing things at home alone. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a good strategy for teaching a patient with an endocrine condition?

options.A: Providing clear written action plans for emergency symptoms
options.B: Tailoring the teaching session to the patient's cultural background
options.C: Giving long medical lectures without checking for understanding
options.D: Using a return-demonstration approach for practical skills

explanation: Correct! Long, boring lectures don't help anyone learn. We always want interactive teaching and plenty of feedback! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h5)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse on a multidisciplinary endocrine care team?

options.A: Acting as the central coordinator and patient advocate
options.B: Performing advanced surgical interventions
options.C: Managing hospital financial budgets
options.D: Prescribing all specialized medications independently

explanation: Spot on! As a nurse, you are the glue that holds the care team together, speaking up for your patient every step of the way. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h6)

question: A diabetic patient is stressed because they cannot afford their monthly insulin. Who should the nurse involve first?

options.A: Radiology technician
options.B: Surgical specialist
options.C: Social worker
options.D: Physical therapist

explanation: Brilliant! Social workers are absolute rockstars at connecting patients with financial aid and community assistance programs. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h6)

question: What is a key clinical marker used to evaluate the success of long-term diabetes management?

options.A: Hemoglobin A1c trends
options.B: Shoe size measurements
options.C: Frequency of dental visits
options.D: Hair color and texture

explanation: That's it! Tracking A1c over time gives a clear, reliable picture of how steady blood sugar levels have been. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h7)

question: Why should nurses look at patient-reported outcomes alongside lab test results in endocrine care?

options.A: Lab numbers alone do not capture the patient's daily quality of life
options.B: Lab results are legally required to be ignored if the patient feels fine
options.C: Patients always understand laboratory science better than doctors
options.D: Patient feelings are the only accurate diagnostic tool available

explanation: Spot on! Good labs are important, but understanding how the patient actually feels and lives day-to-day is what truly matters in nursing. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T17#GNS222_U2_T17_h7)

question: What is the main goal of a fasting blood sugar test?

options.A: To find out the percentage of red blood cells carrying oxygen
options.B: To check how quickly the kidneys filter waste products
options.C: To measure blood sugar levels after a period without eating
options.D: To check the total amount of protein stored in the liver

explanation: You've got this! A fasting blood sugar test simply looks at your glucose levels after you haven't eaten for a while, usually overnight. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h1)

question: When a patient fasts, how does the body keep blood sugar from dropping too low?

options.A: The liver stops all metabolic activity until the next meal
options.B: The pancreas releases extra insulin to store extra sugar
options.C: The muscles absorb all available glucose to build up fat stores
options.D: The pancreas releases glucagon to tell the liver to release stored sugar

explanation: Think of glucagon as the body's natural backup alarm! When food isn't coming in, glucagon tells the liver to share its stored glucose to keep your energy stable. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h1)

question: A fasting blood sugar test is most commonly used to check for which condition?

options.A: Diabetes mellitus
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Hypothyroidism
options.D: Chronic kidney disease

explanation: Spot on! Fasting blood sugar is one of the quickest and most common ways doctors and nurses screen for diabetes mellitus. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h2)

question: Which patient is the best candidate for a routine fasting blood sugar screening?

options.A: A young child recovering from a normal cold
options.B: A healthy athlete with mild muscle soreness after running
options.C: An adult with obesity and a family history of diabetes
options.D: An elderly patient admitted with a broken bone from a fall

explanation: Great thinking! People with risk factors like extra weight and a family history are prime candidates for routine checks so we catch issues early. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h2)

question: How many hours of fasting are normally needed before a fasting blood sugar test?

options.A: 2 to 4 hours
options.B: 18 to 24 hours
options.C: 8 to 12 hours
options.D: Exactly 30 minutes

explanation: An 8 to 12 hour fast (usually overnight) gives the body enough time to clear out food from the last meal so we get a true baseline reading. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h3)

question: Why should nurses tell patients not to chew gum or smoke while fasting for this test?

options.A: They mess up the laboratory machine used to spin blood
options.B: They can trigger digestion and change the blood sugar results
options.C: They cause severe dehydration that collapses arm veins
options.D: They immediately destroy all red blood cells in the body

explanation: Even tiny actions like chewing gum can trick the body into releasing insulin, throwing off the test results. Patient instructions matter! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h3)

question: Which color of blood collection tube is normally used for a fasting blood sugar test?

options.A: Red-top tube
options.B: Lavender-top tube
options.C: Gray-top tube
options.D: Light blue-top tube

explanation: Easy to remember in the ward! Gray-top tubes are your go-to tubes for blood sugar and glucose tolerance tests. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h4)

question: What is the main job of sodium fluoride inside the blood collection tube?

options.A: It stains white blood cells for the microscope
options.B: It speeds up blood clotting so serum separates instantly
options.C: It stops blood cells from consuming the glucose inside the tube
options.D: It stops the blood sample from freezing during transport

explanation: Think of sodium fluoride as a preservative. Without it, the living blood cells inside the tube would keep eating up the glucose, giving you a falsely low lab result! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h4)

question: Which fasting blood sugar level is usually the cutoff for diagnosing diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Less than 70 mg/dL
options.B: 100 to 110 mg/dL
options.C: 80 to 90 mg/dL
options.D: 126 mg/dL or higher

explanation: Keep this number handy for your clinical postings: 126 mg/dL or higher on two separate tests points toward a diabetes diagnosis. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h5)

question: A patient's fasting blood sugar comes back at 115 mg/dL. How should you interpret this?

options.A: It confirms active type 1 diabetes
options.B: It is a completely normal result
options.C: It indicates prediabetes and impaired fasting glucose
options.D: It shows the patient had severe low blood sugar

explanation: Values between 100 and 125 mg/dL sit in the prediabetic zone. It's a great warning sign for patients to adjust their diet and lifestyle early! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h5)

question: Why can a sudden infection or severe physical stress cause a high fasting blood sugar reading?

options.A: White blood cells make sugar to fight germs
options.B: Stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline raise blood sugar
options.C: Infection stops the kidneys from filtering glucose
options.D: Fever destroys insulin receptors in the muscles

explanation: When the body is under stress or fighting sickness, it pumps out emergency hormones (like cortisol) that naturally push blood sugar up to give the body quick energy. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h6)

question: Which of the following does NOT falsely alter a fasting blood sugar result?

options.A: Experiencing emotional or physical stress
options.B: Fasting for longer than 14 hours
options.C: Taking steroid medications in the morning
options.D: Drinking plain water during the fast

explanation: Plain water is totally fine! It has no sugar or calories, so drinking it won't ruin your patient's lab test. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h6)

question: What is a key nursing duty right before a patient takes a fasting blood sugar test?

options.A: Confirming that the patient actually followed the fasting rules
options.B: Giving the patient a small snack to boost energy
options.C: Checking their urine output with a dipstick
options.D: Giving a quick dose of insulin just in case

explanation: Always double-check! Asking 'When was your last meal or drink?' ensures you don't send inaccurate lab samples to the path lab. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h7)

question: A patient waiting for a fasting blood sugar test looks pale, shaky, and dizzy. What should you do first?

options.A: Ask the lab tech to draw their blood right now
options.B: Give them a cup of hot black coffee with sugar
options.C: Check their blood sugar level immediately for low blood sugar
options.D: Tell them to keep waiting patiently for their turn

explanation: Safety first! Shaking, dizziness, and paleness during a fast are classic signs of hypoglycemia. Assess their blood sugar right away before doing anything else. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T18#GNS222_U2_T18_h7)

question: Why is a Random Blood Sugar (RBS) test so handy in everyday clinic or ward work?

options.A: It provides a three-month average of blood sugar
options.B: It is completely painless for every patient
options.C: It does not require a drop of blood
options.D: It can be done at any time without fasting

explanation: You don't need your patient to fast beforehand! That makes RBS a lifesaver during busy shifts and emergency admissions when you need answers right away. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h1)

question: In a busy emergency unit, why do nurses grab the glucometer so quickly?

options.A: It stops the liver from making extra glucose
options.B: It proves whether the patient has diabetes permanently
options.C: It replaces the need for a full medical history
options.D: It helps spot dangerous high or low sugar levels fast

explanation: Portable glucometers give you results in seconds. Catching a dangerously high or low blood sugar early lets you step in and save the day! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h1)

question: A patient's blood sugar drops suddenly. Which classic signs will you likely see first?

options.A: Shaking and sweating
options.B: Persistent high fever
options.C: Extreme thirst and dry skin
options.D: Frequent heavy urination

explanation: When blood sugar crashes, the body sounds an internal alarm (the sympathetic nervous system), making the patient shaky, sweaty, and jittery. Keep some juice nearby! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h2)

question: A confused patient arrives at the emergency ward. What is one of the quickest bedside checks you should do?

options.A: A random blood glucose check
options.B: A twenty-four-hour urine collection
options.C: A complete neurological reflex test
options.D: A fasting lipid profile test

explanation: Always check blood sugar when a patient's mental status changes. It takes seconds to rule out severe hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, which can look just like confusion! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h2)

question: What happens if glucometer test strips are left open to air and moisture for too long?

options.A: The chemical reagents inside them get ruined
options.B: They turn into a liquid gel substance
options.C: They change color to bright neon green
options.D: They become completely sterile to touch

explanation: Test strips are delicate! Moisture and air mess up the sensitive chemicals inside, giving you false readings. Always snap that strip container lid tightly shut. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h3)

question: Why must you check the expiration date on the test strip bottle before testing a patient?

options.A: Expired strips will refuse to fit into the meter
options.B: The glucometer automatically locks out expired strips
options.C: Using expired strips violates hospital electricity codes
options.D: Expired strips may give incorrect readings

explanation: The chemicals on strips degrade as time passes. Using fresh strips means you can trust your numbers and give safe patient care. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h3)

question: After pricking a finger for blood sugar, why should you wipe away the very first drop?

options.A: It contains tissue fluid that can dilute the sample
options.B: The glucometer machine will reject the first drop
options.C: It prevents the puncture site from bruising
options.D: It is contaminated with dangerous skin bacteria

explanation: That initial droplet usually mixes with clear tissue fluid from the skin poke, which throws off the glucose reading. Wiping it away gives you a true blood sample! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h4)

question: What is the right step after cleaning a patient's fingertip with an alcohol swab?

options.A: Wait for the alcohol to dry completely on the skin
options.B: Blow on the finger to speed up the drying process
options.C: Wipe the wet alcohol off with a sterile gauze pad
options.D: Prick the wet finger immediately to save time

explanation: If the alcohol is still wet, it mixes with the blood drop and dilutes it, giving you a false reading. A few seconds of patience guarantees an accurate result! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h4)

question: Along with classic symptoms, what random blood sugar level usually points toward diabetes?

options.A: 200 mg/dL or higher
options.B: 120 to 139 mg/dL
options.C: 90 to 110 mg/dL
options.D: 50 to 70 mg/dL

explanation: An RBS reading of 200 mg/dL or more, paired with signs like extreme thirst and frequent urination, is a strong red flag for diabetes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h5)

question: Why can't a nurse officially diagnose a patient with diabetes based on just one high random blood sugar test?

options.A: Glucometers cannot measure glucose above 150 mg/dL
options.B: Blood sugar levels never stay high for long periods
options.C: It is a screening test and needs confirmatory tests
options.D: Only laboratory nurses are allowed to make a diagnosis

explanation: Meals, stress, and illness can cause temporary spikes. Doctors rely on fasting tests or HbA1c to make a formal diagnosis. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h5)

question: Why might a patient with a severe infection show high blood sugar even if they haven't eaten?

options.A: Fever causes the glucometer to malfunction permanently
options.B: White blood cells consume all the insulin in the body
options.C: Infections directly damage the beta cells in the kidneys
options.D: Stress hormones released during illness raise blood sugar

explanation: When the body fights severe stress or infection, hormones like adrenaline and cortisol surge, telling the liver to dump extra glucose into the blood. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h6)

question: Which common class of medications is well known for pushing a patient's blood sugar up?

options.A: Corticosteroids
options.B: Diuretics
options.C: Antibiotics
options.D: Antacids

explanation: Drugs like prednisolone make the body less sensitive to insulin and push the liver to make more sugar. Good to watch out for in clinical practice! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h6)

question: A conscious patient's random blood sugar is 52 mg/dL and they feel shaky. What should you do right away?

options.A: Give 15 grams of fast-acting oral carbohydrates
options.B: Send the patient for an emergency CT scan of the head
options.C: Inject long-acting insulin into the deltoid muscle
options.D: Wait patiently for two hours and test the blood again

explanation: Since the patient is awake and able to swallow, give them quick-acting sugar (like glucose tablets or juice) to bring their blood sugar back up safely. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h7)

question: Why is it dangerous to give sugary drinks to an unconscious patient with low blood sugar?

options.A: The stomach will reject all sugary liquids
options.B: It can cause choking or enter the lungs
options.C: It will immediately cause a diabetic coma
options.D: It takes three days for the body to digest it

explanation: An unconscious patient cannot protect their airway. Giving them fluids by mouth can cause aspiration, sending liquid straight into their lungs. Safety first! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h7)

question: What is a vital safety item a patient living with diabetes should always carry around?

options.A: An extra pair of clean examination gloves
options.B: A spare blood pressure cuff and stethoscope
options.C: A quick source of sugar like glucose tablets
options.D: A bottle of surgical rubbing alcohol

explanation: Hypoglycemia can strike anywhere. Having glucose tablets or sweets on hand lets the patient treat a sudden crash immediately. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h8)

question: Why is washing hands with soap and water so important before a home blood glucose test?

options.A: Soap adds essential vitamins into the skin capillaries
options.B: Food residue on fingers can falsely raise the reading
options.C: Water activates the electronic screen on the meter
options.D: It is the only way to sterilize the testing strip

explanation: If a patient just ate fruit or biscuits, sticky sugar residue on their fingers will mix with the blood droplet and give a falsely high reading. Clean hands mean honest numbers! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T19#GNS222_U2_T19_h8)

question: What do endocrine glands release straight into the bloodstream?

options.A: Hormones
options.B: Mucus
options.C: Saliva
options.D: Enzymes

explanation: Spot on! Endocrine glands don't use ducts; they release hormones straight into our blood to act as chemical messengers all over the body. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why can taking a health history for hormone problems be tricky for a nurse?

options.A: Symptoms are usually vague and overlap across different disorders
options.B: Patients almost never remember when their symptoms started
options.C: Endocrine problems only affect one specific body system at a time
options.D: Laboratory tests are completely useless without a physical exam

explanation: You got it! Hormonal issues often start with everyday complaints like constant tiredness, making it hard to pin down the exact cause without patient probing. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which group of people is most likely to experience thyroid disorders?

options.A: Having a high-stress occupation
options.B: Living in a rural farming community
options.C: Being female
options.D: Being over the age of seventy

explanation: That's correct! Women are diagnosed with thyroid issues much more often than men, so keep a close eye out during assessments. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why is noting a patient's biological sex important when taking an endocrine history?

options.A: It helps identify conditions like thyroid disorders that affect women more often
options.B: It dictates the exact calorie count the patient needs daily
options.C: It replaces the need to perform a complete review of systems
options.D: It proves whether the patient has a genetic metabolic disease

explanation: Well done! Knowing biological sex helps us suspect certain gender-linked conditions, like thyroid imbalances, right from the start. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h2)

question: What are the classic early signs someone might show when developing new type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Painful joints in the hands and feet
options.B: Sudden swelling in both lower legs
options.C: Excessive thirst and frequent urination
options.D: Yellow discoloration of the skin and eyes

explanation: Spot on! When blood sugar is too high, the body pulls water into the urine to flush it out, leaving the patient super thirsty and running to the toilet constantly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why does a nurse need to ask when a patient's symptoms first started?

options.A: Chronic symptoms never require medical treatment
options.B: Rapid onset points to acute problems, while slow onset suggests chronic imbalances
options.C: Insurance companies require exact dates before approving lab tests
options.D: It helps the patient remember to take their medication on time

explanation: Exactly! The timeline helps you figure out if this is a sudden emergency or a long-standing, slow-burning hormonal issue. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which symptom is a classic sign of an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)?

options.A: A fast and pounding heartbeat
options.B: Shaking hands and muscle tremors
options.C: Intolerance to cold temperatures
options.D: Sudden and unexplained weight loss

explanation: You nailed it! When the metabolism slows down due to low thyroid hormone, patients feel chilly even when everyone else is warm. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h4)

question: A patient complains of putting on weight fast, being constipated, and feeling cold all the time. Which body system is likely acting up?

options.A: Musculoskeletal system
options.B: Respiratory system
options.C: Urinary system
options.D: Endocrine system

explanation: Correct! These are textbook signs of a sluggish metabolism, which points straight to the endocrine system—specifically an underactive thyroid. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is it important to ask if a patient has ever had surgery on their neck?

options.A: It can damage the thyroid or parathyroid glands
options.B: It stops the pancreas from producing insulin
options.C: It leads to chronic respiratory infections
options.D: It always causes permanent high blood pressure

explanation: Spot on! Because the thyroid and parathyroid glands live right in the neck, past surgeries there can sometimes accidentally disrupt hormone control. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why do nurses always ask about a family history of autoimmune diseases?

options.A: Family history determines the exact medication dose a patient needs
options.B: It is only used to fill out mandatory hospital paperwork
options.C: Genetics prevent patients from ever developing metabolic syndrome
options.D: Autoimmune conditions often cluster together in families, increasing endocrine risks

explanation: That's right! Autoimmune troubles like to run in families, putting patients at a higher risk for conditions like type 1 diabetes or thyroid disease. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which common class of medications is known to raise blood sugar levels over time?

options.A: Antibiotics
options.B: Corticosteroids
options.C: Antihistamines
options.D: Pain relievers

explanation: You got it! Steroids push the liver to make more sugar and make the body less sensitive to insulin, which sends blood glucose climbing. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h6)

question: An asthma patient taking steroid medications suddenly has high blood sugar readings. What should you suspect?

options.A: Severe dehydration from lack of water intake
options.B: Medication-induced alteration of glucose metabolism
options.C: A primary failure of the pancreas to produce insulin
options.D: An allergic reaction to the asthma medication

explanation: Spot on! Steroid therapy frequently messes with normal blood sugar control, even in people who have never had diabetes before. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h6)

question: Which hormone does the body pump out in large amounts during long periods of stress?

options.A: Insulin
options.B: Thyroxine
options.C: Cortisol
options.D: Estrogen

explanation: That's correct! Cortisol is our main stress hormone. It helps us deal with short-term stress, but high levels over time can cause real metabolic trouble. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why is checking a patient's daily stress level so important when managing diabetes?

options.A: Stress completely cures low blood sugar episodes
options.B: Stress hormones can raise blood sugar levels and make control harder
options.C: Patients with stress never need to take their medications
options.D: Emotional stress is the only cause of metabolic diseases

explanation: Well done! Stress triggers hormones that drive blood sugar up, making it much harder for the patient to keep their levels steady. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T2#GNS222_U2_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a Glucose Tolerance Test?

options.A: To measure how the body clears a glucose load over time
options.B: To evaluate how quickly the kidneys filter sugar from the blood
options.C: To measure the exact amount of insulin stored in the pancreas
options.D: To determine the average blood sugar level over the past three months

explanation: The GTT tracks how effectively the body processes and clears a specific amount of glucose over several hours. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h1)

question: Why is a GTT often preferred over a simple fasting blood glucose test during pregnancy?

options.A: It is completed in under fifteen minutes with only a single blood draw
options.B: It catches hidden metabolic problems that show up only after a sugar challenge
options.C: It poses zero risk of causing nausea or dizziness in pregnant women
options.D: It requires no prior fasting or dietary restrictions from the expectant mother

explanation: Gestational diabetes often presents only when the body is stressed with a glucose load, making the dynamic test necessary. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h1)

question: During which gestational weeks is a routine GTT typically performed for pregnant women?

options.A: Between 24 and 28 weeks
options.B: Between 8 and 12 weeks
options.C: Between 32 and 36 weeks
options.D: Immediately upon discovering the pregnancy

explanation: Gestational diabetes screening via GTT is standard practice during the late second trimester when placental hormones peak. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h2)

question: Why must a client eat a diet rich in carbohydrates for three days before a GTT?

options.A: To make sure the stomach is completely full before drinking the sweet syrup
options.B: To prevent false-positive results caused by low carbohydrate intake
options.C: To test how fast the liver can store extra glycogen reserves
options.D: To ensure the patient has plenty of energy to sit still during the test

explanation: If a patient restricts carbs beforehand, their body stops producing enough insulin, causing a fake diabetic spike during the test. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h3)

question: How many hours of fasting are typically required before a standard GTT begins?

options.A: No fasting is needed
options.B: 18 to 24 hours
options.C: 8 to 14 hours
options.D: 2 to 4 hours

explanation: An overnight fast of 8 to 14 hours establishes an accurate baseline blood glucose level before the test beverage is consumed. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h3)

question: What is the first blood collection step when performing a standard GTT?

options.A: Drawing blood immediately after drinking the glucose drink
options.B: Drawing a baseline fasting blood sample
options.C: Waiting two hours before taking any blood sample
options.D: Checking urine glucose before touching the patient

explanation: A fasting blood sample must always be collected first to establish the patient's baseline glucose level before giving the drink. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h4)

question: A client vomits twenty minutes after drinking the glucose beverage. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Proceed with the remaining blood draws because enough sugar was absorbed
options.B: Notify the laboratory and physician that the test must be rescheduled
options.C: Collect blood samples on an accelerated schedule to make up for lost time
options.D: Have the client drink a second dose of glucose immediately and continue

explanation: Vomiting means an unknown amount of glucose was absorbed, making the test results invalid; it must be rescheduled for another day. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h4)

question: Which two-hour post-load glucose level indicates impaired glucose tolerance in a non-pregnant adult?

options.A: 70 to 99 mg/dL
options.B: 140 to 199 mg/dL
options.C: 200 mg/dL or higher
options.D: 100 to 125 mg/dL

explanation: A two-hour reading between 140 and 199 mg/dL falls into the prediabetic range known as impaired glucose tolerance. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h5)

question: Why are diagnostic cutoff values for gestational diabetes stricter than those for non-pregnant adults?

options.A: Pregnant women drink larger volumes of glucose solution during the test
options.B: The placenta produces hormones that neutralize laboratory chemical reagents
options.C: High maternal blood sugar can harm the growing fetus and complicate delivery
options.D: Pregnancy causes the body to process and destroy injected insulin much faster

explanation: Strict thresholds protect the fetus from excessive growth, birth injuries, and newborn metabolic complications. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h5)

question: How does acute physical or emotional stress falsely affect a Glucose Tolerance Test?

options.A: It destroys red blood cells and ruins the laboratory blood samples
options.B: It releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol that raise blood sugar
options.C: It slows down digestion so the stomach cannot absorb the glucose drink
options.D: It forces the pancreas to release too much insulin, causing severe hypoglycemia

explanation: Stress hormones mobilize stored energy and push blood glucose levels up, which can mimic diabetes during the test. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h6)

question: Which of the following activities must a client avoid during the GTT waiting period?

options.A: Drinking small sips of plain water
options.B: Smoking cigarettes or drinking coffee
options.C: Sitting quietly in a comfortable chair
options.D: Reading a book or magazine

explanation: Nicotine and caffeine stimulate the nervous system and can alter blood glucose readings, so they are strictly prohibited. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h6)

question: What is the best immediate nursing action after a client finishes the final blood draw of a GTT?

options.A: Instruct the client to continue fasting until they get home
options.B: Administer a small dose of oral insulin to prevent a sugar spike
options.C: Encourage the client to exercise vigorously to burn off the sugar
options.D: Provide a snack containing protein and complex carbohydrates

explanation: Eating a balanced snack helps stabilize blood sugar and prevents the dizziness or fatigue caused by reactive hypoglycemia. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h7)

question: Why might a client feel dizzy or shaky immediately after completing a Glucose Tolerance Test?

options.A: The client has been deprived of clean drinking water for over 24 hours
options.B: A sudden surge of insulin can cause a temporary drop in blood sugar
options.C: Drawing multiple blood samples removes too many red blood cells
options.D: The concentrated sugar solution causes sudden dehydration of the brain

explanation: The large glucose load prompts an insulin spike that can overshoot and drop blood sugar below normal baseline levels, causing shakiness. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h7)

question: What causes the nausea and abdominal discomfort many clients feel right after drinking the GTT solution?

options.A: The solution is highly acidic and burns the lining of the esophagus
options.B: The high concentration of sugar creates an osmotic effect in the stomach and gut
options.C: Drinking cold liquid too quickly triggers an involuntary muscle spasm
options.D: The drink contains toxic chemical preservatives that irritate the liver

explanation: A hypertonic sugar drink draws water into the gastrointestinal tract through osmosis, often causing cramping, nausea, and bloating. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical mild side effect experienced during a GTT?

options.A: Sudden high fever and chills
options.B: Mild dizziness or lightheadedness
options.C: Sweating and feeling shaky
options.D: Nausea and stomach cramping

explanation: Fever and chills are signs of infection, not side effects of consuming a glucose solution. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h8)

question: Which assessment technique is most useful for evaluating most endocrine glands?

options.A: Auscultation of bruits
options.B: Deep organ percussion
options.C: Inspection and palpation
options.D: Direct visual scope

explanation: Because most endocrine structures lie deep within the body, nurses rely on visual inspection of systemic effects and careful palpation of accessible glands like the thyroid. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why do endocrine disorders often present with slow, subtle physical changes?

options.A: Clients hide early symptoms from nurses
options.B: Metabolic pathways stop completely at onset
options.C: Hormones act gradually on target tissues
options.D: Nurses only check clients during late stages

explanation: Endocrine imbalances alter cellular metabolism and growth over long periods, causing gradual shifts rather than sudden acute changes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h1)

question: A client with untreated hypothyroidism is most likely to exhibit which vital sign?

options.A: Hyperthermia
options.B: Tachycardia
options.C: Hypertension
options.D: Bradycardia

explanation: Low thyroid hormone levels slow down the basal metabolic rate, which frequently causes a decreased resting heart rate or bradycardia. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h2)

question: A client reports eating constantly yet losing significant weight. What condition should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Hyperthyroidism
options.B: Hypothyroidism
options.C: Cushing syndrome
options.D: Addison disease

explanation: Excess thyroid hormone revs up metabolism so high that calories burn faster than intake, leading to weight loss despite a hearty appetite. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h2)

question: Generalized skin hyperpigmentation is a classic physical sign of which endocrine disorder?

options.A: Addison disease
options.B: Hyperthyroidism
options.C: Diabetes insipidus
options.D: Cushing syndrome

explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency triggers elevated ACTH production, which shares a precursor molecule that stimulates excess melanin production and skin darkening. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which integumentary finding is most characteristic of severe hypothyroidism?

options.A: Warm and moist skin
options.B: Thin skin with striae
options.C: Dry and coarse skin
options.D: Oily skin with acne

explanation: Reduced sebaceous and sweat gland activity resulting from low thyroid hormone levels causes the skin to become dry, thick, and rough. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the medical term for the forward protrusion of the eyeballs seen in Graves disease?

options.A: Anisocoria
options.B: Strabismus
options.C: Ptosis
options.D: Exophthalmos

explanation: Inflammation and tissue swelling behind the eyes in autoimmune hyperthyroidism push the eyeballs forward, creating a characteristic staring look. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why does the nurse ask the client to swallow water during palpation of the thyroid gland?

options.A: The thyroid rises during swallowing, making it easier to feel
options.B: Water intake helps hydrate the vocal cords for speech testing
options.C: Swallowing prevents the client from coughing mid-examination
options.D: It relaxes the neck blood vessels to lower stroke risk

explanation: The thyroid gland is attached to the trachea and laryngeal cartilage, causing it to move upward noticeably whenever a person swallows. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h4)

question: How do deep tendon reflexes typically present in a client with hypothyroidism?

options.A: Brisk and hyperactive responses
options.B: Normal strength with absent reflexes
options.C: Completely absent without sensory loss
options.D: Sluggish and delayed relaxation phase

explanation: Hypothyroid reflexes feature a characteristic slow snapback during the relaxation phase, which is a classic diagnostic clue for the condition. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which physical test helps a nurse detect fine motor tremors associated with excessive thyroid hormone?

options.A: Pressing feet downward against resistance
options.B: Extending hands straight with spread fingers
options.C: Walking heel-to-toe across a straight line
options.D: Tapping lightly over the facial nerve area

explanation: Holding the arms outstretched with fingers separated makes fine muscular tremors in the hands much easier to observe visually. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the main reason for documenting physical assessment findings with precise measurements?

options.A: To satisfy legal paperwork requirements for insurance
options.B: To track changes and treatment response over time
options.C: To replace the need for laboratory blood testing
options.D: To prevent the client from reading their own chart

explanation: Precise measurements like goiter dimensions or weight changes allow nurses to objectively evaluate whether medical interventions are working. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h6)

question: A nurse notes cold, dry skin, bradycardia, and delayed reflexes in a client. What action should follow?

options.A: Synthesize findings and report potential hypothyroidism to the doctor
options.B: Encourage immediate strenuous exercise to warm up the client
options.C: Administer emergency intravenous insulin based on skin signs
options.D: Document the findings as normal aging changes and discharge

explanation: Recognizing a cluster of symptoms pointing to a specific endocrine disorder allows the nurse to communicate effectively with the healthcare team for diagnosis. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T3#GNS222_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the main goal of diagnostic testing for hormone (endocrine) disorders?

options.A: To destroy overactive hormone-producing tissue
options.B: To permanently replace missing organ functions
options.C: To cure infectious agents causing gland failure
options.D: To measure hormone levels and check organ response

explanation: You've got this! Endocrine tests simply check how much hormone is in the body and see how target organs respond to signals. It is all about checking the balance. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is exact timing so important when collecting blood for hormone tests?

options.A: Hormones break down within seconds after leaving the bloodstream
options.B: Patient fasting has no effect on most endocrine lab results
options.C: Laboratory technicians only process hormone samples in the morning
options.D: Hormone levels change based on daily body rhythms and activities

explanation: Great job thinking like a nurse! Many hormones rise and fall throughout the day or shift with meals, so getting the timing right is key to an accurate result. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h1)

question: What does a 'free hormone' blood test actually measure?

options.A: The rate at which the liver destroys excess hormones
options.B: Only the active hormone not bound to carrier proteins
options.C: Only the inactive hormones attached to transport molecules
options.D: The total amount of protein stored inside the endocrine gland

explanation: Think of free hormones as the ones floating around free and ready to work! Unbound hormones are the active fraction available to affect the body. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h2)

question: Why would a doctor order an antibody blood test for someone with a suspected endocrine problem?

options.A: To test how quickly the kidneys filter out waste products
options.B: To determine if the patient has a bacterial infection
options.C: To check for autoimmune destruction of endocrine tissue
options.D: To measure the exact weight and size of the pituitary gland

explanation: Spot on! Antibody tests help us see if the body's immune system is mistakenly attacking its own hormone glands, like in thyroid disorders. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h2)

question: What is the main perk of doing a 24-hour urine collection instead of just one blood test?

options.A: It captures total hormone output and smooths out hourly spikes
options.B: It measures intracellular hormone synthesis inside the bone marrow
options.C: It requires no special patient preparation or storage rules
options.D: It can be completed in less than five minutes at the bedside

explanation: Hormones can spike and dip all day long. Collecting urine over a full 24 hours gives a complete, average picture of what the body is putting out! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h3)

question: How does a 'stimulation test' help us figure out an endocrine issue?

options.A: It forces the pancreas to stop making insulin during high stress
options.B: It tests if an underactive gland can produce hormones when given a trigger
options.C: It measures the permanent destruction of the pituitary stalk
options.D: It permanently blocks all hormone receptors in peripheral tissues

explanation: You're doing great! If a gland is acting lazy, we give it a special trigger (stimulation) to see if it still has the energy to wake up and produce hormones. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the main goal of an endocrine suppression test?

options.A: To measure how fast the kidneys reabsorb glucose from the urine
options.B: To see if a gland stops producing hormones when given a suppressing agent
options.C: To stimulate a sleeping gland into producing maximum hormone levels
options.D: To permanently destroy overactive cells inside the adrenal cortex

explanation: Exactly! While stimulation tests wake glands up, suppression tests check if an overactive gland knows how to quiet down when it's supposed to. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why is the HbA1c test so helpful for managing diabetes over time?

options.A: It detects acute kidney failure caused by high blood sugar spikes
options.B: It measures the exact amount of insulin stored inside pancreatic beta cells
options.C: It evaluates the immediate effect of the patient's last meal on glucose
options.D: It shows average blood sugar levels over the past two to three months

explanation: Spot on! Because sugar binds to red blood cells for their whole lifespan, HbA1c gives us a reliable historical report card of blood sugar over 2 to 3 months. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which imaging scan is usually best for getting a detailed look at the tiny pituitary gland?

options.A: Superficial ultrasound scanning
options.B: Standard chest X-ray examination
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
options.D: Radioactive iodine uptake probe

explanation: You've got this! MRI gives amazing soft-tissue pictures, making it the top choice for checking out small, deep structures like the pituitary gland. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h5)

question: A patient is getting a CT scan with contrast dye for an adrenal tumor. What is a vital nursing check beforehand?

options.A: Measuring the patient's 24-hour urine cortisol
options.B: Checking for allergies to iodine or shellfish
options.C: Testing the patient for active thyroid antibodies
options.D: Ensuring the patient has swallowed radioactive iodine

explanation: Safety first! Contrast dye often contains iodine, so checking for allergies beforehand helps prevent severe allergic reactions. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h5)

question: What does a 'cold' nodule on a radioactive thyroid scan usually mean?

options.A: A hyperactive area that is producing excessive thyroid hormones
options.B: An allergic reaction to the contrast dye used during imaging
options.C: A normal section of tissue unaffected by the radioactive tracer
options.D: An area of low metabolic activity with a higher cancer risk

explanation: A 'cold' spot means the tissue didn't soak up the tracer well. That sluggish activity can sometimes point toward a higher risk of malignancy, requiring a closer look. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why must patients avoid iodine-heavy foods and meds before a radioactive iodine thyroid test?

options.A: Dietary iodine causes immediate allergic shock in all endocrine patients
options.B: Iodine completely destroys the scanning machine sensors during the test
options.C: Excess iodine can saturate the thyroid and interfere with tracer uptake
options.D: Non-radioactive iodine neutralizes the radiation inside the bloodstream

explanation: Think of the thyroid like a sponge. If it's already full of regular dietary iodine, it won't absorb the radioactive test tracer, messing up the results! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the main reason a doctor performs a fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy on a thyroid lump?

options.A: To obtain cells for microscopic examination to check for cancer
options.B: To inject radioactive isotopes directly into the thyroid tissue
options.C: To completely remove the entire thyroid gland without surgery
options.D: To measure the 24-hour baseline hormone production levels

explanation: Spot on! An FNA takes a tiny sample of cells so the lab can check them under a microscope to confirm or rule out cancer. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is the most crucial nursing check right after a neck biopsy or fine-needle aspiration?

options.A: Monitoring for signs of airway obstruction or bleeding
options.B: Checking for sudden spikes in fasting blood glucose
options.C: Testing the patient's 24-hour urine catecholamine levels
options.D: Encouraging immediate heavy physical exercise

explanation: Always protect the airway! Since the procedure is right in the neck near major blood vessels and the trachea, nurses must watch closely for swelling or bleeding. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which nursing action is a must when managing a timed suppression test?

options.A: Stopping all patient monitoring once the initial baseline is drawn
options.B: Administering the suppression medication at random convenient times
options.C: Ensuring blood samples are drawn at the exact prescribed intervals
options.D: Allowing the patient to eat high-sugar meals during the test procedure

explanation: Precision is everything here! Dynamic tests rely completely on exact timing to track how hormone levels change after giving a medication. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h8)

question: A patient is very anxious about tests for a suspected adrenal tumor. What is the best initial nursing action?

options.A: Tell the patient to refuse all invasive tests until they feel calmer
options.B: Provide clear, simple explanations of the tests and offer emotional support
options.C: Administer a strong sedative without a doctor's prescription
options.D: Reassure the patient that adrenal tumors are never cancerous

explanation: You're a natural! Clear, compassionate communication and emotional support go a long way in calming patient fears and helping them through tests. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T4#GNS222_U2_T4_h8)

question: Which blood vessel delivers nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract directly to the liver?

options.A: Renal artery
options.B: Hepatic portal vein
options.C: Inferior vena cava
options.D: Abdominal aorta

explanation: The hepatic portal vein collects blood from the digestive organs and delivers it straight to the liver for nutrient processing and filtration. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why is the synthesis of albumin by hepatocytes critical for normal physiological function?

options.A: It maintains plasma oncotic pressure and prevents fluid leakage
options.B: It transports oxygen molecules directly to peripheral tissues
options.C: It directly converts toxic ammonia into water-soluble urea
options.D: It provides the primary energy source for cardiac muscle contraction

explanation: Albumin is the main plasma protein responsible for holding fluid inside the vascular space through oncotic pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h1)

question: What pathological change characterizes chronic liver injury and scarring?

options.A: Hypertrophy of functional lobules
options.B: Dilation of the hepatic arteries
options.C: Rapid regeneration of healthy cells
options.D: Fibrosis and architectural distortion

explanation: Chronic injury stimulates stellate cells to deposit collagen, resulting in fibrous scar tissue that alters the normal structure of the liver. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h2)

question: A patient develops liver damage from long-term heavy alcohol use. What is the primary process occurring in the liver tissue?

options.A: Infection of the Kupffer cells by a bacterial pathogen
options.B: Blockage of the renal tubules by precipitated proteins
options.C: Toxic injury leading to inflammation and scarring
options.D: Sudden destruction of red blood cells in the sinusoids

explanation: Alcohol metabolism generates toxic byproducts that directly damage hepatocytes, triggering an inflammatory response and progressive fibrosis. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which type of viral hepatitis is primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route via contaminated water?

options.A: Hepatitis C
options.B: Hepatitis B
options.C: Hepatitis D
options.D: Hepatitis A

explanation: Hepatitis A virus spreads through ingestion of contaminated food and water, often causing acute outbreaks in areas with poor sanitation. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h3)

question: Why do patients with acute viral hepatitis develop pale stools and dark urine?

options.A: The kidneys stop filtering red blood cell waste entirely
options.B: Excess protein breakdown releases abnormal dyes into blood
options.C: Dehydration concentrates all waste products in the bladder
options.D: Bile flow obstruction or backup alters pigment excretion

explanation: Inflammation blocks bile excretion into the intestines, causing urobilinogen to spill into the urine while depriving the stool of its normal pigment. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary hemodynamic consequence of structural scarring in cirrhosis?

options.A: Portal hypertension
options.B: Renal artery stenosis
options.C: Pulmonary congestion
options.D: Systemic hypotension

explanation: Fibrotic tissue compresses intrahepatic blood vessels, raising blood pressure inside the portal venous system significantly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h4)

question: A patient with cirrhosis is at high risk for upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to which physiological change?

options.A: Increased stomach acid secretion caused by poor bile digestion
options.B: Direct irritation of the gastric mucosa by ingested medications
options.C: Development of fragile esophageal varices from high portal pressure
options.D: Excessive production of clotting factors by damaged hepatocytes

explanation: Portal hypertension forces blood through small collateral channels in the esophagus, forming delicate vessels that easily rupture under pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary neurotoxin responsible for causing hepatic encephalopathy in liver failure?

options.A: Creatinine
options.B: Albumin
options.C: Ammonia
options.D: Bilirubin

explanation: The failing liver fails to convert protein-breakdown ammonia into urea, allowing it to accumulate in the bloodstream and affect brain function. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h5)

question: A patient with advanced cirrhosis holds their hands out with wrists extended, and the hands quickly flap downward. What is this clinical sign called?

options.A: Trousseau's sign
options.B: Asterixis
options.C: Homan's sign
options.D: Cullen's sign

explanation: Asterixis, or the 'liver flap', is a classic neurological sign of elevated ammonia levels and impending hepatic encephalopathy. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which blood test result best reflects the synthetic function of the liver?

options.A: Serum creatinine level
options.B: Random blood glucose
options.C: Serum albumin level
options.D: White blood cell count

explanation: Albumin is synthesized exclusively by hepatocytes, making its blood level a direct indicator of the liver's synthetic capacity. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h6)

question: Why is the prothrombin time (PT) or INR typically prolonged in a patient with severe liver failure?

options.A: Platelets are rapidly destroyed inside the enlarged spleen
options.B: The liver cannot produce adequate blood-clotting factors
options.C: Renal clearance of clotting inhibitors is abnormally slow
options.D: Bone marrow suppression prevents normal platelet release

explanation: Most coagulation factors are synthesized in the liver; when liver function declines, clotting times lengthen significantly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h6)

question: How does lactulose work in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy?

options.A: It traps and removes intestinal ammonia through the stool
options.B: It destroys the hepatitis virus inside the bloodstream
options.C: It directly stimulates albumin production in liver lobules
options.D: It widens the narrowed lumen of the hepatic portal vein

explanation: Lactulose acidifies the gut lumen, converting free ammonia into ammonium ions that cannot cross into the blood, clearing them via bowel movements. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of administering non-selective beta-blockers to a patient diagnosed with esophageal varices?

options.A: To increase systemic blood pressure and improve kidney function
options.B: To prevent the absorption of dietary fats and proteins
options.C: To relax the muscular walls of the lower esophagus
options.D: To decrease portal venous pressure and prevent bleeding

explanation: Beta-blockers reduce portal blood flow and pressure, lowering the risk of fragile esophageal varices rupturing. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h7)

question: A nurse is monitoring a patient with cirrhosis for fluid retention. Which assessment method provides the most accurate daily data?

options.A: Checking the skin turgor over the clavicle every morning
options.B: Weighing the client daily at the same time on the same scale
options.C: Measuring the total daily urine output using a graduated jug
options.D: Palpating the lower extremities for firm pitting edema

explanation: Daily weights are the most sensitive indicator of fluid gain or loss in clients with ascites and edema. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T5#GNS222_U2_T5_h8)

question: Which instruction is most important when educating a patient with chronic liver disease regarding self-medication?

options.A: Stop all prescribed blood pressure medications immediately
options.B: Increase dietary protein intake without medical supervision
options.C: Take high doses of vitamin supplements to protect the liver

question: What is the primary function of the gallbladder between meals?

options.D: Metabolism of circulating bilirubin

question: Which hormone is released when you eat fat, causing the gallbladder to contract?

options.A: Gastrin
options.B: Cholecystokinin

explanation: Ingested fats stimulate the release of cholecystokinin from the duodenal mucosa, which directly prompts gallbladder smooth muscle contraction. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h1)

question: What does the medical term cholelithiasis mean?

options.B: Infection of the hepatic ducts

options.D: Necrosis of the liver parenchyma

question: What is the most common cause of acute cholecystitis?

options.A: Excessive dietary fat intake over time
options.B: Primary autoimmune destruction of bile ducts
options.C: Bacterial colonization from systemic sepsis
options.D: Cystic duct obstruction by a gallstone
