question: Which patient factor greatly increases the risk of developing gallstones?

options.A: Female gender
options.B: Male predominance
options.C: Low body weight
options.D: Younger age group

explanation: Hormonal differences, particularly the influence of oestrogen, make women more susceptible to cholesterol gallstones. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h3)

question: Why does rapid weight loss through strict dieting put a person at risk for gallstones?

options.A: Permanent closure of the sphincter of Oddi
options.B: Direct mechanical irritation from fasting
options.C: Increased mobilization of cholesterol into bile
options.D: Infection of the liver by intestinal flora

explanation: Rapid breakdown of body fat releases excess cholesterol into the biliary system, raising the risk of precipitation. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h3)

question: What is the classic physical exam sign for acute cholecystitis?

options.A: McBurney point tenderness
options.B: Murphy sign
options.C: Cullen sign
options.D: Grey Turner sign

explanation: Inspiratory arrest upon deep palpation of the right upper quadrant strongly suggests an inflamed gallbladder. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why does gallbladder pain often spread to the right shoulder?

options.A: Lumbar plexus compression
options.B: Phrenic nerve irritation
options.C: Referred cardiac pathway
options.D: Intercostal muscle spasm

explanation: Inflammation near the diaphragm stimulates the adjacent phrenic nerve, referring pain to the shoulder region. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the main imaging test used to check for gallstones?

options.A: Plain abdominal radiograph
options.B: Abdominal ultrasound
options.C: Barium swallow study
options.D: Magnetic resonance imaging

explanation: Ultrasound is highly sensitive for detecting gallstones and assessing wall thickening without radiation exposure. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h5)

question: Which lab value usually rises first when the common bile duct is blocked?

options.A: Serum alkaline phosphatase
options.B: Blood urea nitrogen
options.C: Serum amylase level
options.D: Fastin blood glucose

explanation: Alkaline phosphatase is concentrated in the biliary epithelium and elevates rapidly when bile flow is impeded. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h5)

question: What is the immediate dietary order for a patient having an acute gallstone attack?

options.A: Nil per os to rest the biliary system
options.B: High-fat diet to empty the organ completely
options.C: Strict clear liquid diet with added oils
options.D: High-fiber meals to bind excess bile acids

explanation: Withholding food prevents the release of cholecystokinin, thereby reducing painful gallbladder contractions. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h6)

question: Oral dissolution medicine using bile acids works best for which type of stones?

options.A: Calcified bilirubinate debris
options.B: Mixed iron-calcium deposits
options.C: Large pigmented stones
options.D: Small cholesterol stones

explanation: Bile acids work by gradually dissolving cholesterol crystals, making them ineffective against hard, calcified stones. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is the standard surgery for treating symptomatic gallstones?

options.A: Percutaneous needle drainage
options.B: Open partial cholecystotomy
options.C: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
options.D: Endoscopic sphincterotomy alone

explanation: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the standard approach due to minimal scarring and rapid patient recovery. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h7)

question: A patient with a T-tube after common bile duct exploration has greenish drainage. What is the primary nursing action?

options.A: Clamp the tube immediately to promote normal digestion
options.B: Notify the surgeon to remove the tube within two hours
options.C: Irrigate the tube routinely with sterile normal saline
options.D: Monitor drainage amount, color, and secure the tubing

explanation: Observing output and preventing accidental dislodgement are critical nursing responsibilities for T-tube management. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h7)

question: Why can a gallstone lead to acute pancreatitis?

options.A: It can obstruct the ampulla of Vater and block pancreatic ducts
options.B: It causes systemic dehydration that destroys pancreatic cells
options.C: It stimulates excessive production of insulin by islets
options.D: It directly damages the pancreatic tail during transit

explanation: A stone lodged at the shared exit point traps pancreatic secretions, leading to autodigestion and inflammation of the pancreas. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h8)

question: Which of these is NOT a known complication of acute cholecystitis?

options.A: Renal cell carcinoma
options.B: Peritoneal perforation
options.C: Empyema formation
options.D: Gangrene of the wall

explanation: Renal cell carcinoma is a kidney malignancy unrelated to the biliary tract, unlike empyema, gangrene, and perforation. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T6#GNS222_U2_T6_h8)

question: What are the hormone-producing cell clusters located within the pancreas called?

options.A: Gastric mucosal pits
options.B: Hepatic portal nodes
options.C: Islets of Langerhans
options.D: Acinar cell clusters

explanation: The endocrine portion of the pancreas contains groups of cells named the islets of Langerhans, which produce insulin and glucagon. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why does damage to the pancreas often lead to both digestive problems and blood sugar issues?

options.A: Digestive enzymes and hormones are stored inside the exact same cells.
options.B: Insulin is required to activate all major pancreatic digestive enzymes.
options.C: The pancreas has both exocrine and endocrine functions in one organ.
options.D: The pancreas shares a direct blood supply with the liver and stomach.

explanation: You've got this! The pancreas is a multitasker. It acts as an exocrine gland to help us digest food, and an endocrine gland to manage our blood sugar. When it gets injured, both jobs take a hit. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h1)

question: What are the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Stomach ulcers and low dietary fiber
options.B: Bacterial infection and high salt intake
options.C: Autoimmune disease and heavy smoking
options.D: Gallstones and chronic alcohol abuse

explanation: Gallstones blocking the bile duct and excessive alcohol consumption account for the vast majority of acute pancreatitis cases. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h2)

question: What main process causes tissue damage inside the pancreas during acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Infection of pancreatic tissue by gut bacteria traveling upward
options.B: Rapid formation of scar tissue blocking the pancreatic duct
options.C: Autodigestion of the pancreas by its own early-activated enzymes
options.D: Complete lack of blood supply caused by sudden heart failure

explanation: Think of it as friendly fire! Digestive enzymes turn on too early while still inside the pancreas, and they accidentally start breaking down the organ's own tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h2)

question: Where is the classic pain of acute pancreatitis felt, and where does it usually spread?

options.A: Chest region radiating to the left arm
options.B: Upper abdomen radiating to the back
options.C: Suprapubic area radiating to the lower back
options.D: Lower right abdomen radiating to the thigh

explanation: Spot on! Pancreatic pain is notorious for being felt right in the upper belly and boring straight through to the back. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h3)

question: A patient asks why their belly pain gets worse after eating a meal. What is the best way to explain this?

options.A: Food stretches the stomach wall, putting physical pressure on the pancreas.
options.B: Eating triggers the pancreas to release enzymes, which irritates the inflamed tissue.
options.C: Eating causes bile to back up instantly into the liver, stopping digestion.
options.D: Food particles enter the pancreatic duct directly, blocking the flow of blood.

explanation: Makes sense, right? When food enters the gut, your body tells the pancreas to pump out digestive enzymes. If the pancreas is already inflamed, sending out those juices just makes it hurt more. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h3)

question: What term describes the fatty, foul-smelling stools seen in patients with chronic pancreatitis?

options.A: Steatorrhea
options.B: Acholuria
options.C: Hematochezia
options.D: Melena

explanation: Great recall! Steatorrhea is the medical term for fatty, oily stools. It happens because the damaged pancreas can't make the enzymes needed to digest fats properly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why do patients with long-standing chronic pancreatitis eventually develop diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Dietary restrictions force the body to rely entirely on stored body fat.
options.B: Scar tissue gradually destroys the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas.
options.C: The liver stops responding to insulin because it is overworked by fat digestion.
options.D: Chronic vomiting causes a permanent chemical imbalance in blood sugar.

explanation: You're doing great! As chronic inflammation forms scar tissue over time, it slowly wipes out the insulin-making cells in the islets of Langerhans, leading to diabetes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h4)

question: Which blood test is more specific for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Hemoglobin
options.B: Lipase
options.C: Creatinine
options.D: Albumin

explanation: Spot on! Serum lipase is the go-to test because it's much more specific to the pancreas than amylase, and it stays elevated longer during an attack. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which imaging test is generally considered the best for viewing tissue death and fluid collections in acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Standard chest X-ray
options.B: Basic abdominal ultrasound
options.C: CT scan with contrast
options.D: Electrocardiogram strip

explanation: You got it! A contrast CT gives doctors the clearest pictures to spot inflammation, dead tissue, and hidden pockets of fluid around the pancreas. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h5)

question: What is the main reason a patient with acute pancreatitis is kept NPO (nothing by mouth)?

options.A: To rest the pancreas and stop the release of digestive enzymes
options.B: To prevent choking during sudden episodes of severe vomiting
options.C: To keep the bowel completely clean for diagnostic X-rays
options.D: To prepare the stomach for emergency surgical removal

explanation: Brilliant! Keeping the patient NPO means no food enters the gut, which gives the hardworking pancreas a well-deserved break so it stops producing damaging enzymes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h6)

question: When should a patient with chronic pancreatitis take their prescribed pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy?

options.A: With every meal and snack
options.B: Only when eating foods high in sugar
options.C: Only when abdominal pain begins
options.D: Once daily right before bedtime

explanation: Spot on! Enzymes need to be taken right along with all food and snacks so they can mix with the nutrients and help the body digest food properly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h6)

question: What early symptom is typically caused by a tumor in the head of the pancreas blocking the bile duct?

options.A: High fever
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Constipation
options.D: Vision loss

explanation: You're crushing it! When a tumor blocks the bile duct, bilirubin backs up into the bloodstream, turning the skin and eyes yellow (jaundice). [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h7)

question: What complex surgery involves removing the head of the pancreas, the duodenum, and the gallbladder?

options.A: Whipple procedure
options.B: Cholecystostomy
options.C: Splenectomy
options.D: Gastric bypass

explanation: The Whipple procedure is a major operation performed to treat tumors located in the head of the pancreas. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h7)

question: What is a major worry when pancreatic fluid leaks from the surgical site after a Whipple procedure?

options.A: Pancreatic fistula and infection
options.B: Immediate high blood pressure
options.C: Chronic kidney stone formation
options.D: Sudden permanent liver failure

explanation: Good to know! A leak at the surgical join creates a pancreatic fistula, which can spill harsh digestive juices into the belly and cause a severe infection. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h8)

question: Which nursing action is MOST important when caring for a patient with active surgical drains after pancreatic surgery?

options.A: Flush the drainage tubing with sterile water every two hours.
options.B: Monitor and record the amount and color of drainage regularly.
options.C: Clamp all surgical drains shut to prevent accidental fluid loss.
options.D: Change the surrounding skin dressings once every week.

explanation: Keep up the great clinical thinking! Tracking your drain output closely helps you catch dangerous warning signs like bleeding or fistulas early. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the main problem in diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Fast sugar breakdown
options.B: Too much insulin produced

options.D: Thick blood

explanation: Diabetes mellitus happens when blood glucose levels remain high because the body has trouble making or using insulin properly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which part of the body makes the hormone insulin?

options.A: Adrenal gland
options.B: Kidneys
options.C: Liver
options.D: Pancreas

explanation: Special cells inside the pancreas called the islets of Langerhans produce and release insulin into the body. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h1)

question: What is the main cause of Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Cells refusing to use insulin
options.B: High sugar intake from diet
options.C: Body attacks its own insulin-making cells
options.D: Temporary stress during pregnancy

explanation: Type 1 diabetes happens when the immune system mistakenly destroys the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas, stopping insulin production completely. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h2)

question: How is Type 2 diabetes different from Type 1?

options.A: The body resists insulin and doesn't make enough
options.B: The body stops making any insulin at all
options.C: It only happens in young children
options.D: It needs lifelong daily insulin from day one

explanation: In Type 2 diabetes, the body still makes some insulin, but the cells do not respond to it well, and the pancreas cannot keep up with the demand. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h2)

question: What is the liver process of making new glucose from fats or proteins called?

options.A: Glycogenolysis
options.B: Lipolysis
options.C: Gluconeogenesis
options.D: Glycolysis

explanation: Gluconeogenesis is how the liver creates fresh glucose from non-carbohydrate sources when the body needs energy. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h3)

question: Why do ketone bodies form when diabetes is not controlled?

options.A: Muscles make proteins too fast
options.B: Cells lack glucose, so the body burns fat instead
options.C: The kidneys filter too much water
options.D: The kidneys turn extra blood sugar into ketones

explanation: When body cells cannot get glucose for energy, they break down stored fat instead, which leaves behind waste products called ketones. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h3)

question: What is the medical term for extreme thirst in diabetes?

options.A: Pyrexia
options.B: Polyuria
options.C: Polydipsia

explanation: Polydipsia means having an abnormally high level of thirst, which happens because the body is losing too much fluid. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why does high blood sugar cause frequent urination?

options.A: A urinary infection starts up
options.B: Extra sugar pulls water into the urine
options.C: High blood pressure pushes fluid directly to the bladder
options.D: Kidneys lose their muscle strength

explanation: High amounts of glucose act like a magnet, drawing water along with it into the urine and causing frequent trips to the bathroom. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h4)

question: How long does an HbA1c test show blood sugar control?

question: What fasting blood sugar level points to a diagnosis of diabetes?

options.D: 10.0 mmol/L

question: What is the usual first drug given for Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Glibenclamide
options.B: Metformin
options.C: Acarbose
options.D: Insulin glargine

explanation: Metformin is the standard first medication because it helps lower liver sugar production and makes body cells more sensitive to insulin. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h6)

question: How does metformin help lower blood sugar?

options.A: By destroying bad beta cells
options.B: By blocking water in the kidneys

explanation: Metformin works mainly in the liver to slow down glucose production while helping body tissues use insulin more effectively. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h6)

question: Which diabetic emergency involves high blood sugar, dehydration, and acid buildup?

options.A: Low blood sugar shock
options.B: Diabetic ketoacidosis

options.D: High sugar hyperosmolar state

question: What is the main difference between microvascular and macrovascular complications?

options.C: Micro affects small blood vessels, macro affects large ones

explanation: The names come from the size of the blood vessels involved, with microvascular affecting tiny vessels in eyes and kidneys, and macrovascular affecting large arteries. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h7)

question: What daily foot care habit should a nurse teach a diabetic patient?

options.C: Put strong medicated ointment between toes

question: Why must nurses teach patients how to spot low blood sugar?

options.A: To stop them from drinking fluids
options.B: Low blood sugar can quickly cause confusion or fainting
options.C: To help them take more pills
options.D: To prevent eye damage

explanation: Hypoglycemia is an urgent situation that needs quick action because dropping blood sugar can rapidly lead to confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T8#GNS222_U2_T8_h8)

question: What does the back part of the pituitary gland (posterior pituitary) actually do?

options.A: It stores and releases hormones made by the hypothalamus.

options.C: It controls blood sugar levels using special insulin cells.
options.D: It filters harmful toxins out of the brain's blood supply.

explanation: Think of the posterior pituitary as a warehouse! It doesn't manufacture its own hormones; instead, it holds onto oxytocin and ADH made by the hypothalamus until it's time to release them. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h1)

question: Why do we call the pituitary gland the 'master gland' of the body?

options.A: It directly controls the activity of several other hormone glands.
options.B: It makes every single hormone needed to keep you alive without help.
options.C: It controls your conscious thought and memory along with the brain.
options.D: It is simply the largest endocrine organ located inside the skull.

explanation: You got this! It earns the title 'master gland' because its hormones act like boss signals telling other glands—like your thyroid and adrenals—when to release their own hormones. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h1)

question: What is the most common cause of trouble in the pituitary gland?

options.A: The body's immune system attacking the back part of the gland
options.B: Severe, long-term bacterial infections spreading through the brain
options.C: Cancerous tumors that have spread to the brain from the lungs
options.D: Benign (non-cancerous) tumors known as pituitary adenomas

explanation: Don't panic when you hear 'tumor'—most pituitary problems come from benign growths called adenomas. They can either pump out too many hormones or squish normal gland tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h2)

question: Why do growing pituitary tumors often cause vision changes like trouble seeing out of the sides of your eyes?

options.A: Not having enough thyroid hormone causes the retina to wear out quickly.
options.B: Too much growth hormone makes the muscles around the eyeballs swell.
options.C: High pressure inside the skull damages the back part of the brain directly.
options.D: The growing mass presses upward directly against the optic chiasm.

explanation: Location is everything! The optic chiasm (where your eye nerves cross) sits right above the pituitary gland. When the gland swells up, it bumps right into those nerves. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h2)

question: What is the main physical sign you will see in an adult with acromegaly?

options.A: Enlargement of the hands, feet, and facial bones
options.B: Sudden and severe hair loss all over the scalp
options.C: Extreme weight loss with rapid muscle wasting
options.D: Sudden, very rapid growth in height during childhood

question: A patient comes in with a 'buffalo hump' of fat, a round belly, and purple stretch marks on their skin. Which condition matches these signs?

options.A: Hypothyroidism
options.B: Cushing's disease
options.C: Acromegaly
options.D: Diabetes insipidus

explanation: These classic changes happen when the body is flooded with too much cortisol. In Cushing's disease, this is often kicked off by a tiny pituitary tumor pushing out extra ACTH. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h3)

question: What exactly is Sheehan's syndrome?

options.A: Immune system attack on the adrenal glands brought on by stress
options.B: Death of pituitary tissue due to severe blood loss right after childbirth
options.C: A benign tumor causing sudden vision loss in older men
options.D: A genetic inability to make antidiuretic hormone after bumping your head

explanation: During delivery, a massive hemorrhage can drop blood pressure so low that the hardworking pituitary gland is starved of blood and oxygen, leading to tissue death (necrosis). [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why is secondary adrenal insufficiency caused by pituitary problems so dangerous for a patient?

options.A: Blood sugar shoots up dangerously high because of a lack of balance.
options.B: The kidneys suddenly stop filtering waste products out of the blood.
options.C: Lacking ACTH makes the adrenal glands stop producing vital cortisol.
options.D: The heart rate goes completely out of control without nerve signals.

explanation: Without ACTH telling them what to do, the adrenal glands shrink and stop making cortisol. That leaves the body completely unable to handle stress, which can quickly lead to shock. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the biggest difference between Diabetes Insipidus (DI) and SIADH?

options.A: DI starts in the front pituitary, while SIADH only happens from kidney failure.
options.B: DI is caused by too much growth hormone, while SIADH is total thyroid failure.
options.C: DI causes fluid overload and high BP, while SIADH causes dehydration.
options.D: DI involves a shortage of ADH causing water loss, while SIADH involves too much ADH causing water retention.

explanation: Think of them as total opposites! DI stands for 'Dry Inside' (you pee out all your water), while SIADH 'Soaks It All In' (your body holds onto too much water and dilutes your blood). [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h5)

question: A patient just had pituitary surgery and is now peeing out 500 mL of very clear, watery urine every single hour, and their blood sodium is climbing. What is happening?

options.A: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH)
options.B: Diabetes insipidus
options.C: Acute adrenal crisis
options.D: Cushing's syndrome

explanation: That massive output of dilute urine right after pituitary surgery is the classic hallmark of diabetes insipidus. The gland is stunned and temporarily (or permanently) stops making enough ADH. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h5)

question: What imaging test is considered the absolute gold standard for spotting a pituitary tumor?

options.A: An ultrasound scan of the blood vessels in the neck
options.B: A plain X-ray picture of the skull from the side
options.C: A standard CT scan of the head without any contrast dye
options.D: An MRI of the brain using contrast dye

explanation: MRI is the best choice because it gives super clear pictures of soft tissues. This lets doctors spot tiny adenomas and see if they are crowding nearby structures like the optic nerves. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h6)

question: Why must nurses regularly check the vision of a patient who has a pituitary tumor?

options.A: Swelling from fluid retention causes temporary double vision.
options.B: High prolactin levels directly burn out the retina and nerve endings.
options.C: Lacking growth hormone makes the eyes unable to focus on close things.
options.D: Growing tumors can press against the optic nerves and cause gradual blindness.

explanation: Because the pituitary lives right below the optic chiasm, any tumor that starts expanding upward will threaten the patient's eyesight first. Regular checks catch this early! [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h6)

question: Through which pathway do surgeons typically reach the pituitary gland during a transsphenoidal hypophysectomy?

options.A: Through a large incision made just above the right ear
options.B: Through a small opening cut directly in the upper jawbone
options.C: Through the nasal cavity and the sphenoid sinus
options.D: Through the back of the neck right near the brainstem

explanation: The 'transsphenoidal' approach means going right through the nose and sphenoid sinus! This lets surgeons reach the pituitary safely without having to cut open the skull or go through brain tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h7)

question: If a patient has their entire pituitary gland surgically removed, which of these medications do they NOT need to take for the rest of their life?

options.A: Thyroid hormone replacement
options.B: Sex hormone replacement
options.C: Cortisol replacement (glucocorticoids)
options.D: Insulin injections

explanation: Insulin is made by your pancreas, not your pituitary gland! Without a pituitary, the patient will need lifelong thyroid, adrenal, and sex hormone replacements, but their pancreas keeps making insulin just fine. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h7)

question: Why must you strictly tell a patient who just had transsphenoidal surgery NOT to blow their nose?

options.A: It triggers terrible allergic reactions to the nasal packing materials.
options.B: It pushes air into the ear tubes and causes permanent deafness.
options.C: It increases pressure inside the head and can ruin the surgical seal.
options.D: It causes too much mucus to form and blocks the sinus completely.

explanation: Blowing your nose spikes intracranial pressure. That sudden pressure can pop the tissue patch the surgeon placed over the surgical site, causing cerebrospinal fluid to leak out. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h8)

question: You notice clear fluid draining from the nose of a patient who just had pituitary surgery. What is a quick bedside test to see if it is cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)?

options.A: Smell the fluid to check for a sharp ammonia or vinegar odor.
options.B: Check the exact temperature of the fluid with a digital probe.
options.C: Shine an ultraviolet light directly onto the wet dressing.
options.D: Test the fluid for glucose using a standard urine dipstick.

explanation: CSF is rich in glucose, whereas normal nasal mucus is not! Touching a glucose test strip to the drainage is a fast, clever way at the bedside to check for a CSF leak. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T9#GNS222_U2_T9_h8)

question: What are the three main functions of the nervous system?

options.A: Digestion, absorption, and elimination
options.B: Sensory input, integration, and motor output
options.C: Protection, support, and movement
options.D: Circulation, respiration, and excretion

explanation: The nervous system constantly gathers information, processes it in the brain and spinal cord, and sends out commands to the body. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why does the nervous system use electrical impulses for communication?

options.A: To store long-term memories in the blood
options.B: To provide rapid and specific responses to body changes
options.C: To produce hormones for the digestive tract
options.D: To filter waste products out of the brain

explanation: Electrical impulses allow the body to react almost immediately to internal and external stimuli, which is essential for survival. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the primary function of the cerebellum?

options.A: Regulating basic breathing and heart rate
options.B: Processing conscious thought and reasoning
options.C: Producing cerebrospinal fluid
options.D: Coordinating balance and smooth body movements

explanation: The cerebellum fine-tunes motor activity and helps maintain posture and balance during movement. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h2)

question: A patient with a head injury shows unstable vital signs and irregular breathing. Which part of the brain is most likely affected?

options.A: Brainstem
options.B: Cerebellum
options.C: Frontal lobe
options.D: Occipital lobe

explanation: The brainstem regulates essential life-sustaining functions including respiration and heart rate. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the main difference between gray matter and white matter in the spinal cord?

options.A: Gray matter contains nerve cell bodies, while white matter contains myelinated fiber tracts
options.B: Gray matter is found only in the neck, while white matter is found in the lower back
options.C: Gray matter is on the outside, while white matter is on the inside
options.D: Gray matter carries motor signals, while white matter carries sensory signals only

explanation: Think of gray matter as the processing hubs (cell bodies) and white matter as the insulated highway cables (myelinated tracts) traveling up and down. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h3)

question: Why are spinal reflexes important for the body?

options.A: They allow the brain to store long-term memories of painful events
options.B: They control conscious decisions made during physical exercise
options.C: They circulate nutrients through the spinal canal
options.D: They provide rapid, automatic responses without waiting for brain processing

explanation: Reflexes bypass the brain to react instantly to danger, such as pulling a hand away from a hot stove. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which part of the peripheral nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscle movement?

options.A: Somatic nervous system
options.B: Parasympathetic division
options.C: Sympathetic division
options.D: Autonomic nervous system

explanation: The somatic system is responsible for conscious control over skeletal muscles. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h4)

question: What happens to the body during activation of the sympathetic nervous system?

options.A: Digestion speeds up to process recent meals
options.B: Heart rate increases and airways dilate for quick action
options.C: Pupils constrict to focus on close objects
options.D: Blood flow is directed entirely to the stomach

explanation: The sympathetic division prepares the body for stressful or emergency situations by boosting alertness and physical readiness. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary function of neuroglial cells?

options.A: To support, insulate, and protect neurons
options.B: To produce hormones for the endocrine system
options.C: To generate electrical impulses for muscle contraction
options.D: To carry sensory messages directly to the cerebral cortex

explanation: Neuroglia act as supportive cells that nourish and protect delicate neurons in the nervous system. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h5)

question: How do dendrites differ in function from axons?

options.A: Dendrites are found only in the brain, while axons are in the spinal cord
options.B: Dendrites carry signals toward the cell body, while axons carry them away
options.C: Dendrites produce myelin, while axons produce neurotransmitters
options.D: Dendrites control voluntary movement, while axons control involuntary actions

explanation: Dendrites act as receiving antennas, whereas axons transmit the nerve impulse outward to other cells. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h5)

question: What causes the initial change in charge when an action potential starts in a neuron?

options.A: Potassium ions leave the cell permanently
options.B: Calcium ions are stored in the nucleus
options.C: Sodium ions rush into the cell
options.D: Neurotransmitters dissolve the cell membrane

explanation: The opening of sodium channels allows positive sodium ions to flood inward, reversing the membrane charge. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the role of a neurotransmitter at a synapse?

options.A: To physically connect the dendrite of one cell to the axon of another
options.B: To chemically bridge the gap and transmit the signal to the next cell
options.C: To generate the original resting membrane potential
options.D: To insulate the axon with a protective fatty layer

explanation: Because electrical signals cannot cross the synaptic cleft, neurotransmitters carry the message chemically across the space. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which layer of the meninges is the tough, outermost layer attached to the skull?

options.A: Choroid plexus
options.B: Arachnoid mater
options.C: Dura mater
options.D: Pia mater

explanation: The dura mater is a thick, durable membrane providing sturdy outer protection for the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricles?

options.A: To generate electrical action potentials for nerve fibers
options.B: To produce hormones that regulate body temperature
options.C: To cushion the brain and provide mechanical protection
options.D: To supply thick insulating myelin to the spinal cord

explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid acts as a shock absorber, shielding the brain from impact against the skull bones. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h7)

question: What three categories are evaluated using the Glasgow Coma Scale?

options.A: Heart rate, breathing rate, and blood pressure
options.B: Eye opening, verbal response, and motor response
options.C: Reflex speed, muscle tone, and pain tolerance
options.D: Cranial nerve integrity, balance, and coordination

explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale measures these three specific behavioral responses to quantify a patient's level of consciousness. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h8)

question: Why is a baseline neurological assessment important for a patient admitted with a head injury?

options.A: To detect subtle changes in status before major complications occur
options.B: To replace the need for physician examinations
options.C: To eliminate the need for ongoing vital sign monitoring
options.D: To diagnose the exact microscopic cellular damage present

explanation: Comparing current neurological findings to an initial baseline helps nurses catch early signs of worsening brain swelling or bleeding. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h8)

question: What is the main goal of an electrophysiologic study (EPS)?

options.A: To clear blocked plaque from the coronary arteries
options.B: To measure the exact volume of blood pumped per minute
options.C: To record surface electrical signals without touching the heart
options.D: To map the electrical system of the heart from the inside

explanation: Think of an EPS as an electrical wiring check! Special tiny wires (catheters) are put right inside the heart chambers to see how the electrical signals are flowing. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h1)

question: Why would a doctor choose an EPS instead of just a regular ECG?

options.A: An EPS can trigger and pinpoint complex arrhythmias from inside the heart
options.B: A regular ECG only works while the patient is asleep
options.C: A regular ECG is completely unsafe for older adults
options.D: An EPS requires no preparation or recovery time for the patient

explanation: A normal ECG is like looking at the house from the outside. An EPS goes inside the rooms to find exactly where the faulty wiring is causing the fast heartbeats! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h1)

question: Which of these clinical situations is a classic reason to order an EPS?

options.A: Unexplained fainting spells
options.B: Newly diagnosed mild anemia
options.C: Chronic lower back pain
options.D: Suspected acute bronchitis

explanation: When a patient keeps fainting and nobody knows why, doctors use an EPS to check if a sudden dangerous heart rhythm is the sneaky culprit. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h2)

question: A patient with a racing heart and frequent fainting is scheduled for an EPS. What is the main goal?

options.A: To permanently cure high blood pressure using catheter pressure sensors
options.B: To locate the exact electrical pathway causing the abnormal heart rhythm
options.C: To check how well the heart valves open and close during exercise
options.D: To widen narrowed coronary arteries with a small balloon

explanation: Spot on! The goal is pure detective work: tracking down the exact electrical short circuit that's making the heart race. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h2)

question: Why are heart-rhythm medications often stopped before an EPS?

options.A: To keep the access site veins from collapsing during catheter insertion
options.B: To allow doctors to successfully provoke the abnormal heart rhythm
options.C: To prevent the patient from falling asleep during the procedure
options.D: To lower the patient's baseline blood pressure safely

explanation: It sounds backwards, but doctors actually *want* to see the bad rhythm happen so they can fix it. If the antiarrhythmic drugs are working too well, they might hide the problem during the test! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h3)

question: Which of these is a standard pre-procedure nursing duty before an EPS?

options.A: Verifying that informed consent has been properly obtained
options.B: Keeping the patient running on a treadmill for a stress baseline
options.C: Permanently implanting a pacemaker before the test
options.D: Administering a double dose of blood thinners that morning

explanation: As a nurse, making sure the patient understands the procedure and has signed their consent form is a vital safety step every single time. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h3)

question: What is a major nursing responsibility while an EPS is actively happening?

options.A: Monitoring continuous heart rhythms and blood pressure
options.B: Performing surgical closure of the blood vessel access site
options.C: Interpreting the final medical billing codes for the procedure
options.D: Personally advancing the catheter electrodes into the heart

explanation: You are the patient's eyes and ears! Keeping a close eye on the monitors and vitals keeps the patient safe while the team works inside the heart. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h4)

question: Why must a working defibrillator be kept close by during an EPS?

options.A: Dangerous heart rhythms are purposely triggered during the test
options.B: Sedation medications frequently cause permanent heart stoppage
options.C: The equipment is required to warm up the contrast dye
options.D: All patients suffer sudden cardiac arrest during catheter insertion

explanation: Because the doctors intentionally spark those weird rhythms to study them, the team must always be ready with a defibrillator just in case the heart needs help getting back to normal. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h4)

question: Why must a patient keep their affected leg straight and flat after a femoral EPS?

options.A: To prevent bleeding and hematoma formation at the vascular access site
options.B: To allow the newly mapped heart chambers to settle into position
options.C: To ensure the patient stays awake during the recovery phase
options.D: To help the local anesthesia wear off faster in the leg muscles

explanation: Bending that leg right after a catheter goes into the groin artery is a recipe for bleeding. Keeping it straight protects the clot so the puncture can heal safely! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h5)

question: What is an essential post-procedure nursing check after an EPS?

options.A: Checking deep tendon reflexes in both upper arms
options.B: Removing all intravenous lines right before transport
options.C: Checking pulses and color in the extremity used for catheter insertion
options.D: Asking the patient to stand up and walk around immediately

explanation: Always check the foot pulses, warmth, and color on the side where the catheter went in. Good circulation checks catch bleeding or blocked blood vessels early! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h5)

question: An EPS report shows dangerous heart rhythms that couldn't be fixed with ablation. What might the medical team look at next?

options.A: Preparing the patient for discussion about an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator
options.B: Removing all cardiac monitoring equipment permanently
options.C: Scheduling an immediate open-heart surgery for valve replacement
options.D: Discharging the patient with no further restrictions or medications

explanation: When an abnormal pathway can't be successfully ablated away, an implantable device (like an ICD) is often the next line of defense to keep the patient safe from sudden cardiac arrest. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h6)

question: What is the nurse's main role when reviewing EPS results with a patient?

options.A: Rewriting the physician's surgical report for legal hospital records
options.B: Diagnosing the primary cause of the heart rhythm disorder independently
options.C: Deciding which antiarrhythmic drug brand the pharmacy should dispense
options.D: Translating technical findings into clear discharge and care instructions

explanation: Medical reports can sound like Greek to patients. As a nurse, you help break down those complex findings so they truly understand how to take care of themselves at home. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T10#GNS222_U3_T10_h6)

question: What is another common name for a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Cerebral shunt
options.B: Spinal tap
options.C: Epidural injection
options.D: Bone marrow biopsy

explanation: A lumbar puncture is commonly referred to as a spinal tap because it involves accessing fluid from the spinal column. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h1)

question: Which main body fluid is collected during a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Synovial fluid
options.B: Lymphatic fluid
options.C: Venous blood
options.D: Cerebrospinal fluid

explanation: Spot on! The procedure draws cerebrospinal fluid from around the spinal cord to help doctors run diagnostic tests. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h1)

question: Which of these is a major reason why a doctor would order a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Suspected meningitis
options.B: Broken vertebrae
options.C: Severe dehydration
options.D: Muscle spasm

explanation: You got it! Testing cerebrospinal fluid is key to diagnosing central nervous system infections like meningitis. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h2)

question: Why is a lumbar puncture very dangerous for a patient with a brain mass causing high pressure inside the skull?

options.A: It will stop the heart instantly
options.B: It leads to instant paralysis
options.C: It causes severe kidney failure
options.D: It can trigger brain herniation

explanation: Exactly. Releasing fluid when pressure is already high can push brain tissue downward. Safety first—always check for high intracranial pressure! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h2)

question: In an adult, around which part of the spine does the main spinal cord usually end?

options.A: Fifth thoracic vertebra
options.B: First lumbar vertebra
options.C: First sacral vertebra
options.D: Twelfth thoracic vertebra

explanation: Well done! The cord ends near L1, which is why doctors insert the needle lower down where it's safer. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h3)

question: Which body landmark helps a clinician easily find the L4 spot for a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Center of the shoulder blades
options.B: Base of the neck vertebrae
options.C: Line connecting the iliac crests
options.D: Bottom edge of the ribcage

explanation: Correct! Drawing an imaginary line across the top of the hip bones (iliac crests) points right to the L4 space. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h3)

question: Which drug history is most important for a nurse to check before a patient has a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Multivitamins
options.B: Antacids
options.C: Antihistamines
options.D: Anticoagulants

explanation: Spot on! Blood thinners (anticoagulants) raise the risk of dangerous bleeding around the spine. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h4)

question: Your patient is heading for a lumbar puncture in 30 minutes. What is a helpful nursing action right now?

options.A: Eat a heavy meal
options.B: Walk around the hallway
options.C: Drink two liters of water
options.D: Empty their bladder

explanation: Great job! An empty bladder keeps the patient comfortable while they curl up on their side for the procedure. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h4)

question: What is the best position for a patient during a standard lumbar puncture?

options.A: Sitting straight upright with arms down
options.B: Lateral fetal position
options.C: Prone face down on pillows
options.D: Flat on the back with legs straight

explanation: You nailed it! Curling up on the side like a fetus opens up the spaces between the back bones. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h5)

question: Why does the nurse gently help the patient tuck their chin and knees tight together during this procedure?

options.A: To keep the back muscles completely relaxed
options.B: To open up the spaces between the vertebrae
options.C: To slow down the heart rate during the tap
options.D: To prevent the patient from biting their tongue

explanation: Exactly! Flexing the spine widens the gaps, making it much easier for the doctor to insert the needle safely. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h5)

question: How is a patient usually positioned immediately after a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Flat in bed
options.B: Trendelenburg position
options.C: High Fowler's position
options.D: Standing up and walking

explanation: Spot on! Lying flat helps the tiny puncture hole seal up and lowers the chance of a stubborn spinal headache. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h6)

question: Why should the nurse encourage the patient to drink plenty of fluids after a lumbar puncture?

options.A: To flush out remaining local anesthetic drugs
options.B: To prevent high blood pressure spikes
options.C: To keep the patient awake and alert
options.D: To help replace the lost cerebrospinal fluid

explanation: You got it! Fluids help the body quickly make up for the cerebrospinal fluid that was removed. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h6)

question: What should healthy, normal cerebrospinal fluid look like?

options.A: Dark red and viscous
options.B: Clear and colorless
options.C: Milky and opaque
options.D: Yellow and thick

explanation: Correct! Normal cerebrospinal fluid looks just like clean, pure water. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h7)

question: What does cloudy cerebrospinal fluid usually tell the medical team?

options.A: Presence of excess oxygen in the brain
options.B: High levels of dietary sugar in the blood
options.C: Presence of white blood cells from infection
options.D: Normal aging process of the nervous system

explanation: Well done! Cloudiness usually means white blood cells are crowded in there fighting off an infection like meningitis. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h7)

question: What is the most common side effect or complication after a lumbar puncture?

options.A: Permanent paralysis
options.B: Severe brain damage
options.C: Chronic high fever
options.D: Spinal headache

explanation: Spot on! A post-dural puncture headache happens quite often when a little fluid continues to leak out. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h8)

question: How can you tell if a patient has a typical post-dural puncture headache?

options.A: It only hurts when the patient eats or drinks
options.B: It disappears completely when the room is dark
options.C: It gets worse when the patient sits or stands up
options.D: It stays the exact same intensity all day long

explanation: You nailed it! These headaches get worse when upright because of lower fluid pressure around the brain, and they feel better when lying flat. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T11#GNS222_U3_T11_h8)

question: Which two main blood vessel systems supply oxygenated blood to the brain?

options.A: Brachiocephalic and thoracic trunks
options.B: Coronary and pulmonary arteries
options.C: Internal carotid and vertebral arteries
options.D: Subclavian and jugular vessels

explanation: Great job! The internal carotid arteries supply the front of the brain, while the vertebral arteries supply the back. Together, they keep the brain well-nourished with oxygen. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h1)

question: What is the main job of the Circle of Willis at the base of the brain?

options.A: To drain deoxygenated blood away from the cerebral cortex
options.B: To cool down the blood before it reaches delicate brain tissue
options.C: To provide alternative blood supply routes if a vessel is blocked
options.D: To produce cerebrospinal fluid for the central nervous system

explanation: Spot on! The Circle of Willis acts like a backup traffic network. If one path gets blocked, it reroutes blood so the brain keeps getting what it needs. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h1)

question: What directly causes an ischemic stroke?

options.A: A sudden drop in systemic body temperature
options.B: A ruptured blood vessel inside the brain
options.C: An infection of the cerebrospinal fluid
options.D: A blood clot blocking a cerebral artery

explanation: You got it! Ischemic strokes happen when a clot cuts off blood flow to a part of the brain, starving those cells of oxygen. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h2)

question: How does a hemorrhagic stroke cause damage to the brain?

options.A: By causing bleeding that increases pressure and compresses brain cells
options.B: By causing a permanent lack of glucose without altering pressure
options.C: By replacing normal neurons with fibrous scar tissue over time
options.D: By triggering widespread bacterial growth in the ventricles

explanation: Spot on! When a blood vessel bursts inside the skull, the pooling blood builds up pressure and squeezes the surrounding delicate brain tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h2)

question: Which of these is the most common and controllable risk factor for having a stroke?

options.A: Male gender
options.B: Advanced age
options.C: Genetic history
options.D: Hypertension

explanation: Correct! High blood pressure puts constant, dangerous strain on the brain's blood vessels, making it the number one risk factor we can manage. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h3)

question: A 55-year-old patient has a 10-year history of poorly controlled high blood pressure. What major condition are they at high risk for?

options.A: Chronic kidney stones
options.B: Cerebrovascular accident
options.C: Iron deficiency anemia
options.D: Degenerative joint disease

explanation: You nailed it! Years of high pressure wear down cerebral blood vessels, putting the patient at high risk for a stroke (cerebrovascular accident). [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h3)

question: In the FAST stroke assessment tool, what does the letter 'A' stand for?

options.A: Arm weakness
options.B: Acute anxiety
options.C: Ataxia severity
options.D: Airway blockage

explanation: Correct! 'A' stands for arm weakness. We check if one arm drifts downward when the patient tries to hold both arms up. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h4)

question: If a patient has a stroke on the right side of their motor cortex, which side of the body will show physical weakness?

options.A: The right side
options.B: The left side
options.C: Only the lower limbs
options.D: Both sides equally

explanation: Brilliant! Brain pathways cross over in the brainstem, so damage on the right side of the brain shows up as weakness on the left side of the body. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h4)

question: Why must an emergency CT scan be done immediately for a suspected stroke patient?

options.A: To check for bacterial meningitis
options.B: To rule out intracranial hemorrhage
options.C: To calculate total intracranial blood volume
options.D: To measure electrical brain wave activity

explanation: Spot on! We need to check if the stroke is caused by bleeding. Giving clot-busting medications during a hemorrhagic stroke would be deadly. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h5)

question: Why does a nurse check blood clotting test results before giving clot-dissolving therapy to a stroke patient?

options.A: To confirm the exact age and size of the blood clot in the vessel
options.B: To ensure the patient does not have an unsafe risk of severe bleeding
options.C: To check if the patient has an active urinary tract infection
options.D: To measure the patient's baseline neurological recovery potential

explanation: Correct! These drugs are powerful. We must make sure the patient's clotting profile is safe so they don't suffer severe, uncontrollable bleeding. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h5)

question: What is the main goal of using clot-busting (thrombolytic) therapy in an acute ischemic stroke?

options.A: To prevent future heart attacks from occurring
options.B: To dissolve the blood clot and restore blood flow
options.C: To lower systemic blood pressure instantly
options.D: To shrink swollen brain tissue caused by edema

explanation: You got it! Thrombolytic therapy breaks down the clot blocking the vessel, getting oxygen flowing back to starving brain cells quickly. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h6)

question: What is the purpose of an endovascular thrombectomy procedure?

options.A: Physically remove a large blood clot from a blocked cerebral artery
options.B: Surgically repair a ruptured blood vessel inside the brain
options.C: Drain excess cerebrospinal fluid from the lateral ventricles
options.D: Bypass a narrowed carotid artery using a synthetic graft

explanation: Spot on! During a thrombectomy, doctors use specialized tools threaded through blood vessels to physically grab and pull out large clots. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h6)

question: What crucial nursing check must be done before giving food or water to a stroke patient who might have trouble swallowing?

options.A: A check for homonymous hemianopsia
options.B: A measurement of 24-hour urine output
options.C: A formal bedside swallow screen
options.D: A complete neurological Glasgow Coma Scale score

explanation: Correct! Swallowing difficulties (dysphagia) can easily lead to aspiration pneumonia. A bedside swallow screen keeps the patient safe before any oral intake. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h7)

question: For a stroke patient with left-sided weakness who is confined to bed, what is the best nursing action to prevent bedsores?

options.A: Keeping the head of the bed completely flat at all times
options.B: Repositioning the patient every two hours and supporting weak limbs
options.C: Restricting oral fluid intake to keep the skin dry
options.D: Massaging the reddened bony prominences vigorously every shift

explanation: You nailed it! Turning the patient regularly relieves pressure on vulnerable skin, while supporting weak limbs protects their joints. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h7)

question: A stroke patient is resting in bed for a long time without moving. What major leg complication are they most at risk for?

options.A: Peripheral neuropathy
options.B: Arterial plaque regression
options.C: Chronic bone demineralization
options.D: Deep vein thrombosis

explanation: Spot on! When a patient cannot move well, blood pools in the lower legs, putting them at high risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h8)

question: What is the main goal of secondary stroke prevention strategies?

options.A: To prevent a recurrent stroke by managing underlying risk factors
options.B: To eliminate the need for any ongoing physical therapy
options.C: To reverse existing brain cell death and restore lost tissue
options.D: To cure the underlying genetic cause of high blood pressure

explanation: Brilliant! Secondary prevention is all about keeping lifestyle habits in check, taking medications properly, and managing blood pressure to stop another stroke from happening. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T12#GNS222_U3_T12_h8)

question: What are the two major parts that make up the human nervous system?

options.A: Spinal cord and vertebral column
options.B: Sympathetic and parasympathetic systems
options.C: Central and peripheral nervous systems
options.D: Brain and cranial nerves

explanation: Spot on! The nervous system splits into two main teams: the central nervous system (your brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (all the nerves branching out to the rest of your body). [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h1)

question: What is the most common cause of injuries to the brain and spine in our communities?

options.A: Workplace chemical exposure
options.B: Congenital weakness
options.C: Road traffic accidents
options.D: Degenerative joint disease

explanation: You got it! High-speed car and motorcycle crashes unfortunately top the list as the leading cause of traumatic brain and spinal injuries globally. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h1)

question: Which type of injury happens at the exact moment a physical blow or crash occurs?

options.A: Metabolic injury
options.B: Primary injury
options.C: Tertiary injury
options.D: Secondary injury

explanation: That's correct! The primary injury is the immediate damage that happens right at the time of impact, like torn tissue or bruising. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h2)

question: As a nurse, what is our main goal when trying to stop a secondary injury after head trauma?

options.A: To permanently numb the patient to eliminate all pain
options.B: To reverse the torn nerve fibers caused by the initial crash
options.C: To prevent further cell death by maintaining oxygen and blood flow
options.D: To repair fractured skull bones without surgery

explanation: Well done! Since we can't always undo the initial impact, our nursing care focuses heavily on keeping oxygen and blood flowing so swelling doesn't destroy more brain cells. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h2)

question: What do we call an actual bruise of the brain tissue that comes with bleeding?

options.A: Contusion
options.B: Hematoma
options.C: Concussion
options.D: Transection

explanation: Spot on! A brain contusion is essentially a bruise on the brain itself. A concussion is different because it usually doesn't show physical tearing or structural damage on scans. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h3)

question: Why is an injury high up on the spinal cord considered a major medical emergency?

options.A: It stops the digestive system from absorbing water
options.B: It automatically causes complete memory loss
options.C: It can paralyze the muscles needed for breathing
options.D: It prevents the heart from producing blood cells

explanation: That's right! High cervical injuries cut off nerve signals to the diaphragm and chest, making it hard or impossible for the patient to breathe on their own without quick support. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h3)

question: What is the standard bedside scale nurses use to quickly check a trauma patient's level of consciousness?

options.A: Braden Scale
options.B: Pain Numeric Rating
options.C: Apgar Score
options.D: Glasgow Coma Scale

explanation: You nailed it! The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) checks eye, verbal, and motor responses so we can quickly tell how alert or responsive a patient is. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h4)

question: If a trauma patient's Glasgow Coma Scale score starts dropping over a couple of hours, what is the most likely reason?

options.A: Successful recovery from the primary injury
options.B: An allergic reaction to pain medication
options.C: Worsening intracranial pressure or bleeding
options.D: The normal healing process beginning

explanation: Spot on! A falling GCS score is a major warning sign that swelling or bleeding inside the head is getting worse and pressing on the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h4)

question: What is the very first thing emergency responders do at an accident scene to protect a patient's spine?

options.A: Administering strong intravenous pain medication
options.B: Standing the patient up to test leg strength
options.C: Applying a rigid neck collar and securing the body
options.D: Massaging the neck muscles to relieve tension

explanation: That's correct! Putting on a stiff neck collar and securing the body keeps the spine still, preventing small fractures from turning into permanent paralysis. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h5)

question: Why might a surgeon need to perform a craniectomy (removing a piece of the skull) after severe brain trauma?

options.A: To remove the primary injury site completely
options.B: To permanently cure the patient's concussion
options.C: To relieve dangerous pressure caused by brain swelling
options.D: To clean out surface dirt from a skull fracture

explanation: You got it! Taking off a piece of the skull gives a swollen brain room to expand outward instead of crushing vital areas inside. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h5)

question: Why do we keep the head of the bed elevated at 30 degrees for a patient with increased pressure inside the head?

options.A: To make it easier for the patient to eat meals
options.B: To help blood drain from the head and lower pressure
options.C: To improve lung capacity during deep breathing
options.D: To prevent the patient from falling out of bed

explanation: Spot on! Gravity helps blood drain down from the head when the bed is slightly raised, which keeps intracranial pressure at a safer level. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h6)

question: You are giving bed bath care to an unconscious patient with a head injury. Which nursing action is most important?

options.A: Massaging the back vigorously to improve general circulation
options.B: Washing the face with cold water to stimulate consciousness
options.C: Removing the cervical collar to wash the neck thoroughly
options.D: Preventing sudden neck twisting and keeping the head aligned

explanation: Well done! Keeping the head and neck straight and neutral stops the neck veins from getting squeezed, which prevents sudden, dangerous spikes in brain pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h6)

question: What is a dangerous emergency complication for patients with high spinal cord injuries, often triggered by something simple like a full bladder?

options.A: Autonomic dysreflexia
options.B: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.C: Malignant hyperthermia
options.D: Acute respiratory alkalosis

explanation: That's right! Autonomic dysreflexia causes a sudden, life-threatening spike in blood pressure triggered by discomfort below the injury, such as a full bladder or tight clothing. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a goal of long-term rehabilitation after a nervous system injury?

options.A: Reversing the primary neural cell death caused by the initial crash
options.B: Helping the client adapt to permanent physical disabilities
options.C: Supporting family members through emotional counseling
options.D: Providing physical therapy to prevent muscle contractures

explanation: You nailed it! Once nerve cells die from the initial heavy impact, they don't grow back. Rehabilitation is all about maximizing the strength and independence the patient has left! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T13#GNS222_U3_T13_h7)

question: What is a primary brain tumor?

options.A: A tumor that originates from metastasized lung cancer cells.
options.B: A tumor that starts directly from central nervous system tissue.
options.C: A tumor that develops only after a head injury.
options.D: A tumor that always spreads rapidly to other body organs.

explanation: Primary tumors originate from cells native to the brain or spinal cord, unlike secondary tumors which spread from elsewhere. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h1)

question: Why can a non-cancerous (benign) brain tumor still be life-threatening?

options.A: Non-cancerous growths actively destroy blood vessel walls.
options.B: Benign brain tumors always turn into aggressive cancers.
options.C: Surgical removal of benign tissue is completely impossible.
options.D: The rigid skull limits space, causing dangerous tissue compression.

explanation: Because the cranial vault cannot expand, any growing mass increases intracranial pressure and displaces vital brain structures. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h1)

question: What key feature distinguishes a grade IV brain tumor?

options.A: Presence of cellular necrosis
options.B: Normal blood vessel growth rates
options.C: Complete absence of dividing cells
options.D: Enclosed fibrous capsule formation

explanation: Grade IV tumors like glioblastoma multiforme typically feature areas of dead tissue due to rapid growth that outstrips the blood supply. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h2)

question: How do brain tumors mainly disrupt normal neurological function?

options.A: By invading tissue, causing swelling, and blocking CSF flow
options.B: By replacing all circulating blood cells in the body
options.C: By stopping electrical activity in the heart
options.D: By increasing systemic blood pressure to dangerous levels

explanation: Expanding masses physically damage local pathways, trigger swelling, and trap cerebrospinal fluid inside the brain ventricles. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h2)

question: Which symptom is a classic sign of increased intracranial pressure?

options.A: Pain radiating down the lower extremities
options.B: Morning headaches that get worse when straining
options.C: Sudden loss of bowel and bladder control
options.D: Permanent hearing loss in both ears

explanation: Intracranial pressure rises during sleep due to changes in breathing, making headaches prominent upon waking and worse with straining. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h3)

question: What causes localized neurological signs in a patient with a brain tumor?

options.A: Widespread inflammation of peripheral nerves
options.B: General reduction of oxygen levels in the lungs
options.C: Rapid electrolyte shifts in the bloodstream
options.D: Destruction or compression of specific brain regions

explanation: Focal deficits reflect the specific job of the brain area being squeezed or destroyed by the growing mass. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h3)

question: What is the standard imaging method for diagnosing brain tumors?

options.A: Abdominal ultrasound
options.B: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
options.C: Electroencephalography
options.D: Standard chest radiography

explanation: MRI provides superior pictures of soft tissue structures, tumor margins, and surrounding swelling compared to other scans. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h4)

question: Why is a tissue biopsy usually performed after brain imaging?

options.A: To immediately relieve dangerous pressure surges
options.B: To determine the precise cellular type of the tumor
options.C: To permanently prevent future seizure activity
options.D: To drain excess fluid from the ventricles

explanation: Imaging shows location and size, but a tissue sample is necessary for grading and cellular profiling to guide treatment. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h4)

question: What is the main role of dexamethasone in brain tumor care?

options.A: Reducing swelling around the brain tumor
options.B: Preventing sudden tonic-clonic seizures
options.C: Killing malignant glioma cells directly
options.D: Lowering systemic arterial blood pressure

explanation: Corticosteroids stabilize the blood-brain barrier and quickly decrease swelling around the tumor, easing pressure symptoms. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h5)

question: When is surgical removal of a brain tumor usually limited?

options.A: When the tumor is classified as a benign meningioma
options.B: When the tumor is located near critical areas that control vital functions
options.C: When the imaging was done using computed tomography
options.D: When the patient has a history of high blood pressure

explanation: Surgeons avoid aggressive removal if it risks damaging vital structures controlling speech, movement, or sensation. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h5)

question: At what angle should the head of the bed be kept after brain surgery (craniotomy)?

options.A: Flat completely horizontal
options.B: Lowered in a steep head-down position
options.C: Rotated sharply to the side
options.D: Elevated thirty to forty-five degrees

explanation: Elevating the head promotes blood return from the head, helping to prevent increases in intracranial pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h6)

question: What should a nurse do immediately if clear fluid leaks from the nose after skull surgery?

options.A: Instruct the patient to blow their nose gently.
options.B: Notify the neurosurgeon immediately for potential CSF leakage.
options.C: Pack the nasal cavity tightly with sterile gauze.
options.D: Document it as normal wound drainage requiring no action.

explanation: Clear fluid draining from the nose or ears after surgery indicates a cerebrospinal fluid leak and a high risk of meningitis. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h6)

question: Which complication is a major risk for bedridden patients recovering from brain surgery?

options.A: Obstructive asthma attack
options.B: Chronic kidney failure
options.C: Blood clots in the veins (venous thromboembolism)
options.D: Iron deficiency anemia

explanation: Immobility and cancer significantly increase the risk of deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in the lungs for these patients. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h7)

question: What is the main goal of rehabilitation for brain tumor survivors?

options.A: Reversing all underlying genetic mutations
options.B: Regrowing lost brain tissue through cell division
options.C: Maximizing independence and adapting to any lasting deficits
options.D: Preventing the need for future medical checkups

explanation: Therapists work to help patients regain as much function as possible and find coping strategies for permanent changes. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T14#GNS222_U3_T14_h7)

question: What is the main characteristic of degenerative neurological disorders?

options.A: Gradual loss of nerve cell function
options.B: Sudden and rapid recovery
options.C: Temporary nerve inflammation
options.D: Infection of the spinal cord

explanation: These conditions involve a slow, ongoing breakdown of neurons over time rather than a sudden injury or short-term infection. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h1)

question: Why are degenerative neurological disorders considered irreversible?

options.A: Neurons cannot easily regenerate once destroyed
options.B: Blood flow to the brain stops completely
options.C: Treatments are never started early enough
options.D: The immune system constantly attacks the brain

explanation: Once nerve cells in the central nervous system are lost, the body cannot easily replace them, leading to permanent structural decline. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h1)

question: What role do abnormal proteins play in degenerative neurological disorders?

options.A: They protect neurons from oxidative stress
options.B: They form harmful clumps that disrupt cell function
options.C: They speed up normal electrical signals
options.D: They help repair damaged nerve pathways

explanation: Proteins that fold incorrectly build up inside or around nerve cells, interfering with normal operations and causing cell death. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h2)

question: What does 'apoptosis' mean when talking about nerve cell damage?

options.A: The blocking of blood vessels
options.B: The sudden growth of new neurons
options.C: The rapid repair of damaged myelin
options.D: The programmed death of cells

explanation: Apoptosis is simply the body's natural process of programmed cell death that happens when neurons get too stressed or damaged. Don't let big medical terms scare you—you're learning them step by step! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h2)

question: Which brain chemical is severely lacking in Parkinson's disease?

options.A: Acetylcholine
options.B: Epinephrine
options.C: Dopamine
options.D: Serotonin

explanation: Parkinson's disease specifically results from the death of neurons that produce dopamine in a part of the midbrain called the substantia nigra. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h3)

question: A patient with ALS is having muscle weakness and wasting. Which part of the nervous system is mainly affected?

options.A: The myelin sheath of peripheral nerves
options.B: Upper and lower motor neurons
options.C: Dopamine receptors in the basal ganglia
options.D: Sensory nerve endings in the skin

explanation: ALS attacks the motor neurons that tell your muscles to move. When these cells weaken, the muscles waste away (atrophy). You are building fantastic clinical knowledge! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical motor symptom of degenerative neurological disorders?

options.A: Muscle stiffness
options.B: Balance problems
options.C: Tremors at rest
options.D: Sudden acute pain

explanation: Sudden acute pain is typically associated with injury or inflammation, whereas degenerative disorders feature gradual motor changes like stiffness, tremors, and balance loss. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h4)

question: A patient with a progressive neurological disorder starts having trouble swallowing and controlling their bladder. What do we call this type of issue?

options.A: Acute infection
options.B: Sensory overload
options.C: Autonomic dysfunction
options.D: Cerebellar excitation

explanation: The autonomic nervous system handles automatic body jobs like swallowing, digestion, and bladder control. When it gets impaired, these tricky symptoms show up. You're mastering patient assessment! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h4)

question: Why do doctors order an MRI when they suspect a neurodegenerative disease?

options.A: To directly count the number of living neurons
options.B: To cure abnormal protein accumulation
options.C: To visualize brain structures and rule out other causes
options.D: To measure electrical brain waves

explanation: An MRI gives a clear picture of the brain so doctors can check for things like strokes or tumors that might look like a degenerative disease. Smart nursing insight! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h5)

question: Why is genetic testing especially important when checking for Huntington's disease?

options.A: It replaces the need for a physical neurological exam
options.B: It measures the exact level of dopamine in the blood
options.C: It immediately stops the progression of the disease
options.D: It proves the patient has a specific inherited gene mutation

explanation: Huntington's disease runs in families. Genetic tests can spot the exact inherited gene mutation responsible for it. Every question you answer makes your future clinical shifts easier! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h5)

question: What is the main goal of medications used for degenerative neurological disorders?

options.A: To replace damaged neurons with new tissue
options.B: To relieve symptoms and improve quality of life
options.C: To speed up the cellular breakdown process
options.D: To completely cure the underlying disease

explanation: Right now, medicines can't cure these diseases or stop nerve loss, but they do a great job easing symptoms so patients stay comfortable. Keep up the awesome studying! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h6)

question: Why is a speech therapist often called in to help patients with advanced neurodegenerative disorders?

options.A: To teach them foreign languages
options.B: To cure their underlying memory loss
options.C: To help manage swallowing and communication issues
options.D: To improve their walking balance and posture

explanation: Speech therapists do more than just speech—they train and protect the muscles used for swallowing, which stops dangerous choking and aspiration. Fantastic nursing awareness! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h6)

question: What is a top nursing priority for a patient who has trouble walking due to a progressive brain condition?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to prevent bathroom trips
options.B: Implementing fall prevention strategies
options.C: Keeping the patient confined to a bed at all times
options.D: Encouraging high-intensity contact sports

explanation: Stiff muscles and poor balance mean falls are a constant risk. Protecting our patients from falls is a core nursing duty. You're thinking like a real nurse! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h7)

question: A nurse is caring for a bedridden patient with advanced Parkinson's disease. What is the best way to prevent bedsores (skin breakdown)?

options.A: Repositioning the patient every two hours
options.B: Keeping the room temperature very high
options.C: Encouraging the patient to run on a treadmill
options.D: Applying lotion once a week

explanation: Turning or repositioning the patient every two hours takes pressure off bony areas, keeping the skin safe and healthy. Excellent bedside care knowledge! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h7)

question: What is a very common and dangerous late-stage complication for many degenerative brain disorders?

options.A: Rapid nerve regeneration
options.B: Aspiration pneumonia
options.C: Sudden high blood pressure
options.D: Severe weight gain

explanation: When swallowing muscles get too weak, food and saliva can easily slip into the lungs and cause a serious infection called aspiration pneumonia. You are building life-saving knowledge! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T15#GNS222_U3_T15_h8)
