explanation: Automatisms are automatic, repetitive actions like smacking the lips, swallowing, or picking at clothes while the patient's mind is cloudy. Spotting these makes you a sharp nurse! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h3)

question: Which imaging scan is best for spotting hippocampal scarring in psychomotor epilepsy?

options.A: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.B: Standard skull X-ray
options.C: Bone density scan
options.D: Abdominal ultrasound

explanation: An MRI gives a clear, high-resolution picture of soft brain tissues, making it the top choice for finding tiny scars or shrinking in the hippocampus. Great job! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h4)

question: Why is information from family members so important when diagnosing seizures?

options.A: Relatives can perform bedside electroencephalogram tests at home
options.B: Family members are legally required to sign consent for medication trials
options.C: Patients often have amnesia for the events and cannot describe the seizure themselves
options.D: Patients exaggerate their symptoms when alone

explanation: Because patients usually don't remember what happened during or right after the seizure, family members or witnesses are vital for filling in the story. You're mastering patient assessment! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T12#GNS222_U4_T12_h4)

question: What is the main goal of taking anti-seizure medications?

options.D: Quaternary prevention

explanation: Pre-marital genotype screening and counseling aim to prevent affected conceptions entirely, which defines primary prevention. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h3)

question: What defines an individual who is a 'carrier' of an autosomal recessive genetic disorder?

options.A: They have two mutant gene copies causing rapid degeneration
options.B: They display severe physical symptoms of the actual disease
options.C: They are completely immune to all forms of genetic illness
options.D: They possess one mutant gene copy and show no symptoms

explanation: Carriers have a single altered gene alongside a normal gene, protecting them from the disease while allowing potential transmission. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h4)

question: Why is pre-test and post-test counseling essential when conducting carrier screening tests?

options.A: To prepare clients for the emotional and social impact of results
options.B: To force the patient to pay for expensive hospital equipment
options.C: To diagnose unrelated infectious diseases during the session
options.D: To ensure the laboratory technician processes the blood faster

explanation: Genetic findings carry heavy emotional weight and potential stigma, requiring professional support before and after testing. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h4)

question: Which of the following is a classic example of secondary prevention in a newborn?

options.A: Routine newborn screening for congenital metabolic disorders
options.B: Conducting community town halls on environmental health
options.C: Administering long-term physical therapy for adult paralysis
options.D: Providing genetic counseling to prospective parents before marriage

explanation: Newborn screening detects hidden anomalies early in life so treatment can start before severe symptoms manifest. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h5)

question: What is the primary benefit of early detection through secondary prevention screening?

options.A: It guarantees a complete cure for all degenerative illnesses
options.B: It removes the need for any future medical appointments
options.C: Prompt intervention can slow disease progression and minimize damage
options.D: It completely eliminates the mutated genes from the human body

explanation: While it cannot cure the genetic defect, early detection allows medical teams to intervene before permanent tissue destruction occurs. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h5)

question: A parent expresses intense guilt after learning they passed a genetic disorder to their child. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Provide a supportive, non-judgmental space to validate their complex emotions
options.B: Explain that genetic inheritance is a deliberate choice they made
options.C: Tell the parent firmly that dwelling on the past is a waste of time
options.D: Ignore the emotional comment and focus entirely on charting vital signs

explanation: Parents often struggle with self-blame, requiring compassionate nursing presence and emotional validation without judgment. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h6)

question: What is a core component of nursing advocacy in genetic healthcare?

options.A: Protecting patient autonomy and defending their right to healthcare
options.B: Reporting carriers of genetic diseases to public newspapers
options.C: Deciding which medical treatment the family must accept
options.D: Charging patients fees for counseling services provided

explanation: Advocacy ensures patients retain their decision-making power and receive fair, unbiased care free from coercion. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h6)

question: What is the main role of the nurse within a multidisciplinary degenerative care team?

options.A: Replacing the dietician and physiotherapist during hospital shifts
options.B: Performing all specialized surgical procedures independently
options.C: Making final legal decisions regarding patient insurance coverage
options.D: Acting as a central communication hub between the family and specialists

explanation: Nurses coordinate care across different disciplines to ensure smooth communication and holistic patient management. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h7)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team necessary for patients with inherited degenerative disorders?

options.A: Specialists alone can handle all emotional and social family needs
options.B: Hospital policies mandate that at least five doctors see every patient
options.C: The conditions affect multiple body systems and require diverse expertise
options.D: Nurses are not qualified to provide any form of direct care

explanation: Because degenerative disorders cause widespread physical and metabolic decline, input from various specialists ensures comprehensive support. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h7)

question: What is another widely used name for disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: Multiple sclerosis
options.B: Myasthenia gravis
options.C: Muscular dystrophy
options.D: Motor neuron disease

explanation: Disseminated sclerosis is the older or alternative term for multiple sclerosis, a condition marked by widespread nervous system damage. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why do symptoms of disseminated sclerosis differ so much from one patient to another?

options.A: Damage occurs randomly across different areas of the central nervous system
options.B: Different patients have completely different blood types
options.C: The disease only affects the peripheral nerves in the arms and legs
options.D: Infection rates change depending on the weather

explanation: Think of it like scars forming in different places in the brain or spinal cord. The symptoms depend entirely on which exact nerve pathways are affected! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which part of the nerve cell is mainly destroyed during the demyelination process in disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: Cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Gray matter neurons
options.C: Myelin sheath
options.D: Acetylcholine

explanation: You've got this! The immune system mistakenly attacks and strips away the myelin sheath, which normally acts like an insulation cover to protect nerves and speed up signals. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h2)

question: How do hard scars (plaques) cause symptoms in disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: They cause excess production of spinal fluid in the brain ventricles
options.B: They stimulate muscles to contract constantly without rest
options.C: They repair the damaged nerves completely back to normal
options.D: They block and slow down electrical signals traveling along nerve fibers

explanation: When inflammation creates scar tissue (plaques), it gets in the way of smooth electrical conduction—leading to the physical and sensory changes patients feel. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which group of people is diagnosed with disseminated sclerosis more often?

options.A: Inhabitants of high-altitude deserts
options.B: Children under five
options.C: Elderly men
options.D: Women

explanation: Studies consistently show that disseminated sclerosis affects women about twice as often as men. Good to keep in mind for your exams! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which of the following is linked as an environmental trigger for developing MS?

options.A: Living close to sea level in tropical zones
options.B: Engaging in heavy physical labor outdoors
options.C: Eating a diet high in processed carbohydrates
options.D: Past viral infections like Epstein-Barr virus

explanation: While the exact cause isn't fully pinned down, certain past viral infections are believed to help trigger this abnormal immune response in vulnerable people. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is a very common early sign that patients with developing disseminated sclerosis report?

options.A: Complete paralysis of both legs
options.B: Vision changes like optic neuritis
options.C: Severe high blood pressure
options.D: Total loss of long-term memory

explanation: Keep an eye out for this: inflammation of the optic nerve causing blurry vision or eye pain is frequently one of the very first warning signs of MS. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h4)

question: A patient has sudden flare-ups of numbness and weakness that completely clear up after a few weeks, followed by long periods of normal health. What pattern is this?

options.A: Secondary progressive
options.B: Relapsing-remitting
options.C: Primary progressive
options.D: Benign transient paresis

explanation: This is the classic 'relapsing-remitting' pattern—clear flare-ups (relapses) followed by periods where the patient recovers and feels fine (remissions). [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the main imaging test doctors use to see brain and spinal cord plaques in disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: Barium swallow
options.B: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.C: Chest X-ray
options.D: Abdominal ultrasound

explanation: An MRI is the gold standard here because it gives a clear picture of scarring and inflammation inside the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why would a doctor perform a lumbar puncture (spinal tap) when investigating suspected disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: To drain excess blood following an acute head injury
options.B: To check cerebrospinal fluid for signs of abnormal immune activity
options.C: To inject medication that stops nerve pain immediately
options.D: To measure the exact pressure inside the heart chambers

explanation: Testing the spinal fluid helps find specific markers (like oligoclonal bands) that point straight to inflammation in the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which medication class is quickly given to calm down inflammation during a sudden MS flare-up?

options.A: Antibiotics
options.B: Corticosteroids
options.C: Anticoagulants
options.D: Antihistamines

explanation: High-dose corticosteroids are the go-to treatment to quickly quiet down acute inflammation when a patient has a relapse. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the main goal of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) in treating disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: To immediately repair severed nerve axons overnight
options.B: To reduce relapse frequency and slow long-term disability
options.C: To completely cure the underlying autoimmune response
options.D: To lower elevated blood pressure caused by stress

explanation: While they don't offer an instant cure, DMTs help calm the immune system over time, preventing future attacks and keeping the patient independent longer. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is a key nursing care action for a patient dealing with extreme fatigue from disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: Keeping the patient confined strictly to bed
options.B: Restricting all fluid intake after midday
options.C: Scheduling planned rest periods throughout the day
options.D: Encouraging intense daily marathon training

explanation: Pacing is everything! Balancing daily activities with scheduled rest helps patients conserve their energy without burning out. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h7)

question: For a patient with severe mobility problems due to disseminated sclerosis, which complication should nurses watch out for and prevent?

options.A: Kidney stone formation
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Type 2 diabetes
options.D: Pressure injuries

explanation: When patients spend a lot of time in bed or a wheelchair, their skin is at high risk. Regular turning and meticulous skin care are vital nursing duties! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of physiotherapy in long-term MS care?

options.A: Maintaining mobility and preventing joint stiffness
options.B: Analyzing cerebrospinal fluid laboratory samples
options.C: Performing surgical repair of demyelinated nerves
options.D: Prescribing disease-modifying drug dosages

explanation: Physiotherapy keeps muscles working, improves balance, and prevents tight joints (contractures), helping the patient stay active for as long as possible. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h8)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team (doctors, nurses, physiotherapists) so important for patients with advanced disseminated sclerosis?

options.A: Physicians are not permitted to manage neurological disorders alone
options.B: The disease affects many different physical, cognitive, and emotional functions
options.C: It eliminates the need for any ongoing medical drug therapy
options.D: Patients require daily surgical procedures to replace damaged nerves

explanation: Because MS touches movement, speech, mood, and daily living, it takes a whole team of specialists working together to give the patient the best quality of life. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T3#GNS222_U4_T3_h8)

question: In Parkinson's disease, which part of the brain is mainly damaged, leading to low dopamine levels?

options.A: Cerebellar cortex
options.B: Substantia nigra
options.C: Medulla oblongata
options.D: Frontal lobe

explanation: You've got this! The substantia nigra is the brain area packed with dopamine-producing cells. When these cells break down, movement problems start to show. Spotting this early helps you understand why Parkinson's affects movement so much! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h1)

question: What do Lewy bodies do inside the brain cells of someone with Parkinson's disease?

options.A: They protect neurons from inflammatory damage in the midbrain.
options.B: They accumulate inside nerve cells and disrupt normal cellular function.
options.C: They produce excessive amounts of dopamine to compensate for cell loss.
options.D: They repair damaged myelin sheaths around peripheral nerves.

explanation: Think of Lewy bodies like unwanted trash piling up inside the cell. These abnormal protein clumps build up, causing the nerve cells to get damaged and eventually die off. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h1)

question: What is the medical term for the slowness of voluntary movement seen in Parkinson's patients?

options.A: Akathisia
options.B: Dyskinesia
options.C: Ataxia
options.D: Bradykinesia

explanation: Great word to know! 'Brady' means slow, and 'kinesia' means movement. Together, bradykinesia means it takes a patient much longer to start and finish simple physical actions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h2)

question: How does a typical resting tremor look in a patient with early Parkinson's disease?

options.A: As rhythmic head nodding that worsens only during high-stress situations
options.B: As violent shaking of both arms when reaching out to grab an object
options.C: As a pill-rolling movement of the thumb and forefinger when the hand is relaxed
options.D: As sudden muscle jerks throughout the entire body during deep sleep

explanation: Picture someone gently rolling a tiny pill back and forth between their thumb and index finger while resting—that's the classic Parkinson's resting tremor! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h2)

question: How is Parkinson's disease usually diagnosed in clinical practice?

options.A: Clinical history and physical neurological examination
options.B: Routine blood tests measuring complete blood count
options.C: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for infectious agents
options.D: Magnetic resonance imaging of the spinal cord

explanation: There's no single blood test for Parkinson's! Doctors rely on a careful physical exam, watching how the patient moves, and taking a detailed medical history. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h3)

question: According to the Hoehn and Yahr scale, what does Stage 1 Parkinson's disease mean?

options.A: Symptoms are limited to one side of the body with minimal disability.
options.B: Bilateral disease is present with severe impairment of balance.
options.C: Symptoms are completely absent during physical exertion.
options.D: The patient is confined strictly to a wheelchair or bed.

explanation: Stage 1 is the very beginning of the journey. The symptoms affect only one side of the body (unilateral) and cause very little disruption to daily life. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h3)

question: Why is carbidopa always given alongside levodopa when treating Parkinson's?

options.A: To act as a direct replacement for lost acetylcholine
options.B: To sedate the patient and prevent involuntary tremors
options.C: To prevent the breakdown of levodopa before it reaches the brain
options.D: To completely cure the underlying neuronal degeneration

explanation: Think of carbidopa as the bodyguard for levodopa. It stops levodopa from breaking down too early in the body so that enough of it actually reaches the brain to do its job! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h4)

question: What does the 'wearing-off' phenomenon mean for a patient taking Parkinson's medication?

options.A: The medication loses its effectiveness before the next scheduled dose is due.
options.B: The patient develops a permanent allergic reaction to the drug ingredients.
options.C: The patient no longer requires any treatment due to spontaneous recovery.
options.D: The dosage must be permanently reduced to prevent severe liver toxicity.

explanation: It's like a battery running low before you can plug it in. The medicine wears off too early, causing the patient's symptoms to return right before it's time for their next pill. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is the main goal of deep brain stimulation (DBS) for Parkinson's disease?

options.A: To surgically remove Lewy bodies from the cerebral cortex
options.B: To deliver electrical impulses that block abnormal brain signals
options.C: To regenerate lost dopamine-producing neurons in the midbrain
options.D: To replace damaged cerebrospinal fluid with synthetic dopamine

explanation: DBS uses tiny implanted wires to send gentle electrical pulses, acting like a pacemaker for the brain to block the faulty signals causing tremors and stiffness. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h5)

question: Which patient factor would usually make someone a poor candidate for deep brain stimulation surgery?

options.A: Significant cognitive impairment or dementia
options.B: Intolerable side effects from oral levodopa therapy
options.C: Severe motor fluctuations and on-off periods
options.D: Persistent resting tremor despite high medication doses

explanation: Surgery like DBS requires a clear mind to handle the device and follow-up care. If a patient already has severe memory or thinking issues (dementia), the surgery can sometimes make those worse. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h5)

question: As a nurse, what is a major safety risk you must watch out for in patients with advanced Parkinson's disease?

options.A: Aspiration due to swallowing difficulties
options.B: Spontaneous regeneration of nerve tissue
options.C: Sudden permanent paralysis of the lower limbs
options.D: Excessive weight gain from hyperactive metabolism

explanation: Swallowing problems (dysphagia) are very common in late-stage Parkinson's. If food or saliva goes down the 'wrong pipe', it can lead to dangerous chest infections or choking. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h6)

question: You are helping a patient with severe bradykinesia get ready in the morning. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Withholding morning medication until physical therapy is finished
options.B: Allowing extra time for the patient to complete tasks independently
options.C: Completing all hygiene tasks quickly for the patient to save time
options.D: Restricting oral fluid intake to prevent frequent bathroom trips

explanation: Patience is key! Bradykinesia means everything takes longer. Giving them extra time keeps their dignity intact and encourages them to do as much as they can for themselves. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is a helpful technique when a Parkinson's patient suddenly 'freezes' and cannot move their feet while walking?

options.A: Firmly push the patient forward from behind to restart momentum
options.B: Instruct the patient to lean backward to shift their center of gravity
options.C: Tell the patient to close their eyes and try to run quickly
options.D: Ask the patient to step over a visual cue on the floor or count out loud

explanation: Freezing can be scary! Using a visual trick—like stepping over a line on the floor—or counting a steady rhythm gives the brain a new cue to help break the freeze. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a safe home environment practice for a patient with Parkinson's disease?

options.A: Ensuring hallways and stairwells have bright, even lighting
options.B: Installing secure grab bars in the bathroom and shower
options.C: Clearing pathways of electrical cords and clutter
options.D: Placing loose decorative throw rugs over slick tile floors

explanation: Watch out for loose rugs! Because Parkinson's patients often shuffle their feet, throw rugs are a major tripping hazard that should always be removed. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h7)

question: Why is taking Parkinson's medication right on time, every single day, so important?

options.A: Delayed timing makes the medication completely toxic to the kidneys.
options.B: Missed doses cause the brain to permanently stop producing acetylcholine.
options.C: Delays in taking doses can quickly trigger severe symptom recurrence or off-periods.
options.D: Taking pills late can cause permanent liver failure within twenty-four hours.

explanation: Parkinson's drugs have a very short lifespan in the body. If a dose is even a little late, the drug levels drop and the shaking or stiffness rushes right back. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h8)

question: What is a major benefit of connecting family caregivers to local support groups?

options.A: It helps reduce caregiver burnout by sharing coping strategies and emotional support.
options.B: It provides free prescription medications directly to the household.
options.C: It completely cures the neurodegenerative disease process in the patient.
options.D: It eliminates the need for professional physical and occupational therapy.

explanation: Looking after someone with a chronic illness is tough work. Support groups give families a safe space to vent, share tips, and remember they are not alone in the journey. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T4#GNS222_U4_T4_h8)

question: What kind of infectious agent causes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)?

options.A: A slow-acting bacterial spore
options.B: An abnormally folded prion protein
options.C: A parasitic protozoan in brain tissue
options.D: A mutant strand of DNA virus

explanation: Spot on! CJD is caused by prions, which are unique proteins that misfold and don't even carry DNA or RNA. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h1)

question: What classic structural change happens to the brain tissue in CJD?

options.A: Massive swelling of the blood vessels
options.B: Excessive growth of new nerve endings
options.C: Development of sponge-like holes
options.D: Hardening of the protective skull bone

explanation: Correct! As those rogue proteins build up, they damage the brain cells and leave tiny, sponge-like holes behind. Great job remembering that! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h1)

question: In a healthy human body, where do normal prion proteins naturally live?

options.A: Along the lining of the gut
options.B: On the membranes of neurons
options.C: Inside red blood cells
options.D: Within the fluid of joints

explanation: You got it! Normal prions hang out peacefully on the surface membranes of our nerve cells. It's only when they change shape that trouble starts. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h2)

question: How do disease-causing prions spread and multiply inside the brain?

options.A: By forcing normal proteins to change shape
options.B: By dividing rapidly through simple cell fission
options.C: By absorbing nutrients from nearby blood vessels
options.D: By replicating their own viral RNA strands

explanation: Spot on! Prions don't reproduce like normal germs; instead, they act like bullies, forcing healthy proteins to fold into the abnormal shape just like them. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which category makes up the vast majority of all CJD cases?

options.A: Iatrogenic CJD
options.B: Variant CJD
options.C: Sporadic CJD
options.D: Familial CJD

explanation: Correct! Most CJD cases happen sporadically—meaning they appear out of nowhere for no known reason, without any inherited gene or infection link. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h3)

question: How would a patient most likely contract iatrogenic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?

options.A: Through a contaminated surgical tool
options.B: Through a mosquito bite in a tropical zone
options.C: By inheriting a mutated genetic trait
options.D: By eating undercooked beef products

explanation: You nailed it! 'Iatrogenic' means it happened accidentally during a medical or surgical procedure, such as using instruments that previously touched infected tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h3)

question: What is a very common early physical sign in someone developing CJD?

options.A: Involuntary muscle jerks
options.B: High fever and sweating
options.C: Severe joint swelling
options.D: Yellowing of the skin

explanation: Spot on! Sudden, involuntary muscle jerking (called myoclonus) is a classic physical sign as the disease progresses. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h4)

question: In the late stages of CJD, what does the term 'akinetic mutism' mean?

options.A: The patient is completely immobile and unresponsive.
options.B: The patient experiences sudden episodes of paralysis.
options.C: The patient has lost the ability to digest solid food.
options.D: The patient is restless and shouts continuously.

explanation: Correct! Akinetic mutism means the patient can no longer move or speak, remaining entirely quiet and unresponsive to their environment. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which test gives the definitive, 100% confirmation of CJD?

options.A: Chest X-ray examination
options.B: Complete blood cell count
options.C: Neuropathological brain tissue exam
options.D: Cerebrospinal fluid culture

explanation: You got it! While other tests help doctors look at clues, final confirmation requires checking brain tissue for those hallmark sponge-like changes. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why is an MRI scan so helpful when evaluating a patient with suspected CJD?

options.A: It checks the electrical activity of skeletal muscles.
options.B: It reveals characteristic patterns of brain tissue damage.
options.C: It measures the exact level of circulating antibodies.
options.D: It clears away abnormal prion protein deposits safely.

explanation: Spot on! An MRI can show distinct bright spots and damage patterns in specific areas of the brain, guiding the medical team. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary focus of medical care for a patient diagnosed with CJD?

options.A: Relieving symptoms and providing comfort
options.B: Stopping the replication of prions
options.C: Restoring lost memory and brain cells
options.D: Reversing the genetic mutation

explanation: Correct! Because there is currently no cure for CJD, treatment is all about palliative care—keeping the patient comfortable and easing their symptoms. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h6)

question: As a nurse caring for a bedbound patient in the late stages of CJD, what is your top priority?

options.A: Daily physical therapy to rebuild muscle mass
options.B: Regular position changes to prevent skin breakdown
options.C: Active range of motion exercises for independence
options.D: Frequent neurological testing to track recovery

explanation: You nailed it! Since the patient can't move on their own, turning them regularly is vital to protect their skin from pressure sores. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h6)

question: Which of these methods is NOT reliable for destroying infectious prions?

options.A: Using disposable instruments
options.B: Extended chemical disinfection
options.C: Standard boiling in water
options.D: Specialized high-heat autoclaving

explanation: Spot on! Prions are super tough and survive normal boiling. They need heavy-duty, specialized sterilization protocols to be destroyed. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h7)

question: Why do hospitals often prefer single-use instruments for procedures involving suspected CJD patients?

options.A: They are cheaper to purchase in large quantities.
options.B: Standard sterilization fails to eliminate prions reliably.
options.C: Patients prefer disposable tools for surgical safety.
options.D: They prevent the spread of common viral infections.

explanation: Correct! Because standard hospital cleaning methods don't always kill prions, using disposables keeps future patients completely safe. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the typical life expectancy after CJD symptoms first appear?

options.A: Up to ten years
options.B: About one year
options.C: Around five years
options.D: More than twenty years

explanation: You got it! CJD moves very fast, and sadly, most individuals do not survive past one year after their initial symptoms show up. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h8)

question: How can nurses best support families dealing with a loved one's CJD diagnosis?

options.A: By teaching them how to reverse the disease at home
options.B: By connecting them with palliative care and support
options.C: By promising a full recovery with experimental drugs
options.D: By restricting all visiting hours to prevent stress

explanation: Spot on! A CJD diagnosis is heartbreaking for families. Guiding them to palliative care and emotional support resources makes a world of difference. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h8)

question: Pick's disease mainly affects which areas of the brain first?

options.A: Frontal and temporal lobes
options.B: Occipital and parietal lobes
options.C: Thalamus and hypothalamus
options.D: Cerebellum and brainstem

explanation: Pick's disease zeroes in on the frontal and temporal parts of the brain, which handle our personality, behavior, and language. Spotting this early helps you understand why patients act differently long before memory issues start! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h1)

question: How does early Pick's disease usually look different from Alzheimer's disease?

options.A: Alzheimer's disease exclusively affects people under age fifty.
options.B: Alzheimer's disease causes rapid physical paralysis unlike Pick's disease.
options.C: Pick's disease alters behavior and personality first rather than memory.
options.D: Pick's disease begins with severe visual hallucinations.

explanation: You've got this! While Alzheimer's usually attacks memory first, Pick's disease changes how a person acts, talks to others, and handles their emotions right from the start. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which abnormal protein builds up inside the nerve cells in Pick's disease?

options.A: Tau protein
options.B: Beta-amyloid
options.C: Alpha-synuclein
options.D: Prion protein

explanation: Think of tau proteins as building blocks that go rogue and clump up inside the brain cells in Pick's disease. Knowing this pathology makes the rest of the topic much easier to master! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h2)

question: What exactly are 'Pick bodies' seen under a microscope in brain tissue?

options.A: Scars from previous traumatic head injuries
options.B: Deposits of calcium in the brain blood vessels
options.C: Clumps of abnormal tau protein inside nerve cells
options.D: Infections caused by bacteria in the spinal fluid

explanation: Pick bodies are just microscopic clumps of tangled tau protein. When neurons get weighed down by these clumps, they start to struggle and break down. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which behavior do you typically see first in someone with Pick's disease?

options.A: Sudden tremors and rigidity in all four limbs
options.B: Inability to recognize familiar faces in mirrors
options.C: Loss of social inhibitions and personality changes
options.D: Complete loss of bladder and bowel control

explanation: Because the frontal lobe gets damaged, patients lose their 'social filter.' They might act very impulsively or say things they normally wouldn't, which is a classic sign to watch out for. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h3)

question: A patient with Pick's disease tries to eat paper wrappers and craves tons of sugar. How should you understand this?

options.A: It indicates the patient is suffering from severe iron-deficiency anemia.
options.B: It is a typical oral and dietary manifestation caused by temporal lobe damage.
options.C: It is a deliberate attempt by the patient to seek attention from staff.
options.D: It proves the patient has developed a secondary bacterial throat infection.

explanation: When the temporal lobe is affected, patients often develop strange eating habits, like craving sweets or trying to swallow non-food items. It's not for attention—it's the disease at work! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is the classic scan finding for a patient with Pick's disease?

options.A: Atrophy localized to the frontal and temporal lobes
options.B: Swelling and inflammation throughout the cerebellum
options.C: Multiple blocked blood vessels in the deep brain
options.D: Enlargement of the occipital cortex exclusively

explanation: Spot on! 'Atrophy' just means shrinkage. Scans of Pick's patients clearly show shrinking right in the frontal and temporal areas of the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h4)

question: Why can diagnosing Pick's disease be tricky in the beginning?

options.A: Its behavioral symptoms can be mistaken for psychiatric disorders.
options.B: Standard MRI scanners cannot image the frontal lobes clearly.
options.C: Routine blood tests can easily confuse it with normal aging.
options.D: Patients usually retain perfect memory until the final days.

explanation: Because the very first signs are personality changes and apathy, doctors sometimes mistake it for depression, anxiety, or mental health issues rather than a brain disease. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is the main goal of medical treatment for Pick's disease?

options.A: Restoring lost brain tissue in the frontal lobe
options.B: Reversing the underlying cellular tau accumulation
options.C: Curing the primary neurodegenerative process
options.D: Managing behavioral symptoms and improving comfort

explanation: Since we can't cure or reverse the disease yet, our nursing care focuses on keeping the patient comfortable, calm, and managing tough behavioral symptoms. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why are standard Alzheimer's drugs usually avoided or used carefully in Pick's disease?

options.A: They accelerate memory loss within the first week of use.
options.B: They interfere with routine blood pressure medications.
options.C: They do not target the underlying pathology and can worsen agitation.
options.D: They cause immediate and permanent paralysis of the lower limbs.

explanation: Alzheimer's medications don't help frontotemporal issues and can actually make behavioral outbursts worse. It's a great clinical pearl to remember for your exams! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h5)

question: A patient with Pick's disease tries to wander out of the ward wearing only a hospital gown. What is your best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Apply soft wrist restraints immediately to prevent wandering attempts.
options.B: Gently redirect the patient toward a quiet lounge area with a familiar activity.
options.C: Explain firmly and logically why leaving the ward is dangerous for health.
options.D: Lock the patient inside the hospital room until visiting hours are over.

explanation: Redirection is your best friend here! Arguing or reasoning usually fails because of brain damage, but gently steering them to a cozy spot keeps them safe without a fight. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h6)

question: What is a major safety risk for patients with Pick's disease due to temporal lobe changes?

options.A: Developing sudden and severe bone fractures from walking
options.B: Inability to feel pain when touching hot stove surfaces
options.C: Sudden loss of hearing making them unable to hear fire alarms
options.D: Attempting to eat non-food objects or dangerous substances

explanation: Because of changes in how they experience things orally, these patients might try to chew or swallow harmful objects. Keeping hazardous items out of reach is a crucial nursing priority! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h6)

question: Why is caring for someone with Pick's disease often so emotionally draining for families?

options.A: The disease progresses much faster than any other form of dementia.
options.B: Patients require constant surgical procedures throughout the illness.
options.C: Family members are legally required to pay for all hospital care.
options.D: The loss of personality and social filter can feel emotionally rejecting.

explanation: It hurts deeply when a loved one changes personality, loses their warmth, or acts out of character. Families need plenty of empathy and support from nurses to cope with this grief. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h7)

question: When is the best time to talk about end-of-life wishes and care planning with the family?

options.A: As early in the disease trajectory as possible
options.B: When the patient develops sudden aspiration pneumonia
options.C: Immediately after the final post-mortem examination
options.D: Only after the patient becomes completely mute and bedbound

explanation: Having these conversations early lets the patient share what they want while they still can, making future medical choices much easier for everyone involved. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T6#GNS222_U4_T6_h7)

question: Wernicke encephalopathy is caused by a severe shortage of which vitamin?

options.A: Vitamin D
options.B: Vitamin B12
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Vitamin B1

explanation: Spot on! Wernicke encephalopathy happens specifically when the body lacks enough thiamine, which is Vitamin B1. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h1)

question: Why do nurses treat Wernicke encephalopathy as a true emergency?

options.A: It triggers sudden high blood pressure that never responds to drugs
options.B: It can cause quick, permanent brain damage if treatment is delayed
options.C: It quickly spreads as a contagious infection
options.D: It causes immediate paralysis in all four limbs

explanation: You got it! Because it affects the brain so fast, replacing thiamine right away is crucial to prevent lasting harm. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h1)

question: What is the main job of thiamine (Vitamin B1) in our cells?

options.A: It wraps around nerves to speed up signals
options.B: It helps brain cells turn glucose into energy
options.C: It stops white blood cells from overreacting
options.D: It carries oxygen through the bloodstream

explanation: That's right! Thiamine acts like fuel for the brain, helping cells process glucose so they can stay alive and active. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h2)

question: What happens inside the brain when there is a severe shortage of thiamine?

options.A: Nerve cells multiply too fast and form lumps
options.B: Blood vessels in the head become too thick
options.C: Brain cells run out of energy and get damaged or die
options.D: Brain tissue fills up with excess water

explanation: Spot on! Without thiamine, cells can't make energy. This leads to cell stress, bleeding, and eventually cell death. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h2)

question: What is the most common reason people develop Wernicke encephalopathy?

options.A: A sudden head injury
options.B: A bad food allergy
options.C: Eating too much sugar
options.D: Chronic alcohol misuse

explanation: Correct! Long-term heavy alcohol use stops the gut from absorbing thiamine properly, making it the top cause of this condition. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h3)

question: Which of these patients is NOT at risk for Wernicke encephalopathy?

options.A: A patient recovering from weight loss surgery who vomits a lot
options.B: A patient eating a balanced diet with normal digestion
options.C: A patient on long-term kidney dialysis without supplements
options.D: A patient with an eating disorder who refuses to eat

explanation: You nailed it! Someone with normal nutrition and digestion gets plenty of daily thiamine, so they are not at risk. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h3)

question: What are the three classic signs of Wernicke encephalopathy?

options.A: Chest pain, high fever, and skin rash
options.B: Tremors, stiffness, and slow movement
options.C: Eye problems, poor balance, and confusion
options.D: Severe headache, stiff neck, and sudden paralysis

explanation: Great job! Watch out for trouble with eye movements, unsteady walking, and confusion—they form the classic triad. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h4)

question: A patient with a history of heavy drinking stumbles when walking and has jerky eye movements. What should you suspect?

options.A: An epileptic seizure
options.B: Acute appendicitis
options.C: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.D: Wernicke encephalopathy

explanation: Spot on! Stumbling, eye issues, and a history of heavy drinking are textbook signs of Wernicke encephalopathy. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h4)

question: Why must thiamine always be given BEFORE glucose to a deficient patient?

options.A: Glucose burns up the remaining thiamine and can worsen brain injury
options.B: Glucose stops the body from absorbing any vitamins
options.C: Thiamine stops glucose from causing an allergic reaction
options.D: Glucose mixes with the vitamin and makes it poisonous

explanation: Exactly! Giving sugar without thiamine forces starving cells to work, using up their last bits of vitamin and causing rapid brain damage. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h5)

question: How is thiamine usually given during an acute crisis of Wernicke encephalopathy?

options.A: By injection (IV or IM) in high doses
options.B: As a tiny swallowable tablet once a week
options.C: Rubbed onto the skin as a lotion
options.D: Mixed into cold fruit juice

explanation: You got it! Because the gut doesn't absorb nutrients well during a crisis, doctors order high-dose injections or IV drips. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h5)

question: What is a vital safety step when nursing a patient with Wernicke encephalopathy?

options.A: Setting up fall precautions because of poor coordination
options.B: Encouraging heavy gym workouts to build leg strength
options.C: Restricting all fluids to stop brain swelling
options.D: Keeping the room pitch black all day

explanation: Spot on! Because these patients struggle with balance (ataxia), keeping them safe from nasty falls is a top nursing priority. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h6)

question: A doctor orders IV glucose for a suspected Wernicke patient. What should you check first?

options.A: Warm the IV bag to room temperature
options.B: Confirm that thiamine has already been given
options.C: Check the patient's blood pressure every 5 minutes
options.D: Ask if they want fruit juice instead

explanation: Brilliant! Always verify that thiamine went in first to protect the patient's brain from crashing when glucose is introduced. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h6)

question: What condition often develops if Wernicke encephalopathy is left untreated?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.B: Chronic kidney failure
options.C: Type 2 diabetes
options.D: Korsakoff syndrome

explanation: That's correct! If Wernicke's isn't caught and treated, it often rolls into Korsakoff syndrome, which brings long-term memory troubles. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h7)

question: Which behavior is typical in a patient with Korsakoff syndrome?

options.A: Confabulation, where they make up stories to fill memory gaps
options.B: Uncontrollable shaking of both hands while eating
options.C: Throwing angry tantrums at family members
options.D: Being completely mute and refusing to talk to anyone

explanation: Spot on! Patients with Korsakoff often unconsciously invent details (confabulate) to cover up the blank spots in their memory. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T7#GNS222_U4_T7_h7)

question: Which vitamin deficiency is the main cause of Korsakoff syndrome?

options.A: Niacin deficiency
options.B: Thiamine deficiency
options.C: Cobalamin deficiency
options.D: Ascorbic acid deficiency

explanation: Spot on! Korsakoff syndrome happens when the body lacks vitamin B1 (thiamine), which the brain really needs to keep memory working smoothly. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h1)

question: What does 'confabulation' mean when caring for a patient with Korsakoff syndrome?

options.A: Making up stories to fill memory gaps without intent to lie
options.B: Refusing to speak to anyone about personal history
options.C: Deliberately deceiving healthcare workers about past events
options.D: Experiencing vivid visual hallucinations during the night

explanation: Don't worry, they aren't trying to trick you! Confabulation is when a patient unconsciously fills in memory blanks with made-up details, and they genuinely believe it happened. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h1)

question: Which parts of the brain are usually damaged in Korsakoff syndrome?

options.A: Broca area and the temporal lobe
options.B: Occipital cortex and the cerebellum
options.C: Mammillary bodies and thalamic nuclei
options.D: Basal ganglia and the motor strip

explanation: These specific deep brain structures have massive energy needs, making them the first casualties when thiamine runs out. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h2)

question: Why does lacking thiamine cause brain cells to die so quickly?

options.A: It disrupts critical energy pathways and glucose metabolism in neurons
options.B: It causes massive bacterial infections inside the cerebrospinal fluid
options.C: It triggers an autoimmune attack directly targeting the myelin sheath
options.D: It increases intracranial pressure by blocking the reabsorption of CSF

explanation: Think of thiamine as the spark plug for brain cells to burn glucose. Without it, the cells literally starve for energy and shut down. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h2)

question: How are Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome related?

options.A: They are completely unrelated disorders affecting different organs
options.B: Korsakoff syndrome always occurs years before Wernicke develops
options.C: Wernicke is a mild form of memory loss caused by normal aging
options.D: Wernicke is the acute stage and Korsakoff is the chronic stage

explanation: They are actually two sides of the same coin! Wernicke is the sudden, early emergency phase, and Korsakoff is the long-term memory issue that follows if it's not treated quickly. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h3)

question: A patient with a history of heavy drinking suddenly looks confused and has trouble moving their eyes. What is the most likely condition?

options.A: Alzheimer dementia
options.B: Korsakoff syndrome
options.C: Wernicke encephalopathy
options.D: Parkinson disease

explanation: That classic mix of confusion, eye movement problems, and a history of heavy alcohol use is a textbook warning sign for acute Wernicke encephalopathy. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a risk factor for getting Korsakoff syndrome?

options.A: Regular aerobic exercise
options.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum
options.C: Chronic alcohol abuse
options.D: Prolonged malnutrition

explanation: Exercise keeps you healthy! It doesn't cause vitamin shortages, unlike severe vomiting, poor diet, or heavy drinking. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h4)

question: How does heavy alcohol use lead to a lack of thiamine?

options.A: By speeding up kidney filtration so the vitamin is quickly sweated out
options.B: By neutralizing stomach acid so that protein digestion stops entirely
options.C: By destroying stored body fat where the vitamin is primarily stored
options.D: By interfering with intestinal absorption and liver storage of the vitamin

explanation: Alcohol irritates the gut lining and stresses the liver, making it impossible for the body to properly take in and hold onto vitamin B1 from food. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h4)

question: A patient remembers their childhood clearly but cannot recall what they ate an hour ago. What kind of memory loss is this?

options.A: Global retrograde amnesia wiping out all past decades
options.B: Anterograde amnesia with preserved remote memory
options.C: Pure procedural amnesia affecting motor skills only
options.D: Transient global amnesia that will resolve in hours

explanation: You've got it! 'Anterograde' means trouble making *new* memories, while older childhood memories ('remote memory') stay safe in the back of the mind. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h5)

question: What emotional change do we often see in patients with Korsakoff syndrome?

options.A: Extreme violent outbursts toward staff members
options.B: Apathy and lack of emotional spontaneity
options.C: Constant hyperactivity and pacing the hallways
options.D: Hyper-fixation on learning new complex hobbies

explanation: Patients often seem very indifferent, flat, or lacking in energy and initiative. It's part of how the brain injury affects their drive. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h5)

question: How do doctors usually confirm a diagnosis of Korsakoff syndrome?

options.A: An electrical muscle test of the upper and lower limbs
options.B: A simple finger-prick blood glucose test done at the bedside
options.C: Clinical history, neurological assessment, and neuroimaging
options.D: A 24-hour urine collection measuring total protein content

explanation: Since there isn't one quick blood test for it, clinicians look at the patient's story, test their memory, and use brain scans like an MRI. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h6)

question: A patient who has been in the hospital for weeks insists they just went to the market this morning. What should you suspect?

options.A: Confabulation due to underlying memory gaps
options.B: A normal reaction to boredom in the hospital
options.C: Deliberate lying to escape hospital restrictions
options.D: Early signs of a severe bacterial meningitis

explanation: They aren't trying to pull your leg! They are confabulating—innocently making up details to fill in the blank spots in their memory. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h6)

question: Why must you always give thiamine BEFORE IV glucose to a malnourished patient?

options.A: Glucose lowers blood pressure too quickly without thiamine present
options.B: Thiamine makes the veins less fragile before a large fluid bolus is given
options.C: Glucose interacts with IV tubing and causes the medication to crystallize
options.D: Giving glucose first can use up remaining thiamine and worsen brain damage

explanation: This is a crucial clinical pearl! Pouring sugar (glucose) into the body forces cells to burn energy, which completely drains the tiny bit of thiamine left and can trigger severe brain damage. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h7)

question: What happens to a patient's memory once you start giving them thiamine treatment?

options.A: It cures the underlying liver disease and repairs all brain tissue
options.B: It completely reverses all memory loss within forty-eight hours
options.C: It has no effect whatsoever on the patient's neurological state
options.D: It prevents further worsening, but full recovery of memory is rare

explanation: Thiamine is amazing for stopping the damage from getting worse, but unfortunately, the deep brain changes that already happened are usually permanent. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h7)

question: A patient with Korsakoff syndrome insists on going home to feed a pet dog that died years ago. How should you respond?

options.A: Agree that the dog is waiting at home for them
options.B: Gently redirect the patient to a current activity without arguing
options.C: Ignore the patient and leave the room immediately
options.D: Argue firmly until the patient admits the dog is dead

explanation: Arguing will only upset or confuse them. The kindest nursing move is to stay calm, validate their feelings softly, and smoothly guide them to a new activity. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h8)

question: What is the main goal of nursing care for someone living with long-term Korsakoff syndrome?

options.A: Completely restoring lost declarative memories from childhood
options.B: Training the brain to regrow lost neurons through intense puzzles
options.C: Teaching the patient how to fabricate stories more convincingly
options.D: Maximizing remaining functional independence using environmental aids

explanation: Since memory loss sticks around, we focus on helping them stay safe and independent using daily routines, calendars, and friendly cues. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h8)

question: Roughly what percentage of patients with full Korsakoff syndrome make a complete recovery?

options.A: Zero percent
options.B: Exactly 75 percent
options.C: Nearly 90 percent
options.D: About 20 percent

explanation: Only a small fraction (around one in five) recover fully, which is why catching and treating early Wernicke signs is so important! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h9)

question: Why do many patients with severe Korsakoff syndrome eventually need assisted living or structured care?

options.A: Severe chronic pain requires round-the-clock narcotic management
options.B: Patients require constant intravenous antibiotics for infections
options.C: Continuous physical therapy is needed to reverse limb paralysis
options.D: Inability to form new memories makes independent daily living unsafe

explanation: Because they cannot safely remember new instructions or manage daily tasks on their own, a structured, supportive environment keeps them safe. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T8#GNS222_U4_T8_h9)

question: How many unprovoked seizures are typically required to diagnose epilepsy?

options.A: Ten recurring seizures
options.B: Four or more seizures
options.C: At least two seizures
options.D: Only a single seizure

explanation: Diagnosing epilepsy generally requires two or more unprovoked seizures spaced more than 24 hours apart. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h1)

question: What is the main difference between epilepsy and a single isolated seizure?

options.A: The complete absence of motor symptoms
options.B: Strict occurrence only during sleep cycles
options.C: Instantaneous recovery of normal brain wave activity
options.D: The tendency for recurrent, unprovoked events

explanation: Epilepsy is defined by a lasting tendency to experience repeated, unprovoked seizures over time. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h1)

question: Which chemical messenger acts as the primary calming or inhibitory agent in the brain?

options.A: Dopamine transmitters
options.B: Gamma-aminobutyric acid
options.C: Excitatory glutamate
options.D: Acetylcholine molecules

explanation: GABA reduces brain activity by slowing down nerve cell signals, acting as the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h2)

question: What happens in the brain to directly trigger a seizure?

options.A: Depleted stores of intracellular water
options.B: Complete cessation of electrical activity
options.C: Equal levels of sodium and potassium
options.D: Excessive electrical excitation compared to inhibition

explanation: Seizures happen when nerve cell excitation overpowers calming signals, causing a sudden burst of synchronized electrical firing. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h2)

question: What is a common infectious cause of secondary epilepsy in sub-Saharan Africa?

options.A: Chronic uncomplicated urinary tract infections
options.B: Uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Neurocysticercosis and cerebral malaria
options.D: Primary upper respiratory infections

explanation: Infections affecting the brain, such as cerebral malaria and parasites, can scar brain tissue and trigger seizures. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h3)

question: Why is a traumatic brain injury considered a risk factor for developing epilepsy later on?

options.A: It permanently lowers resting body temperature
options.B: It accelerates the production of red blood cells
options.C: Scar tissue forms and alters normal nerve pathways
options.D: It permanently increases daily dietary salt intake

explanation: Physical head injuries create scar tissue that disrupts normal electrical wiring in the brain, making seizures more likely. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h3)

question: Which seizure type originates in both cerebral hemispheres simultaneously?

options.A: Focal aware seizures
options.B: Partial motor events
options.C: Simple sensory spells
options.D: Generalized seizures

explanation: Generalized seizures engage networks across both brain hemispheres right from the onset. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h4)

question: A patient is observed staring blankly for a few seconds without falling or convulsing. What seizure type is this?

options.A: Myoclonic spasm
options.B: Tonic-clonic seizure
options.C: Focal motor event
options.D: Absence seizure

explanation: Absence seizures present as brief, sudden lapses in awareness often mistaken for daydreaming. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h4)

question: What term describes the period of confusion and deep sleep immediately following a seizure?

options.A: Prodromal stage
options.B: Aura period
options.C: Post-ictal phase
options.D: Tonic interval

explanation: The post-ictal phase is the recovery period right after a seizure where the brain rests, leading to tiredness and confusion. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h5)

question: What is Todd's paresis, which can be seen after a focal seizure?

options.A: Irreversible cognitive memory decline
options.B: Temporary muscle weakness in the affected limbs
options.C: Permanent loss of visual field perception
options.D: Complete paralysis of respiratory muscles

explanation: Todd's paresis is a temporary weakness in a specific part of the body following a seizure that wears off after a few hours. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h5)

question: Which diagnostic tool is primarily used to record abnormal brain electrical activity?

options.A: Electrocardiogram
options.B: Electromyogram
options.C: Echocardiogram
options.D: Electroencephalogram

explanation: An EEG measures voltage fluctuations resulting from ionic current within the neurons of the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h6)

question: Why do doctors order a brain scan (neuroimaging) when someone has a new-onset seizure?

options.A: To assess heart rhythm abnormalities
options.B: To detect physical brain damage, scars, or tumors
options.C: To measure exact salt levels in the blood
options.D: To evaluate how well oxygen is moving through the lungs

explanation: Imaging scans like an MRI help find physical issues like strokes, scars, or tumors that may be causing the seizures. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h6)

question: What is the main medical treatment used to manage epilepsy day-to-day?

options.A: Intravenous electrolyte infusions
options.B: Daily immunosuppressive drugs
options.C: Anti-seizure medications
options.D: Long-term antibiotic therapy

explanation: Anti-seizure medications are the main treatment used to calm electrical activity and prevent future seizures. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h7)

question: When is surgery usually considered for a patient with epilepsy?

options.A: When medication side effects are extremely mild
options.B: Immediately following the first unprovoked episode
options.C: Only when an EEG test is completely normal
options.D: When seizures cannot be controlled by multiple medications

explanation: Surgery is kept as an option for drug-resistant epilepsy when medications fail and a clear seizure source can be safely removed. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h7)

question: What duration of continuous seizure activity defines status epilepticus?

options.A: Less than one minute
options.B: Exactly thirty seconds
options.C: Longer than five minutes
options.D: More than two hours

explanation: Seizures lasting beyond five minutes carry a high risk of permanent neuronal damage and define status epilepticus. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h8)

question: What is the most important immediate nursing action during an active convulsive seizure?

options.A: Give the patient water immediately to prevent dehydration
options.B: Force a padded wooden spatula into the oral cavity
options.C: Attempt to physically hold down all moving limbs
options.D: Protect the patient from injury and keep the airway clear

explanation: Safety comes first: clear dangerous objects, turn the patient onto their side to keep the airway open, and never force anything into their mouth. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h8)

question: Which lifestyle factor is a very common trigger for breakthrough seizures in epilepsy patients?

options.A: Drinking clean water
options.B: Eating balanced meals
options.C: Regular moderate exercise
options.D: Not getting enough sleep

explanation: Poor rest or sleep deprivation lowers the brain's seizure threshold, making breakthrough seizures much more likely. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h9)

question: Why is psychosocial support so important in the overall care of an epilepsy patient?

options.A: To eliminate the need for regular EEG testing
options.B: To replace the requirement for daily medication
options.C: To permanently cure underlying brain malformations
options.D: To help them cope with social stigma and feelings of isolation

explanation: Psychosocial support helps patients deal with the emotional weight, anxiety, and social stigma that often come with a chronic condition. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h9)

question: Why are the testes located outside the main body cavity in the scrotum?

options.A: To produce testosterone for secondary sex traits
options.B: To store mature sperm cells before ejaculation
options.C: To keep the testes cooler than core body temperature
options.D: To secrete fluid that forms the bulk of semen

explanation: You've got this! Sperm production works best at a slightly lower temperature than our normal body heat. That is why nature designed the scrotum to hang outside the body to keep the testes nice and cool. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which part of the penis directly wraps around and surrounds the urethra?

options.A: Dartos muscle layer
options.B: Corpus spongiosum
options.C: Corpora cavernosa
options.D: Tunica albuginea

explanation: Great job thinking through the anatomy! The corpus spongiosum is the single column of spongy tissue that houses and protects the urethra as it runs down to the tip. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h1)

question: Where exactly inside the testes are sperm cells made?

options.A: Leydig cells
options.B: Seminiferous tubules
options.C: Tunica albuginea
options.D: Epididymis head

explanation: Think of the seminiferous tubules as tiny, packed-together factories inside the testes where germ cells constantly grow and transform into brand new sperm! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is the main job of the Leydig cells found in the testes?

options.A: Protecting developing germ cells from immune attack
options.B: Providing nutritional support to immature spermatids
options.C: Transporting mature sperm out of the lobules
options.D: Producing and secreting the hormone testosterone

explanation: You're doing great! Leydig cells hang out right between the sperm-producing tubes and are responsible for pumping out testosterone, the key male hormone. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h2)

question: What happens to sperm when they hang out in the epididymis?

options.A: To allow sperm to mature and gain swimming ability
options.B: To cool down the testes during physical exertion
options.C: To filter out abnormal sperm cells using white blood cells
options.D: To add fructose-rich fluid to the seminal mixture

explanation: Think of the epididymis as a training ground! Newly made sperm aren't ready to swim yet; they spend time here resting, maturing, and learning how to swim. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h3)

question: How do sperm travel upward through the long vas deferens during ejaculation?

options.A: By beating their flagella very rapidly
options.B: By suction created by the prostate gland
options.C: By smooth muscle peristaltic contractions
options.D: By gravity pulling them down into the urethra

explanation: Just like food moves down your gut, the walls of the vas deferens use wave-like muscle squeezes (peristalsis) to push sperm smoothly along their journey. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which male reproductive gland adds the most fluid volume to semen?

options.A: Seminal vesicles
options.B: Prostate gland
options.C: Testicular interstitium
options.D: Bulbourethral glands

explanation: Spot on! The seminal vesicles are generous contributors, providing about 60% of semen fluid along with sugary fructose to give the sperm energy. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why do the bulbourethral glands release a clear mucus right before ejaculation?

options.A: To neutralize any leftover acid from urine in the urethra
options.B: To provide the main energy source for sperm motility
options.C: To activate sperm flagella for faster swimming
options.D: To cause the semen to clot firmly inside the vagina

explanation: Urine is quite acidic and can harm delicate sperm. This clever little mucus fluid cleanses the urethra path first so the sperm can pass safely! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which hormone signals the Leydig cells in the testes to make testosterone?

options.A: Luteinizing hormone (LH)
options.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
options.C: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)
options.D: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)

explanation: You've got this! Luteinizing hormone (LH) travels from the brain's pituitary gland down to the testes, giving the green light for testosterone production. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h5)

question: How would you explain a negative feedback loop of hormones to a curious patient?

options.A: It allows the brain to control your heart rate and breathing rate simultaneously.
options.B: It prevents the testes from ever changing in size throughout your lifetime.
options.C: It stops the body from producing too much testosterone when levels are already high.
options.D: It ensures that the pituitary gland stops working completely during physical rest.

explanation: Think of it like an air conditioner thermostat! When hormone levels get high enough, a signal goes back to the brain to slow things down so the body doesn't overproduce. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which gland releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone to trigger the female reproductive cycle?

options.A: The anterior pituitary gland
options.B: The adrenal cortex
options.C: The hypothalamus
options.D: The posterior pituitary gland

explanation: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone is synthesized and released by the hypothalamus in the brain to kick off the hormonal cascade. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h1)

question: What usually happens when the delicate hormonal balance of the female reproductive system is disrupted?

options.A: Secondary sex characteristics reverse themselves instantly
options.B: Estrogen production permanently stops across all age groups
options.C: The reproductive organs immediately undergo complete atrophy
options.D: It can lead to issues ranging from irregular periods to more serious health concerns

explanation: Think of hormones like a delicate chain reaction! When one part is out of balance, it can throw off the whole cycle, leading to skipped periods or other reproductive challenges. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h1)

question: What is the medical term for abnormally heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding?

options.A: Oligomenorrhea
options.B: Dysmenorrhea
options.C: Menorrhagia
options.D: Amenorrhea

explanation: Menorrhagia describes periods that are excessively heavy or last longer than normal, often draining the body's iron stores. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h2)

question: A patient with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is most likely to show which group of signs?

options.A: High male hormone levels, failure to release eggs regularly, and insulin resistance
options.B: Heavy bleeding, low blood pressure, and severe weight loss
options.C: Complete absence of pubic hair and early menopause
options.D: Frequent fever, pelvic pain, and purulent vaginal discharge

explanation: PCOS is a very common hormonal condition. It usually involves high levels of androgens (male hormones), irregular ovulation, and trouble handling insulin properly. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is a cystocele?

options.A: Benign smooth muscle tumors growing inside the myometrium
options.B: Bulging of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall
options.C: Herniation of the rectum into the posterior vaginal canal
options.D: Downward displacement of the uterus through the cervix

explanation: A cystocele happens when the supportive tissue between a woman's bladder and vaginal wall weakens, allowing the bladder to sag into the vagina. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h3)

question: Why do pelvic organ prolapse conditions often lead to problems with urination?

options.A: Estrogen surges cause the bladder to double in physical size
options.B: Infection destroys the smooth muscle tissue of the ureters
options.C: The kidneys stop producing urine due to chronic pelvic pressure
options.D: The shifted position of the organs changes normal urine flow mechanics

explanation: When supportive pelvic structures weaken and sag, organs like the bladder shift out of place. This makes it hard to empty the bladder fully, leading to frequent urges or retention. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h3)

question: Which germs are the most common causes of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)?

options.A: Candida albicans and Trichomonas vaginalis
options.B: Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus
options.C: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.D: Human papillomavirus and Herpes simplex virus

explanation: PID usually happens when sexually transmitted bacteria travel upward from the vagina and cervix into the uterus and fallopian tubes. Always good to remember for clinicals! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h4)

question: A young female patient has lower abdominal pain and cries out in severe pain when the nurse moves her cervix during a pelvic exam. What is the most likely condition?

options.A: Uterine fibroids
options.B: Primary dysmenorrhea
options.C: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
options.D: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

explanation: That intense pain when moving the cervix is called 'cervical motion tenderness' (or a positive chandelier sign), and it's a classic red flag for PID. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h4)

question: Persistent infection with high-risk strains of which common virus is the primary cause of cervical cancer?

options.A: Epstein-Barr Virus
options.B: Human Papillomavirus
options.C: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
options.D: Cytomegalovirus

explanation: High-risk types of HPV can cause gradual changes in the cells of the cervix. Over time, these changes can turn cancerous if not caught early by a Pap smear. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why is ovarian cancer so often diagnosed at an advanced stage?

options.A: Patients refuse pelvic examinations until pain becomes unbearable
options.B: Early symptoms are vague and easily mistaken for normal tummy trouble or gas
options.C: Tumors spread exclusively through the lymphatic system
options.D: There are no reliable blood tests or imaging studies available

explanation: Ovarian cancer is tricky because early signs like bloating, mild fullness, or tummy ache look just like common digestive issues, so people often ignore them at first. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h5)

question: What tool does a doctor use to look closely at abnormal cervical tissue under a special magnifying lens?

options.A: Transvaginal ultrasound
options.B: Hysterosalpingography
options.C: Laparoscopy
options.D: Colposcopy

explanation: A colposcopy uses a special magnifying scope to take a closer look at the cervix, vagina, and vulva, usually following up on an abnormal Pap smear result. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h6)

question: What is the main reason a patient would have a hysterosalpingography (HSG) procedure done?

options.A: To measure circulating levels of follicle-stimulating hormone
options.B: To check if the fallopian tubes are open and examine the inside of the uterus
options.C: To visualize ovarian cysts and measure their exact physical dimensions
options.D: To scrape the endometrial lining for suspected malignant cells

explanation: During an HSG, a special dye is gently put into the uterus while taking X-rays. It helps doctors see if the fallopian tubes are blocked or clear. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which specific cells in the testes are responsible for making testosterone?

options.A: Seminiferous tubules
options.B: Bulbourethral glands
options.C: Cells of Leydig
options.D: Epididymis

explanation: Great job! The interstitial cells of Leydig are found inside the testes and do the heavy lifting of making testosterone. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h1)

question: What is the main job of the fluid made by the seminal vesicles?

options.A: Storing mature sperm cells
options.B: Nourishing sperm with fructose
options.C: Lubricating the urethra
options.D: Neutralizing acidic urine

explanation: You've got this! Seminal vesicle fluid is packed with fructose, giving sperm the energy boost they need to swim toward the egg. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h1)

question: What actually happens to the prostate gland in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?

options.A: Non-cancerous cell overgrowth
options.B: Infection-driven tissue necrosis
options.C: Malignant tumor invasion
options.D: Fibrotic tissue shrinking

explanation: Spot on! 'Benign' means non-cancerous. In BPH, the prostate cells simply overgrow, which is very common as men age. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h2)

question: If an older male patient has an enlarged prostate (BPH), what urinary symptom is he most likely to complain about?

options.A: A weak and slow urinary stream
options.B: Total absence of urine production
options.C: Inability to control bowel movements
options.D: Severe pain during bladder filling

explanation: Makes total sense, right? When the prostate grows, it presses on the urethra like a pinched garden hose, making the urine flow slow and weak. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is a major sign that sets acute bacterial prostatitis apart from chronic prostate issues?

options.A: Gradual hair loss on the legs
options.B: Sudden high fever and chills
options.C: Enlarged painless lymph nodes
options.D: Completely painless urination

explanation: Spot on. Acute infections hit hard and fast! Patients usually run a high fever and feel very sick, unlike chronic cases. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why is it so important to figure out the exact type of prostatitis a patient has?

options.A: It indicates that immediate surgical removal of the prostate is needed
options.B: It prevents the future development of benign prostatic hyperplasia
options.C: It proves whether the patient has concurrent testicular cancer
options.D: It dictates whether antibiotics or non-infectious management is required

explanation: Brilliant! Bacterial infections need antibiotics, while other types of pelvic pain need a totally different, non-infectious treatment plan. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why is testicular torsion treated as an absolute medical emergency?

options.A: It causes irreversible damage to the prostate gland
options.B: Loss of blood supply can lead to tissue death within hours
options.C: It always leads to permanent systemic high blood pressure
options.D: It immediately spreads severe infection to the kidneys

explanation: You nailed it. When the cord twists, it cuts off blood flow. If we don't fix it right away, the testicle can die. Every minute counts! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h4)

question: During a physical exam for a patient with testicular torsion, which reflex is usually missing?

options.A: Cremasteric reflex
options.B: Patellar reflex
options.C: Gag reflex
options.D: Babinski reflex

explanation: Correct! Normally, stroking the inner thigh makes the testicle rise (cremasteric reflex). In torsion, that reflex is completely absent. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h4)

question: Testicular cancer is most commonly diagnosed in which age group?

options.A: Young men aged 15 to 35
options.B: Middle-aged men aged 50 to 65
options.C: Pre-pubertal boys under 10
options.D: Elderly men over 75 years
