explanation: If a baby can't pee, it could mean swelling is blocking the urethra. That's an urgent sign that needs immediate medical review! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h9)

question: Why do nurses give medications through an IV line instead of having the patient swallow a pill?

options.A: It lasts much longer in the bloodstream than oral pills.
options.B: It prevents all known systemic side effects from occurring.
options.C: It is completely painless for every patient receiving treatment.
options.D: It provides a much faster onset of drug action in the body.

explanation: Spot on! Because IV fluids go straight into the bloodstream, the body skips the digestive tract entirely and goes to work right away. You've got this! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: A patient arrives at the clinic with severe vomiting and dehydration. Why is an IV line started instead of just giving them oral rehydration drinks?

options.A: The patient's digestive tract cannot absorb any liquids safely.
options.B: Oral fluids take too long to reach the stomach lining.
options.C: IV fluids rapidly restore circulating blood volume and correct electrolytes.
options.D: Intravenous fluids taste much better than oral rehydration salts.

explanation: Great thinking! When someone is vomiting heavily, IV fluids are the quickest way to restore circulating blood volume and get their electrolytes balanced safely. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: Where is the median cubital vein located, which is a favourite spot for starting an IV?

options.A: Near the inside of the ankle joint
options.B: Along the lateral side of the upper arm
options.C: On the back of the hand
options.D: In the antecubital fossa of the elbow

explanation: Exactly! The median cubital vein sits right across the bend of the elbow (the antecubital fossa), making it super accessible for quick IV lines and blood tests. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: When you gently tap and feel a patient's arm to find a good vein, what should a healthy peripheral vein feel like?

options.A: A hard, rigid cord that does not bounce back
options.B: A soft, bouncy vessel that refills after being pressed
options.C: A deep vessel that cannot be felt but looks dark blue
options.D: A pulsing vessel that moves strongly under the finger

explanation: Spot on! Healthy veins feel spongy, elastic, and refill promptly with blood after you press them. You'll get great at spotting these on the ward! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which of these commonly used IV fluids is classified as an isotonic fluid?

options.A: 0.45% Sodium Chloride
options.B: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.C: 10% Dextrose in Water
options.D: 3% Sodium Chloride

explanation: Well done! Normal saline has a salt and water balance very close to human blood plasma, so it stays nicely inside the vessels without causing weird fluid shifts. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: A patient has severe brain swelling, and you need a fluid that will draw excess water out of the swollen cells and back into the bloodstream. What type of IV solution do you need?

options.A: Hypoosmolar solution
options.B: Isotonic solution
options.C: Hypertonic solution
options.D: Hypotonic solution

explanation: You got it! Hypertonic fluids are concentrated, creating an osmotic pressure that pulls fluid out of tissue cells and safely back into the blood vessels. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: Why do we apply a tourniquet to a patient's arm before trying to insert an IV cannula?

options.A: To sterilize the outer skin surface before cleaning
options.B: To completely stop arterial blood flow to the limb
options.C: To numb the local skin area and reduce sharp pain
options.D: To trap venous blood and make the veins swell up

explanation: Exactly! The tourniquet pauses blood from returning to the heart, causing the veins underneath to plump up so they are much easier to see and feel. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: Why do nurses prefer to use a clear, transparent dressing over an IV insertion site?

options.A: It completely stops the patient from feeling any accidental movement pain.
options.B: It allows the nurse to inspect the skin for redness without removing the cover.
options.C: It keeps the cannula warm so the IV fluid flows much faster.
options.D: It permanently seals the vein shut so no blood can ever leak out.

explanation: Spot on! Clear dressings keep outside germs away while letting you quickly check the site for early signs of swelling or redness without peeling anything back. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: At what angle should you hold your needle when inserting a peripheral IV cannula through the skin?

options.A: 15 to 30 degrees
options.B: 45 to 60 degrees
options.C: 90 degrees straight down
options.D: 5 to 10 degrees

explanation: Great job! A shallow 15 to 30-degree angle lets you glide smoothly into the vein without accidentally poking right through the back wall of the vessel. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: During an IV insertion, what lets you know for sure that your needle has successfully entered the vein?

options.A: The infusion bag begins to drip rapidly without any pressure.
options.B: The surrounding skin turns pale and cool to the touch.
options.C: The patient reports a sudden cooling sensation in the arm.
options.D: A flash of blood appears inside the flashback chamber of the device.

explanation: That's right! Seeing that little 'flash' of dark red blood in the chamber is the classic sign that you're in the vein. Beautiful work! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: When programming an electronic IV infusion pump on the ward, what unit of measurement do you normally use?

options.A: Milliliters per hour (mL/hr)
options.B: Liters per 24 hours (L/day)
options.C: Drops per minute (gtt/min)
options.D: Drops per second (gtt/sec)

explanation: Spot on! Pumps are designed to deliver a precise volume of fluid every hour, so we program them in mL/hr. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: You need to run 1000 mL of normal saline over 8 hours using a manual gravity tubing set with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What is the approximate flow rate in drops per minute?

options.A: 31 gtt/min
options.B: 125 gtt/min
options.C: 21 gtt/min
options.D: 42 gtt/min

explanation: You're doing great with math! Multiply 1000 mL by 15 to get 15,000 drops, then divide by 480 total minutes (8 hours x 60 mins). That gives you roughly 31 drops per minute! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: As a student nurse, how often should you check and inspect an active peripheral IV site on your patient?

options.A: Once every 48 hours during dressing changes
options.B: Only when the patient complains of severe pain
options.C: Only when the infusion bag runs completely empty
options.D: At least once every nursing shift

explanation: Exactly! Regular checks each shift help you catch tiny problems like early swelling or soreness before they turn into bigger issues. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: Why do nurses flush an intermittent IV line with normal saline right after giving a medication?

options.A: To clear remaining drug residue and prevent line clotting
options.B: To dilute any air bubbles that entered during the injection
options.C: To numb the vein so the patient feels less soreness
options.D: To cool down the internal walls of the plastic tubing

explanation: Well done! Flushing pushes any leftover medication completely through the catheter, keeping the line clear and preventing clots. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: Which of these signs is the classic giveaway that an IV has 'infiltrated' (leaked into the tissue)?

options.A: A warm, red, hard streak running all the way up the arm
options.B: Severe chest pain accompanied by audible lung crackles
options.C: Bright red bleeding gushing out around the plastic catheter
options.D: Swelling, coolness, and pallor around the insertion site

explanation: Spot on! When IV fluid leaks into the tissue instead of the vein, it makes the skin look pale, feel cool, and swell up. Time to restart the line! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: A patient receiving a strong chemotherapy drug through a peripheral IV suddenly complains of a burning pain, and the area starts swelling up. What is your very first action?

options.A: Stop the infusion immediately and disconnect the tubing.
options.B: Flush the IV line rapidly with normal saline to clear the drug.
options.C: Massage the arm firmly to help the drug spread out faster.
options.D: Apply a cold ice pack directly over the swollen area.

explanation: Safety first! Stopping the infusion right away prevents any more harsh fluid from leaking into the tissue and causing damage. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: Why must you always inspect the tip of an IV catheter immediately after taking it out of a patient's arm?

options.A: To see if the patient's blood type has changed during therapy
options.B: To test the sterility of the plastic surface before disposal
options.C: To check if the plastic tip broke off inside the vein
options.D: To measure how much blood remains inside the hollow needle

explanation: Great nursing habit! Always check the removed cannula to make sure the entire plastic tip came out cleanly and nothing was left behind. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)

question: What is the proper technique for pulling a peripheral IV cannula out of a patient's skin?

options.A: Pull it out smoothly and parallel to the skin surface.
options.B: Twist the catheter in a full circle before lifting it out.
options.C: Tug it quickly and firmly to make the removal as fast as possible.
options.D: Pull it straight up toward the ceiling at a sharp 90-degree angle.

explanation: You've got it! Pulling it out smoothly and low to the skin prevents unnecessary scratching or trauma to the fragile vein wall. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)

question: What is the main focus of cancer epidemiology?

options.A: Testing new chemotherapy drugs in the laboratory
options.B: Studying cancer patterns and causes in populations
options.C: Performing surgical removal of malignant tumors
options.D: Providing daily bedside care to cancer patients

explanation: Cancer epidemiology looks at whole groups of people to see how and why cancer occurs in different populations. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why do public health planners rely on epidemiological data?

options.A: To decide where to direct health resources and programs
options.B: To diagnose individual patients in emergency rooms
options.C: To write personal care plans for recovering clients
options.D: To determine the exact cost of hospital equipment

explanation: Population data helps health authorities see where disease rates are highest so they can build facilities and plan interventions accordingly. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which cancer is the most common among Nigerian women?

options.A: Liver cancer
options.B: Breast cancer
options.C: Cervical cancer
options.D: Ovarian cancer

explanation: Breast cancer is recorded as the leading malignancy among women in Nigeria and globally. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is a major viral infection linked closely to cervical cancer in Nigeria?

options.A: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
options.B: Hepatitis B virus
options.C: Epstein-Barr virus
options.D: Human Papillomavirus

explanation: Persistent infection with high-risk strains of Human Papillomavirus is the primary driver behind most cervical cancer cases. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What does incidence measure in a population?

options.A: The number of new cases diagnosed
options.B: The total number of existing cases
options.C: The percentage of people who die
options.D: The cost of treating the disease

explanation: Incidence specifically counts the new diagnoses appearing over a set timeframe, showing the rate at which a disease develops. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: A public health nurse wants to know the total burden of chronic leukemia in a community, including people diagnosed years ago. Which measure should she look at?

options.A: Risk ratio
options.B: Prevalence
options.C: Incidence
options.D: Mortality rate

explanation: Prevalence measures all existing cases at a given time, capturing both new diagnoses and survivors living with the condition. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following is a non-modifiable risk factor for cancer?

options.A: Smoking
options.B: Alcohol use
options.C: Diet
options.D: Age

explanation: Age is an inherent biological factor that cannot be altered, making it non-modifiable. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why are infectious agents like Hepatitis B classified as cancer risk factors?

options.A: They immediately destroy all red blood cells in the body
options.B: They lower body temperature and stop normal digestion
options.C: They block the absorption of vital nutrients in the gut
options.D: They cause chronic inflammation and cellular damage over time

explanation: Certain viruses and bacteria lead to long-term tissue damage and inflammation, which increases the chance of cellular mutations. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the origin of most cancer-causing mutations?

options.A: Passed down exclusively through maternal bloodlines
options.B: Inherited directly from parents in every single diagnosed case
options.C: Acquired over a lifetime from environmental and lifestyle factors
options.D: Caused entirely by sudden bacterial infections in childhood

explanation: Most cancers arise from acquired mutations that build up over time due to exposure to external agents like tobacco, radiation, and unhealthy diets. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why do people with the same genetic background sometimes have different cancer risks?

options.A: Genetics is the only factor that ever influences disease
options.B: Inherited genes change completely every five years
options.C: Their environmental exposures and lifestyle choices vary
options.D: Lifestyle habits have no real impact on cellular health

explanation: Environmental and lifestyle factors interact with genes, meaning different habits will alter overall risk even among family members. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of cancer screening programs?

options.A: To replace traditional biopsy procedures entirely
options.B: To detect cancer or precancerous changes early
options.C: To cure late-stage metastatic disease completely
options.D: To measure the exact cost of hospital stays

explanation: Screening aims to identify disease before symptoms appear so treatment can start when it is most effective. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: A community health nurse is planning a cervical cancer screening outreach. Which test is she most likely to utilize?

options.A: Liver biopsy
options.B: Chest X-ray
options.C: Pap smear
options.D: Prostate-specific antigen test

explanation: A Pap smear is a standard, widely used screening tool for detecting cervical cell abnormalities and precancerous lesions. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: How do nurses directly help with cancer epidemiology in clinical and community settings?

options.A: Funding public health research grants through private banks
options.B: Designing blueprints for modern oncology radiation bunkers
options.C: Manufacturing new chemotherapy drugs in hospital pharmacies
options.D: Accurate data collection and maintaining cancer registries

explanation: Nurses play a huge role by gathering precise patient data and keeping records updated, which helps researchers track cancer trends. You're making great progress! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: Why are community health nurses in a great position to promote cancer prevention?

options.A: They are the only healthcare professionals permitted to diagnose tumors
options.B: They hold exclusive authority over national public health budgets
options.C: They interact directly with individuals and families on a regular basis
options.D: They spend all their time working inside high-tech molecular laboratories

explanation: Because nurses interact regularly with everyday people and families, they are perfectly placed to teach about risk factors and encourage healthy habits. Well done! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is the main job of chemotherapy in cancer treatment?

options.A: To cool down inflamed skin tissues
options.B: To physically remove large solid tumors
options.C: To supply essential vitamins to the blood
options.D: To target and destroy rapidly dividing cells

explanation: You've got this! Chemotherapy drugs travel through the body specifically seeking out and killing cells that divide very quickly, which is what cancer cells love to do. Great job learning the basics! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why do doctors often combine surgery with radiation or chemotherapy?

options.A: To prevent the patient from losing too much weight
options.B: To make the patient immune to future infections
options.C: To permanently boost the patient's red blood cell count
options.D: To eliminate any remaining microscopic cancer cells left behind

explanation: Think of it as teamwork! Surgery removes the main tumor, but combination therapies help sweep up any tiny stray cancer cells that are too small to see. You are doing brilliantly! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h1)

question: What is the top nursing priority right after major cancer surgery?

options.A: Withdrawing all intravenous fluids immediately
options.B: Preventing complications and managing acute surgical pain
options.C: Discharging the patient within twenty-four hours
options.D: Starting intensive physical exercise right away

explanation: Right after surgery, keeping your patient comfortable and watching out for issues like infection or blood clots are your most important duties. You are well on your way to becoming an amazing nurse! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h2)

question: A patient after cancer surgery refuses to get out of bed to walk. What is the best thing to do?

options.A: Allow the patient to stay in bed all day without moving
options.B: Wait until the surgeon arrives before attempting any movement
options.C: Scold the patient for being uncooperative with recovery
options.D: Explain that early walking helps prevent blood clots and lung problems

explanation: Kind patient education works wonders! A gentle explanation helps them see why moving early is vital for preventing serious issues like clots. You've got the nurse's touch! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h2)

question: What does the word 'vesicant' mean when talking about certain chemo drugs?

options.A: Natural supplements that cure nausea caused by treatment
options.B: Solutions used to clean the skin before a surgical incision
options.C: Drugs that cause severe tissue damage if they leak outside the vein
options.D: Medications that are only given orally in pill form

explanation: Vesicants are tricky drugs! If they escape the vein into the skin, they can cause blistering and tissue damage, which is why nurses watch IV sites so closely. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h3)

question: Why must nurses check absolute neutrophil counts before giving chemotherapy?

options.A: To measure how fast the kidneys are filtering urine
options.B: To check if the patient has a hidden vitamin deficiency
options.C: To see if the patient is eating enough protein
options.D: To ensure the patient's immune system is strong enough to handle the drug

explanation: Chemo can lower white blood cells, so checking neutrophils first keeps your patient safe from dangerous infections. Safety first, nurse! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h3)

question: How should a nurse instruct a patient to care for skin receiving radiation therapy?

options.A: Scrub the treatment area firmly with a washcloth daily
options.B: Use heating pads on the skin to relieve soreness
options.C: Wash the area gently with mild soap and warm water
options.D: Apply strong perfumed lotions right before treatment

explanation: Treated skin is extra fragile. Gentle cleansing with mild soap and water protects the delicate skin barrier. You're mastering patient care! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h4)

question: A patient having radiation for breast cancer asks if she can wear her tight underwire bra. What should you say?

options.A: Yes, as long as it is washed in hot water
options.B: Yes, underwire provides necessary support during healing
options.C: No, choose a soft, loose-fitting garment to avoid friction on the skin
options.D: Only wear it during the actual radiation treatment session

explanation: Tight clothing rubs against fragile skin and causes irritation. Recommending soft, loose clothes keeps your patient comfortable! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h4)

question: What does 'myelosuppression' mean?

options.A: A sudden swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck
options.B: An infection located directly on the outer layer of the skin
options.C: The suppression of blood cell production in the bone marrow
options.D: The overproduction of red blood cells in the bone marrow

explanation: Big medical word, simple meaning! It just means cancer treatments slow down bone marrow activity, leading to low blood counts. You're learning fast! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why are anti-nausea meds usually given before chemo starts instead of waiting for nausea to begin?

options.A: Preventing nausea before it starts is much more effective than treating it later
options.B: They help the patient fall asleep during the long infusion
options.C: Chemotherapy drugs will not dissolve properly without them
options.D: They taste better when taken on an empty stomach

explanation: Prevention is key! Giving these meds early blocks the vomiting center before chemo triggers it. Brilliant clinical thinking! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h5)

question: Which condition causes facial swelling, neck vein bulging, and trouble breathing due to a blocked major vein?

options.A: Spinal Cord Compression
options.B: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome
options.C: Febrile Neutropenia
options.D: Tumor Lysis Syndrome

explanation: When a tumor presses on the superior vena cava, blood gets backed up in the upper body, causing that distinct facial swelling. Spotting this makes you a sharp nurse! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h6)

question: Why is a fever in a neutropenic patient considered a medical emergency?

options.A: It causes severe bleeding that is impossible to stop
options.B: A compromised immune system means a mild infection can rapidly turn fatal
options.C: It always causes permanent paralysis in the legs
options.D: It instantly stops the kidneys from producing any urine

explanation: Without enough white blood cells to fight back, a small fever can quickly become overwhelming. Quick action with antibiotics saves lives here! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h6)

question: What is a great food tip for a patient who feels nauseated and has a poor appetite during cancer treatment?

options.A: Eat three large heavy meals at traditional times
options.B: Offer small, frequent meals that are high in protein
options.C: Avoid all protein and eat only plain white sugar
options.D: Eat food straight from the oven while it is piping hot and aromatic

explanation: Large meals can overwhelm a weak tummy. Small, protein-rich snacks are much easier to handle and help keep their strength up! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h7)

question: A cancer patient says food smells too strong and tastes like metal. What is a helpful nursing tip?

options.A: Suggest serving foods cool or at room temperature to reduce strong smells
options.B: Tell the patient to force themselves to eat large portions anyway
options.C: Advise the patient to stop eating completely until treatment ends
options.D: Recommend adding extra iron supplements to every meal

explanation: Warm foods release strong vapors that trigger nausea. Serving meals cool helps hide those metallic tastes and smells. Clever nursing care! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h7)

question: When is the best time to introduce palliative care to a cancer patient?

options.A: Early alongside active disease treatment to improve quality of life
options.B: Only when the patient refuses to take prescribed oral medications
options.C: Only during the final twenty-four hours of life
options.D: After all chemotherapy and radiation treatments have failed completely

explanation: Palliative care isn't just for the end of life—it teams up with curative treatments from day one to keep the patient comfortable. Excellent holistic nursing! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h8)

question: How does early palliative care help a patient going through tough cancer treatments?

options.A: It completely replaces the need for any surgical operations
options.B: It lowers hospital bills by shortening surgical procedures
options.C: It focuses on relieving symptoms, pain, and emotional distress
options.D: It guarantees that the cancer will completely disappear

explanation: Palliative care is all about comfort, helping patients manage tough physical and emotional symptoms every step of the way. You are doing wonderful work today! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the main goal of cancer rehabilitation?

options.A: Curing the primary cancer diagnosis
options.B: Preventing the recurrence of tumors
options.C: Managing acute surgical site infections
options.D: Restoring physical and emotional well-being

explanation: You got this! Cancer rehab is all about helping patients get back their strength, independence, and good quality of life after treatment. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h1)

question: When should the cancer rehabilitation process ideally start?

options.A: Only after chemotherapy is fully completed
options.B: At the time of cancer diagnosis
options.C: After permanent disabilities develop
options.D: When the patient enters palliative care

explanation: Starting early is key! When we begin rehab right from diagnosis, we can stop long-term physical problems before they even start. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h1)

question: What do we call a rehab goal that tries to stop side effects before they even happen?

options.A: Preventative goal
options.B: Supportive goal
options.C: Palliative goal
options.D: Restorative goal

explanation: Think of this as stopping trouble before it starts. Preventative rehab jumps in early to block expected physical losses. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: A patient with advanced, progressive cancer is admitted for rehab. Which goal makes the most sense?

options.A: Maximizing comfort and dignity
options.B: Reversing all chemotherapy side effects
options.C: Restoring pre-treatment athletic ability
options.D: Preventing future tumor growth

explanation: When the disease is advanced, our main priority shifts to keeping the patient comfortable, peaceful, and full of dignity. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: Which health worker helps patients learn how to dress, cook, and do daily chores again?

options.A: Physical therapist
options.B: Oncology social worker
options.C: Speech-language pathologist
options.D: Occupational therapist

explanation: Great job! Occupational therapists (OTs) focus on everyday life skills and help patients master their daily self-care tasks independently. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why do we need a whole team of different specialists for cancer rehab?

options.A: The physical and emotional needs of survivors are too diverse for one discipline
options.B: It lowers the overall cost of hospital administration
options.C: Hospital rules require multiple signatures for every session
options.D: Doctors are no longer involved in direct patient care

explanation: Cancer touches every part of a person's life, so it takes a collaborative team of different experts to provide truly great care. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: As a nurse, what common myth about weakness in cancer patients should you avoid?

options.A: Thinking it has no relationship to chemotherapy
options.B: Assuming it is simply due to aging or lack of effort
options.C: Believing it can only be cured by heavy weightlifting
options.D: Stating that it always resolves immediately after surgery

explanation: Never assume a weak patient is just being lazy or getting old! Cancer weakness comes from the disease, poor nutrition, and heavy treatments. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why do nurses need to check and re-check a patient's physical abilities regularly during cancer care?

options.A: Therapists need to change their billing codes frequently
options.B: Initial assessments are usually inaccurate due to stress
options.C: Hospital accreditation requires weekly paperwork updates
options.D: A patient's functional status can fluctuate rapidly during treatment

explanation: Because treatments and cancer can change a patient's strength quickly up or down, regular check-ins help us keep our care plan on track. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: How is cancer-related fatigue different from everyday tiredness?

options.A: It does not improve with regular rest or sleep
options.B: It exclusively affects older adult populations
options.C: It only occurs during the first week of diagnosis
options.D: It can only be treated with high-dose intravenous vitamins

explanation: Cancer fatigue is heavy and overwhelming. Unlike normal tiredness, sleeping or resting doesn't make it go away. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: Why is getting pain under control so important before starting rehab exercises?

options.A: Therapy sessions are legally required to be painless
options.B: Uncontrolled pain prevents patients from participating in therapy
options.C: Pain medication replaces the need for any physical movement
options.D: Physical therapists are not allowed to touch patients who have pain

explanation: It makes total sense: if a patient is hurting badly, they won't want to move, and they won't be able to do their recovery exercises. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: When planning exercises for a patient whose cancer has spread to the bones, what must you guard against?

options.A: Respiratory alkalosis
options.B: Pathological fractures
options.C: Acute kidney injury
options.D: Iron deficiency anemia

explanation: Bones weakened by cancer metastases are very fragile. We must avoid high-impact movements to prevent unexpected bone breaks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: A cancer patient is exercising. Which sign means you should stop the activity right away?

options.A: A slight increase in heart rate during active movement
options.B: Mild muscle soreness in the legs after walking twenty steps
options.C: Sudden chest pain, severe shortness of breath, and dizziness
options.D: Desire to rest after completing a supervised stretching routine

explanation: Always watch out for red flags! Chest pain, dizziness, and trouble breathing mean the heart or lungs are struggling during exercise. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: Why is poor nutrition (malnutrition) such a big problem during cancer treatment?

options.A: It causes immediate and permanent hair loss
options.B: It increases the likelihood of bone fractures
options.C: It prevents medications from dissolving in the stomach
options.D: It impairs wound healing and reduces treatment tolerance

explanation: Good food is body fuel! Without proper nutrition, the body struggles to heal wounds and handle harsh cancer treatments. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the best eating strategy for a patient dealing with severe nausea and poor appetite?

options.A: Encouraging three large, heavy meals to catch up on lost calories
options.B: Forcing the patient to finish everything on a large dinner plate
options.C: Withholding all food until appetite returns spontaneously
options.D: Serving small, frequent nutrient-dense meals throughout the day

explanation: Huge meals can make a nauseous patient feel worse. Small, tasty bites spaced through the day are much easier to manage! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: Besides the patient, who else is at high risk and needs emotional support during cancer recovery?

options.A: Pharmaceutical suppliers
options.B: Billing department staff
options.C: Hospital administrators
options.D: Family caregivers

explanation: Don't forget the family! Caregivers pour so much energy into helping others that they often face severe stress and burnout themselves. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h8)

question: How should a nurse respond when a patient expresses deep fear that their cancer will return?

options.A: Change the subject immediately to something more positive
options.B: Acknowledge their feelings and provide a safe space to talk
options.C: Assure them with certainty that the cancer will never come back
options.D: Tell them not to worry because worrying brings the cancer back

explanation: Empathy first! Validating their fears and being there to listen helps them process heavy emotions instead of bottling them up. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of a survivorship care plan?

options.A: To manage acute surgical complications in the hospital
options.B: To replace the need for any further primary care visits
options.C: To guarantee that cancer will never return in the future
options.D: To outline treatment history and schedule ongoing surveillance

explanation: Think of it as a roadmap. A survivorship plan summarizes past treatments and maps out future health check-ups. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h9)

question: Which nursing activity is vital for long-term cancer survivors?

options.A: Administering initial chemotherapy cycles in the acute ward
options.B: Performing major reconstructive surgeries in the clinic
options.C: Prescribing high-dose narcotic pain medications
options.D: Monitoring for late-appearing side effects of treatment

explanation: Even years later, survivors can develop delayed side effects affecting their heart or lungs, making watchful nursing care essential. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h9)

question: What is the primary characteristic of a malignant neoplasm compared to a benign one?

options.A: It invades nearby tissues and spreads to other parts of the body.
options.B: It stops growing entirely after a few weeks without treatment.
options.C: It only affects older adults and ignores younger populations.
options.D: It stays localized in one spot and never grows very large.

explanation: Malignant neoplasms are cancerous because they can break away, invade surrounding structures, and travel through the blood or lymph system. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why is prevention so important in cancer care?

options.A: It replaces the need for surgical removal of tumors in every single patient.
options.B: It completely eliminates the requirement for diagnostic lab testing.
options.C: It stops the disease early, reducing suffering and healthcare costs.
options.D: It guarantees that patients will never experience any genetic mutations in their lifetime.

explanation: Preventing cancer or catching it early spares your future patients from aggressive treatments and helps them live longer, healthier lives. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: What is the main goal of primary prevention?

options.A: Rehabilitating a patient after major cancer surgery
options.B: Catching an existing disease during its very early stages
options.C: Providing palliative comfort during end-of-life care
options.D: Preventing a disease from ever occurring in a healthy person

explanation: Think of primary prevention as stopping trouble before it even starts—like protecting healthy people by reducing risk factors. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which nursing intervention is the best example of primary cancer prevention?

options.A: Teaching a patient how to care for a surgical wound after tumor removal
options.B: Helping a newly diagnosed patient manage chemotherapy side effects
options.C: Administering the HPV vaccine to a group of adolescent students
options.D: Scheduling a routine screening mammogram for a 50-year-old woman

explanation: Giving the HPV vaccine prevents a viral infection that can lead to cervical cancer, fitting the definition of primary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of secondary prevention, like routine screenings?

options.A: Stopping environmental toxins from entering the local community
options.B: Preventing healthy individuals from ever encountering risk factors
options.C: Restoring full physical strength after cancer treatment finishes
options.D: Detecting disease early when it is easiest and most successful to treat

explanation: Secondary prevention is all about catching things early through screening so you can tackle them before they grow into a bigger problem. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why is a colonoscopy considered a secondary prevention tool?

options.A: It completely cures advanced metastatic tumors in the large intestine.
options.B: It boosts the patient's immune system to fight off new infections.
options.C: It prevents a person from ever eating foods that cause inflammation.
options.D: It finds and removes abnormal growths before they develop into full cancer.

explanation: Screenings like colonoscopies let us spot small polyps and take them out early, stopping cancer in its tracks! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: When does tertiary prevention happen along the care continuum?

options.A: After a diagnosis and treatment have already occurred
options.B: While administering vaccines in a community health clinic
options.C: During routine screening tests for healthy people
options.D: Before any exposure to environmental toxins happens

explanation: Tertiary prevention steps in after treatment to help patients recover, manage long-term effects, and get back to daily life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: Which nursing action best demonstrates tertiary cancer prevention?

options.A: Encouraging a young adult to stop smoking cigarettes before any disease develops
options.B: Teaching arm exercises to a patient recovering from breast cancer surgery to prevent lymphedema
options.C: Providing educational pamphlets about the importance of getting a regular Pap smear
options.D: Administering a routine hepatitis B immunization to a healthcare worker

explanation: Managing complications and rehabilitating a patient post-treatment are core goals of tertiary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: When should a nurse refer a patient for genetic counseling regarding cancer?

options.A: The patient has a strong family history suggesting an inherited gene mutation.
options.B: The patient needs immediate chemotherapy for an active lung tumor.
options.C: The patient wants to quit smoking and needs nicotine replacement therapy.
options.D: The patient requires physical therapy to recover from radiation fatigue.

explanation: If a family history points to inherited genes, genetic counseling helps patients understand their risks and plan ahead. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a role for a nurse doing community cancer advocacy?

options.A: Prescribing targeted chemotherapy drugs for newly diagnosed patients
options.B: Promoting clean air and smoke-free public spaces
options.C: Dispelling cultural myths about cancer transmission in local neighborhoods
options.D: Advocating for policies that provide affordable cancer screenings

explanation: Nurses rock at education and community advocacy, but prescribing medications is reserved for doctors and specialized nurse practitioners. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)

question: What are the three main categories of oncologic emergencies?

options.A: Respiratory, cardiac, and renal
options.B: Acute, chronic, and terminal
options.C: Primary, secondary, and tertiary
options.D: Metabolic, structural, and hematologic

explanation: Oncologic emergencies are traditionally grouped into metabolic, structural, and hematologic categories to help guide rapid assessment and intervention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why is early recognition by the nurse vital in oncologic emergencies?

options.A: It shortens the patient's hospital stay to one day
options.B: It completely cures the underlying cancer
options.C: It prevents permanent organ damage and death
options.D: It eliminates the need for any laboratory tests

explanation: Because these conditions develop rapidly and threaten life, catching them early stops the cascade toward permanent organ failure. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h1)

question: What electrolyte abnormality is a key feature of Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: High potassium
options.B: Low phosphate
options.C: High calcium
options.D: Low sodium

explanation: When massive numbers of cancer cells burst open, they flood the bloodstream with intracellular potassium, causing hyperkalemia. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h2)

question: A patient with breast cancer and bone metastases is drowsy, confused, and very weak. Which metabolic emergency is most likely occurring?

options.A: Hyponatremia
options.B: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
options.C: Hypercalcemia
options.D: Hypoglycemia

explanation: Tumors affecting the bones release excess calcium into the blood, causing neurological dullness, muscle weakness, and profound fatigue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h2)

question: What is the classic early symptom of Spinal Cord Compression in cancer patients?

options.A: Inability to swallow
options.B: New, persistent back pain
options.C: Sudden visual loss
options.D: Severe chest pain

explanation: Back pain that worsens when lying flat is almost always the earliest warning sign of a tumor pressing on the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h3)

question: Why does Superior Vena Cava Syndrome cause facial swelling?

options.A: Allergic reactions to chemotherapy puff up the face
options.B: Lymph nodes in the neck shrink and pull skin tight
options.C: Blood flow from the head and neck is blocked from reaching the heart
options.D: Fluid retention is caused by failing kidneys

explanation: When a tumor blocks the superior vena cava, blood backs up in the upper body, causing noticeable swelling in the face, neck, and arms. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h3)

question: What defines febrile neutropenia in a cancer patient?

options.A: High fever and high white blood cell count
options.B: Low red blood cells and high platelets
options.C: Fever and low white blood cell count
options.D: Normal temperature and low platelets

explanation: Febrile neutropenia is diagnosed when a patient has a fever alongside a dangerously low count of infection-fighting neutrophils. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why is a fever in a neutropenic patient treated so aggressively?

options.A: It means the cancer has spread to the skin
options.B: They lack enough white blood cells to fight off hidden infections, leading to rapid sepsis
options.C: Chemotherapy drugs stop working completely if a fever develops
options.D: Fever automatically causes permanent brain damage within minutes

explanation: Without neutrophils, a minor infection can quickly overwhelm the body and cause fatal septic shock, requiring instant antibiotic therapy. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is a common trap nurses must avoid when assessing oncology patients?

options.A: Relying too much on lab results instead of talking to the patient
options.B: Dismissing subtle confusion or fatigue as normal chemotherapy side effects
options.C: Measuring fluid intake and output when the patient is stable
options.D: Checking vital signs too often during a night shift

explanation: Subtle mental status changes can be the first clue of a serious metabolic or structural emergency, not just everyday treatment fatigue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h5)

question: Which nursing action is most helpful for catching fluid balance problems early in patients at risk for Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: Restricting all oral fluids
options.B: Checking blood pressure twice a week
options.C: Weighing the patient once a month
options.D: Tracking daily intake and output

explanation: Strict monitoring of fluid input and output helps nurses evaluate kidney function and hydration status during high-risk treatment periods. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of giving intravenous fluids in Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: To raise blood pressure to normal levels
options.B: To shrink the size of the primary tumor
options.C: To flush out uric acid and protect the kidneys
options.D: To replace lost red blood cells

explanation: Aggressive hydration forces urine production, helping the kidneys wash away dangerous breakdown products like uric acid and potassium. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h6)

question: How should a nurse position a patient experiencing Superior Vena Cava Syndrome to help ease their symptoms?

options.A: Flat on their back with no pillow
options.B: With their legs raised higher than their head
options.C: On their left side in the recovery position
options.D: Upright with the head elevated

explanation: Keeping the head of the bed elevated uses gravity to help reduce venous pressure and swelling in the head and neck. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of teaching oncology patients about emergency warning signs?

options.A: To ensure they seek help quickly before symptoms become life-threatening
options.B: To prevent them from ever experiencing another tumor recurrence
options.C: To train them to manage medical emergencies at home without calling a doctor
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of hospital stays

explanation: Early reporting of red-flag symptoms allows healthcare teams to intervene swiftly before minor issues become full-blown emergencies. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h7)

question: Which home monitoring task is most critical for a patient undergoing chemotherapy who is at risk for infection?

options.A: Checking body temperature daily
options.B: Measuring blood pressure every four hours
options.C: Testing urine sugar levels twice a day
options.D: Weighing oneself every morning before eating

explanation: Because fever is often the only sign of neutropenic infection, daily temperature tracking is vital for catching early sepsis risks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h7)

question: What do we call an abnormal, new growth of tissue that forms a tumor?

options.A: Atrophy
options.B: Neoplasm
options.C: Metaplasia
options.D: Hypertrophy

explanation: Great start! A neoplasm is simply an abnormal mass of tissue that grows when cells divide more than they should. Think 'neo' (new) + 'plasma' (formation). You've got this! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h1)

question: What happens when the chemical signals that control normal cell division break down?

options.A: Cells transform into normal bone
options.B: Cells multiply uncontrollably
options.C: Cells stop dividing permanently
options.D: Cells immediately shrink and die

explanation: Spot on! When the body's natural brakes on the cell cycle fail, cells lose their stop signals and keep dividing, leading to abnormal growth. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which of these is the main feature of a benign tumor?

options.A: It travels through the blood to distant organs
options.B: It has poorly differentiated cells
options.C: It remains localized and does not spread
options.D: It invades surrounding nearby tissues

explanation: You got it! Benign tumors stay put in one place. They don't invade nearby tissues or spread around the body like malignant ones do. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h2)

question: What does it mean when a cancer cell is called 'poorly differentiated'?

options.A: The cancer cells look very different from normal tissue cells
options.B: The tumor cells have stopped growing completely
options.C: The cells are surrounded by a thick protective capsule
options.D: The mass is unable to attract a blood supply

explanation: Well done! 'Differentiated' means looking like the original tissue. Poorly differentiated cells have lost their specialized look, which usually means the cancer is more aggressive. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the normal job of tumor suppressor genes in our bodies?

options.A: To stimulate rapid cell growth during injury
options.B: To supply blood vessels directly to growing tissues
options.C: To carry oxygen to rapidly dividing cancer cells
options.D: To slow down cell division and repair damaged DNA

explanation: Exactly! Think of tumor suppressor genes as the body's molecular brakes. They pause cell growth to fix DNA mistakes or clear out damaged cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h3)

question: How do normal proto-oncogenes cause trouble when they mutate?

options.A: They permanently shut down all cellular activity in the organ
options.B: They cause the immune system to destroy healthy tissue
options.C: They stop the tumor from getting a blood supply
options.D: They become overactive oncogenes that drive constant cell division

explanation: Spot on! When proto-oncogenes mutate, they turn into hyperactive oncogenes that act like a stuck accelerator pedal, shouting for the cell to multiply nonstop. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which phase of cancer development involves a permanent change or mutation in a cell's DNA?

options.A: Initiation
options.B: Progression
options.C: Metastasis
options.D: Promotion

explanation: You nailed it! Initiation is always step one—it's the very first moment a trigger causes a permanent genetic change in a normal cell. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the main job of promoting agents during the second stage of cancer?

options.A: To help the immune system destroy early cancer cells
options.B: To stimulate previously mutated cells to divide and multiply
options.C: To stop blood vessels from growing into the tumor
options.D: To cause the initial DNA damage inside the cell nucleus

explanation: Correct! Promoters don't start the mutation themselves, but they act like fertilizer, encouraging those already-mutated cells to multiply and grow. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the term for the process where a tumor grows its own new blood supply?

options.A: Metastasis
options.B: Pinocytosis
options.C: Angiogenesis
options.D: Apoptosis

explanation: Awesome! 'Angio' (vessels) + 'genesis' (creation). Tumors rely on angiogenesis to build their own private network of blood vessels to keep growing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why is angiogenesis so important for a growing malignant tumor?

options.A: It supplies necessary oxygen and nutrients while removing waste
options.B: It prevents the immune system from noticing the tumor mass
options.C: It encapsulates the tumor to keep it from spreading locally
options.D: It repairs damaged DNA inside the fast-growing cancer cells

explanation: You got it! Without a fresh blood supply delivering nutrients and carrying away waste, a tumor would quickly starve and stop growing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h5)

question: What do we call the spread of cancer cells to other parts of the body?

options.A: Carcinogenesis
options.B: Metastasis
options.C: Hyperplasia
options.D: Apoptosis

explanation: Fantastic! Metastasis is when cancer cells break away from the main tumor, travel through the body, and set up secondary tumor camps elsewhere. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h6)

question: How do migrating cancer cells manage to break into nearby blood vessels?

options.A: They secrete enzymes that break down surrounding tissue barriers
options.B: They attract white blood cells to carry them into circulation
options.C: They wait for the blood vessel walls to rupture from high pressure
options.D: They shrink in size until they slip through normal cell walls

explanation: Spot on! Cancer cells release special chemical enzymes that chew through tissue barriers and blood vessel walls, letting them slip right into circulation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which immune cells are on the front lines, patrolling tissues to destroy abnormal cells?

options.A: Albumin and globulin proteins
options.B: Eosinophils and basophils
options.C: Red blood cells and platelets
options.D: T-cells and natural killer cells

explanation: You got it! T-cells and natural killer (NK) cells are the heavy lifters of the immune system, constantly hunting down and destroying abnormal or infected cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h7)

question: How do malignant cells often manage to survive even when a healthy immune system is present?

options.A: They absorb all circulating antibodies to block inflammation
options.B: They coat themselves in thick layers of calcium and iron
options.C: They turn into benign tumors to trick white blood cells
options.D: They release chemical signals that suppress immune cell activity

explanation: Well done! Clever cancer cells can send out decoy signals that turn down immune responses, tricking the body's defenses into leaving them alone. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h7)

question: What kind of tumor grows into nearby tissues and travels to other parts of the body?

options.A: Benign tumor
options.B: Metaplastic lesion
options.C: Malignant tumor
options.D: Hyperplastic growth

explanation: Spot on! Malignant tumors are cancerous because they don't stay in one place—they can invade local tissues and travel through the blood or lymph to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is the very first thing that happens during the initiation stage of cancer development?

options.A: The tumor develops its own blood supply to grow
options.B: Promoting agents cause the mutated cells to multiply rapidly
options.C: Malignant cells travel through the blood to distant organs
options.D: A permanent mutation occurs in the cellular DNA

explanation: You got it! Initiation is step one, where a harmful agent (carcinogen) causes a permanent, irreversible change right inside the cell's DNA. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which of these is a clear example of primary cancer prevention?

options.A: Starting chemotherapy for a diagnosed breast lump
options.B: Undergoing a routine screening colonoscopy
options.C: Receiving the Hepatitis B vaccine
options.D: Performing a monthly self-breast examination

explanation: Brilliant! Primary prevention stops a disease before it even starts. Giving vaccines against cancer-linked viruses like Hepatitis B is a classic way to protect the body early. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h2)

question: A patient asks how to lower their colon cancer risk through food. What is the best nursing advice?

options.A: Eliminate all forms of dietary fat from the daily menu
options.B: Eat more processed red meat and smoked foods daily
options.C: Increase intake of fresh vegetables and whole grains
options.D: Take high-dose iron supplements with every meal

explanation: Well done! Eating plenty of fiber-rich veggies and whole grains keeps the bowel healthy and protects against colon issues. Balance is key! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the main goal of secondary cancer prevention?

options.A: Managing chronic pain in end-stage terminal patients
options.B: Detecting cancer early before symptoms appear
options.C: Providing rehabilitative care after surgical removal
options.D: Stopping initial exposure to environmental carcinogens

explanation: Spot on! Secondary prevention is all about catching the disease early through screening tests when it is easiest to treat. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why must a patient still do a biopsy after a routine screening test comes back positive?

options.A: A biopsy is necessary to cure the disease without surgery
options.B: Biopsies are required by law before any medication can be prescribed
options.C: Screening tests are always completely inaccurate for internal organs
options.D: Screening tests only suggest risk and cannot definitively diagnose cancer

explanation: Exactly! Screening tests only raise a red flag or show a risk. A biopsy (checking actual tissue cells) is the only way to say for sure that it's cancer. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h3)

question: Which low-cost test is commonly used in Nigerian primary health clinics to check for early cervical cell changes?

options.A: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography
options.B: Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid
options.C: Positron emission tomography scans
options.D: Magnetic resonance imaging scans

explanation: Correct! VIA (Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid) is quick, affordable, and works wonderfully in everyday primary care clinics where high-tech scanners aren't available. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why do many cancer patients in Nigeria often come to the hospital at a very advanced stage?

options.A: Government policies strictly prohibit early diagnostic testing
options.B: Malignant tumors grow much slower in tropical climates
options.C: Financial barriers, limited access, and reliance on traditional remedies
options.D: Early screening tests are overly accurate and cause false alarms

explanation: Spot on. Distance to clinics, money constraints, and trying local herbs first often delay proper hospital visits until the disease has progressed. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h4)

question: In the CAUTION mnemonic for warning signs of cancer, what does the letter 'U' stand for?

options.A: Urinary frequency and burning
options.B: Ulceration of the skin surface
options.C: Unusual bleeding or discharge
options.D: Unexplained upper abdominal pain

explanation: You nailed it! The 'U' stands for unusual bleeding or discharge from anywhere in the body. It's an important red flag that needs checking. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h5)

question: An older adult has had a nagging cough and hoarseness for three months that won't go away. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Instruct the patient to purchase over-the-counter cough syrup
options.B: Advise the patient to return only if they cough up blood
options.C: Report these findings to the clinician for further diagnostic evaluation
options.D: Reassure the patient that common colds often last for several months

explanation: Great clinical thinking! A cough that lasts that long without healing is a classic warning sign that needs a proper doctor's assessment right away. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h5)

question: What does the letter 'M' stand for in the TNM cancer staging system?

options.A: Muscle involvement
options.B: Microscopic grading
options.C: Distant metastasis
options.D: Malignant potential

explanation: Spot on! In the TNM system, M tells us if the cancer has traveled (metastasized) to distant organs far away from where it started. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why is cancer staging so important after a patient receives a confirmed diagnosis?

options.A: It guides treatment decisions and helps determine the overall prognosis
options.B: It identifies the exact environmental toxin that caused the disease
options.C: It guarantees that the patient will achieve full remission
options.D: It completely replaces the need for any laboratory blood tests

explanation: You got it! Staging lets the team know how far the cancer has spread, which helps them choose the best treatment plan and understand what lies ahead. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which of these is a key responsibility for a nurse working in public health cancer advocacy?

options.A: Organizing community awareness and teaching early detection methods
options.B: Diagnosing cancer stages without the need for pathology reports
options.C: Performing independent surgical removal of malignant tumors
options.D: Manufacturing chemotherapy medications in hospital pharmacies

explanation: Brilliant! Nurses play a leading role in public health by educating communities, spreading awareness, and encouraging early screening. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h7)

question: A community nurse notices women in a village avoiding breast screening due to cultural fears. What is the best way to handle this?

options.A: Report the village residents to local government authorities for non-compliance
options.B: Insist that screening is mandatory under all circumstances
options.C: Ignore the cultural beliefs and hand out clinical pamphlets silently
options.D: Provide culturally sensitive health education and address community fears openly

explanation: Spot on! Building trust through gentle, respectful conversations and addressing fears openly is always the best nursing approach for community health. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is the very first step in how cancer starts in the body?

options.A: Chronic dehydration of body tissues
options.B: Excessive intake of dietary proteins
options.C: Rapid spread of bacteria in the blood
options.D: Genetic mutation in a single cell

explanation: Cancer kicks off when a change happens in a cell's genes, making it grow and divide without stopping. You've got this! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is the nurse's role so important when a patient is first told they might have cancer?

options.A: To determine the final pathological tumor grade
options.B: To perform surgical removal of the tumor mass
options.C: To prescribe and administer initial chemotherapy doses
options.D: To reduce anxiety and guide patients through complex tests

explanation: Finding out about cancer is super scary. Nurses step in as guides and educators to help patients understand tests and calm their fears. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which special scan uses a tiny, safe radioactive substance to check for active changes in body tissues?

options.A: Basic fluoroscopy
options.B: Ultrasound
options.C: PET scan
options.D: Standard X-ray

explanation: A PET scan uses a special tracer to light up how tissues and organs are working on a cellular level. Pretty neat technology! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h2)

question: A healthy 50-year-old woman asks why she needs a routine mammogram when she feels fine. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Routine screening is legally required for all women over the age of forty in this country.
options.B: Screening tests catch cancer early before symptoms develop, which makes treatment more successful.
options.C: These tests are designed to prevent normal cells from ever mutating into cancerous growths.
options.D: Mammograms are only performed after a physician feels a distinct lump during a physical exam.

explanation: Screening is all about catching things early before they turn into bigger problems. Early detection makes treatment much easier! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h2)

question: What does tumor 'staging' mainly tell the healthcare team?

options.A: The exact microscopic appearance and shape of the cells
options.B: The size of the tumor and how far it has spread
options.C: The speed at which the patient's hair falls out
options.D: The specific type of chemotherapy needed for cure

explanation: Staging helps doctors figure out how big the tumor is and if it has traveled to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h3)

question: How do high-grade cancer cells usually act compared to low-grade cancer cells?

options.A: High-grade cells never metastasize to lymph nodes.
options.B: High-grade cells are easier to destroy with basic antibiotics.
options.C: High-grade cells look identical to healthy tissue under a lens.
options.D: High-grade cells grow and spread much more rapidly.

explanation: High-grade cells are fast-growing and more aggressive, meaning doctors need to act quickly. You're doing great learning this! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why is a biopsy a must-have test when checking for cancer?

options.A: It replaces the need for laboratory blood testing entirely.
options.B: It lowers systemic blood pressure during diagnostic scans.
options.C: It completely cures the patient by removing all toxins.
options.D: It provides definitive microscopic proof of malignancy.

explanation: Looking at actual cells under a microscope is the only way to be 100% sure whether cancer cells are present. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the nurse's main job right after a tissue sample (biopsy) is taken?

options.A: Place the tissue sample in a household refrigerator until the morning shift
options.B: Examine the cells under the ward microscope to give an early report
options.C: Wash the specimen with sterile water to remove any residual blood
options.D: Ensure correct labeling and prompt placement in the proper preservative solution

explanation: Good lab results start with proper handling! Labeling it right away and putting it in the right preservative keeps the sample safe for testing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the most important nursing check right after a patient has a liver biopsy?

options.A: Remove all intravenous access lines right away
options.B: Monitor vital signs and check the puncture site for bleeding
options.C: Feed the patient a large high-fiber meal immediately
options.D: Encourage the patient to walk briskly around the hospital ward

explanation: Since the liver has a huge blood supply, watching closely for bleeding and checking vital signs is top priority after this procedure. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h5)

question: A patient scheduled for a procedure with mild sedation asks for a glass of water an hour beforehand. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Explain that fasting guidelines must be followed to prevent aspiration during sedation.
options.B: Ignore the question because fluid intake does not affect anesthesia safety.
options.C: Tell the patient to drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated before the test.
options.D: Allow the patient to drink a small cup of water since it is just a liquid.

explanation: Fasting (NPO) keeps the stomach empty so the patient doesn't accidentally choke or inhale stomach contents while sedated. Safety first! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h5)

question: How should a nurse respond when a patient is extremely scared while waiting for biopsy results?

options.A: Tell them not to worry because most lumps turn out to be harmless
options.B: Remind them that other patients have much worse conditions
options.C: Change the subject immediately to cheer them up
options.D: Acknowledge their feelings and listen attentively to their concerns

explanation: Just being there, listening, and validating their worries can be a huge comfort to a terrified patient. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is a very normal emotional reaction for patients waiting to find out if they have cancer?

options.A: Uncontrolled physical hunger
options.B: Extreme happiness and relief
options.C: Intense anxiety and shock
options.D: Complete emotional numbness

explanation: Waiting for big health news is terrifying. Shock and heavy anxiety are very common reactions that nurses need to be ready to support. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which medical expert spends their day looking at tissue samples under a microscope to diagnose cancer?

options.A: Dietitian
options.B: Pathologist
options.C: Surgeon
options.D: Radiologist

explanation: Pathologists are the lab detectives who study cells and tissues to give us a clear diagnosis. Teamwork makes the dream work! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why do healthcare workers use a team approach (doctors, nurses, pharmacists, etc.) in cancer care?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any nursing involvement in patient education.
options.B: It reduces hospital costs by avoiding diagnostic imaging tests.
options.C: It combines various specialties to ensure accurate diagnosis and comprehensive treatment planning.
options.D: It allows a single doctor to make all clinical decisions without consulting others.

explanation: Cancer care is complex! Working together ensures that every single physical, emotional, and medical need of the patient is met. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h7)

question: During which phase of the cell cycle does a cell make a copy of its DNA?

options.A: First gap phase
options.B: Mitotic phase
options.C: Resting phase
options.D: Synthesis phase

explanation: You got this! The S phase (synthesis phase) is specifically when the cell replicates its genetic material before dividing. Think 'S' for 'Synthesis' or 'Copying'! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the main job of checkpoints in the normal cell cycle?

options.A: To stop division if DNA damage is found
options.B: To speed up tissue growth
options.C: To provide energy for the cell to split
options.D: To turn active cells into resting cells

explanation: Great try! Cell checkpoints act like security guards—they inspect the cell and halt the cycle if anything looks damaged, keeping the body safe. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: When one mature cell type changes into another mature cell type due to ongoing irritation, what is it called?

options.A: Anaplasia
options.B: Hyperplasia
options.C: Metaplasia
options.D: Apoptosis

explanation: Spot on! Metaplasia is like a cellular makeover; cells switch to a tougher type to better handle chronic stress, such as smoke irritation in the airways. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: A lab report describes tissue with disordered growth and cells of varying shapes and sizes. Which term describes this?

options.A: Metaplasia
options.B: Dysplasia
options.C: Hyperplasia
options.D: Atrophy

explanation: Well done! Dysplasia means disordered growth where cells lose their normal shape and organization—often an early warning sign that nurses watch closely. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: What do we call the process where cancer cells break away and spread through the blood or lymph to other parts of the body?

options.A: Mitosis
options.B: Metastasis
options.C: Metaplasia
options.D: Apoptosis

explanation: You're doing great! Metastasis happens when malignant cells travel via blood or lymph to set up secondary growths in distant organs. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: Which of these is a typical feature of a benign (non-cancerous) tumor?

options.A: Surrounded by a fibrous capsule
options.B: Infiltrates surrounding normal tissues
options.C: Rapid and uncontrolled cellular division
options.D: Ability to form secondary tumors

explanation: Correct! Benign tumors usually stay put inside a neat fibrous capsule, meaning they don't invade nearby tissues or spread around. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: What are the two big features that define all stem cells?

options.A: Programmed death and shrinkage
options.B: Rapid mutation and anaplasia
options.C: Self-renewal and potency
options.D: Encapsulation and metastasis

explanation: Spot on! Stem cells are amazing because they can both make copies of themselves (self-renewal) and turn into specialized cells (potency). [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why is cellular differentiation so important for the human body?

options.A: It ensures that all cells in the body remain identical
options.B: It stops normal cells from resting
options.C: It allows basic cells to mature into specific functional cells
options.D: It keeps the immune system calm

explanation: Brilliant! Differentiation is how a simple stem cell becomes a specialized muscle, nerve, or blood cell to do specific jobs in the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the main underlying cause of uncontrolled cell growth in cancer?

options.A: Accumulated mutations in cellular DNA
options.B: Permanent resting state in the cells
options.C: A total lack of cellular respiration
options.D: Eating too many vitamins

explanation: You've got it! Cancer starts when genetic errors build up over time, breaking the normal rules that tell cells when to stop growing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why do advanced tumors often become resistant to medical treatments like chemotherapy?

options.A: The body's immune system destroys the medication before it reaches the tumor
options.B: Chemotherapy drugs turn normal cells into malignant cancer cells
options.C: Genetic diversity creates varied cell populations with different drug resistance traits
options.D: Tumor cells develop a protective bone shell that blocks all medications

explanation: As mutations accumulate, cancer cells become diverse; while some cells die from treatment, resistant clones survive and multiply. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the normal, healthy job of proto-oncogenes in our bodies?

options.A: Triggering cell suicide immediately
options.B: Encapsulating benign tumors
options.C: Promoting normal cell growth and division
options.D: Repairing broken DNA strands

explanation: Spot on! Proto-oncogenes are normal, helpful genes that tell cells when it's time to grow and repair tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: What happens when a tumor suppressor gene experiences a loss-of-function mutation?

options.A: The cell immediately transforms into a benign fibrous cyst
options.B: The cell loses its molecular brakes and divides uncontrollably
options.C: The cell creates an outer capsule to prevent metastasis
options.D: Normal cellular division stops permanently in the G0 phase

explanation: Tumor suppressor genes normally slow down cell growth; losing them removes these protective brakes, allowing rapid tumor growth. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the main role of apoptosis in the body?

options.A: Removing damaged or unneeded cells in a neat, orderly way
options.B: Causing sudden inflammation after an injury
options.C: Turning normal tissue into tumors
options.D: Encouraging rapid stem cell division

explanation: Correct! Apoptosis is the body's clean-up process—it gently removes old or damaged cells without causing messy inflammation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: How do cancer cells frequently manipulate apoptosis to survive and multiply?

options.A: They trigger excessive external death receptor signals
options.B: They replace damaged mitochondria with healthy ones
options.C: They mutate regulatory genes to evade programmed cell death
options.D: They speed up the intrinsic pathway to destroy healthy tissue

explanation: Cancer cells often survive by disabling the normal suicide signals that would normally force a damaged cell to die. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why do traditional chemotherapy drugs commonly cause side effects like hair loss and mucosal sores?

options.A: They cause the patient's immune system to attack hair follicles
options.B: They attack all rapidly dividing cells, both cancerous and normal
options.C: They block the formation of protective fibrous tumor capsules
options.D: They stimulate normal cells to enter permanent resting phases

explanation: Traditional chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells, which inadvertently damages healthy tissues with high turnover like hair follicles and gut linings. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h8)

question: A patient on chemotherapy has a very low white blood cell count. What is the top nursing priority?

options.A: Stopping the process of metastasis
options.B: Giving medication to help hair grow back
options.C: Preparing the patient for emergency surgery
options.D: Monitoring closely for signs of infection

explanation: Brilliant nursing judgment! Low white blood cells (neutropenia) mean the immune system is weak, so watching for and preventing infection is your #1 priority. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h8)

question: What is the literal meaning of the medical term neoplasm?

options.A: Inflamed tissue
options.B: Normal healing
options.C: New growth
options.D: Cell death

explanation: The term neoplasm comes from Greek roots meaning new formation or growth, which describes the abnormal tissue mass formed by runaway cell division. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do neoplastic cells form a tumor instead of behaving normally?

options.A: They expand rapidly because they are fighting off local infections
options.B: They grow larger to replace dead tissue in the organ
options.C: They absorb too much water from surrounding blood vessels
options.D: They multiply uncontrollably due to failed growth regulation

explanation: You've got this! Normally, our body tells cells when to rest and when to divide. In a tumor, those control signals fail, and the cells just keep multiplying without stopping. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which feature is typical of a benign tumor?

options.A: It destroys neighboring healthy organs
options.B: It is enclosed by a fibrous capsule
options.C: It looks completely different from normal cells
options.D: It spreads quickly through the bloodstream

explanation: Benign growths typically form a distinct capsule that separates them from surrounding tissue, making them easier to excise. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: Even though a benign tumor is non-cancerous, why can it still be dangerous to a patient?

options.A: It always releases toxic poisons into the bloodstream
options.B: It can press on vital structures inside confined spaces
options.C: It frequently turns into widespread blood cancer
options.D: It destroys the immune system completely

explanation: Think about a crowded room! Even if things are peaceful, if a tumor grows inside a tight space like the skull, it can press on vital organs and cause serious trouble. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the term for cancer cells spreading to distant parts of the body?

options.A: Metastasis
options.B: Hyperplasia
options.C: Angiogenesis
options.D: Differentiation
